symbols with which that and the other Mexican paintings abound. It may further be remarked, that in the same 
manner as the prophets used very strong language when predicting God's indignation against the Jews on account 
of their sins, and his retributive vengeance, so the Mexicans would naturally, if they had wished to symbolize that 
language by paintings, have made use of very terrible and revolting images, to do justice to the energy of the 
prophet’s conceptions. How, except by a revolting picture, could they have expressed in painting the following 
denunciation contained in the thirty-fourth chapter of Isaiah—“< The sword of the Lord is filled with blood, it is 
made fat with fatness, and with the blood of lambs and goats, with the fat of the kidneys of rams: for the Lord 
hath a sacrifice in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Idumea. And the unicorns shall come down with 
them, and the bullocks with the bulls; and their land shall be soaked with blood, and their dust made fat with 
fatness. For it is the day of the Lord’s vengeance, and the year of recompences for the controversy of Zion.” 
Some of the representations contained in the Mexican paintings seem to be not unallied to events which happened 
at a very early period of Hebrew history, and which became the theme and boast of the Jews of all succeeding 
ages. Of this description was the exploit of Jael, who, although a woman, destroyed Sisera, the captain of 
the enemies’ host, by driving a nail into his temples while he was sleeping in his tent,—a faint tradition of which 
might have been preserved amongst the Mexicans. In a Mexican painting in the Bodleian library at Oxford is 
a symbol very much resembling the jaw-bone of an ass, from the side of which water seems to flow forth ; which 
might allude to the story of Samson slaying a thousand of the Philistines with such a bone, which remained mi- 
raculously unbroken in his hands, and from which he afterwards quenched his thirst. In the first page of the 
Borgian MS. a remarkable representation of Quecalcoatle (as the head-dress of the figure seems to indicate) vomited 
from the jaws of some amphibious animal occurs ; in reference to which curious painting it would be interesting to 
know whether the Jews had any tradition that their Messiah would be devoured by a monster, who would afterwards 
be compelled to yield up his prey, like the serpent in the seventy-fifth page of the Lesser Vatican MS., which a fierce 
eagle forces to disgorge a rabbit,—the symbol of suffering innocence amongst the Mexicans, according to Baron de 
Humboldt, which corresponded to the lamb of the Hebrews, and which perhaps was a type substituted for the latter 
by the Jews of Mexico, and referred by them to Quecalcoatle, in the same manner as their brethren of Peru appear to 
have replaced the sacrifices of sheep in the Old Continent by those of llamas in the New, the former species of animal 
being unknown to the Indians before the arrival of the Spaniards amongst them. Or, finally, shall we suppose that 
the Mexicans might have had some acquaintance with the Book of the prophet Jonah, and have transferred a portion 
of his history to the mysterious page of their own, which recorded the disappearance of Quecalcoatle in the Red Sea. 
The writings of that prophet being amongst the most ancient in the world, (since he lived as is generally supposed. 
about the time of the Trojan war,) and the adventures of his life being connected with the present subject of inquiry, 
we shall here insert his entire Book, which we shall be the more readily excused for doing, since it is very brief, and 
occupies only two octavo pages of the Old Testament; affording at the same time a new argument in favour of the 
Jews having colonized America, and transported thither their rites and traditions: “ Now the word of the Lord came 
unto Jonah the son of Amittai, saying, Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wicked-

The cause of the prophet Jonah’s anger, it may be remarked, was, that God by sparing Nineveh should have made 
him a false prophet, who had foretold unconditionally its destruction within forty days. But if our admiration for the 
prophet be not in consequence diminished, will our feelings of respect for the man undergo no alteration? Jonah was, 
nevertheless, the most famous type of the Messiah, to whom Christ himself refers in the following passage of the 
twelfth chapter of the Gospel of Saint Matthew, on occasion of the Scribes and Pharisees asking him for a sign to 
satisfy them that he was the Messiah: from whence it may be inferred in what estimation the Book of Jonah was 

NOTES. 363 

held by the Jews, who, having lost so many other books of Scripture, had preserved this for nearly nine hundred 
years, until the age of Christ. “Then certain of the Scribes and of the Pharisees answered, saying, Master, we 
would see a sign from thee. But he answered and said unto them, An evil and adulterous generation seeketh 
after a sign; and there shall no sign be given to it, but the sign of the prophet Jonas: for as Jonas was three 
days and three nights in the whale’s belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart 
of the earth.” Many of the Mexican paintings would seem to imply that the Mexicans were acquainted with 
various books of the Old Testament, and had even attempted to express in brilliant colouring and in hieroglyphics 
the very same metaphors as had been employed by the prophets, whose frequent denunciations of vengeance 
against the Jews and other nations, on account of their sins, might have laid the foundation of a school for 
painting amongst the Mexicans, which sought to convey the same ideas of religious terror to the imagination, 
but through the medium of another sense. How, it may be demanded, could so many Scriptural allegories 
and images have presented themselves to the minds of the Mexicans, if they had not had some acquaintance 
with the forcible, not to say gross, language (but well adapted to the morals of the people addressed,) in which 
the prophets Ezekiel, Isaiah, and Jeremiah upbraid the Jews? and from what other source could they have been 
derived? Sahagun says, that in the reign of Ytzcoatl, the lords and principal persons amongst the Mexicans 
(who were the priests, the Mexican government being a theocracy,) burned all their ancient paintings, that they 
might not, by falling into the hands of the laity, smk into contempt. If this passage be not, as we suspect it is, 
wholly an interpolation, (since no sufficient reason is assigned why the Mexicans, after having preserved for so many 
ages the ancient Tultec paintings, should have destroyed them at a comparatively late period of time, not long 
before the arrival of the Spaniards amongst them,) but, on the contrary, founded on a tradition partly true,—it might 
relate to the destruction of the Teoamoxtli (or divine book of the Tultecas) in the reign of the above-mentioned 
Mexican king; from which the Mexicans might have borrowed these notions and metaphors. The following are 
passages in the Old Testament which seem to have suggested types and symbols to the Mexican painters. The 
prophet Jeremiah in the twenty-first verse of the eighth chapter of his Prophecies thus figuratively describes the 
grief which he felt at the afflicted state of his countrymen; which passage of Scripture might likewise have induced 
the Mexican priests to paint their faces black, as a symbol that they mourned and were afflicted for the sins of the 
people: “ For the hurt of the daughter of my people am I hurt; I am black ; astonishment hath taken hold on me. 
Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there? why then is not the health of the daughter of my people 
recovered?” That the Hebrew prophets sometimes blackened their faces, is evident from the very curious account 
of the type (which, like that mentioned in the first chapter of the prophet Hosea, was more than mere words,) which 
is contained in the twentieth chapter of the First Book of Kings, by which Ahab was made to pronounce judgment 
against himself. Habakkuk, uttering a denunciation against the Jews on account of their wickedness, in the six- 
teenth verse of the second chapter of his Prophecies thus apostrophizes Jerusalem: “Thou art filled with shame for 
glory: drink thou also, and let thy foreskin be uncovered: the cup of the Lord’s right hand shall be turned unto 
thee, and shameful spewing shall be on thy glory.” The following passage in the first chapter of the same prophet 
has something mysterious in it, in reference as well to a curious representation in the twenty-sixth page of the Bor- 
gian MS. of fish taken in a net, (which perhaps were named by the Mexicans Tlacamichin, (or men-fish,) on account 
of the configuration of their heads,) as to a custom existing amongst the Matlatzincas noticed by Sahagun. It also 
seems to imply a charge of cannabalism against the Jews, which is darkly hinted at in more places than one in 
Scripture. “Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil, and canst not look on iniquity: wherefore lookest thou 
upon them that deal treacherously, and holdest thy tongue when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous 
than he? and makest men as the fishes of the sea, as the creeping things, that have no ruler over them? They take 
up all of them with the angle, they catch them in their net, and gather them in their drag: therefore they rejoice 
and are glad. Therefore they sacrifice unto their net, and burn incense unto their drag; because by them their por- 
tion is fat, and their meat plenteous. Shall they therefore empty their net, and not spare continually to slay the 
nations?” The prophet Nahum, in the fifth and sixth verses of the third chapter of his Prophecies, denouncing the 
fall of Nineveh, puts the following expressions into the mouth of God: “ Behold, I am against thee, saith the Lord 
of hosts ; and I will discover thy skirts upon thy face, and I will show the nations thy nakedness, and the kingdoms 
thy shame. And I will cast abominable filth upon thee, and make thee vile, and will set thee as a gazingstock.”

Terror is an attribute with which all the Hebrew prophets loved to invest the Deity. Thus Habakkuk, in the third 
chapter of his Book of Prophecies, describing the presence of Jehovah, says ; “Before him went the pestilence, and 
burning coals went forth at his feet.” And David, in the eighteenth Psalm, employs similar language : “ There went 
up a smoke out of his nostrils, and fire out of his mouth devoured: coals were kindled by it.” The voice of God is 
in various places of the Old Testament likened to the roaring of a lion; as in the thirtieth verse of the twenty-sixth 
chapter of the Book of Jeremiah: “ Therefore prophesy thou against them all these words, and say unto them, The 
Lord shall roar from on high, and utter his voice from his holy habitation ; he shall mightily roar upon his habita- 
tion ; he shall give a shout, as they that tread the grapes, agaist all the inhabitants of the earth.” And in the 
thirteenth verse of the forty-second chapter of Isaiah: “The Lord shall go forth as a mighty man, he shall stir up 
jealousy like a man of war: he shall cry, yea, roar; he shall prevail against his enemies.” The latter prophet twice 
borrows a simile from the hissing of a serpent: “ And he will lift up an ensign to the nations from far, and 
will hiss unto them from the end of the earth: and, behold, they shall come with speed swiftly.” “ And it shall 
come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, 
and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria.” The twenty-sixth verse of the fifth chapter of Isaiah, and the 
eighteenth verse of the seventh chapter, are the passages of Scripture referred to. As terror was, according to: the 
Jewish belief, the chief attribute of the Deity ; so fire, as being the most destructive of the elements, was the symbol 
to which the prophets most frequently resorted to heighten their descriptions of his power and majesty. Thus Daniel, 
in the seventh chapter of his Book of Prophecies, recording a vision in which he beheld God, says; “I beheld till 
the thrones were cast down, and the Ancient of days did sit, whose garment was white as snow, and the hair of his 
head like the pure wool: his throne was like the fiery flame, and his wheels as burning fire. A fiery stream issued 
and came forth from before him: thousand thousands ministered unto him, and ten thousand times ten thousand 
stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened.” 

Daniel’s description of his vision resembles in its imagery (if we may be permitted to make use of that term) a 
passage in the ninth chapter of the sixth book of Sahagun’s History of New Spain, in which the newly elected king 
of Mexico returns thanks to Tezcatlipoca, who it is to be presumed was Xiuhtecutli, which proper name signifies 
literally ‘the God of Heaven,’ or ‘the God of years.’ The following is the passage alluded to: “Quien soy yo, Seftor 
mio? y que es mi valor, que me pongais entre los que vos amais y conoceis, y teneis por amigos y escogidos, y dignos 
de toda honra, y nacidos y criados para las dignidades y tronos reales, y para este efecto los criasteis habiles y pru- 
dentes, tomados de nobles y generosos padres, y para esto criados y ensefados, y que fueron nacidos y bautizados 
en signos y constelaciones en que nacen los Sefiores, y para ser vuestros instrumentos y vuestras imagenes para regir 
yuestros reinos, esténdo dentro de ellos, y hablando por su boca y pronunciando ellos vuestras palabras, y paraque se 
conformen con el querer del antiguo Dios y padre de todos los Dioses, que es el Dios del fuego, que esta en la alberca 
de agua entre almenas cercado de piedras como rosas, el quel se llama Xiuhtecutli, el qual determina, examina y con- 
cluye los negocios y litigios del pueblo y de la gente popular, como lavandoles con agua, al qual siempre acompafan 
y estan en su presencia las personas generosas arriba dichas?” “Who am I, O Lord? and of what account, that you 
should place me in the rank of those whom you love and know, and number amongst your friends and your elect, 
whom you esteem as persons worthy of the highest honours, and to be such as are born and educated for dignities 
and royal thrones, and accordingly have endowed them with talents and prudence, selecting for the purpose those 
who are descended from noble and illustrious parents, who have been brought up with these expectations, and who 
have been baptized in the signs and constellations which preside at the birth of kings, that they might become your 
instruments and your images to govern your kingdoms, you being in them and speaking through their mouth, and 
they pronouncing your words, that thus they might act in conformity to the will of the ancient God and father of 
all the Gods, who is the God of fire, whose habitation is in the waters, which battlements encompass where he dwells, 
surrounded with rocks as it were with roses, whose name is Xiuhtecutli, who determines, examines, and brings to an 
issue the controversies and disputes of the people and of the multitude, cleansing them as it were with water, before 
whom are ever present and in attendance the noble persons above mentioned?” The supposed habitation of Xiuhte- 
cutli (the Mexican god of fire) in the waters, might almost lead us to imagine that the Mexicans had perused the 
following verses of the eighteenth Psalm, and thence borrowed the notion: “There went up a smoke out of his 
nostrils, and fire out of his mouth devoured: coals were kindled by it. He bowed the heavens also, and came down:

and darkness was under his feet. And he rode upon a cherub, and did fly: yea, he did fly upon the wings of the 
wind. He made darkness his secret place; his pavilion round about him were dark waters and thick clouds of the 
skies *. At the brightness that was before him his thick clouds passed, hail stones and coals of fire. The Lord 
also thundered in the heavens, and the Highest gave his voice; hail stones and coals of fire.” 

It has elsewhere been observed, that the deity worshiped by the Peruvians under the names of Pachacama and of 
Viracocha (the former of which signifies the Creator) was probably the same as Tezcatlipoca; and it might be conjec- 
tured, from the figure of a man riding upon some unknown animal, which is carved upon the cover of the box said to 
contain the quipoes, (or records of the Peruvian monarchy,) that the Peruvians were not ignorant of the metaphor “And 
he rode upon a cherub, and did fly: yea, he did fly upon the wings of the wind”—and had even attempted to make it 
the subject of an ornamental device. Reserving for another place all further mention of these quipoes, we shall only 
remark here, that whatever opinion may be formed of them, there cannot be the least doubt that the box is a specimen 
of ancient Peruvian workmanship. Exact delineations of the various figures carved upon the sides of this box will 
be found in the fourth volume of plates, each of which it will be observed, except the lower, represents a religious 
subject. On one side is a model of the famous temple of the sun at Cuzco, and on the other of that of the moon, 
before it is the pond in which, when the image of the moon became reflected, the priests and people offered up 
their homage to the queen of night-}. At each end are figures of the sun and the moon encircled with rays, with a 
human figure in the orb of each,—the symbol perhaps of the Peruvian trinity, which, according to Acosta, was one 
god, “ trinus uno ” and “ unus trino,” consisting of three persons, the father of the sun, the sun, and the brother of 
the sun; to the last of whom the moon might have been dedicated, as the sun seems to have been to the first. 
Upon the top or principal side of this box, Pachacama seems to be represented riding upon an animal not unlike a 
cherub, the velocity of whose flight may be typified by the swallow carved upon its wing ; the speed of the former 
being thus made to appear equal to that of the latter, since the swallow, the swiftest of birds, seems here unable to 
outstrip the cherub. The figures of the birds, beasts, fishes and creeping things around, may allude to the epithet of 
Pachacama (or Creator), under which the Peruvians adored their principal deity: for although they believed, as did 
also the Mexicans, that that deity was incorporeal, they still, like the Jews, personified him in human shape. To the 
objection which may be urged against our hypothesis, derived from the graceful attitude in which the person there 
represented appears to sit upon the animal which he is riding, and the proper position of his knees and legs,—implying 
that the carver of the box was not entirely unacquainted with European horsemanship,—four solutions may be 
offered. First, that he had seen some Tultec paintings in which men were represented riding on horses; secondly, that 
that position was chosen by the artist because it appeared to him the most graceful ; thirdly, that it was the effect of 
accident rather than of design ; or, lastly, that the Indians might have had horses before the arrival of the Spaniards 
in the New World. The last supposition may perhaps appear absurd; nor would it have been here had recourse to, if 
Peter Martyr, the most celebrated historian of America and the first in order of time, had not seemed in one passage 
of his Ocean Decades to be in doubt upon this point, and to have been embarrassed by conflicting statements ; scep- 
ticism being moreover admissible regarding every thing either asserted or denied of the Indians, but more especially 
of the Peruvians and the Ingas, by the licensed Spanish authors, whose works appeared in the sixteenth century. 
We shall here remark, that the Peruvians entertained as much or even greater superstition for fire than the Mexicans, 
believing like them that that element was an instrument of destruction in the hands of the deity. Many 
passages in Scripture might have induced the Jews to entertain such a notion; from whom the Indians probably 
derived it : but we shall here only refer to the mysterious mention of it in the seventh chapter of the prophet Amos: 
“Thus hath the Lord God showed unto me ; and, behold, he formed grasshoppers in the beginning of the shooting up 
of the latter growth ; and, lo, it was the latter growth after the king’s mowings. And it came to pass, that when they 
had made an end of eating the grass of the land, then I said, O Lord God, forgive, I beseech thee: by whom shall 
Jacob arise? for he is small. The Lord repented for this: It shall not be, saith the Lord. Thus hath the Lord

miracle interposed to prevent the completion of the sacrifice, it was a sign that Heaven willed it to take place, and 
that the act itself would be meritorious. That the Jews, like the Peruvians, entertained notions of the efficacy of a 
vicarial human sacrifice and atonement, is evident from what the prophet Micah says in the seventh verse of the 
sixth chapter of his Prophecies, reprobating their customs: “ Will the Lord be pleased with thousands of rams, 
or with ten thousands of rivers of oil? shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the 
sin of my soul?” In the sixth verse of the nineteenth chapter of Exodus, God commands Moses to address the 
following language to the Jews: “Ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation.” And Josephus, in 
his Treatise against Apion, boasts that his countrymen were a kingdom of priests, who rendered a pure homage to one 
God, the Creator of the universe *. The Mexicans resembled the Jews in being also a nation of priests ; and their pro- 
phets were not unlike the Hebrew prophets, who are so frequently accused in Scripture of deceiving the people with lies. 
It is very remarkable that both nations were equally inclined to pay superstitious attention to dreams: the Mexicans 
had paintings expressly for their interpretation ; and it is highly probable that “‘hinc fons et origo malorum.” The 
Jews believed in two kinds of divine inspiration, the distinct nature of which will be more clearly understood from 
the perusal-of the twelfth chapter of Numbers; from which (but more especially from the sixteenth chapter of the 
same book) it would appear not improbable that the whole tribe of Levi laid claim to the possession of inspiration 
by dreams ; for that is the only inference to be drawn from the address of Korah and the princes of the congrega- 
tion to Moses and Aaron: “ Ye take too much upon you, seeing all the congregation are holy, every one of them, 
and the Lord is among them ;” since presumptuous and impious as those men were, they would scarcely have ven- 
tured to have told Moses to his face that the Lord spoke mouth to mouth with them as with him (the only other 
mode of inspiration), it being so easy moreover to disprove the fact. A broad line of distinction is drawn in the 
sixth and eighth verses of the above-mentioned chapter of Numbers between these two kinds of inspiration; the 
former of which was received by the priest or prophet in a sleeping state, and the latter by Moses in his full senses 
and awake. This chapter we the more readily insert here at full length, because it has been elsewhere referred to 

* Some writers have contended that the licentiousness of the Poets having lessened the respect which the Romans entertained for their

a reform in real religion, which they judged to be nothing more than a pure and spontaneous feeling of gratitude from man towards the 
unknown Author of his existence and happiness. They soon, however, discovered their error, and perceived that such a religion would be

and learning on its side, with the great disadvantage of being obliged to defend many old abuses to the prejudice of reform; the other 
called in the aid of foreign superstition, availed itself of the passions and physical force of the multitude, conciliated the favour of the 
government, obtained imperial decrees, silenced their opponents by appealing to laws and penalties, of which they were themselves both 
the framers and executors, and soon acquired absolute power,—establishing at the same time a reign of terror and of persecution.

make myself known unto him in a vision, and will speak unto him in a dream. My servant Moses is not so, who 
is faithful in all mine house. With him will I speak mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches ; 
and the similitude of the Lord shall he behold: wherefore then were ye not afraid to speak against my servant Moses ? 
And the anger of the Lord was kindled against them ; and he departed. And the cloud departed from off the taber- 
nacle; and, behold, Miriam became leprous, white as snow: and Aaron looked upon Miriam, and, behold, she was 
leprous. And Aaron said unto Moses, Alas, my lord, I beseech thee, lay not the sin upon us, wherein we have done 
foolishly, and wherein we have sinned. Let her not be as one dead, of whom the flesh is half consumed when he 
cometh out of his mother’s womb. And Moses cried unto the Lord, saying, Heal her now, O God, I beseech thee. And 
the Lord said unto Moses, If her father had but spit in her face, should she not be ashamed seven days? let her be 
shut out from the camp seven days, and after that let her be received in again. And Miriam was shut out from the 
camp seven days; and the people journeyed not till Miriam was brought in again. And afterward the people 
removed from Hazeroth, and pitched in the wilderness of Paran.” The displeasure of Moses as recorded in the 
above chapter, who, although slow to provocation and very meek, could not help on that occasion, as it would appear, 
making an appeal to God against Aaron and Miriam, renders their justification very difficult. One thing, however, 
may be said in palliation of their conduct : Moses had contracted two idolatrous marriages in succession, in defiance 
of Abraham’s admonition to Eliezer his steward not to make choice of a wife the daughter of an idolater for Isaac, 
which he could not have been unacquainted with, and of a law afterwards promulgated by himself; for the first wife 
of Moses was a woman of Midian, the daughter of the priest of that land, and his second wife was an Ethiopian, 
whom it would be wrong to confound with the former; since the supposition would be absurd that Aaron and Miriam 
should have quarrelled with Moses so long afterwards, on account of a marriage to which it is evident that they had 
already become reconciled. In reference to an observation made above, that the Jews and Mexicans were inclined to 
consider dreams as ri Pevov, (or possessing a divine nature,) we cannot help here expressing the strongest conviction that 
never would those two nations have fallen into such abominable superstitions, or suffered their priests so grossly to 
deceive them, but for the strange persuasion which they were under, that the Deity commonly communed with mortals 
by means of dreams and visions. What opinion would the ancient philosophers have pronounced on such a doctrine ? 
In what language would the orators have sought to expose to public contempt those witnesses whose evidence could 
not be disproved, because they unblushingly asserted that they had dreamt that the fact was so, and impiously main- 
tained that their dream was God, or in other words a vision of the deity? If the great mind of Brutus, when harassed 
with anxiety for the fate of his country, could have created a phantom of its own imagination which appeared to 
address him in his tent ?—what monstrous visions might not the Mexican and Jewish priests, who had employed the 
day in sacrificing, and whose hands and garments had been so lately drenched in blood, have fancied that they beheld 
when sleep took possession of their frame? The Mexican priests fasted to excess ; and it is admitted that fasting 
makes the imagination more active in dreams. They probably, therefore, when in the morning they took up the 
brush to compose their mythological paintings (a task which Torquemada says belonged more peculiarly to a class of 
Mexican priests remarkable for the austerity of their lives), found their invention much sharpened. The Jews might 

9 

be emphatically styled “a dreaming people ;” and it is probable that whenever any disaster threatened their state, public 
attention was more generally directed to dreams; the population became more credulous, and impostors more numerous 
and bold. Supposing for a moment that the inhabitants of this vast metropolis (London) could be induced to surrender 
up their judgments to the guidance of a few persons, who told them to place implicit faith in dreams,—what disorders 
would not ensue? Some of the multitude of dreamers would necessarily dream what would turn out.true, who would 

be accounted prophets and inspired persons ; the truth of their dreams would be insisted upon; and if religion could 

368 NOTES. 

once be identified with them, the popular delusion would be confirmed. Since no event can have more than two issues, 
when a prediction relates simply to the fact of its future accomplishment,—and the lying Hebrew prophets, as Scripture 
designates them, often prophesied on both sides of the question,—it necessarily followed that they even were sometimes 
true prophets. Saint Jerome has observed that it is no difficult thing to deceive the people; and he might have added, 
that it is frequently a very profitable thing. If the Roman augurs, whom Cicero is disposed to ridicule—affirming that 
they could scarcely meet each other in the streets without smiling, from the consciousness that their art was only cal- 
culated to cajole the populace,——had wished to heighten the respect which the public felt for their order, by encouraging 
the belief that they could predict the future through dreams, as well as by the usual way of divination; such preten- 
sions might possibly have been maintained by the stratagem of depositing, either in the temple of Jupiter or of 
Minerva, predictions framed so as to be adapted to all probable contingencies. One might have foretold and recorded 
his prophecy in writing, that the third Punic War would take place; another that it would not: one that if it did, it 
would be disastrous to the Romans; another that it would be fatal to the Carthaginians. And these prophecies 
having been laid up for some future race of priests to consult, and put in order after the event to which they related 
had occurred, they, by selecting the true from the false, and treating the latter as the Sibyl did her books, might by 
dexterously producing the former, and appealing to signatures and the faded character of the hand-writing as the 
proof of their genuine nature and authenticity, have easily induced the people, who are naturally inclined to the mar- 
vellous, to credit them, and who are disposed, moreover, to think it sinful to doubt any thing which their priests pledge 
their words to be the fact. But if it be objected to this fictitious case, that a preceding generation of mankind cares 
in general very little for those who follow them ; the reverse, it may be replied, experience shows to be the feelings 
of religious corporations, with whom the credit of their order is always a paramount consideration. We shall here

Commentators have been at no little trouble in endeavouring to explain to others, and rightly to comprehend 
themselves, the meaning of Jeremiah’: apostrophe, J am called by thy name, O Lord God of Hosts ; and some have 
even, rather than admit that the passage was too difficult for their ingenuity, taken refuge in a supposed mistrans- 
lation of the Hebrew: the literal interpretation of the text of Scripture seems, however, to furnish its right meaning; 
which is no other than that Jeremiah was called by his countrymen by the honorary appellation of the God whose 
priest and prophet he was. This text may receive some illustration from the following curious passage of Sahagun’s 
History of New Spain, in which that learned author gives some account of the ancient Tultecas: “Eran muy 
devotos y grandes oradores, oraban a un solo Sefior, que tenian por Dios, al qual le Hamaban Quetzalcoatl, cuyo 
sacerdote tenia el mismo nombre que tambien le Ilamaban Quetzalcoatl, el qual era muy devoto é aficionado 4 las 
cosas de su Sefor y Dios, y por esto tenido en mucho entre ellos, y asi lo queles mandaba lo hacian y cumplian y 
no excedian de ello; y le solia decir muchas veces que habia un solo Sefior y Dios que se decia Quetzalcoatl, y que 
no queria mas que culebras y mariposas que le ofreciesen y diesen en su sacrificio.” Historia Universal de las Cosas 
de Nueva-Espaia, lib. x. cap. 29. sec. 1. “They were very religious and much addicted to prayer; they worshiped 
only one Lord, whom they considered God, and they named him Quetzalcoatl; whose priest bore lkewise the same 
appellation, being also named Quetzalcoatl, who was very devout and zealous in the service of the Lord his 
God, and on that account held in great veneration by them; so that whatever he commanded them to do they did, 
without failing in any part of their obedience to him; he was accustomed frequently to declare that there was one 
only God and Lord, whose name was Quetzalcoatl, and that he required no other sacrifices but snakes and 
butterflies.” We have elsewhere observed, that Scriptural phrases, a Jewish train of sentiment and Hebrew 
metaphors, present themselves abundantly in almost every line of the sixth Book of Sahagun’s History of New 
Spain, which contains the prayers which the Mexicans addressed to the gods, the speeches which on solemn 
occasions they made to their kings, and the advice which they gave to their children. We here only wish to refer to 
the 376th page of the fifth and preceding volume of the present work, in order to point out the probability that 
God's promise to Jeremiah, “Thou shalt be as my mouth,” was known to the Mexicans; since the newly elected king 
of Mexico, in a prayer of thanksgiving to Tetzcatlipoca, there emphatically says of kings in general, “ Vuestros 
instrumentos y vuestras imagenes para regir vuestros reynos, estando dentro de ellos y hablando por su boca, y pro- 
nunciando ellos vuestras palabras.” “They are thine instruments and thine images to govern thy kingdoms, thou being 
in them, and speaking through their mouth, and they pronouncing thy words.” We may further remark, that the 
Mexicans, like the Jews, used very free language in remonstrating with the Deity. Torquemada and Acosta assert 
(perhaps exaggerating querulous chiding into positive insolence) that the Mexicans did not hesitate to apply the epithet 
bellaco to Tetzcatlipoca, when they imputed some bitter disappointment to his rejecting their vows. One more 
passage shall be adduced from Scripture, to show in what utter contempt the Jews held even that prophet, whose 
denunciations of vengeance and unchastened invective render his Book (laying aside its inspiration) one of the most 
extraordinary that can be found in any language. Ezekiel in his twentieth chapter thus bears witness to the little 
estimation in which his predictions were held by his countrymen; “ Moreover the word of the Lord came unto me, 
saying, Son of man, set thy face toward the south, and drop thy word toward the south, and prophesy againt the forest 
of the south field; and say to the forest of the south, Hear the word of the Lord; Thus saith the Lord God; Behold, 
I will kindle a fire in thee, and it shall devour every green tree in thee, and every dry tree: the flaming flame shall not 
be quenched, and all faces from the south to the north shall be burned therein. And all flesh shall see that I the Lord 
have kindled it : it shall not be quenched. Then said I, Ah Lord God! they say of me, Doth he not speak parables?”

One reflection must occur to those who meditate upon the history of the Jews and Mexicans,—that the two 
nations were equally addicted to idolatry, and that human sacrifices were quite as common amongst the Hebrews in 
the days of the prophets, as they afterwards became among the Mexicans and the Peruvians: the temple itself was 
profaned by them, and it cannot be doubted that men were devoted and sacrificed to Jehovah. This state of things 
being considered, it is not at all surprising that from time to time prophets should have risen up amongst the Jews 
who endeavoured to bring their countrymen to a sense of their guilty excesses, by threats of speedy and dreadful 
divine vengeance. Since, where was the rational Jew whose heart must not have sickened at the name of Tophet, 
and of the valley of the Son of Hinnom? Or who could have required inspiration to teach him that human sacrifices 
were displeasing to the Deity? The Hebrew prophets were all of them believers in a Deity of a purer nature as 
regarded the acceptance of sacrifice, than the mass of the people imagined the God who brought them ont of Egypt to 
be; and who, as we have elsewhere observed, seem to have put a false construction upon that Mosaic ordinance which 
declared, that none devoted of men should live ; and to have perverted to a dangerous precedent the faith of Abraham 
in offering up his son Isaac; as also not to have benefited by that page in their own history, which recorded the 
destruction of all the first-born in the land of Egypt ina single night, by the same Deity who immediately afterwards 
ordered the first-born, both of man and of beast, to be set apart (or devoted) unto him, in commemoration of that 
dreadful decree. If Mexican history had been handed down to us entire, we should probably have found that the 
Mexicans were not entirely destitute of prophets who denounced the vengeance of Tetzcatlipoca against those who 
sacrificed human victims at his shrine; since it has not failed to inform us that Nezahualcoyotl and Nezahualpilli dis- 
approved of such sacrifices and proposed to the people their abolition ; and that the former of those renowned kings 
built a temple in Tezcuco in honour of the Supreme Being, in which he only allowed incense to be burned, prayers to 
be offered up, music by means of plates of metal to be sounded, but o image whatsoever to be placed. As regards the 
idolatry of the Greeks and Romans, it may confidently be asserted, that it was the purity of their idolatry, compared 
with that of the Jews and the Mexicans, that was the sole reason why their philosophers did not all become prophets. 
Yet still it should be recollected that Socrates fell a victim to his zeal for reforming the religion of the state; and it 
cannot be doubted, if human sacrifices had been customary in Greece in the days of Pythagoras, that he who pronounced 
even sacrifices of animals to be impious, would have loudly protested against them; and if his protest had been written 
down by his disciples and been accompanied with threats, that Jupiter to punish the Greeks would either excite a 
civil war amongst them, or cause a Persian invasion, or finally would afflict them with any other evil which he might 
have thought near or probable,—he perhaps in after ages would have been revered in Greece as an inspired prophet. 

We pass, by an easy transition, from dreams and visions to fables. It may, however, be deemed a more rational 
task to compare the laws of the Mexicans and the Jews with each other: than their fables, which were infinite in 
number and similar in kind; for the imagination both of the former and the latter people,—unlike that of the 
Greeks, which loved to soar to the sunny heights of Olympus and the purple pavilions of the gods, or to repose 
on the banks of winding streams, or visit the battle plain,—delighted in exploring the hidden centre of the earth, 
and in compelling, with magic rings, spells, and incantations, genii to reveal hidden treasures, and witches 
to conjure up the ghosts of the dead. We shall therefore leave to others the task of unravelling the meaning of 
the Mexican and Hebrew fables; who, if they can obtain the assistance of a learned Rabbi, will find their labour 
much lightened; although we cannot refrain from inserting here two Mexican fables, extracted from Boturini’s 
short but learned treatise, because the former seems to contain a confused tradition of Christ and the prophet

The following is the translation of the latter fable. “The justice of the above observations is further confirmed 
by another fable of these same Indians, which is founded upon historical fact. They affirm, then, that on the year 
of Seven Rabbits the Sun stood still; when, the earth becoming scorched to an excessive degree, a mosquito presented 
itself before him and addressed him, ‘ Lord of the World, is it your intention to burn up the whole earth and to 
reduce the universe to cinders; since, fatigued as it were in your regular course, you stop and remain immoveable to 
the prayers of mortals?’ When receiving no answer, the Sun continuing motionless, the mosquito approached nearer 
to him and stung him upon the leg, which, drawing back he again renewed his course.” This fable is particularly 
deserving of attention, because it furnishes strong grounds for supposing that the Mexicans were not only acquainted 
with some of the circumstances preceding and attending the flight of the children of Israel from Egypt, and their 
subsequent wanderings in the desert, but had also preserved traditions of the events which immediately followed 
their occupation of the land of Canaan under Joshua. It must also be admitted, that this tradition cannot be 
classed amongst the number of those which connected with a belief in the Deluge, in the existence of giants, and 
with legends of the golden age, have been discovered nearly amongst all nations. On the contrary, it bears a Hebrew 
stamp and character; for, although the fancy of Ovid induced him poetically to describe the consternation which the 
gods and men were thrown into by the rashness of Phaéton, who drove the chariot of the Sun out of its old course, 
when Jupiter interposed to restore order to nature; and Pope has sublimely imagined the effect which the suspension 
of the laws of gravity for one moment would produce throughout the universe, in the often-quoted lines of his 

Essay on Man,— 
« And, if each system in gradation roll 

Alike essential to the amazing whole, 

The least confusion but in one, not all 

That system only, but the whole, must fall. 

Let earth unbalanced from her orbit fly, 

Planets and suns run lawless through the sky ; 
Let ruling angels from their spheres be hurld, 
Being on being wreck’d, and world on world ; 
Heaven’s whole foundations to their centre nod, 
And nature trembles to the throne of God. 

All this dread order break—for whom? for thee? 
Vile worm !—Oh madness! Pride! Impiety !”— 

we are not at liberty to seek in the region of poetry and fiction grave arguments on which to found historical 
conclusions. The annals of the Jews alone inform us, that thrice within the last four thousand years, words pro- 
nounced by mortal lips have effected the greatest changes in the sun, both as regards its orbicular motion and the 
motion of its rays. The following miracle is recorded in the tenth chapter of Exodus as having been performed 
by Moses, in order to compel Pharaoh to let the children of Israel depart out of Egypt, (the representation of which 
occurs in the twelfth page of the Borgian MS.): “ And the Lord said unto Moses, Stretch out thine hand toward 
heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, even darkness which may be felt. And Moses stretched 
forth his hand toward heaven; and there was a thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days. ‘They saw not one 
another, neither rose any from his place for three days: but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings.” 
In the tenth chapter of the Book of Joshua we read, that at the command of that chieftain of the Jews the 
solar orb stood still for a considerable period of time: “Then spake Joshua to the Lord in the day when the 
Lord delivered up the Amorites before the children of Israel, and he said in the sight of Israel, Sun, stand 
thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon. And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, 

NOTES. 375 

until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies. Is not this written in the Book of Jasher*? So the 
sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and hasted not to go down about a whole day. And there was no day 
like that before it or after it, that the Lord hearkened unto the voice of a man: for the Lord fought for Israel.” 

Frem a comparison of the following passages, taken from the twentieth chapter of the Second Book of Kings, and 
the thirty-eighth chapter of the Prophecies of Isaiah, it is evident that there was a time when the sun’s motion, whether 
it should go backward or forward, depended upon the will of king Hezekiah: “And Hezekiah said unto Isaiah, 
What shall be the sign that the Lord will heal me, and that I shall go wp into the house of the Lord the third day? 
And Isaiah said, This sign shalt thou have of the Lord, that the Lord will do the thing that he hath spoken: shall 
the shadow go forward ten degrees, or go back ten degrees? And Hezekiah answered, It is a light thing for the 
shadow to go down ten degrees: nay, but let the shadow return backward ten degrees. And Isaiah the prophet 
cried unto the Lord: and he brought the shadow ten degrees backward, by which it had gone down in the dial of 
Ahaz.” “Then came the word of the Lord to Isaiah, saying, Go, and say to Hezekiah, Thus saith the Lord, the 
God of David thy father, I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears: behold, I will add unto thy days fifteen 
years. And I will deliver thee and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria: and I will defend this city. 
And this shall be a sign unto thee from the Lord, that the Lord will do this thing that he hath spoken; Behold, I 
will bring again the shadow of the degrees, which is gone down in the sun-dial of Ahaz, ten degrees backward. So 
the sun returned ten degrees, by which degrees it was gone down.” 

Sacred history. declaring that the sun has stood still, and profane history being altogether silent on the subject, it 
is evident, or at least highly probable, (if the Mexican fable was founded upon historical truth, as Boturini supposes 
it to have been,) that it was derived from a Hebrew source. This assumption will acquire further corroboration if it 
can be shown that this fable is accompanied with any of the characteristics that usually belong to the miracles 
which are related in the Old Testament. Those miracles are in general the greatest that can be conceived, brought 
about by the most insignificant means, and frequently wrought for the purpose of accomplishing ends which to 
erring human judgment must appear comparatively trivial: since of what importance, after all, can the issue of the 
greatest battles in support of the most just of causes, and fought by the most glorious of nations, appear when 
compared with the derangement of the laws of the universe? We are not informed of the precise object of the 
sun’s standing still in the Mexican fable; but a mosquito or some stinging fly was that which caused it to go on 
again: and it deserves to be remarked, that flies are particularly alluded to by Moses as instruments by which 
the Deity accomplished great ends. One of the plagues sent upon the Egyptians was a plague, as it is probable, 
of stinging flies, which is thus described in the eighth chapter of Exodus: “ And the Lord said unto Moses, Rise 
up early in the morning, and stand before Pharaoh; lo, he cometh forth to the water; and say unto him, Thus 
saith the Lord, Let my people go, that they may serve me. Else, if thou wilt not let my people go, behold, I will 
send swarms of flies upon thee, and upon thy servants, and upon thy people, and into thy houses: and the houses of 
the Egyptians shall be full of swarms of flies, and also the ground whereon they are. AndI will sever in that day the 
land of Goshen, in which my people dwell, that no swarms of flies shall be there ; to the end thou mayest know that 
Tam the Lord in the midst of the earth. And I will puta division between my people and thy people: to-morrow shall 
this sign be. And the Lord did so; and there came a grievous swarm of flies into the house of Pharaoh, and 
into his servants’ houses, and into all the land of Egypt: the land was corrupted by reason of the swarm of flies.” 
In the twenty-seventh and twenty-eighth verses of the twenty-third chapter of Exodus, God promises to extirpate 
the enemies of the children of Israel who dwelt in the land of Canaan, by means of hornets: “I will send my fear 
before thee, and will destroy all the people to whom thou shalt come, and I will make all thine enemies turn their 
backs unto thee. And I will send hornets before thee, which shall drive out the Hivite, the Canaanite, and the 
Hittite, from before thee.” The same promise is repeated in the twentieth verse of the seventh chapter of 
Deuteronomy: “ Moreover the Lord thy God will send the hornet among them, until they that are left, and hide 
themselves from thee, be destroyed.” And it is referred to as having been carried into execution in the twelfth verse 
of the twenty-fourth chapter of Joshua: “And I sent the hornet before you, which drove them out from before 
you, even the two kings of the Amorites; but not with thy sword.” It is evident from the passages of Scripture 
which have been quoted, that the mosquito’s agency introduced into the Mexican fable of the Sun having stood still,

makes it still more probable that it was derived from a Hebrew source. It may be also proper to remark, that there 
are certain prophecies in Scripture respecting the sun, which seem all to be represented as fulfilled in the Mexican 
paintings. “The sun shall be darkened,” “it shall be turned into blood,” are denunciations which often occur in the Old 
Testament; and the sun is frequently painted in the superstitious calendars of the Mexicans darkened and streaming 
with blood. The great wonder in heaven, a woman clothed with the sun, which is mentioned by St. John in the 
twelfth chapter of the Revelations, appears also to have presented itself to the imagination of the Mexican painters ; 
and commentators, by consulting the plates contained in the present work, will be relieved from the difficulties which 
one and all confess that they have felt in guessing what this curious costume could have been. As regards an ob- 
servation which we have made above respecting the miracles recorded in the Old Testament,—that in general neither 
the end to be attained, nor the means by which the miracle itself is effected, bear any proportion in magnitude to it, 
—we must do the Rabbis the justice to give their solution of this difficulty, which they explain on the principle of 
Aaron’s rod, which became a serpent, swallowing up the rods of the magicians which became serpents also, as 
narrated in the twelfth verse of the seventh chapter of Exodus, giving us to understand by this explanation, that the 
Jews rest their claim to be considered God’s peculiar people, solely upon the magnitude of the miracles which he 
performed in their favour, and on their superiority over all other miracles: for they absurdly suppose that to work 
miracles, provided those miracles be neither great nor many, may be the lot of common mortals, even when their end 
is mischievous. If this mode of reasoning of the Rabbis be just, the whole system which they are anxious to uphold 
would fall to the ground ; since what could be proved by miracles, if the origin ascribed to them be of so precarious 
a nature, and if they may be referred to more than one cause? yet this is the only solution which the Rabbis offer 
for God’s accomplishing the most trivial ends by the greatest miracles. The ancient philosophers believed that they 
understood too little of the Deity, of nature, or of man, to place much faith in miracles and prophecies, or to admit 
any extravagant inferences to be drawn from them. They would have allowed little more to the man who called 
himself a prophet, than that he was to be credited in those particular predictions which he had uttered, which time 
had already shown were true ; and his further demands would have been rejected with contempt. If to reason by 
analogy on physical questions can never lead to more than probable conclusions, how manifest is it that such a mode 
of reasoning must be much more inconclusive, where the subject itself is above nature and consequently beyond 
reason, which miracles confessedly are! And yet the Hebrew people, the most ignorant and unphilosophical of all 
nations, were those who deduced conclusions of the greatest latitude from them. That the Jews were a very un- 
philosophical nation, may be proved from the literal sense in which they chose to understand the thirteenth verse of 
the tenth chapter of Joshua; inferring that, as the moon was commanded to stand still as well as the sun, not only 
had the latter motion, but likewise that, since the second command could not have been for the sake of adding to the 
light of the sun, it must have been to prevent the moon coming into collision with the sun, which would have been a 
necessary consequence on the supposition that those luminaries were two large balls which revolved in the same 
circle round the earth. The ancients entertained in common the erroneous belief in the sun’s annual motion 
through the signs of the zodiac: but the Jews are the only people in the world who seem to have been ignorant of 
the earth’s motion round its own axis. Before terminating these notes, we shall point out some analogies in the 
miscellaneous customs of the Jews and the Mexicans. Both nations were most punctual in the payment of their 
religious offerings, first-fruits, &c. The Mexicans, as Montezuma informed Cortes, feared if they failed in this 
portion of their religious duties that they would incur the severest vengeance of the gods: and the prophet Malachi, 
or rather God speaking through the mouth of that prophet, assures the Jews that they would lie under a peculiar 
curse if they did not bring the full quantity of tithe to the temple. It is probable, from the curse denounced and the 
blessing promised in the following passage of the third chapter of the Book of Malachi, that the Rabbis would soon, 
on establishing themselves in the New World, have taught their Mexican and Peruvian converts the necessity of 
complying with this precept of the old law; “ Will a man rob God? yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherem 
have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings. Ye are cursed with a curse: for ye have robbed me, even this whole 
nation. Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now 
herewith, saith the Lord of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that 
there shall not be room enough to receive it. And I will rebuke the devourer for your sakes, and he shall not 
destroy the fruits of your ground ; neither shall your vine cast her fruit before the time in the field, saith the Lord 
of hosts. And all nations shall call you blessed: for ye shall be a delightsome land, saith the Lord of hosts.” The

‘paintings of the Mexicans show that censers were used in profusion in the ceremonies of their religion: and it. ap- 
pears from the sixteenth and seventeenth verses of the sixteenth chapter of Numbers, that they were in as common 
use amongst the Levites: “ And Moses said unto Korah, Be thou and all thy company before the Lord, thou, and 
they, and Aaron, to-morrow: and take every man his censer, and put incense in them, and bring ye before the Lord 
every man his censer, two hundred and fifty censers ; thou also, and Aaron, each of you his censer.” The Mexicans 
were accustomed to mark their respect for the persons of ambassadors by burning odoriferous perfumes in censers 
before them, which it would seem from the forty-sixth verse of the second chapter of the prophet Daniel. was a 
ceremony with which the Jews were acquainted: “Then the king Nebuchadnezzar fell upon his face, and worshiped 
Daniel, and commanded that they should offer an oblation and sweet odours unto him.” The Mexicans, like the 
Jews, used the ceremony of prostration when admitted to the presence of their kings. How gratifying, therefore, 
must it have been to the vanity of the latter people, who were at that time captives in Babylon, to learn that the 
haughty ruler of Asia had prostrated himself to the earth before a child of their nation! And into what repute must it 
have brought the art of interpreting dreams! The Mexicans were accustomed to decorate the inner walls of their 
temples and palaces with figures painted in vermilion. And we learn from the twenty-third chapter of Ezekiel that 
a similar custom prevailed amongst the Jews; since the prophet, describing Samaria and Jerusalem under the type 
of the two sisters Aholah and Aholibah, there says of the latter, ““ When she saw men portrayed upon the wall, the 
images of the Chaldeans portrayed with vermilion, girded with girdles upon their loins, exceeding in dyed attire 
upon their heads, all of them princes to look to, after the manner of the Babylonians of Chaldea, the land of their 
. nativity: and as soon as she saw them with her eyes, she doted upon them, and sent messengers unto them into 
Chaldea.” The Mexican priests lodged round their temples in chambers built for the express purpose; and it says 
in the twenty-seventh verse of the ninth chapter of the First Book of Chronicles, that a certain portion of the Levites 
lodged round the temple constructed by Solomon: “ And they lodged round about the house of God, because the 
charge was upon them, and the opening thereof every morning pertained to them.” The Mexican temples contained 
fountains or ponds in their court-yards in which the priests performed their ablutions ; and Solomon is said, in the 
seventh chapter of the First Book of Kings, to have made a molten sea which contained two thousand baths, which 
served the same purpose, and it is to be supposed stood in the court of the temple. Although images were forbidden 
to the Jews, still frequent mention is made in Scripture of cherubim carved as ornaments upon wood: these cherubim 
were perhaps sometimes merely winged heads, such as now decorate tombs; and it is probable that the Jews orna- 
mented the outside of their edifices with similar heads sculptured in stone. M. Dupaix has observed that heads 
sometimes of a very cadaverous aspect were inserted by the Mexicans into their walls, for the purpose, as he supposes, 
of giving a relief to their monotonous appearance. (Representations of these mural ornaments will be found in the 
fifth plate of the second part of his Monuments of New Spain.) The Mexican priests were accustomed to pierce 
their bodies with lancets formed out of a diaphanous stone named the Yztli; and to draw blood from their arms, 
legs, wrists, tongues, ears, &c. And it is said of the idolatrous Hebrew prophets, in the twenty-eighth verse of the 
eighteenth chapter of the First Book of Kings, “ And they cried aloud, and cut themselves after their manner with 
knives and lancets, till the blood gushed out upon them.” very thing that related to the preserving unextinguished 
the sacred fire which burnt in their temples, was considered by the Mexicans as a matter of the utmost consequence. 
And it would appear from the following passage of the first chapter of the Second Book of Maccabees, that the Jews 
attached scarcely less importance to the keeping in the fire of their altar: “For when our fathers were led into 
Persia, the priests that were then devout took the fire of the altar privily, and hid it in an hollow place of a pit 
without water, where they kept it sure, so that the place was unknown to all men. Now after many years, when it 
pleased God, Neemias, being sent from the king of Persia, did send of the posterity of those priests that had hid it 
to the fire: but when they told us they found no fire, but thick water; then commanded he them to draw it up, and 
to bring it; and when the sacrifices were laid on, Neemias commanded the priests to sprinkle the wood and the 
things laid thereupon with the water. When this was done, and the time came that the sun shone, which afore was 
hid in the cloud, there was a great fire kindled, so that every man marvelled.” The manner in which the Jews kindled 
their sacred fire is not precisely known. That it was a religious rite, accompanied with certain ceremonies, cannot be 
doubted: and we may even be permitted to believe, from the expression in the fourteenth verse of the nineteenth 
chapter of Ezekiel,—* And fire is gone out of a rod of her branches which hath devoured her fruit,’—that they were 
acquainted with the Mexican method of kindling fire from wood. Many passages in the Old Testament would lead

us to imagine that the ground plan, at least, of the greater temple of Mexico resembled that of the temple of

rock, the four sides of which were fashioned and rendered smooth by the labour of man, (according to Josephus,) 
upon which the Hebrew temple was built; whilst its upper area, divided into different courts, with porticoes having 
light against light, and containing various edifices, might have imitated in some degree Herod’s temple, in the inner

Book of Chronicles ; and can assure them that they will reap little assistance from consulting the vision of Ezekiel, 
as recorded in the forty-seventh and forty-eighth chapters of that prophet’s Book. What is here asserted admits the 
most simple proof; since it is only necessary to recur to plans of that temple, which celebrated scholars have caused 
to be engraved and inserted in their works, to find that they almost all materially differ from each other; whilst the 
Rabbis in their plans mix absurdity with ignorance. It cannot be expected that much light should be thrown upon 
the question by Josephus, whose description of Herod’s temple is inapplicable to that which was founded so many 
ages before by Solomon, and who is besides an historian who is guilty of the greatest exaggerations: but an obscure 
passage in the fourteenth chapter of his Jewish Antiquities, seems to afford grounds for supposing that the Hebrew 
temple was built upon a hollow artifical platform, like many of the Mexican temples. The following is the passage

priest, the son of Onias, who in his life repaired the house again, and in his days fortified the temple: and by him 
was built from the foundation the double height, the high fortress of the wall about the temple.” This description 
would be almost applicable to the architecture of the temple of Palenque, or to the platforms of more than one 
story upon which the Mexican temples were built. The roof and the windows of the house of the forest of 
Lebanon, built by Solomon, are thus described in the seventh chapter of the First Book of Kings ; from which it 
would appear that the roof of that house was supported by transverse beams resting upon three rows of pillars ; 

* Tt deserves to be remarked, that the name of the holy house, which Josephus always bestows upon the temple of Jerusalem, is the 
literal signification of the Mexican term teocalli.

which was the plan adopted by those who constructed the palaces of Mictlan, although in those palaces, the halls 
being long and narrow, single rows of pillars were judged sufficient to support the roof: “And it was covered with 
cedar above upon the beams, that lay on forty-five pillars, fifteen in a row. And there were windows in three rows, 
and light was against light in three ranks. And all the doors and posts were square, with the windows: and light 
was against light in three ranks. 

M. Dupaix has remarked, that the sides of the Mexican temples almost invariably corresponded to the four 
cardinal points, whilst the staircases were always on the east, because the chapel above looked towards the east ; 
and when the ascent was by a single staircase, faced the upper landing-place. The same was the position of the 
temple which Ezekiel beheld in his vision, as is evident from the first verse of the forty-seventh chapter of his 
Prophecies: “ Afterward he brought me again unto the door of the house; and, behold, waters issued out from 
under the threshold of the house eastward: for the forefront of the house stood toward the east, and the waters 
came down from under from the right side of the house, at the south side of the altar.” The stairs of the altar 
appertaining to this temple are said, in the following passage of the forty-third chapter of the same prophet, to have 
looked towards the east: “And the altar shall be twelve cubits long, twelve broad, square in the four squares 
thereof. And the settle shail be fourteen cubits long and fourteen broad in the four squares thereof; and the 
border about it shall be half a cubit; and the bottom thereof shall be a cubit about; and his stairs shall look 
toward the east.” It had also many courts, like the greater temple of Mexico, as Ezekiel declares in the twenty- 
first verse of his forty-sixth chapter: “Then he brought me forth into the utter court, and caused me to pass by the 
four corners of the court; and, behold, in every corner of the court there was a court.” From the fourteenth verse 
of the thirty-eighth chapter of Jeremiah, it appears that the temple of Solomon had many courts likewise : “Then 
Zedekiah the king sent, and took Jeremiah the prophet unto him into the third entry that is in the house of the Lord: 
and the king said unto Jeremiah, I will ask thee a thing; hide nothing from me.” A causeway is also mentioned in 
the sixteenth verse of the twenty-sixth chapter of the First Book of Chronicles, as leading to the latter temple: “To 
Shuppim and Hosah the lot came forth westward, with the gate Shallecheth, by the causeway of the going up, ward 
against ward.” The Jews were commanded by Moses not to make an altar of hewn stone: smooth uncut stones were 
therefore probably used by them in the construction of the altars belonging to their temple. And Sahagun affirms 
that the court of the greater temple of Mexico was paved with smooth and uncut stones as slippery as glass. 
Josephus records the vast size of the blocks of hewn stone of which the temple of Jerusalem was built. And 
M. Dupaix expresses his astonishment at the equally large masses of granite which he discovered in the walls of 
the palaces of Mictlan; wondering at the same time by what means they had been worked, since their perfectly 
smooth surface bore no marks of the chisel; and he could not believe it possible that the founders of Mictlan had 
reduced those blocks to proper shape and dimensions merely by the friction of one stone against another. It did 
not occur to M. Dupaix that emery might have been employed in working them, with several kinds of which 
Sahagun says the Mexicans were acquainted; which in conjunction with the saw would have given to those 
stones the smooth surface that he describes. It appears from the ninth verse of the seventh chapter of the First 
Book of Kings, that the stones with which the temple of Solomon was constructed were sawed both on the inner 
and the outer side: “ All these were of costly stones, according to the measures of hewed stones, sawed with saws, 
within and without, even from the foundation unto the coping, and so on the outside toward the great court.” 

That the Tultecas were the founders of many of the most splendid monuments of the New World may be inferred, 
not only from the signification of the proper name Tulteca, which means an architect, but likewise because the 
figure of a feathered serpent is sometimes represented in Mosaic on their walls, which undoubtedly referred to their god 
Quetzalcoatl. A gigantic serpent of this description ornaments the ruins of the fortress of Xochicalco; and here 
we may observe, that the original drawing of that monument (from which the fifteenth plate in the first part of the 
Monuments of New Spain has been taken) has suffered considerable mutilation, one half of it having been torn off. 
Since nothing appears more admirable in the architecture of the New World than the beautiful and durable Mosaic 
ornaments which cover the walls of the palaces of Mictlan, it is highly probable that those structures were erected 
by the Tultecas ; and they furnish an argument in favour of the belief, that the Tultecas were originally a Jewish 
colony which in remote ages had settled in America; since we do not read that any other nation of the old continent, 
except the Jews, ever introduced this style of ornament into architecture; whilst Josephus, it should be remarked, 
commends in the highest terms the skill which his countrymen displayed in uniting together the stones of which 

380 NOTES. 

the walls of the temple were composed, the joints of which were scarcely visible. And the art of working in mosaic 
seems probably alluded to in the sixth verse of the third chapter of the Second Book of Chronicles, where the 
embellishments which Solomon added to the temple are thus described; “And he garnished the house with 
precious stones for beauty, and the gold was gold of Parvaim.” The walls of the Mexican temples were delicately 
plastered, and frequently ornamented with stucco, especially those of the temple of Palenque, the exterior of which 
presented to the eye groups of colossal figures, which viewed from the ground must naturally have suggested to the 
mind of the beholder the relievos which decorate the temple of the Parthenon; save that in the former, the 
immortal genius of the Greeks was wanting. That the Jews were accustomed to add this kind of ornament to their 
buildings we learn from the simile contained in the seventeenth verse of the twenty-second chapter of Ecclesiasticus : 
“ A heart settled upon a thought of understanding is as a fair plastering on the wall of a gallery.” M. Dupaix, in 
describing the figures in plaster upon the walls of the temple of Palenque, notices, as a peculiarity in them all, the 
excessive size of the nose. He did not perhaps know that Solomon ascribed beauty and majesty to countenances 
distinguished by that characteristic, as he intimates in the comparison introduced in the fourth verse of the seventh 
chapter of his Song: “Thy neck is as a tower of ivory, thine eyes like the fishpools in Heshbon, by the gate of 
Bath-rabbim, thy nose is as the tower of Lebanon which looketh toward Damascus.” Since it cannot be doubted 
that Solomon was the arbiter elegantiarum of Jewish taste, it may be inferred that the peculiar physiognomy of the 
above-mentioned figures, (which induced M. Dupaix to think that they represented an extinct race of mankind,) was 
only, as regarded the junction of the nose with the forehead, an exaggeration of the Hebrew line of beauty into a 
complete curve. 

In some of the temples of Yucatan, according to the testimony of Captain Don Antonio del Rio, statues of men with 
palms m ther hands, in the act of beating drums and dancing, are formed in stucco on the walls: and it should be 
observed, that to rejoice with branches of the palm-tree was peculiarly a Hebrew custom, the observance of which 
Moses strictly enjoined to the Jews.—The following passage is extracted from Captain Don Antonio del Rio’s narrative 
of his visit to the ruins of Palenque, (which preceded, and probably led to, the more extensive researches of M. 
Dupaix,) in which he takes occasion to mention other ancient temples existing in Yucatan. 

“The Rey. Father Thomas de Soza, a Franciscan friar of the convent of Merida, many years collector of alms 
destined for the holy house of Jerusalem, who, in pursuing the duties imposed upon him from his situation, had 
repeatedly traversed the province, fortunately happening to be at Palenque, favoured me with a circumstantial 
account of that country, of which I shall now avail myself in his own words. 

“‘ At the distance of twenty leagues from the city of Merida southward, between the curacy called Mona y Ticul 
and the town of Nocacab, are the remains of some stone edifices ; one very large building has withstood the ravages of 
time, and still exists in good preservation: the natives give it the name of Oxmutal. It stands on an eminence of 
twenty yards in height, and measures two hundred yards on each facade. The apartments, the exterior corridor, the 
pillars with figures in medio-relievo, and decorated with serpents, lizards, &c. formed in stucco, beside which are 
statues of men with palms in their hands in the act of beating drums and dancing, resemble in every respect those 
observable in the buildings at Palenque. Hight leagues distant from the same city to the northward are the ruined 
walls of several other houses, which increase in number as you advance in an easterly direction. In the vicinity of 
the river Lagartos, at a town called Mani, which is under the actual jurisdiction of the Franciscan friars, in the 
middle of the principal square, stands a pillory of a conical shape, built of stones ; and to the southward rises a very 
ancient palace, resembling that at Palenque, which, according to tradition, was inhabited, upon the arrival of the 
Spanish conquerors, by a petty Indian sovereign called Htulrio, who resigned it to the Franciscans for a residence 
while their new convent was building, after which it was used for several years as a public hospital. The erection 
of this palace was long anterior to the time of Htulrio, who replied to the inquiries of the fathers relative to the 
period of its construction, that he was totally ignorant of its origin, and only knew that it had been inhabited 
by his ancestors. From hence we may draw some inference respecting the very remote antiquity of the Pa- 
lencian edifices, buried for so many ages in the impenetrable thickets covering a mountain, and unknown to the 
historians of the New World, by whom no mention whatsoever is made of their existence. On the road from 
Merida to Bacalar there are also many other buildings both to the north and south, according to my informant’s 
narrative, a description of which I conceive unnecessary, not only from being desirous of avoiding prolixity, but 
because the identity of the ancient inhabitants of Yucatan and Palenque is, in my opinion, evidently proved by the

strong analogy of their customs, buildings, and acquaintance with the arts, whereof such vestiges are discernible in 
those monuments which the current of time has not yet swept away.” 

M. Dupaix observes, that he sometimes discovered a plain cylindrical stone at no great distance from the Mexican 
temples. This stone he is inclined to think might have been destined for gladiatorial sacrifices : but from the absence 
of the groove through which the rope ran that was fastened round the waist of the combatant, (which Sahagun 
makes particular mention of in describing those sacrifices, we imagine that this stone was a Tehuehuetl, or stone 
dedicated to acts of penance. And here again the manners of the ancient Jews and the Mexicans seem to approximate ; 
for the latter did penance by ascending upon a cylindrical stone, and the former by sitting in a czrcle, as the two fol- 
lowing extracts (the one from Boturini’s Treatise, the other from A View of the Jewish Religion,) will more fully 
show.

We cannot refrain from observing, in reference to the fable of Yappan, (under which proper name that of Job may 
perhaps be disguised;) that it has a tincture of Jewish superstition: for although the Jews were left completely in 
the dark by Joses in every thing relating to the doctrines of heaven, hell, the devil, a future state of rewards and 
punishments, and the immortality of the soul, which furnished the chief grounds of the disputes between the Pha- 
risees and the Sadducees ; they still believed in an evil spirit who accused them before God, when watching their 
actions he became aware of their having sinned, whom they named Satan, or the adversary: and this doctrine they 
collected from the Book of Job. We may add, in reference to the second quotation, that the Mexicans, like the 
Jews, were accustomed to do penance by sitting on the ground, in which posture their priests are often represented 
in the Mexican paintings. The object of this penance frequently was to obtain rai ; and they might have imitated 
either Quecalcoatl, who procured rain by fasting, or the prophet Jeremiah, who declares in the third verse of the 
third chapter of his Prophecies, that the wickedness of the Jews was the cause of showers having been withholden ; 
and in his prayer for the people to God, in the fourteenth chapter of the same Book, he expresses himself in lan- 
guage very analogous to that which we find in the eighth chapter of the sixth book of Sahagun’s History of New 
Spain was used by the Mexican priests in their prayer to Tlaloc for rain. The Mexicans attached great importance 
to the sacred vestments worn by their priests, which were carefully preserved in their temples; and in this they 
resembled the Jews. In the twenty-fourth verse of the eighteenth chapter of the Wisdom of Solomon, the following 
virtues are ascribed to the pontifical costume of Aaron: “ For in the long garment was the whole world, and in the 
four rows of the ‘stones was the glory of the fathers graven, and thy majesty upon the diadem of his head.” They 
were fond of wearing dresses of scarlet and of showy colours, as were also the Jews. The exclamation of the prophet, 
“‘ Who is this that cometh from Bozrah?” and many other passages of the Old Testament might be cited to show that 
the Jews entertained a great predilection for scarlet: and a coat of many colours was given as a mark of peculiar 
kindness by the patriarch Jacob to his favourite son Joseph, as we learn from the following verse of the thirty-seventh 
chapter of Genesis : “ Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age: 
and he made him a coat of many colours.” ‘The Mexicans not only excelled in the fabrication of cloth and hangings, 
but delighted likewise in introducing monstrous and uncouth figures into the labours of their loom ;'a taste that in 
former days prevailed amongst the Jews, who being forbidden by their law to imitate things that existed in EUG, 
had no choice left but to imagine monsters. To this Jewish custom, Claudian alludes in the following verses : 

“ Jam frugibus aptum 
Bquor, et assuetum sylvis delphina videbo ; 
Jam cocleis homines junctos, et quidquid inane 
Nutrit Judaicis que pingitur India velis.” 

It may be proper to remark that some critics, unwilling to allow the Jews the fame which Claudian ascribes to 
them, have, witha total disregard to prosody, wished to substitute the word A/talicis for Judaicis. A cross somewhat 
resembling the Greek letter ¢aw occurs not unfrequently in the Mexican paintings. And it deserves to be noticed, that 
in the kingdom of Naples the Jews in former ages were compelled to wear a badge of that description, as Bayle and 
other authors assert. The representations of ravenous beasts tearing and eagles devouring are so often found in
