the same paintings, that it might almost induce one to suppose that there was an intended allusion to the third verse 
of the fifteenth chapter of the Prophecies of Jeremiah: “ And I will appoint over them four kinds, saith the Lord: 
the sword to slay, and the dogs to tear, and the fowls of the heaven, and the beasts of the earth, to devour and 
destroy.” 

The last argument which we shall adduce to prove that the Jews in early ages colonized America, is the prophetical 
denunciations of the Old Testament, that they should be removed into a// the kingdoms of the earth ;—which required 
for their literal fulfilment (since what dependence can be placed on prophecies that are not to be literally fulfilled ?) 
that the Jews should be removed to Peru and Mexico ; and could never have contemplated that an entire hemisphere 
would remain until the sixteenth century after the Christian era untrodden by the chosen people of God. Nor will 
it avail those who wish, by giving less latitude to the words of Moses, to contend that his prediction has been fully 
accomplished,—to insinuate that he was perhaps ignorant of the existence of America, and therefore did not mean to 
prophesy that the Jews would be scattered over that continent: since this would be arguing absurdly, that human 
knowledge prescribes limits to Divine inspiration. Since the prophecy relating to the dispersion of the Jews, and 
its alledged fu? accomplishment, has always been used as a lever to lift and support an enormous weight,—the 
acknowledgement that we should not have recurred to it here but for the sake of one class of persons, who will 
prefer this to every other kind of proof, and that we do not now address this argument to any others, may appear 
somewhat gratuitous. But we hope that by doing so, those that may henceforward find it disagreeable to admit that 
the Jews had in early ages colonized America, will find it impossible to recede; and that an accumulation of evidence 
will compel them to confess that the old law has been revived in that continent, and that the sceptre has been 
restored to Judah. The reasons that induce us not to consider this last argument of a general kind, are the 
following : First, the Mosaic records are not admitted by all persons to be inspired: and arguments drawn from their 
inspiration to prove that America was colonized by the Jews, would evidently be thrown away upon those who did 
not believe in them. Secondly, The Jews themselves may feel in doubt,—understanding in a limited signification, as 
Christians have done, the words of Moses, “shall be removed into allthe kingdoms of the earth;” and not con- 
sidering their dispersion to be a judgment inflicted upon them on account of the crucifixion of Christ, (to which 
Moses makes not the slightest allusion,) but a punishment on account of their disobedience to his law, which he 
threatened them would actually happen,—whether the accomplishment of all the prophecies relating to their dispersion 
might not have occurred at the time of the Babylonian captivity ; for the second temple wanting prophecy as well as 
Urim and Thummim, of course there could have been no prophecies of more dispersions after the return from 
that captivity: and the predictions uttered during the seventy years might have referred to the probable future lot 
of the Jews dispersed in Egypt and elsewhere. The Jews may therefore ascribe their dispersion after the subjugation 
of their state by the Romans until the present time, first to political and afterwards to religious causes, and not 
consider the argument drawn from Prophecy as affording conclusive evidence that they had in remote ages colonized 
America. Amongst the following denunciations pronounced by Moses against the Jews, will be found that, relative 
to their future dispersion, which is contained in the twenty-fifth verse of the twenty-eighth chapter of Deuteronomy: 
“ But it shall come to pass, if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the Lord thy God, to observe to do all his 
commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day ; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and 
overtake thee : Cursed shalt thou be in the city, and cursed shalt thou be in the field. Cursed shall be thy basket 
and thy store. Cursed shall be the fruit of thy body, and the fruit of thy land, the increase of thy kine, and the 
flocks of thy sheep. Cursed shalt thou be when thou comest in, and cursed shalt thou be when thou goest out. 
The Lord shall send upon thee cursing, vexation, and rebuke, in all that thou settest thine hand unto for to do, 
until thou be destroyed, and until thou perish quickly ; because of the wickedness of thy doings, whereby thou hast 
forsaken me. The Lord shall make the pestilence cleave unto thee, until he have consumed thee from off the land, 
whither thou goest to possess it. The Lord shall smite thee with a consumption, and with a fever, and with an 
inflammation, and with an extreme burning, and with the sword, and with blasting, and with mildew; and they shall 
pursue thee until thou perish. And thy heaven that is over thy head shall be brass, and the earth that is under 
thee shall be iron. The Lord shall make the rain of thy land powder and dust: from heaven shall it-come down 
upon thee, until thou be destroyed. The Lord shall cause thee to be smitten before thine enemies: thou shalt go 
out one way against them, and flee seven ways before them: and shalt be removed into all the kingdoms of the 

earth.”

If the prophecy of Moses related to the dispersion of the Jews after the Christian era, how very remarkable must it 
appear that he should denounce vengeance against them in case they should disobey those laws which Christ him- 
self came into the world to repeal, and that the Apostles should have attempted to make proselytes of the Jews! It 
may therefore be inferred that neither Moses, nor the other prophets who followed him, contemplated any other 
dispersion than that caused by the Babylonian captivity. It would even seem, from the following passage of the 
twenty-fourth chapter of Jeremiah, that if the prophecy of Moses was not fully accomplished at the period of the 
Babylonian captivity, as far as it related to Zedekiah, the princes of the tribe of Judah, the residue of the Jews that 
were unwilling to quit Babylon, and their brethren who had fled into Egypt to escape from the Chaldean yoke ; it 
was with respect to those who returned to their country and rebuilt Jerusalem. But it was the descendants of the 
latter who crucified Christ, whose dispersion is imputed to that cause, and appealed to as a standing miracle at the 
present day. “ Again the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Thus saith the Lord, the God of Israel; Like 
these good figs, so will I acknowledge them that are carried away captive of Judah, whom I have sent out of this 
place into the land of the Chaldeans for their good. For I will set mine eyes upon them for good, and I will bring 
them again to this land: and I will build them, and not pull them down; and I will plant them, and not pluck them up. 
And I will give them an heart to know me, that I am the Lord: and they shall be my people, and I will be their God: 
for they shall return unto me with their whole heart. And as the evil figs, which cannot he eaten, they are so evil; 
surely thus saith the Lord, So will I give Zedekiah the king of Judah, and his princes, and the residue of Jerusalem, 
that remain in this land, and them that dwell in the land of Egypt: and I will deliver zhem to be removed into all the 
kingdoms of the earth for their hurt, to be a reproach and a proverb, a taunt and a curse, in all places whither I 
shall drive them.” 

It may truly be observed, that what is named an appeal to a standing miracle, whether it proceed from the mouth of 
Christian, Jew, or Mahometan, is generally an argument addressed by the unlearned to the completely ignorant, who 
judge by their senses of the truth of that respecting which their reason cannot assist them in forming any conclusion ; 
and who have not leisure to reflect, or means to know, whether the effects which surprise them may not have been 
brought about by a train of physical and moral causes. There was atime when the colour of the skin of the negro 
was reckoned a standing miracle; the Jews consider the preservation of their Talmud a miracle of that description ; 
and Protestants, and all other seceders from the Church of Rome, declare that the locality of the Holy See upon 
seven hills is a standing miracle, and the fulfilment of prophecy; even the temple of Jerusalem in ruins, has been 
maintained by some learned writers to be astanding miracle. The dispersion of the Jews may either be a miracle or 
may not, since it might have been brought about by the operation of political and religious causes combined. ‘The 
geographical situation of Judea, placed exactly in an angle between Europe, Asia, and Africa, and in the vicinity of 
the sea, favoured a political dispersion after their city and territory had been reduced under the Roman yoke. This 
dispersion, in the first instance compulsory, might afterwards have assumed a voluntary character, when the love of 
gain, for which the Jews have in all ages been distinguished, had taught them the advantages of spreading themselves 
through the various cities of the Roman empire, which comprehended in its vast extent all civilised Africa, Asia 
to the Euphrates, and Europe as far north as Britain, and west as the Ocean. They were then a dispersed 
people, before they felt the rage of Christian persecution, from political causes only: but other causes soon combined 
to disperse them still more, and to entail dispersion and reproach upon their posterity. The Church declared that 
the dispersion of the Jews was a proof of the truth of Christianity, that they were an accursed race, who had cruci- 
fied the Saviour of mankind; and pointing to the prophetical books of the Old Testament, which denounced such a 
judgment against them, called upon the laity to cooperate with prophecy to vex and harass the Jews; who from that 
moment became like the unconscious pieces on a chess-board,—instruments that were moved about by the hands of 
those who played a deep game; whilst the various Christian states, aiding the ecclesiastical with the secular arm, 
permitted and encouraged their several corporations to pass laws and regulations, the object of which was to scatter 
and disperse the Jews, and never to permit them to remain beyond a certain time within the same city or town. 

We have here shown by what natural causes the present dispersed state of the Jews may have been effected. But 
those who prefer miraculous agency to plain and simple probabilities, will, we fear, cut short our reasoning upon the 
subject, in the usual manner, by putting a question with a conditional promise annexed,—that if we can point out to 
them another nation on the globe that has remained for ages a dispersed and separate people like the Jews, they will 
admit that their dispersion is not miraculous. To which we must reply, by promising to do so after they have in- 

NOTES. 385 

formed us of some other nation, who, like the Jews, have been accused by a number of powerful states and empires 
contiguous to their own, of having crucified their God, who—believing that that God had ages before denounced 
his bitterest vengeance against the entire nation of those whom he foresaw would become his murderers, and had 
sentenced them to be dispersed,—resolved to cooperate with prophecy and to carry into execution the will of God, 
External political causes, over which the Jews could exercise no controul, combined in the first instance to make them 
a dispersed people; but religious causes, to which they themselves lent willing aid, contributed, after they became 
dispersed, to keep them a separate people, however identified by local habitation with the subjects and citizens 
of other states. Amongst these may be enumerated the following: The rite of circumcision, and the ridicule 
attached to it immediately after it ceased by the abolition of the old law to be a religious symbol in the opinion of 
Christians: The feast of the passover, and the ceremonies attendant upon it, as described in the twelfth chapter of 
Exodus, which necessarily congregate the Jews together once a year in the cities of the several states in which they 
may reside, and form a kind of national, as well as religious, bond between them: Their strict observance of their 
oral laws respecting marriages, which at the same time that they serve to remedy the evil which their dispersed state 
would seem to entail upon them, viz. diminution of population, strictly forbid them to intermarry with persons ofa 
different faith: The entire spirit of the Mosaic law, which was framed for the express purpose of making and keeping 
the Jews a distinct people; and finally, The crime of which they are accused, of having crucified the Saviour of 
mankind. If due regard be paid to all these natural causes, which in former ages, when Christendom groaned 
itself under despotism and was enveloped in ignorance, operated powerfully on the condition of the Jews, and which 
still continue to affect them in a mitigated degree,—the unreasonableness of the demand of those who are 
determined not to imitate the incredulity of Saint Thomas, and who require that another nation precisely cir- 
cumstanced as the Jews should be pointed out to them before they will cease to believe that their dispersion is a 
miracle, must be apparent to all. 

The time has perhaps arrived when authentic monuments, affording matter upon which to found reasonable dis- 
cussion, will enable men of information to decide upon the certainty or the probability of the Jews having in early 
ages colonized America. The notion prevailed—the conviction was probably felt in Europe at the beginning of the 
sixteenth century, that this was the case: but those who entertained these sentiments, although furnished with the 
necessary proofs, might have been compelled to keep the secret locked up in their breasts, lest they should have 
cast a scandal upon a received religious notion, that the dispersion of the Jews was the fulfilment of Prophecy : since 
how, if it could have been shown that the riches of Peru, or the throne of Mexico, or political ascendancy in any 
part of the New World, had become the lot of the dispersed Jews, would the prophecy seem to be accomplished 
respecting them, where it says that they should borrow and not lend, and that they should ‘be the ¢ai/ and not the 
head? We cannot refrain from inserting in this place a passage from the 424th page of the fifth volume of the 
present work, because the expression outcasts (desechados), as applied by the Mexicans to themselves, is there so 
singularly introduced, and savours so strongly of the tone of complaint in which the Jews, wherever residing and 
however well off in their temporal concerns, have heen accustomed to indulge ever since the fall of their empire. 
“ Nota, hijo, esta palabra, que lo que te tengo dicho te sea espina y aire frio que te aflija, paraque te haga humillar 
y volver en ti. Mira, hijo, que has nacido en tiempo de trabajos y aflicciones, y te ha enviado Dios al mundo en 
tiempo de gran pobreza; mira, que yo soy tu padre; mira, que vida pasamos yo y tu madre, que no somos tenidos 
en nada, ni hay memoria de nosotros; aunque nuestros antepasados fueron grandes y poderosos dejarronnos aquella 
potencia y grandeza? No, por cierto; mira 4 tus parientes y 4 tus afines, que no tienen ser ninguno en la reptiblica 
sino que viven en pobreza y como desechados ; y aunque tu seas noble y generoso de claro linage, conviene que 
tengas delante tus ojos, como has de vivir.” “ Remember the words which I now address to thee, my son; let them 
be a thorn in thy heart and a cold blast to afflict thee, that thou mayest humble thyself and betake thee to inward 
meditations. Consider, my son, that it has been thy lot to be born in a time of trouble and sorrow, and that God 
hast sent thee into the world at a period of extreme poverty. Behold me, who am thy father; see what a life I and 
thy mother lead, and how we are accounted as nothing, and the memory of us has passed away. Although our 
ancestors were powerful and great, have they bequeathed to us their power and greatness? No, truly; cast thine 
eyes upon thy relations and kindred, who fill no public offices, but who live in poverty and as outcasts. Wherefore, 
although thou thyself art noble and illustrious and of famous lineage, it becomes thee to have ever present before thine 
eyes how thou oughtest to live.” The Jews themselves, as it has been elsewhere observed, have entertained a strong

belief that America has been colonized by their race, grounding that belief on what is said in certain chapters of the 
Old Testament of the People of the Isles, (to which isles a Hebrew appellation, derived from a Hebrew word sig- 
nifying the West, has been given; evidently showing that they could not have been Ceylon, or the islands of the 
Indian Archipelago,) as also on many analogies in the laws, rites; customs, and ceremonies of the Indians, but 
more especially in the following passage of the thirteenth chapter of the second apocryphal Book of Esdras: “ And 
whereas thou sawest that he gathered another peaceable multitude unto him; those are the ten tribes which were 
carried away prisoners out of their own land, in the time of Osea the king, whom Salmanasar the king of Assyria 
led away captive, and he carried them over the waters, and so came they into another land. But they took this 
counsel among themselves, that they would leave the multitude of the heathen, and go forth into a further country, 
where never mankind dwelt, that they might there keep their statutes, which they never kept in their own land. And 
they entered into Euphrates by the narrow passages of the river. Wor the Most High then showed signs for them, 
and held still the flood, till they were passed over. For through that country there was a great way to go; namely, 
of a year and a half: and the same region is called Arsareth. Then dwelt they there until the latter time; and now 
when they shall begin to come, the Highest shall stay the springs of the stream again, that they may go through: 
therefore sawest thou the multitude with peace.” Assuming on the best grounds that the apocryphal Books of 
Esdras are not inspired,—since except on good grounds learned men would not have pronounced the judgment which 
they have upon them, the Church would have made greater use of their authority, and time would not have convicted 
any portion of their narrative of falsehood,—we shall not notice the reveries to which the above passage has given 
rise amongst the Rabbis; but shall,as a way of promoting the end of science, which is truth, endeavour to invalidate 
by just objections what ill deserves the name of proof of any kind. It will be at once admitted that if the Apocryphal 
Books of Esdras are not inspired they are a forgery; and that in that case it would be improper to attach more 
weight to arguments drawn from any passages contained in them, favouring the conclusion that the Jews had colo- . 
nized America, than to mere human authority. The following, then, are reasons. for believing those books not to 
be inspired. First, since it is admitted that the truth of the Christian religion, and that Christ was the real Messiah, 
the Son of God, are mainly proved by the prophecies contained in the Old Testament; and a more famous pre- 
diction relating to his advent, with the time clearly defined (which is seldom the case in Hebrew prophecies), is 
contained in the seventh chapter of the Second Book of Esdras, than can be found in any of the other prophetical 
books of the Old Testament, in which he is mentioned by name four hundred years before his birth ;—it must be 
presumed, the Church making such little use of the authority of this book, and none of the Evangelists referring to 
it, it was not considered genuine. ‘The silence of the Evangelists may be accounted for by supposing that it was 
not in existence when they wrote; and the Church’s rejecting it altogether in the beginning, and afterwards pro- 
nouncing it to be merely apocryphal, was probably because the real story of its fabrication was in the beginning 
well known, and became in after-ages forgotten. The dream of Esdras, as recorded in the eleventh chapter of the 
Second Book of Esdras, which is penned so exactly in the style of the prophet Daniel, bears evident allusion to the 
Roman empire, the triumvirate, and the twelve Cesars, as must immediately suggest itself to the mind of even a 
careless reader, on the perusal of the first verse of that chapter: “Then saw I a dream, and, behold, there came up 
from the sea an eagle, which had twelve feathered wings, and three heads.” 

The time when this book was composed may therefore easily be inferred; and the circumstances of the forgery 
coming to the knowledge of the philosopher Porphyry, might have induced him to form the opinion which he did 
of the Book of the prophet Daniel. The following is the prophecy of Esdras relating to the advent of the Messiah : 
“ Behold, the time shall come, that these tokens which I have told thee shall come to pass, and the bride shall appear, 
and she coming forth, shall be seen, that now is withdrawn from the earth. And whosoever is delivered from the 
aforesaid evils, shall see my wonders. For my son Jesus shall be revealed with those that be with him, and they that 
remain shall rejoice within four hundred years. After these years shall my son Christ die, and all men that have life. 
And the world shall be turned into the old silence seven days, like as in the former judgments: so that no man shall 
remain.” Secondly, because time has convicted Esdras of falsehood, when speaking of the age of the world and the 
time which it had still to last, he definitely says in the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth verses of the fourteenth chapter 

- of his Second Book: “ For the world hath lost his youth, and the times begin to wax old. For the world is divided 
into twelve parts, and the ¢en parts of it are gone already, and half of a tenth part: and there remaineth that which 
is after the half of the tenth part.” But how, according to Scripture chronology,—the age in which Esdras lived being 

NOTES. 387 

considered, and the time which has since elapsed,—can the declaration contained in the chapter referred to be consi- 
dered otherwise than as manifestly false? At the same time we cannot omit to notice here an analogous usage 
of the Jews and the Mexicans,—that of dividing time into a certain number of ages; nor refrain from observing that 
the expression of Esdras dike as in the former judgments affords an indication that he at least, and perhaps many 
other Jews in his age, believed, like the Mexicans, that the world had been several times destroyed. Thirdly, 
because if the apocryphal Books of Esdras are to be considered as inspired, the other books of the Apocrypha 
which possess equal claim to inspiration must be considered inspired likewise : but some of these History convicts 
of falsehood, and others are replete with absurdities: for example, the united testimony of all profane historians 
contradicts the account given in the first chapter of the First Book of Maccabees, of Alexander the Great dividing 
during his life-time his kingdom; and nothing can be more absurd than the eighth chapter of the Book of Tobit. 
We trust that the reasons which have been adduced for rejecting as inspired the testimony of Esdras, will induce 
those who may in future discuss so obscure a question in history as the time when, and the passage by which, 
the Jews migrated to America, not to refer to that author in proof of their marvellous journey by dry land through 
the midst of the Euphrates; since it is evidently borrowed from the Mosaic history of the division of the waters of 
the Red Sea, at which it may be observed Esdras elsewhere glances, when he says that God spoke to him out ofa 
bush, as ages before he had done to Moses. We have already alluded to several causes which conspired to spread 
the veil of oblivion over the history of the New World; to which may be added, that the attention of the learned in 
Europe, at the latter end of the fifteenth and the beginning of the sixteenth century, was diverted from dwelling long 
upon any one event, by the magnitude of others, which had either recently happened or which were continually 
occurring around them, such as were the magic effects of the art of printing, and the rescuing from oblivion many 
of the long-lost works of antiquity; the progress of the Reformation, the destruction of the Greek empire, and the 
gigantic and sudden growth of the Ottoman power in Europe; as also the Portuguese discoveries in the Kast. 
Europe in fact knew and cared very little in the sixteenth century about the proceedings of the Spanish . Inquisition 
and the clergy in America. Since, however, nothing will now tend so much as free discussion to throw light upon 
a most mysterious page of history, we shall conclude these remarks by citing,—in anticipation to the objections 
of those who may choose to contend that Jewish antiquities will be profaned by coming in contact with Mexican,— 
a passage from Aristotle’s Treatise on Rhetoric, that contains an argument which furnishes a complete refutation 
to all the reasoning of those who in the present day assert (protesting by so doing against the very principle of 
the Reformation) that it is for the interest of Religion, that the truths which she teaches, and the ordinances of 
Leviticus and Deuteronomy, should be part and parcel of the law of England; which is in other words to deny the 
truth of that approved motto of antiquity, “Magna est veritas et prevalebit ;” to maintain that error is in its nature 
superior to truth, darkness to light, and evil to good; and to attempt to compel the people to acknowledge by 
means of excessive fines and arbitrary imprisonment, that the Jews were the chosen people of God. The Brahmin 
who pronounced Pope’s Universal Prayer to be deserving of being inscribed in golden letters upon a tablet in the 
temple of Vishnou, would probably have judged this sentence of the Stagirite worthy to have been uttered by 
the lips of Brahma, to whom hypocrites were odious, since hypocrisy is here met on its own ground of argument, 
and left altogether without a reply : © Aiew radnOn Kar ra Bedrw ry voc evovlAoyiororepa Kar mOavwrepa, OG aTAws 
etme, (ciot Twy évaytwy.)”—~ That which is true, and by its own nature Jetter, can always, simply speaking, be more

SUPPLEMENTARY REMARKS. 

Four and eight were very favourite numbers among the Mexicans. They fasted every fourth year eight days, in 
memory of the destructions of the world, and every eighth year four days in recollection of the fall of man. But 
besides the invention of fasts and feasts as a method of keeping alive religious reminiscences (in which they strongly 
resembled the Jews), they devised other means. And if we may believe Boturini, the Tultecas actually built towers 

388 NOTES. 

in memory of the tower of Babel,—perhaps he might have said of the temple of Jerusalem. It would also appear 
from a drawing in the collection of M. Dupaix, representing a curious coin obtained by him in the city of Ciudad 
Real, that they recorded in medals the temptation of Eve and the loss of Paradise. Boturini, in the 113th page of 
his Idea of a New General History of North America, says, “The Indians likewise celebrated their said origin in 
ancient songs, and retained such perfect recollection of the Tower of Babel, that they sought to imitate it in various 
monstrous edifices of the New World.” “Celebraron assimismo los Indios su dicho origen en antiguos cantares, y 
tuvieron tan viva la memoria de la Torre de Babel, que la quisieron imitar en America con varios monstruosos 
edificios.” 

Never was there a nation that attached the importance which the Jews did to types and memorials. In their 
persons, on their clothes, in their eating and drinking, in what would be considered the most indifferent actions 
of life, the past and the future were ever present before their eyes. Circumcision reminded them of their 
covenant with God, which nevertheless they were continually breaking; their fringes and the phylacteries which 
they wore on their foreheads, of the obligation imposed upon them to keep his laws; their not eating the sinew 
of the thigh of a sheep or of any other animal, of Jacob’s wrestling and prevailing with God, when the sinew of 
his thigh shrank. Hence it is not too much to suppose, without going so far back as to the era of the tower of 
Babel, that the Jews did on their arrival in America, and on their acquiring wealth and power in that continent, 
determine to commemorate their ancient temple, by building there other temples of great magnificence in imitation 
of it; such as were the temple of Pachacama, (or of the Creator,) situated at the distance of four miles from the city 
of Lima; and the greater temple of Mexico. The foundation stones of the former of these temples are said by some 
Spanish writers to have been soldered together with gold and silver, and the interior was plated with gold; as was also 
the still more famous temple in Cusco, which was likewise dedicated to Pachacama, who, as the priests pretended, deli- 
vered oracular answers to those who came to inquire of him. The Tultecas, who were great artists, and who excelled in 
working in jewellery, an art, the name of which both in French and English is derived from the proper name Jew, 
probably recollected that exclamation of David in the Psalms: “ If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, may my right hand 
forget her cinning.” But David alludes more particularly to the temple: and it is a fact notorious to all, that 
wherever Jews exist, the recollection of their temple and of its destruction is preserved amongst them; and the 
coming of the Messiah, their own restoration, the New Jerusalem, and the rebuilding of the temple, continually occupy 
their thoughts. Do such feelings, we may inquire, proceed from religion or from patriotism? From the latter we 
should be inclined to imagine, kept up and cherished by the Rabbis; for what Christians believe religiously, the 
Jews believe patriotically. 

The retrospect, however, of the city and the holy hill, which their ancestors seem to have founded in the New 
World, and called Churula after Jerusalem, and Tlachihualtepetl (or the Hill of Sacrifice) after Mount Sion, will not be 
so agreeable to the Jews of the present age as the prospect of the ‘sceptre returning to Israel.’ Many customs of the 
Mexicans, strongly savouring of Judaism, besides that of circumcision, have already been noticed: such as their wearing 
fringes fastened to their garments; practising frequent ablutions ; attending constantly public places of worship, to 
which they were summoned by the blowing of horns, as the Jews are to the synagogues; anointing themselves with 
oils; addressing each other with the appellation of Brother * and Sister; their priests allowing their hair to'grow long

But something remains to be said of the external religious marks or signs which both the Jews and the Mexicans 
wore on their faces and bodies. In the thirteenth chapter of Exodus, the following ordinance occurs: “ And it shall 
be for a sign unto thee upon thine hand, and for a memorial between thine eyes, that the Lord’s law may be in thy 
mouth.” As among the Jews the head, as being the nobler part of the body and the seat of reason, was adjudged 
the place most worthy of receiving the memorials of the law,—so among the Mexicans the nose and ears, parts 
corresponding to the eyes and temples of the Jews, were the places destined to receive their religious badges or 
memorials. It is impossible, on viewing the singular symbols attached to the noses of many of the figures 
represented in the Mexican paintings, not to imagine that they were religious memorials, or to refrain from 
instituting a comparison between them and those worn by the Jews, especially as they seem to contain obvious 
Hebrew allusions. The reversed temple or teocalli might have been worn by the Mexicans as a memorial of the 
destruction of the second temple; as the feasts of Purim, and of the dedication of the temple in the days of Judas 
Maccabeus, were instituted by the Jews in ages long after that of Moses,—one of them at least being a civil rather 
than a religious enactment, although religiously observed. The serpent which is sometimes substituted in the place 
of the teocalli, might have alluded to the temptation of Eve; since the fall of man and the loss of Paradise were 
events which the Spaniards found the Mexicans in the sixteenth century still bewailing. But the amphisbcena or 
double-headed serpent probably refers to the two chiefs designated by the common name of Ometeuli, and fre- 
quently represented in the Mexican paintings by the figure of two persons seated back to back, the one holding a

It may very reasonably be doubted whether the Jews of the present day know exactly the nature of the memorial 
which their ancestors wore between their eyes: Some believe it to have been a jewel which was fastened on the top 
of the nose between the eyes. If this opinion be correct, the change of place from the upper to the lower part of 
the nose would be no great deviation from ancient usage or the letter, of the law; since the memorial would still be 
between their eyes, and the greater convenience of fastening it might in the first instance have caused the transition. 
But if it be objected, that it was customary with the Jews to wear a jewel, but that the Mexican symbols were an 
ornament of a different kind, it must be recollected that the expression ‘jewels of gold and jewels of silver’ occurs 
in Scripture without any reference to precious stones; and that the reversed temple worn by the Mexicans was a 
plate of gold or of silver, and consequently a jewel of one of those metals. Coatl, likewise, the primitive mean- 
ing of which in the Mexican language is a serpent, and the secondary signification @ twin, is said by some writers 
to mean a gem also; in the same way as the Latin word gemma is derived from gemellus, the same analogies 
suggesting the use of this metaphor in both languages ; for we associate with a gem the idea of harmony and exact 
correspondence with something else of the same kind. . If, therefore, coaéd signified in the Mexican language both 
a serpent and a gem, and the Mexicans considered it a religious duty to wear a coatl as.a memorial, they might have 
worn indifferently either a plate of gold or a serpent. Other nations have also worn ornaments on the head as 
memorials. Unlike as the Greeks were in every respect to the Jews, whose wisdom appeared even foolishness in 
their eyes, still Thucydides records that the Athenians wore golden grasshoppers in their hair as a memorial of 
their origin, that they were not descended from foreign tribes, but sprung from the earth which they then inhabited. 
This, however, was a civil and not a religious. institution. If memorials. were in use in Greece, they consisted 
of solemn games, instituted in commemoration of departed heroes, whose souls they imagined were enjoying 
happiness in the Elysian Fields, or translated to the society of the immortal gods. A greater calumny has never 
been uttered against the most famous men of antiquity, than that of denying that they believed in the immortality 
of the soul, or in a future state of rewards and punishments. And since the Jews have been very forward in making 
this accusation, we may be permitted to ask them, what gave rise to the bitter hatred which existed between their 

NOTES. 391 

two most famous sects, of Pharisees and Sadducees; and. how, since both appealed to the written word of God 
and to the law.of Moses, could they have interpreted the Scriptures in such a manner as to elicit contrary doctrines 
from them on such a great question as that of the resurrection? If it be true, (and it is a remarkable truth,) that the 
Mosaic code of laws, voluminous as it is, and delivered as it was from Mount Sinai, contains no allusions to a future 
state of rewards and punishments or to an after life, but only promises temporal rewards to virtue; such as long 
life, riches, abundant seasons and rain, victory over the enemy, freedom from pestilence, famine, and invasion ; 
denouncing corresponding evils against the wicked, as may be seen in the twenty-sixth chapter of Leviticus, and in 
almost every chapter of the Pentateuch; the Sadducees might perhaps have opposed the silence of Moses and of 
God in the Pentateuch, to what they considered the inferior authority of the Book of Job, supposing that if such 
important doctrines as those of a future life and of a state of rewards and punishments after death had been taught 
from the chair of Moses, to which all bowed, they would have been repeated over and over again distinctly in the 
Pentateuch, as was the case with other inferior points of the law, and would not have been obscurely alluded to in 
such vague terms as that of ‘showing mercy unto thousands.’ Being Jews likewise, and believing that the covenant 
which they made with God was to be an everlasting covenant, they expected no new dispensation ; and the essence 
ofa covenant being the conditions of which it consists, those conditions being changed, the covenant does not 
remain the same: and hence they might have supposed that the insertion. of any new articles in that which God 
had made with their fathers, would be falsifying the oath which he.sware unto Abraham and unto Isaac and unto 
Jacob, which: did not contemplate the abolition of the old law, and was totally silent on the subject of the immor- 
tality of the soul and a future state of rewards and punishments. And since it is said of Moses, in the last chapter 
of Deuteronomy, “And there arose-not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses, whom the Lord knew face to 
face,” they might have been unwilling to receive from later and inferior prophets, doctrines which had not been 
revealed to him, and therefore have rejected those vital articles which Moses knew that the Kgyptians held most 
sacred. That the ancients fully believed in the immortality of the soul, and in a divine retribution in another world 
for good or evil actions. performed in this, is attested by the surviving works of their greatest philosophers and 
poets. - Aristotle’s hymn, beginning with the words “’Apern woduvpoyOa yever Bporew,” would alone be sufficient to 
vindicate Philosophy from the unfounded charge of atheism; and the odes of Pindar perpetually inculcate the same 
salutary doctrines. Five hundred years before the Christian era, the Greeks assembled at the Olympic games 
listened with rapture to the following verses of the Theban bard, in which he describes the rewards and punishments 
ofa future state. “Ei de pu éyer ru, oidev ro peAAoy, ore Davovrwv pev evOad avtix’ aadapvor Ppeves Towae éricay; va 8 ev

'To return to the consideration of the memorials in use among the Jews.—That which was placed between their 
eyes was not the only one which they wore on their faces. They fastened phylacteries likewise to their temples, 
which were pieces of paper containing written portions of the law. Memorials of this kind the Mexicans, who were 
not acquainted with the art of writing, could not have worn; but the Zemes, or charms, which Peter Martyr says that 
the Indians of Haiti, or the island of Saint Domingo, bound on their foreheads when they went to war, seem to have 
been a remnant of Jewish superstition: nor, when we recollect that the Jews laid the foundation of their cabalistic 
art in Scripture, and used the letters of the divine name, or the tetragram, in their magical incantations, need we feel 
at all surprised that the Hebrew phylacteries should have degenerated into Zemes? Some persons may feel inclined 
to suppose that the Mexicans substituted for those phylacteries pieces of cloth or cotton, which they inserted in their 
ears ; since the former ceasing to contain portions of Scripture, and their use and intention having been probably 
long forgotten, they could have only been looked upon as religious ornaments, which it might have been found more 
convenient to wear in the ears than to fasten to the hair above the temples :—boring the ears for the reception. of 
these ornaments was a religious ceremony amongst the Mexicans and the Peruvians, which Acosta and Torquemada 
both record. The former of these writers, in the twenty-eighth chapter of the Fifth Book of his Natural History of 

392 Ne Ome Ers: 

the Indies, says of the Peruvians: “Hoc mense (Ayamara), qui nobis November est, pro pueris istis quibus postero 
mense aures pertundende erant, necessaria omnia parabantur, et seniores lustrabantur.” “In this month (Ayamara), 
which is November with us, every thing necessary was prepared for those boys whose ears were to be bored in the 
following month, and the elders purified themselves, and other similar preparations were made.” And Torquemada, in 
the thirtieth chapter of the Tenth Book of the Indian Monarchy, describes the Mexican ceremony which took place 
on the last festival of their year, which was named that of Xiuhtecutli*; “ Este mismo dia luego en riyendo el alva, 
comencaban 4 agugerar las orejas 4 los nifios, y los becos de la boca, y hechavanles en las cabecas un casco de plumas 
de papagaio pegado con ocogotl, que es resina de pino, dando 4 todos los nifios y niflas sus padrinos y madrinas, 
para que los instruiesen y ensefiasen en las ceremonias y servicio de este y de todos los otros dioeses.” “ On this same 
day when morning dawned, they began to pierce the ears and the lips of the boys, and to put upon their heads 
a plume of parrots’ feathers glued together with ococotl, which is resin of the pine, giving to all the boys and girls 
their own godfathers and godmothers, in order that they might teach and instruct them in the ceremonies and services 
of this and of all the other gods.” 

This accordance in the practice of an arbitrary rite in the case of two nations, so remote from each other and so 
different as were the Mexicans and the Peruvians, might lead us to expect a correspondence in some of their other 
rites and ceremonies: and since Boturini informs us that he discovered one of those knotted cords called by the 
Peruvians Quipus, and by the Mexicans Nepohualtzitzin, in the possession of a principal Indian of the province 
of Tlaxcallan (although he adds, “ Estaba tan carcomido de Ja antiguedad, que solo me pudo instruir de que los huvo, 
aunque escasos.” (“It was so consumed by age, that it only served to convince me that they had been used, 
although sparingly”),—it would appear equally probable that paintings resembling those of the Mexicans, had 
formerly existed in Peru, although consigned to perpetual oblivion by the prudence of those who thought that 
such documents had better never be brought to light. The same reason may be assigned for Kurope after the 
lapse of three centuries, being, before the publication of the American Monuments of Baron de Humboldt, ignorant 
whether the soil of the New World possessed any remarkable monuments of antiquity. Garcia citing Laet, 
and likewise on his own authority, says that paintings were used in Peru, but that the style of their execution 
was rude; which he seems to have inferred from the inspection of some confessional paintings of the Peruvians. 
We have had an opportunity of seeing some specimens of a similar nature, painted by the Mexicans after their 
conversion to Christianity, exceedingly rude, in which hardly a trace of the old style of Mexican painting can 
be discerned: and the same may have been the case with the later Peruvian paintings, from which it would be 
wrong to form an estimate of the degree of excellence which the art of painting had attained in the time of the 
Ingas; since it is probable, that, identified with the fables of a false religion, it was speedily consigned with them 
to oblivion. It is certainly very extraordinary to find from the “Oronoco Illustrado” of Gumilla, and Coreat’s 
Voyages to the West Indies, that Indian nations so remote from each other as those of the Oronoco and the tribes 
who lived on the confines of Peru on the banks of the La Plata, as well as the Chalchaques, a people situated 
between Peru and Tucuman, all used circumcision, and strictly abstained from the flesh of swine. Captain Cook 
also discovered that circumcision had extended itself to the Islands of the South Sea. How, to use the words of 
Gumilla, are these moral phenomena to be explained? That the Jews were always eager to make proselytes, and, 
like Saint Paul before he became a Christian, would not hesitate to employ force as well as persuasion to effect 
conversion, is a notorious fact; and circumcision being amongst them, what baptism is with Christians, a means of 
grace, and the rite by which in fact a heathen was admitted to be a Jew-, it is highly probable that their zeal, or

From an examination of some of the Mexican paintings, it would appear that circumcision amongst the Indians was

The Mexicans, besides using this rite, marked the breasts and arms of their children on the festival of Toxcatl with 
another sign or token, which Torquemada compares, in the following passage of the sixteenth chapter of the tenth 
book of his Indian Monarchy, with the analogous ceremony of marking the sign of the cross upon the breasts and 
the foreheads of the faithful amongst Christians with the holy oil or chrism: “It is no slight thing to note, that on 
this day the priests made a scar on the breasts and stomachs of all the male and female children, and on the wrists 
and fleshy parts of the arms of others, imprinting them as it were with the iron and mark of the Devil, to whose 
service they offered them, in order that they might be known as his, in the same way as God commands that those of 
his fold should be anointed on their breasts with the holy oil, and on their foreheads with the most blessed cross of his 
passion and death; since this is the sign with which God is accustomed to mark those who are his, as circumcision 
was formerly amongst his ancient people, which is now the cross and the holy chrism. Hence Saint John bade the 
persecutors and murderers desist from their work of slaughter until the people of God and his servants were marked 
on their foreheads, since this is a kind of sign by which he distinguishes those who are his, as the owners of cattle 
mark their herds with some particular print or sign.” Whether the Indians of the Island of Saint Domingo and of 
Cuba,—whose language is said to have been half Hebrew, and who in many of their customs nearly resembled the 
Jews,—practised the same rites as those in use amongst the Indians of the continent, it would be difficult to say; 
but that they possessed traditions in common with them, evidently derived from a Hebrew source, is plain from the 
following relation of Torquemada, which we cannot refrain from inserting here in the original Spanish: “ Verdad 
es que los de los Indios de la Isla de Cuba dicen que tuvieron conocimiento que havia sido el cielo y las otras cosas 
criadas ; y decian que por tres personas, y que la una vino por tal parte, y las otras dos de otras; y que tuvieron 
gran noticia del diluvio, y que se havia perdido el mundo por mucha agua; y decian los viejos de mas de setenta y 
ochenta afios, luego al principio que entraron los nuestros en equella isla, que un viejo sabiendo que havia de venir 
el diluvio, hico una grande nao, y se metidé en ella con su casa y muchos animales, y que embié un cuervo, y no 
bolvié por comer de los cuerpos muertos, y que despues embiéd una paloma, la qual bolvié cantando, y trajo una 
rama con hoja que parecia hobo, pero que no era hobo; el qual salié del navio, y hico vino de las parras monteses, y 
se embriagé; y teniendo dos hijos, el uno se rid y dijo al otro, Hechemonos con 1; pero que el otro le rifio, y cubrié 
al padre; el qual despues de dormido el vino, y sabida la desverguenca de el hijo, le maldijo ; y que al otro did 
bendiciones, y que de aquel havian procedido los Indios de estas tierras ; y que por esto no tenian saios ni capas ; 
pero que los Castellanos procedian del otro, por lo qual andaban vestidos, y tenian cavallos. Lo sobredicho refirié 
un Indio viejo de mas de setenta afios 4 Gabriel de Cabrera; porque un dia rifiendo con el, y llamandole perro, 
respondié que por qué le refiia, y Ilamaba perro, pues todos eran hermanos? Vosotros, le dijo, no procedeis de un 
hijo de aquel que hico la nao grande para salvarse del agua, y nosotros del otro? Y lo mismo refirié el mismo 
Indio delante de muchos Castellanos, haviendolo publicado su amo. Esto dijo aquel Indio; y parece atinar con lo 
que la Sagrada Escritura dice de Noe, y de sus hijos ; aunque ierra en decir que no fueron mas de dos; y si por lo 
dicho quisiere alguno arguirme que estos son descendientes de Can, no se lo concedo ; pero tampoco se lo negaria, 
quando quisiese afirmarlo, por lo que dejamos dicho ; aunque caso tan dudoso y obscuro debemos remitirlo a Dios, 
que es claridad de todas las cosas y las sabe como ellas son, y no cabe duda en su saber infinito.” Monarquia

“Tt is true that the Indians of the Island of Cuba say that they knew that the heaven and other things had been 
created ; and they affirm by ¢hree persons, one of whom came from such a part, and the other two from other parts ; 
that they were perfectly informed also of the deluge, and that the world had been destroyed by a quantity of water. 
The old men above seventy and eighty years of age reported, when first our countrymen settled in that island, that 
an old man knowing that the deluge was about to happen, built a large ship, in which he embarked with his house- 
hold and many animals, and that he dispatched from thence a crow, which did not return, staying to prey upon the 
dead carcases ; and that he afterwards sent a dove, which came back cooing, bringing a leafy branch which resembled 
a hop, although not one: on which he quitted the ship, and made wine of mountain grapes and became drunk; and

having two sons, one of them laughed, and said to the other, Turn him into jest; but the other reproved him, and 
covered his father ; who having slept off the effects of the wine, and knowing the impudence of his son, cursed him, and 
pronounced a blessing on the other: and that from the former of these the Indians of those countries were descended, 
who on that account were without coats and cloaks: but that the Spaniards proceeded from the other, and were 
therefore well apparelled and rode horses. The above story was told by an old Indian more than seventy years of 
age to Gabriel de Cabrera; who quarrellmg with him on a certain day, and calling him a dog, he asked him why 
he quarrelled with him and named him a dog, since they were all brothers? You, (says he to him,) do you not 
descend from the one son of him who built the large ship to escape from the water, and we from the other? And the 
same story was told by the same Indian before many Spaniards, his master having spread it abroad. This was the 
account given by that Indian: and it seems to allude to that which the Holy Scripture says of Noah and his sons; 
although he errs in saying that the sons were only two: should any one hence endeavour to persuade me that the 
Indians are the descendants of Cham, I do not admit it, but neither will I deny it, should they choose to affirm it 
on the grounds of what we have just stated; although we ought to leave a matter, so obscure and doubtful, to God, 
who is the light of all things, and understands their nature and essence, and to whose infinite’ wisdom the 
portion of doubt does not fall.” This curious relation Torquemada judges to be so well authenticated, that 
he not only gives it a place in his History, but allows that it may serve as a basis on which to reason respecting the 
origin of the Americans ; although he at the same time professes that he will not be bound by the conclusions which 
others might be tempted to draw from it. The tradition of the inhabitants of Cuba certainly deserves to be com- 
pared with those of the people of Michuacan and Nicaragua, who also approximated to the Mosaic history in 
their accounts of the Deluge; although the former of the last-mentioned nations believed that it was the colibri, or 
the humming-bird, and not the dove, that returned with the branch of the tree. The Indians of Chili, according to 
Rosales, had likewise a tradition of the Deluge: but he observes, that shells and other fossil remains discovered in 
abundance on their highest ranges of mountains, might have suggested that idea to them. And it cannot be denied 
that even the sagacity of savages might have arrived at this conclusion, totally unaided by divine inspiration: nor 
would it have exceeded their moral comprehension to believe that such a convulsion was caused by the sins of 
mankind provoking God to vengeance. On the contrary, they would have been more inclined to attribute such an 
event to that, than to any other cause; for savages and ignorant and superstitious nations are frequently disposed, 
in proportion as calamities are great, which befall numbers of persons or single individuals, to attribute them to a 
particular and signal divine judgment inflicted upon them for their sins: although such a mode of reasoning is 
not more to be despised for its absurdity than condemned for its injustice, since it tends to deprive misfortune of 
all sympathy, and to involve innocence and guilt ina common mass. That the Indians of Chili;—reading in the 
volume of Nature that their highest mountains had been submerged in the ocean, and the bones of animals mixed 
with shells testifying to them that that inundation had been accompanied with a destruction of animal life,—should 
not have suppose” that such an accident might have occurred in the order of the universe, is likely enough; as 
likewise that their piaques, or Priests—who pretended to be in the secrets of Heaven, and to have rain, thunder, and 
good and bad seasons at their command,—should have sought, by appealing to this past judgment, to render their 
own denunciations of the future more probable, and to maintain by these means their ascendancy over the deluded 
minds of the people. But, as Rosales observes, this argument alone is not sufficient to prove that Saint Thomas, or 
any other Apostle, had preached the Gospel in Chili. It is a very remarkable fact, that the curse which Noah 
in the twenty-fifth verse of the ninth chapter of Genesis pronounces against the posterity of his son Ham or Cham, 
to which the traditions of the Island of Cuba evidently referred,—*“ Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall 
he be unto his brethren;” by which expression, brethren, is meant mankind in general, and not the Jews in 
particular; for the descendants of the three sons of Noah comprise all mankind,—justified slavery in the eyes of 
the early Christians, and of some of the Fathers of the Church; which was also sanctioned by the Mosaic laws, 
and is not forbidden in the New Testament, except in the case of Christians, who were not permitted to have other 
Christians for their slaves; -although by the feudal laws, the ascripti gleba, or vassals of the soil, were in a 
much worse situation than the domestic slaves amongst the Greeks. It cannot be denied that that is the most 
goading system of slavery where the law, not content with vesting in the owner a right to the industry and personal 
labour of his slave, impowers him likewise to use cruel treatment towards him, and does not protect his honour 
and civil rights by the same penal enactments and provisions as those of the other members of the community,—as 

NOTES. 395 

in the case of the betrothed female slave amongst the Jews, the violation of whose faith was only to be punished 
with scourging, whilst the other party seems to have escaped with impunity, for the reason alleged in the twentieth 
verse of the nineteenth chapter of Leviticus, “because she was not free.” A great distinction is made, in the code of 
laws professedly delivered by God himself from Mount Sinai to Moses, between slaves and those who were free, and 
between Hebrew slaves and such as were bought by the Jews from other nations. It is ordained in the twenty-first 
chapter of Exodus, that “if'a man smite his servant, or his maid with a rod, and he die under his hand, he shall be 
surely punished. Notwithstanding, if he continue a day or two he shall not be punished, for he as his money.” It 
would little avail a West Indian planter of the present day, if his slave died on the third day from a beating which 
he had inflicted upon him on the first, to urge this obsolete Hebrew law, even in palliation of the crime of murder, 
much less to excuse it. But we must recollect what God says by the mouth of the prophet Ezekiel, in the twentieth 
chapter of his Book of Prophecies, in reference probably to this as well as to many other laws of the Pentateuch : 
“Wherefore I gave them also statutes that were not good, and judgments whereby they should not live.” The Ten 
Commandments are but a small portion of the laws which Moses received from God in the various conferences 
which he from time to time held with him; but the greater part of the others are inapplicable to modern times, as 
may be proved from their not being found in the statute books of England, France, and the other enlightened states 
of Europe, or from their having been expunged from them*. It is said in the eighteenth and nineteenth verses of 
the thirty-fourth chapter of Jeremiah, that “the princes of Judah, the princes of Jerusalem, the eunuchs, and the 
priests, made a covenant before God when they passed between the parts of the calf which they cut in twain.” The 
eunuchs, who it is singular should be mentioned as parties to this covenant, were slaves whom the Jewish princes 
and nobles, in the true spirit of Oriental jealousy, retained in great numbers in their houses and palaces. And it is 
to be supposed, as well from their being included in the covenant as from their being kept by the Jews, that the silence 
of Moses sanctioned a barbarous custom amongst the owners of slaves, which Acosta observes was also prevalent in 
Peru. The modern opposers of slavery (and we trust that their laudable efforts will be crowned with the fullest 
success) will hardly believe that-its ancient advocates justified it on the authority of the Scriptures, reasoning in the 
following manner, according to Torquemada: “God created man free, and not only free, but possessing lordship: for 
as soon as he had created him, he gave him the entire dominion over every thing ; and made him lord over the birds 
which fly in the air, and the fish of the sea, andthe beasts ofthe earth. He created him in his own image and like- 
ness, and did not ordain that one man should be lord over another, which was the reason why the first righteous men 
were shepherds, and not kings, that in this manner we might understand the order of nature, and the evil which resulted 
from sin. The name of servant is not found in Holy Scripture, until it is related in Genesis, that righteous Noah 
having drunk of the wine of the vine which he had planted, fell on the ground drunk, with his body shamefully exposed. 
Cham, his son, saw him, and called his two other brothers that they might likewise see their father and turn him into 
jest ; but the two good sons, impressed more strongly with feelings of propriety, approached him with their faces 
turned backwards, and covered him. Noah afterwards recovering from his intoxication, and knowing the turpitude 
of his bad son, pronounced a malediction against Canaan, the son of Cham, and said, ‘Cursed be Canaan ; let him 
be a servant to his brethren.’ These words afford grounds for the conclusion, that captivity and servitude were the 
punishment of sin; since this curse which the holy patriarch uttered, was not to avenge himself of an injury, but a 
prophecy, and a denunciation of what was to befall his posterity, the descendants of Cham; and St. Chrysostom 
remarks, as if wondering that a brother born of one womb, and the son of the same mother, became, on account 
of the sin which he committed against his father, the slave (esc/avo) of his brother; since before this fault and 
transgression, servitude and slavery did not exist, for, each possessing enough to satisfy his own wants, no one 
thought of deriving profit from the service of another. Saint Augustin likewise says, that God, on account of his 
having created man in his own image, did not grant him dominion over men, but only over irrational animals ; the

as was the cause in which it originated, it is not too much to say, that dire have been its consequences in destroying 
the peace and the happiness of mankind. It has been the scourge of two vast continents, Africa and America, and 
of the populous islands of the Western Atlantic sea; it has retarded the progress of civilization: and if a tree is 
to be judged of by its fruit, the vine planted by Noah should be execrated by every friend of the human race. In 
the breast of that holy patriarch it is true that it only awoke the hilarity of intemperance, and in that of another 
the fire of unlawful lust; but it has steeled the hearts and the consciences of succeeding generations of mankind ; 
and, far more cruel than the sword of Agag, it has rendered millions of mothers childless amongst women. The 
Jews themselves, if they had wished to stigmatize and to brand with ignominy all the enemies of their tribe, could 
not have invented a fable more proper for the purpose than what we learn from Moses in the Pentateuch to be 
matter of real history. If for a moment we consider who the near and remote enemies of the Jews were, we shall 
find that the lineage of all of them may be traced up to one or other of the cursed descendants of Cham, or to Lot 
and his two daughters. The Moabites and the Ammonites were the bitterest enemies of the Jews; they were the 
incestuous progeny of Lot. The Canaanites, the dispossessed inhabitants of the land of Canaan, who were to he 
utterly destroyed, were the immediate descendants of Canaan the fourth son of Cham, who is said to have first told 
his father of the intoxication and nakedness of Noah. Under this general name were comprehended many different 
nations, which the Scripture declares to have been equally descended from Canaan, of which the principal were the 
Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgasites, the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites, the Arvadites, the Hittites, and the 
Sidonians, or Phoenicians, whose ancestor was Sidon, the e/dest son of Canaan ; whose posterity, notwithstanding the 
curse pronounced against him by his grandfather, laid the foundation of the future glories of Carthage, the rival in 
after ages of imperial Rome. The friendship which existed between Hiram king of Tyre and Solomon, may 
perhaps be alleged as a proof that the Sidonians were not reckoned by the Jews amongst the number of their 
enemies: but they being de facto the possessors of a territory which de jure belonged to the seed of Abraham, and 
addicted to the same idolatries as the other inhabitants of the land of Canaan, were equally included by Moses in 
the sentence of utter destruction; and could not, except in direct disobedience to the word of God and by the basest 
duplicity, have been treated by the Jews as friends and allies: since, professing friendship to the Tyrians, the issue of 
the first-born of Canaan, against whom the curse of Noah was chzefly directed, could only have been smiling to 
deceive those whom they knew that they had irrevocably sworn to destroy. If the judgment pronounced by Moses 
against the Pheenicians was never executed by the Jews, the only reason was, that they were too formidable a people 
for them to attack ; although it is probable that not without repining they beheld themselves masters of only a 
comparatively small territory in Palestine, whilst their origznal grant comprehended all the country lying between 
Egypt and the great river Euphrates, although on that side the name “horrendum late” of the kings of Babylon 
was an effectual barrier to their ambition. The remaining enemies of the Jews, although with the exception of the 
Philistines in a secondary degree so, were the Assyrians or Babylonians, the Syrians, the Egyptians, the Philistines, 
and the Edomites. All these nations were bitterly hated by them; and, although their nearest neighbours, were the 
constant theme of the denunciations of their prophets; and the genealogies of all, one excepted, are traced up in 
Scripture to Cham. The Assyrians were descended in the line of Nimrod from Cush the eldest son of Cham, as 
were also the Syrians ; the Egyptians were the posterity of Mizraim his second son, and likewise the Philistines ; 
but the Edomites, who are coupled in the Psalms with the Moabites, where David speaking in the name of God in 
the first person, as was usual with the Jewish prophets, says, “Moab is my wash-pot, over Edom will I cast out my 
shoe,” were of the seed of Abraham and of the lineage of Shem ; although the Scripture has likewise affixed a stain 
on their nativity, by declaring them to be of the outcast race of Esau, who sold his birthright to his brother Jacob 
for a mess of pottage; Edom the eldest son of Esau, and by the mother’s side a descendant from Cham, being 
their progenitor. It is singular that some of the early Spanish writers who were much more inclined to believe 
that the Indians were descended from the Jews than from the Canaanites, should have imagined that Yucatan was 

* This should silence the disputations of geologists about extinct species of animals.

named after Joktan the brother of Peleg, and the son of Heber the ancestor of the Hebrews. It has been already 
observed that the Egyptians, the ancient task-masters of the children of Israel, were the offspring of Mizraim the 
son of Cham, whose slaves the Hebrews were for more than three hundred years; the curse pronounced by Noah 
being for that long period of time reversed, and the enslavers in their turn the enslaved, the posterity of Shem 
becoming in fact the servants of the servants of Cham. Later prophecies, however, doomed Egypt to be the basest 
of kingdoms, which (according to the interpretation which many commentators put on Scripture) arts, science, 
and naval and military power are never again to adorn: but modern events clearly show that these prophecies are 
not to be understood in the sense which commentators choose to assign to them. Reasoning by analogy fails us 
in the case of Egypt; or we should say, that if the sceptre had not departed from Judah when Shiloh came, because 
Herod the Tetrarch governed in Judea as viceroy of the Cesars,—neither is it wanting in Egypt now that, under the 
Sultan, Mahomet~Pacha rules that fertile region, which promises again to be the centre of arts, industry, and civili- 
zation, and which (let the part which its fleet took at the battle of Navarin decide) begins to resume a respectable 
rank amongst nations. If it may appear surprising to some that so remote a cause as the curse pronounced by Noah 
against his son Cham should have operated by itself so powerfully in Spain and Portugal as to have laid the foundation 
of the slave-trade ; turning our attention nearer home, we shall find that about the same period another dead letter 
text of the Pentateuch produced a train of consequences, not so important, because neither so lasting nor so pro- 
ductive of human misery as the former, but which, nevertheless, afforded the Spanish king a pretext for sending the 
Armada against England, threatening to inundate Europe with blood ; and which, if queen Elizabeth had had children, 
would have revived feuds as deadly as those of the rival houses of York and Lancaster, and caused Britain to weep 
as bitterly for a verse in the Old Testament, as she has made Ireland rue others contained in the New. Who 
for a moment could have supposed that a law that was made only for the Jews,—namely, that brothers should 
marry brothers’ widows,—and which no other nation ever adopted, would have accelerated the progress of the Refor- 
mation, altered the succession to the English crown, nearly plunged the country into civil war, and cost a queen of 
Scotland and of France her head. There is not the least difficulty im tracing all these effects to this main, though 
remote cause. If Moses had not commanded, and Christ had decidedly condemned such marriages when the Sad- 
ducees came to him, tempting him, as was their custom, to induce him to contravene some part of the Mosaic law, 
and thereby to draw on himself the indignation of the people, Julius the Second would not have granted a dispen- 
sation to Henry the Eighth to marry Catharine of Arragon; nor would Ferdinand of Spain have given his consent, 
or Henry the Seventh have solicited it. But the Pope was persuaded that where morals and not ritual observances 
were in question, the doctrines of the New Testament could not zmpugn those contained in the Old*: for although 
in the case of divorces, when the Pharisees tempted Christ with the Mosaic law, which permitted a man to divorce 
his wife for the most trivial causes and to marry again, his reply was, that because of the hardness of their hearts 
they were permitted to do so, although it was not so in the beginning: still the case of marriages of brothers- and 
sisters-in-law was very different ; since the Mosaic law not only permitted but positively commanded such marriages; 
and to refrain from them was to transgress the express will of God, as declared by the mouth of Moses his prophet. 
When the Sadducees, therefore, who denied the doctrine of the resurrection, appealed to the laws of Moses to disprove 
it; they argued on the assumption that if souls were immortal, the laws of Moses could not be just, and therefore 
could not be from God; for that it would have been unjust in Moses to have deprived the first husband at the resur- 
rection of his wife, by compelling her to invalidate her former by a later contract. The reply of Christ to the Sadducees 
is remarkable, not so much on account of the assurance which he gives them that marriages do not take place in a 
future state, as because he omits the opportunity which presented itself of expressing any opinion on these Hebrew 
marriages ; although on another occasion he censured the frequent divorces of the Jews, which the law of Moses 
authorized. And therefore it is the more astonishing that those divines, who on account of their denying the supre- 
macy of the Pope have been named the champions of the Reformation, should have shared Henry’s antipathy to 
one part of the Mosaic law which had not been condemned by Christ, and yet have retained a strong predilection for 
another which he had formally disapproved: for although they protested against the king’s marriage, they did not

protest against his numerous divorces ; nor did a conscientious scruple arise in their minds, as to whether the unfortu- 
nate women whom he beheaded during the life-time of Catharine of Arragon could be really guilty of the crime of 
adultery; or in other words, whether they were in point of law his wives. Assuredly if such marriages as are here alluded 
to had been instituted amongst any other nation than the Jews, or by any other legislator than Moses, they would 
have incurred lasting infamy ; and later ages would not have hesitated to have imputed them to the sordid avarice of 
the people amongst whom they were encouraged, who recurred to such means to secure to families the dowry which 
the marriage of the widow into another family would have deprived them of. Even amongst the Jews, (if we may be 
permitted to attempt to penetrate the-designs of Moses,) the securing the dowry and inheritance of the widow to the 
family of her deceased husband,—which could only be done by a compulsory law, obliging her to marry his next brother, 
was as much the object of the Hebrew legislator, as the other plea of raising up seed to the elder brother in Israel : 
for the Jewish laws, which aimed by every possible means at increase of population,—unlike those of most other 
nations, which had a greater regard for female delicacy,—not only sanctioned but commanded, under the penalty of 
legal disgrace, reiterated marriages to widows. And hence we have an example in the New Testament of a woman who 
married seven brothers in succession and survived them all, who if a Roman matron had expostulated with her on 
her conduct, would probably have scornfully demanded of her, “Id cinerem, aut manes, credis curare sepultos 2?”—so 
different are the manners and ways of thinking of different countries, and so repugnant were the morals of the Jews 
to those of the Romans and the Greeks ! It is easy to see the distinction which Moses makes between the sanction 
which he gave to divorces, and the obligation which he imposed on brothers to marry brothers’ widows: but if 
further proof be wanting to show that the latter law was not only permissive but imperative, it is afforded in the 
example of divine punishment which Scripture holds out to the disobedient, in the history of Judah and his three 
sons, Kr, Onan, and Shelah. This history is contained in the thirty-eighth chapter of Genesis ; and two things are 
very remarkable in it: The first is, that although special inspiration had not informed the more ancient patriarchs 
that they ought not to marry their own sisters, it had revealed to them the law of circumcision, and of raising up 
seed to an elder brother, which four hundred years later were again to be ratified amidst thunder and lightning from 
Mount Sinai; since, except on this supposition, Judah’s command to Onan in the eighth verse of the same chapter, 
and his apology for Tamar in the twenty-sixth verse, “She hath been more righteous than I,” (after having previously 
ordered her to be brought forth and burnt,) would be quite inexplicable, or would involve that patriarch by his own 
confession in a crime somewhat analogous to that which drew down his father’s curse on his eldest brother Reuben. 
The other is, that Saint Matthew in the first chapter of his Gospel traces up the genealogy of the Messiah, (who, 
according to ancient prophecy, was to be of the tribe of Judah,) to Judah and Tamar through Phares, which doubtless 
involves a mystery which has not been suffered to pass unheeded by the ancient commentators on Scripture; as 
here it was not the younger brother, but the father himself, who raised up seed to his eldest son, and preserved his 
own name in Israel. Since the reflux of religious opinions is generally as violent as their resistless tide, and it has 
become the fashion of modern times to condemn slavery chiefly on Christian grounds, we fear that, reprobating in 
the highest degree such an odious traffic with our fellow-creatures, we shall offend a class of persons whose zeal 
much exceeds their knowledge, by candidly avowing that the Old Testament history, the Mosaic law, the customs of 
the Jews, and the curse pronounced by Noah against Cham, appear to give a strong sanction to it; neither would 
it be very difficult to show, if the occasion required, by appealing to the experience of past ages, and opposing the 
opinions of many centuries to those of the present day, that our ancestors interpreted Scripture, on this and many 
other important points, in amanner very different from ourselves, and deduced from it doctrines in every sense most 
opposed to ours. It was certainly not the publication of a book like Doctor Sepulveda’s in justification of slavery, 
but a decree of the Emperor Charles the Fifth,—who had taken the advice of all the learned in the land, and consulted 
_ the Spanish universities, whose fame in theology was in that age great,—that doomed the inhabitants of the islands 
and continent of America to slavery. This decree was sanctioned-by the Council of the Indies ; anda more solemn 
act could not have emanated from higher constituted authorities. If it was reversed not many years afterwards, this 
was in consequence of the evils which followed, but was no condemnation of a conceded point in divinity and law. 
Those who may wish to learn more of the opinions of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries on the subject of slavery, 
can consult the writings of Las Casas and of Doctor Sepulveda, who although the supporters of contrary systems, at 
least as far as American slavery was concerned, pretended equally to ground their conflicting reasonings on Scripture. 
Doctor Sepulveda’s work has been termed by later authors a bloody book; but Las Casas’s short and pathetic nar-
