* Las Casas has sometimes been called a fanatic; but were it even the case, how much more desirable would it be if modern religious 
fanaticism flowed in a similar channel. His fanaticism was merely an ardent desire to oppose the dignity of his sacerdotal character, his 
acknowledged talents and learning, and the mildness of old age, to brutal oppression and injustice. How different was zeal like his from that 
of Mr. Irving’s, or some other popular preachers of the present day, to whom a crowded audience flocks, scarcely knowing why, except 
that they expect to hear new truths delivered in a new manner. We fear, however, that the speech of Festus to Paul would not have been 
addressed with much propriety to them. But nothing appears more intolerable than their wilful ignorance of modern history, or at least 
open defiance to the principles laid down at the Reformation ; since, although belonging themselves to no ostensible church, and de- 
nying many of the Articles of the Church of England, they still would make the soil of Britain that of persecution. Neither do they 
pay the slightest regard to the Christian precept of—not speaking evil of dignities ; but, as it were in mockery of Saint Jude, pour forth 
unceasing railing accusations against him whose majestic station is quite forgotten by them, because they know that his power is remote, 
and that they are protected by the laws of another state. The principle, that any church has a right to force the conscience, or to impose 
silence on the tongues or pens of the lowest members of the community, should be rejected; but this right, when assumed by new and 
schismatic churches, becomes odious in the extreme, and differs as much from the exercise of the former, as the usurping ruffian from the 
crowned king. Itis impossible that any one can read and meditate on the history of the Protestant Reformation without having his mind 
assailed by such a conviction. But if we are inclined to recoil with horror from flames lit up by Orthodox persecution, with what un- 
qualified disgust must we turn from the page of history that records the death of the unfortunate Servetus,—whilst imagination pictures to 
us the gloomy founder of Calvinism seated in the shape of an ill-omened vulture upon a neighbouring rock, and contemplating with 
steady eye the expiring fires of a pile that might well have drawn down the deadliest bolt of Almighty wrath. Servetus may be considered, 
in reference to Calvin and the pernicious tenets of his sect, to have “ vindicated the ways of God to man;” for how shortsighted must 
those of that school be, who do not perceive that if their doctrines of absolute predestination are inconsistent with’ the notion of man’s 
being an agent possessed of free will,.all moral evil must be referred to God! who would afterwards (far be from us the thought) have to 
be viewed in the light of an unjust and inexorable judge, who would condemn those to eternal punishment who were not able to avoid the 
commission of sin, because their will was under the control of a necessity caused by himself. That poet, whom Lord Byron pronounces to 
be the greatest in our language, in the beautiful line 

“« Who binding nature fast in fate left free the human will,” 

destroys, by making a just distinction between man and inanimate nature, the entire of Calvin’s clumsy and. sophistical web.

sino de las dichas en el parrafo pasado, que estos Indios, y todos los que en otras Regiones son de color baco, 
seran Descendientes de aquellos Hijos de Can, t de alguno de sus Descendientes ; y siendo esto asi, como no siguen 
estas Gentes 4 sus antepasados en las costumbres, en las fuercas, y facciones, y color ?” 

Nore II. 

AMERICAN TRADITIONS WHICH APPEAR TO BE DERIVED FROM A HEBREW SOURCE. 

THE present note (which is referred to in the preceding,) contains some American traditions, evidently derived from 
the Old Testament, and tending to prove that the Indians were at least acquainted with that portion of it designated 
the Pentateuch. It is impossible on reading what Mexican Mythology records of the war in heaven, and of the fall 
of Zontemoque and the other rebellious spirits; of the creation of light by the word of Tonacatecutli, and of the 
division of the waters ; of the sin of Yztlacoliuhqui, and his blindness and nakedness; of the temptation of Suchi- 
quecal, and her disobedience in gathering roses from a tree, and the consequent misery and disgrace of herself and 
all her posterity,—not to recognise Scriptural analogies. But the Mexican tradition of the Deluge is that which bears 
the most unequivocal marks of having been derived from a Hebrew source. This tradition records that a few 
persons escaped in the Ahuehuete, or ark of fir, when the earth was swallowed up by a Deluge, the chief of whom 
was named Patecatle or Cipaquetona ; that he invented the art of making wine; that Xelua, one of his descendants, 
or at least one of those who had escaped with him in the ark, was present at the building of a high tower, which the 
succeeding generation constructed with a view of escaping from the deluge should it again occur ; that Tonacatecutli, 
incensed at their presumption, destroyed the tower with lightning, confounded their language, and dispersed them ; 
and that Xelua led a colony to the New World. This age, which was the first of the Mexican ages, and named by 

(5x) 

402 NOTES. 

them Atonatiuh, or the age of water, closely bordered upon that of the Tzocuillicxeque, or age of giants; and it will 
be recollected that the age of the Flood in Scripture was that of giants also. The fact of the Mexicans recording» 
both in their paintings and songs, the deluge, the building of the Tower of Babel, the confusion of tongues, 
and the dispersion of tribes, being generally admitted by the early Spanish writers on America, it is almost 
unnecessary to refer to the authority of any particular writer to prove what no one will deny. Since Gomara, 
however, in his History of the Indies, describing the conference of Nicaragua with Gil Gonealez and the ecclesi- 
astics, introduces that chief as putting a variety of questions to the Spaniards; the first of which was, whether they 
were acquainted with the deluge, and others no less curious, showing that the Indians were not unaccustomed to 
abstruse speculations, and that besides their knowledge of many traditions contained in the Old Testament, they 
possessed some information respecting the predictions of the New. It may be interesting to insert the entire 
passage of Gomara giving an account of this conference. 

“Nicaragua, who was acute and skilled in the knowledge of the rites and antiquities of his own country, had a 
long conference and dispute with Gil Goncalez and the ecclesiastics. He inquired if the Christians were acquainted 
with the great deluge, which had swallowed up the earth, men, and animals; and whether another was to happen? 
whether the earth was to be revolutionized (trastornar), or heaven to fall? when and how the sun, moon, and stars, 
should be deprived of their motion and light? since they were of such vast magnitude, who moved and kept them 
in their orbits ? He inquired the cause of the darkness of night, and of cold, blaming Nature for not having made 
light and heat perpetual, since they were best? What were the honour and reverence due to the triune God 
of Christians, who had created the heaven, and the sun whom they adored as god in those countries, the sea, 
the earth, and man, who rules over the birds which fly and the fish which swim? where souls would go after 
death ; and what would be their occupations after having left the body, since being immortal they lived for so short 
a time? He inquired likewise if the Holy Father at Rome, the Vicar of Christ, who was the god of Christians, 
died? and how Jesus being a God is a man, and his mother being a virgin brought forth? and whether the Emperor 
and King of Spain, whose prowess, virtue, and power they had so vaunted, was mortal ? and why such a handfull of 
men were anxious to obtain so much gold ?”—La Istoria de las Indias, fo. cviii. 

From this account it will be perceived, that as not only in New Spain and in Peru, but likewise in Nicaragua, the 
tradition of the Deluge was generally received among the Indians; that of the temptation of Eve, of the fall of man, 
and of the loss of Paradise, was no less general in the New World. Torquemada, in the thirty-first chapter of the sixth 
book of his Indian Monarchy, gives this description of the goddess Cihuacohuatl, who is named by many writers 
the Aztec or Mexican Eve. “ One of the goddesses greatly esteemed by the natives of New Spain was Cihuacohuatl, 
which name signifies ‘the woman serpent ;’ and they say that she always has twins or brings forth two children at a 
birth. This woman or goddess, whom they named Cihuacohuatl, was according to the etymology of the name, as 
Father Bernard de Sahagun says, the first woman who existed in the world, the mother of the whole of the human race, 
who it is true was tempted by the serpent who appeared to her in the terrestrial Paradise, and discoursed with her to 
persuade her to transgress the command of God. And it is likewise true, that after having committed sin, she con- 
ceived and bore a son and a daughter, both at the same birth, and that the son was named Cain and the daughter Cal- 
mana: and that afterwards she brought forth, at a second birth, Abel and his sister Delborah ; so that she bore them by 
twin births, and continued from that time onwards to give birth to twins, as has been observed ; the Indians therefore 
designated her from these two properties, Cihuacohuatl, which signifies ‘the woman of the serpent, that is to say, whom 
the serpent tempted; and which also signifies, ‘the woman who brought forth two infants at a birth, a girl and a boy ;’ 
for they call twins and infants born at the same birth Cocohua, which name signifies ‘ serpents, as if they called them 
serpents born from the woman serpent. This appears to be a confused knowledge, which they had received by tradi- 
tion, of the ancient truth of the origin of the human race, and of the temptation of the serpent.” The above account of 
Torquemada (or rather of Sahagun, whose authority he cites,) is very curious, and is further confirmed by the repre- 
sentation (in the forty-eighth page of the lesser Vatican MS.,) of the goddess Cihuacohuatl or Suchiquecal, with two 
infants and a serpent near her. Another painting, (contained in the seventy-fourth page of the same MS.,) is more 
remarkable, since it seems clearly to allude to the threat pronounced in the third chapter of Genesis against the 
serpent, “ And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed: it shall bruise thy 
head, and thou shalt bruise his heel :” as in fact the seed of the woman appears to be there in the act of bruising 
the head of the serpent with a staff, whilst the latter has bitten off, and is holding in his jaws, the foot of his 

NOTES. 4.03 

adversary. Mexican traditions seem also to refer to the creation of the one sex from the bone of the other, as is 
recorded in the second chapter of Genesis: “And the Lord God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he 
slept: and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh instead thereof. And the rib, which the Lord God 
had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man. And Adam said, This is now bone of my 
bones, and flesh of my flesh: she shall be called Woman; because she was taken from man:”—since the Mexicans 
believed that both sexes had been created from a bone which Xolotle had obtained from Mictlantecutli, who is said 
to have stumbled and fallen down in running away from the God of the dead, who was anxious to take back his 
gift; and that the bone, which had been at first of a single piece, having been broken by the fall into many small 
fragments of unequal sizes, the stature of mankind became in consequence unequal. The Peruvian tradition of men 
having been created by Viracocha, after the likeness of images made by himself, seems also to allude to what is said 
in the twenty-sixth verse of the first chapter of Genesis: “And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our 

9 

likeness :” and in the next verse, “So God created man in his own image; in the image of God created he him.” 
This tradition is mentioned by Garcia in the seventh chapter of the fifth book of the Origin of the Indians, where, 
treating of the origin of the Peruvians, he says: “We have still to state what the Indians of Peru relate of their 
origin, which I shall narrate as Juan de Betancos wrote it, who was one of the first who entered that kingdom, (of 
whom we have already made mention in other places,) who was well acquainted with the general language of the 
Indians, called the Quichua or language of the Inga*; and being thus qualified, served as interpreter or linguist in 
that kingdom, and was on that account ordered by Don Antonio de Mendoga, who was at that time viceroy of Peru, 
to compose a history of the origin and succession of the Ingas, kings of Peru, and of their conquests, deeds, and 
exploits, to the period when the Spaniards entered their country, procuring the necessary information from the oldest 
Indians. Juan de Betancos obeyed the order of the viceroy, and compiled with great diligence and care a history, 
which on account of the death of Don Antonio de Mendoga, to whom he had dedicated it, was not at that time brought 
to light and published; neither was it afterwards printed, by reason of the death of Betancos, who, proceeding to 
give an account of the origin of the Ingas, relates what the Indians told him of the origin of all the first inhabitants 
of that kingdom, which is as follows: ‘Formerly, in ancient times, the kingdom and provinces of Peru were 
enveloped in an obscurity in which neither light nor sun existed, and were consequently without day. A certain 
race of people inhabited them at that period, who were ruled and governed by a lord, whose name as well as that of 
his subjects they forget. The Indians further say, that at this time, in which all was night, and when neither light nor 
day existed, a lord named Contice Viracocha came out of a lake which is in the province of Collasuyo, and brought 
along with him a certain number of persons; and having come from thence, proceeded to a place adjoining to the 
lake, where at present is the city called Tiaguanaco, where as soon as he had arrived with his people, he created in 
an instant the sun and day, commanding the former to encircle and revolve with rapid motion round the whole 
world. He next created the moon, the planets, and the stars, which are in the eighth heaven and firmament. But 
since it may be inquired, when did this Viracocha create the earth, and the people who had lived in that obscurity, 
and those who came with him out of the lake? the Indians say that Contice Viracocha had on a former occasion 
come out of the lake, and that he then created the heaven and the earth, leaving it without sun or light to illu- 
minate it; and made those who came out of the lake with him, and the people who existed at that period, who were 
guilty of some offence against Viracocha, on which account he became incensed at last against them, and as 
a punishment and chastisement for their sins changed them and their lord into stones. He then created the sun, 
the day, and the stars, as has already been said; and having so done, he formed out of stone, (on the same spot and 
site of Tiaguanaco,) figures and images of men and women, some in a state of pregnancy, and others to represent 
mothers with their children in cradles, according to their usages and customs, which were to serve as a model and 
sample of the people whom he was about to create. Having completed the formation of these figures, he removed 
them and put them into some particular province, and afterwards created another province of people of the same kind, 
dividing it from the former; and lastly, he formed out of stone the entire population of Peru, in the same manner as 
he had formed the others. Having finished his work, he said to the people who had come out of the lake with him, 
Mark very attentively the images and busts of stone which I have made, and observe that some of them shall be named

This account of Viracocha forming man after the likeness of images fashioned by himself, seems to refer to the 
above-mentioned verse in Genesis: but the following tradition bears a less equivocal mark of having been derived 
from a Scriptural origin. It is taken from an inedited History of Chile by Diego de Rosales: “ De proposito y no 
por olvido he dexado para la postre, por darse le bueno a este capitulo, las lagunas de Taguatagua, que no es digno 
de olvido, sino de perpetua memoria, el caso tan raro y singular que sucedio en ellas. Caen estas lagunas veinte 
leguas al sur de la Ciudad de Santiago cerca del pueblo de Malloa, tienen seis leguas de circunferencia, muchas 
truchas, varios generos de pezes, y muchedumbre de paxareria de varios colores que sobre las aguas forman un 
hermoso jardin de flores vivientes. 'Tiene en medio una pequefia isla, que muchas vezes se ve nadar por encima de 
la laguna y moverse con el impulso de los vientos. No es esto lo singular y raro, que Dausqueyo, y Pomponio 
Mela traducido o illustrado por Joseph Antonio Gonzales de Salas, dicen lo mismo de otras islas que fluctuan en 
las lagunas y se mueven en ellas, y entre otras es muy nombrada la isla de Chemnis, que esta en un lago de Egipto 
poblada de muchas selvas y ennoblecida con el famoso templo dedicado al dios Apolo. Lo singular y de grande 
ensefianza es, que se conserva una tradicion de tiempo immemorial entre los Indios, que en aquel sitio antiguamente, 
antes de la venida de los Espafioles, avia un hermoso valle muy ameno y poblado de infinita gente, y que no avia 
laguna ni sefial de ella, sino mucha amenidad, y sementeras en abundancia para las delicias de los naturales. Pero 
que con la abundancia y el regalo eran sus costumbres tan estragadas y tan enormes sus vicios, que no conten- 
tandose con la muchedumbre de mugeres proprias, y agenas, se desenfrenaban como bestias en los torpisimos vicios 
de la sodomia y bestialidad. Entraron un dia en aquel valle dos hermosos mancebos en el trage y rostros nunca 
vistos, y en la hermosura y gravedad admirables, que en la realidad eran Angeles, y les dixeron a todos los 
habitadores de aquella tierra que venian embiados del Seftor del cielo y la tierra, del mar y de los vientos, del sol, 
luna, y estrellas, y que venian a requerirles de su parte como los requerian, que se enmendasen de tan enormes 
vicios, y obsenidades con que gravissimamente offendian al autor de la naturaleza, ya su Dios y Senor a quien 
devian todo amor y obediencia, y que si no se enmendaban, serian del gravissimamente castigados en esta vida, y 
mas rigurosamente en la otra con eternas penas y tormentos, y dicho esto desaparecieron, y no los vieron mas. 
Causoles alguna novedad al principio, pero no enmienda, porque perseveraron en sus torpezas. O gran paciencia 
de Dios y grande su misericordia que no se contento con este aviso! sino que passados algunos afios, volvieron los 
dos Angeles en figura humana y en el trage y hermosura, dando muestras de que no eran hombres terrenos, sino 
espiritus celestiales. Volvieronles a requerir a los Indios, afearonles sus vicios, y dixeron les que estaba ya cercano 
el castigo de Dios, sino se enmendaban de sus pecados. Desaparecieronse, y los Indios endurecidos en sus malas 
costumbres, y ciegos a tanta luz, perseveraron en sus delitos, incredulos del castigo como los de Sodoma, mas 
despues de pocos dias vino el castigo de Dios sobre ellos, porque temblo la tierra y se estremecio con tanta furia, 
que abriendose en differentes grutas, y por diversas bocas, pronuncio la sentencia y executo el castigo, vomitando 
tanta cantidad de agua, que inundo todo aquel valle, y anego a quantos en el avia, sus casas, haziendas, y sementeras, 
sin dexar memoria de aquella tan nefanda gente, y quedando para eterna memoria y escarmiento de los demas 

aquella laguna, que oy se ve, y a permanecido despues de tantos afios que ha que sucedio este tan maravilloso caso,

and when such phantoms present themselves to the low and timorous rabble, they immediately begin to fly, and their spirits are so

paths, desirous of seeing them, in order to obtain from them some piece of good fortune, or a present of thorns of the aloe, which were

and will not let you go. ‘These words he frequently repeated whilst the struggle continued between them; and when the conflict had 
lasted for a length of time, on the approach of morning the phantom spoke, and said, Let me go, for you weary me; tell me what you 
wish, and it shall be granted to you. On which the soldier replied, What will you give me? when the phantom said, Hereis athora. To

portance it must be confessed) arises, viz. Whether Jacob suffered one or two accidents in his conflict with God? It is evident on the latter 
supposition that his thigh which had been put out of joint must immediately afterwards have been restored to its proper place, or he never 
would have been able to have walked again. Considering the importance which the Jews attached to this mysterious incident in the 
life. of the most revered of their patriarchs, it is surprising that Moses did not record in a more circumstantial manner an event in Hebrew 
history which redounded so much to the glory of Jacob, the founder of the house of Israel; although his reserve makes it only the more 
probable that the Rabbis corrupted with their traditions the simple narrative of the Pentateuch. ‘They undoubtedly considered the 
shrinking of the sinew of Jacob’s thigh a sign of the blessings,—amongst which riches must be numbered,—which were in store for him 
and his descendants; and it may be a question, whether, in their usual style of absurd reasoning upon every unexplained point in 
Scripture, they might not have argued, that since a mere touch could not have caused the sinew of his thigh to shrink, it might have been 
punctured; and that, as God had appeared to Moses in a bush, so he might on this other occasion have pierced the patriarch’s 
thigh with a¢horn. Itis vain, from the nature of the subject which affords grounds for these discussions, to attempt to refute any thing that 
may be said by the Rabbis, by demanding of them whether a viler fable or one more derogatory to the majesty of the Deity, can be 
found in the whole range of heathen mythology than that which their perverse genius may suggest as a solution of these doubts. At the 
same time, since the Mexicans considered the thorns of the aloe, which the soldier received from the phantom of Tezcatlipoca, to be the 
sign of his having prevailed and of his future good fortune, it is probable that Jewish traditions laid the foundation for this gross super- 
stition amongst them.”

The following passage, containing the tradition of the Mexicans respecting their own genealogy and that of the 
other nations of New Spain, is taken from the 120th page of Gomara’s Conquest of Mexico, where, treating of their 
antiquities, he says, “ According to their own books, and the common opinion of their learned men, and such as are 
acquainted with their ancient history, the Mexicans came from a country called Chicomuztotlh, and descended all 
from one father, whose name was Iztacmixcoatlh, who had two wives. By Wancueitl, (which was the name of one 
of them,) he had six sons, the eldest of whom was named Xelhua, the second Tenuch, the third Ulmecatlh, the fourth 
Xicalancatlh, the fifth Mixtecatlh, the sixth Otomitlh. By Chimalmatlh, (which was the name of the other,) he had 
Quecalcoatlh.” Gomara next proceeds to state in what part of New Spain each of these sons settled, and the 
names of the cities which they founded. Of Quecalcoatlh he says, “‘he built, or, according to other accounts, 
rebuilt Tlaxcallan, Huexocinco, Chololla, and many other cities. The same Quecalcoatlh was an upright, temperate, 
religious, and holy man, and, as they believe, a god. He never was married or acquainted with women. He lived a 
life of the greatest chastity, performing rigid acts of penance, accompanied with fasting and other austerities. He 
preached, according to report, the law of nature, and inculcated it with diligence, setting an example of morals. He 
instituted fasting, which had not been before practised; and was the first who in that country offered sacrifices of 
blood, but not, in the manner which is now customary with these Indians, with the death of infinite numbers of men, 
but by drawing blood from the ears and tongue, as an act of penance, and as a punishment and remedy against the 
sin of lying and of listening to lies, which are no small vices amongst these people. They believe that he did not 
die, but that he disappeared in the province of Coacacoalco, close to the sea. They paint Quecalcoatlh such as I 
have described; and either because they do not know, or because they conceal his death, they believe him to be the 
god of the air, and worship him in all that country, but principally in Tlaxcallan and Chololla, and in the other 
cities which he founded, and accordingly they celebrate strange rites and sacrifices in them to him.” 

It would be an omission in this place, speaking of American traditions which seem to connect the Mosaic history 
with the mythology of the New World, not to mention Votan, who was a celebrated saint amongst the Chiapanese 
and the Capotecas ; and it is much to be regretted that Nufiez de la Vega, Bishop of Chiapa and Soconusco, should 
have destroyed or consigned to oblivion the historical work which he wrote, (or which at least was written by some 
other person,) concerning him; as it would probably have thrown much light on the ancient history of America and 
the communications which undoubtedly subsisted in early ages between the Old and New Continent. Boturini, in 
the 115th page of his Idea of a New General History of North America, gives an account of the discovery, by 
Nufiez de la Vega, whilst engaged on a visitation of his diocese in the year 1691, of this historical work, together 
with some ancient calendars, which he caused to be publicly burnt in the square of Huehuetan ; an act of mistaken zeal. 
that Boturini thus laments : “These burnings have been frequent and very fatal in New Spain. The Indians deplore 
them, and so do learned Spaniards; and I lament them, because I am convinced that these ancient paintings contained 
not only particular notices of great literary treasures, but likewise of immense riches stored up in the times of 
paganism, and hid on the occasion of the conquest; and I do not despair of being able to perform, some day or 
other, a notable service to Your Majesty.” 

The following account of Votan is taken from a recent publication, but of no great authority. It contains, however, 
a statement of some curious facts relative to him, which bear the appearance of probability; and as that part of 
it which relates to the discovery of the abovementioned history by Nufiez de la Vega is extracted from the Diocesan 
Constitutions, (a work written by that bishop, and published at Rome in 1702,) it is so far entitled to full credit. It 
is necessary however to observe, that the English translation, “he wrote an historical tract in the Indian idiom,” is 
incorrect, as the Spanish passage should have been translated, “ and in an historical tract which was written in the 
Indian idiom, mention is made;” since it is not expressly stated who the author of the book was, whether Votan 
himself or some other person. The account itself is from the pen of Doctor Cabrera, who says: “ Among the 
many small historical works that fell into the hands of this illustrious prelate (Nufiez de la Vega),—who was not 
more zealous for the glory of God than he was mistaken in the interpretations he applies to many of them, and 
particularly when he attributes the whole of them to superstition,—he instances one that was written by Votan, of 
whom he speaks as follows, in No. 34, section 30, of the Preface to his Constitutions: ‘ Votan is the third Gentile 
placed in the calendar: he wrote an historical tract in the Indian idiom, wherein he mentions by name the people 
with whom, and the places where, he had been. Up to the present time there has existed a family of the Votans in 
Teopizca. He says also that he is lord of the Tapanahuasec (‘the wooden drum’); that he saw the great house 

” 408 NOTES. 

(meaning the Tower of Babel), which was built, by the order of his grandfather Noah, from the earth to the sky ; 
that he was the first man whom God sent hither to divide and portion out these Indian lands; and that at the place 
where he saw the great house a different language was given to each nation.’ 

“ This illustrious prelate could have communicated a much greater portion of information relative to Votan, and 
to many other of the primitive inhabitants, whose historical works he assures us were in his own possession; but 
feeling some scruples on account of the mischievous use the Indians made of their histories in the superstition of 
the Nagualism, he thought proper to withhold it, for the reasons assigned in No. 36, section 32, of his preface. — 
‘ Although,’ says he, ‘ in these tracts and papers there are many other things touching primitive paganism, they are 
not mentioned in this epitome, lest, by being brought into notice, they should be the means of confirming more 
strongly an idolatrous superstition. I have made this digression, that it may be observed in the notices of the 
Indians, and the substance of the primitive errors in which they were instructed by their ancestors.’ It is to be 
regretted that the place is unknown where these precious documents of history were deposited; but still more is it 
to be lamented that the great treasure should have been destroyed. This treasure, according to the Indian tradition, 
was placed by Votan himself, as a proof of his origin anda memorial for future ages, in the casa lobrega (house 
of darkness) that he had built in a breath, that is in the space of a few breathings,—a metaphorical expression, 
intended to imply the very short space of time employed in its construction. He committed this deposit to a 
distinguished female and a certain number of plebeian Indians appointed annually for the purpose of its safe 
custody. His mandate was scrupulously observed for many ages by the people of Tacoaloya, in the province of 
Soconusco, where it was guarded with extraordinary care; until being discovered by the prelate before mentioned, 
he obtained and destroyed it. Let me give his own words, from No. 34, section 30, of his preface. ‘This treasure 
consisted of some large earthen vases of one piece, and closed with covers of the same material, on which were 
represented in stone the figures of the ancient Indian pagans whose names are in the calendar, with some 
Chalchihuites, which are solid hard stones of a green colour, and other superstitious figures. These were taken 
from a cave by the Indian lady herself and the Tapianes or guardians of them, and given up, when they were 
publicly burnt in the square at Hueguetan, on our visit to that province in 1691. 

“ Tt is possible that Votan’s historical tract alluded to by Nuhez de la Vega, or another similar to it, may be the 
one which is now in the possession of Don Ramon de Ordofiez y Aguiar, a native of Ciudad Real. He is a man of 
extraordinary genius, and engaged at this time in composing a work, the title of which I have seen, being as 
follows, ‘ Historia del Cielo y de la Tierra,—that will not only embrace the original population of America, but 
trace its progress from Chaldea immediately after the confusion of tongues, its mystical and moral theology, its 
mythology, and most important events. His literary acquirements, his application and study of the subject for 
more than thirty years, his skill in the Tzendal language, (in which idiom the tract just spoken of is written,) and 
the many excellent authors he has collected, lead us to anticipate,” &c. &c. The writer proceeds to say, “To the 
important information of Nufiez de la Vega, I will add the no less valuable notices communicated to me by Don 
Ramon Ordofiez y Aguiar. The memoir in his possession consists of five or six folios of common quarto paper, 
written in ordinary characters in the Tzendal language,——an evident proof of its having been copied from the original 
in hieroglyphics shortly after the conquest. At the top of the first leaf the two continents are painted in different 
colours in two small squares placed parallel to each other in the angles: the one representing Europe, Asia, and 
Africa, is marked with two large SS upon the upper arms of two bars drawn from the opposite angles of each square, 
forming the point of union in the centre: that which indicates America has two S S placed horizontally on the bars ; 
but I am not certain whether upon the upper or lower bars; I believe, however, upon the latter. When speaking of the 
places he had visited on the Old Continent, he marks them on the margin of each chapter with an upright S, and those 
of America with a horizontal S. Between these squares stands the title of his history, ‘ Proof that I am Culebra, 
(a serpent), which title he proves in the body of his work by saying that he is Culebra because he is Chivim. He 
states that he conducted seven families from Valum Votan to this continent, and assigned lands to them; that he is 
the third of the Votans; that, having determined to travel until he arrived at the root of heaven, in order to 
discover his relations the Culebras and make himself known to them, he made four voyages to Chivim, which is 
expressed by repeating four times, from Valum Votan to Valum Chivim, from Valum Chivim to Valum Votan ; that 
he arrived in Spain, and that he went to Rome; that he saw the great house of God building ; that he went by the 
road which his brethren the Culebras had bored; that he marked it, and that he passed by the houses of the thirteen.

Culebras. He relates that in returning from one of his voyages, he found seven other families of the Tzequil 
nation, who had joined the first inhabitants, and recognised in them the same origin as his own, that is, that of the 
Culebras. He speaks of the place where they built their first town, which from its founders received the name 
of Tzequil. He affirms the having taught them refinement of manners in the use of the table, table-cloth, dishes, 
basins, cups, and napkins: that in return for these, they taught him the knowledge of God and of his worship, his 
first ideas of a king, and of obedience to him; and that he was chosen captain of all these united families.” 

So far Doctor Cabrera; from whose treatise, entitled “Teatro Critico Americano,” this long paragraph has been 
extracted. It is unnecessary to attempt in this place to trace out any further Scriptural analogies in the traditions 
and mythology of the New World, since the coincidences which have been already mentioned are sufficiently 
strong to warrant the conclusion that the Indians, at a period long antecedent to the arrival of the Spaniards in 
America, were acquainted with a portion at least of the Old Testament, although time, superstition, and, above all, 
such an imperfect mode of transmitting to posterity the memory of past events as that of paintings, had greatly 
corrupted their ancient traditions. We shall close these observations with the following curious extract from 
Torquemada, from which it might appear that even the New Testament had been known to the Indians: “ Another 
ecclesiastic, named Brother Diego de Mercado, a grave father, who has been definitor of this province of the Holy 
Gospel, and one of the most exemplary men and greatest doers of penance of his time, relates, and authenticates 
this relation with his signature, that some years ago conversing with an aged Indian of the Otomies, above seventy 
years old, respecting matters concerning our faith, the Indian told him that they in ancient times had been in 
possession of a book which was handed down successively from father to son, in the person of the eldest, who was 
dedicated to the safe custody of it and to instruct others in its doctrines. These doctrines were written in two 
columns, and between column and column Christ was painted crucified, with a countenance as of anger. They 
accordingly said that God was offended; and out of reverence did not turn over the leaves with their hands, but 
with a small bar which they had made for that purpose, which they kept along with the book. On this ecclesiastic’s 
questioning the Indian as to the contents of that book and its doctrines, he was unable to give him further 
information, but simply replied that if the book had not been lost, he would have seen that the doctrine which he 
taught and preached to them, and those which the book contained, were the same; that the book had rotted in the 
earth, where the persons who kept it had buried it on the arrival of the Spaniards. He likewise informed him that 
they knew the world had been destroyed by the deluge, and that only seven persons had escaped in the ark, and 
that all the rest had perished, together with the animals and birds, excepting those which had been saved therein. 
They were also acquainted with the embassy of the angel to Our Lady, under a figure, relating that something very 
white, like the feather of a bird, fell from heaven, and that a virgin stooped down and took it up, and put it in her 
bosom and became pregnant; but what she brought forth they could not tell. What they say of the Deluge is 
attested likewise in Guatemala by the Indians named Achies, who assert that they possessed paintings recording 
that event, with other matters of antiquity, all of which the Brothers, with the spirit and zeal with which they were 
animated for the destruction of idolatry, took from them and burnt, holding them to be suspicious.” 

Nore III. 
REASONS FOR SUPPOSING THAT CHRISTIANS IN EARLY AGES COLONIZED AMERICA. 

Ir is so singular a fact that the Indians of Mexico and Peru should have believed with Christians in many 
doctrines which are held to be peculiarly and exclusively Christian, and to constitute a line of demarcation 
between Christianity and all other religions, that it appears a convincing proof that Christianity must in early 
ages have been established in America, and that ancient communications subsisted between the old and new 
continent at a period long antecedent to the age of Columbus. In pointing out some of the leading doctrines 
of Christianity, the knowledge of which was likewise found amongst the Indians, it may be proper to observe, that 

(5m ) 

410 NOTES. 

although it might be easily shown that the Indians believed in the existence of the Deity, in the immortality 
of the soul, and in a future state of rewards and punishments; still, as these are intuitive truths which all 
religions teach, which all ages have believed, no inferences will be attempted to be drawn from them; since the 
Romans or the Greeks, the Mahometans or the Hindoos, might by the same arguments be proved to have 
_carried on intercourse in former ages with the Indians. The doctrines more peculiarly Christian, a belief in which 
the Indians likewise professed, however mixed up with other superstitions, and from which inferences may be fairly 
drawn, are the following: That of a Trinity, of original sin, of repentance and penance, of a vicarial atonement, of a 
future redeemer, and of the resurrection of the body. But, besides exhibiting a certain degree of conformity on these 
doctrinal points, they likewise seem to have been formerly acquainted with the sacraments, although superstition had 
lamentably perverted these ancient mysteries of the Christian Church, since traces of them may be found in various 
rites and ceremonies common alike to the Mexicans and Peruvians. Having briefly mentioned what the particular 
doctrines of Christianity were, which the gravest writers assert were known to the Indians before the arrival of the 
Spaniards in the New World, we shall proceed separately to adduce proofs to show that the above-mentioned doc- 
trines did in reality constitute a portion of the Indian faith ; and although many testimonies from different authors 
might be cited in confirmation of each article, it will be sufficient in this place to quote the single authorities of men 
like Acosta, Peter Martyr, Garcia, and Torquemada, whose writings are highly appreciated in Spain, and are also known 
to the rest of Europe.—And first with respect to the doctrine of a Trinity *. Acosta says that the belief of the Peru-

* The following observations are taken from the English edition of “ Volney’s Ruins,” and they refer to a strange heresy that sprung 
up in the earliest ages of Christianity, which identified Christ in a sort of ézeve1 with the sun. That celebrated writer commenting on 
the word chris, which he says signifies to preserve, and was a name belonging to Vishnou, writes as follows: “The Greeks used to 
express by # or the Spanish iota, the aspirated hd of the Orientals, who said hdris : in Hebrew, héres (p5n) signifies the sun; but in Arabic, 
the radical word means to guard, to preserve, and haris, guardian, preserver. It is the proper epithet of Vichenou, which demonstrates 
at once the identity of the Indian and Christian trinities, and their common origin. It is manifestly but one system, which divided into 
two branches, one in the East, and the other in the West, assumed two different forms: its principal trunk is the Pythagorean system 
of the soul of the world, or Ioupiter. The epithet pater or father having been applied to the Demi-ourgos of the Platonicians, gave rise 
to an ambiguity which caused an inquiry to be made after the son. In the opinion of the philosophers it was the understanding, vous and 
Aoyos, from which the Latins made their verbum; and thus we clearly perceive the origin of the eternal father and of the verb his son, 
proceeding from him (mens ex Deo nata, says Macrobius); the anima or spiritus mundi was the Holy Ghost ; and it is for this reason 
that Manes, Basilides, Valentinius, and other pretended heretics of the first ages, who traced things to their source, said that God the 
Father was the supreme inaccessible light of heaven (the first circle, or the émaaves); the Son the secondary light resident in the sun, and 
the Holy Ghost the atmosphere of the earth.—See Beausob. vol. ii. p. 586. Hence, among the Syrians, his emblem of a dove, the bird 
of Venus Urania, that is of the air. ‘The Syrians (says Nigidius in Germanico) assert that a dove sat several days in the Euphrates on

sun. They bestowed the same appellations also on Chuquulla, that is, the god whose habitation they supposed was 
in that tract or region of the air whence proceed thunder, rain and snow, as they had done on the three images. 
In Chuquisaca an idol was once shown to me to which the Indians were accustomed to pray; they called it Tanga- 
tanga, and believed it to be a god who was one in three, and three in one.’—Acosta, lib. v. cap. xxviii. Several 
historians of the New World mention Suchiquecal, and the sin which she committed in eating of the fruit of a tree; 
although they do not expressly state that that fruit was an apple: whilst others assert, that with the Mexicans each 
succeeding year was merely a new anniversary of the fall of man, and that every day in their calendar was dedicated 
to the performance of some cruel austerity intended to blot out the remembrance of that sin; it will therefore be un- 
necessary to appeal to the testimony of any particular author to prove that the doctrine of original sin was believed 
by the Indians. ‘With respect to penitence and penance, these were doctrines introduced by Quecalcoatl, and strictly 
inculcated by the religion of the Mexicans. Gomara (speaking of Quecalcoatl) says, “He was the god of the air, 
that he founded the city of Chollula, and was by tradition chaste, and a great doer of penance, the institutor of fasts, 
and of drawing blood from the tongue and the ears; and that he permitted no sacrifices except those of quails, doves, 
and such animals as were taken in the chace; that he wore a long narrow vest of white cotton, and over it a mantle 
coyered with red crosses.”—Gomara, La Conquista de Mexico, fo. xxxviii. The doctrine of a vicarial atonement, or 
of a sacrifice for sin, whereby the guilt of the one party is expiated and atoned for by the zmnocent blood of the other, 
was also well known to the Indians; and the question is curious, how traces of this doctrine should have been disco- 
vered in America, and how, on the supposition of these traces affording indications of Christianity having in earlier 
ages existed in that continent, the doctrines of a purer faith could have thus degenerated, and in time have become 
mingled with such barbarous superstitions. The following extract is from the History of Chili by Rosales ; since the 
work of Rosales is inedited, the passage in the original Spanish is here inserted, to which the translation is subjoined. 
“ En Culacoya prosiguiendo con su conquista en tierras del gran Sefior Quinchatipai, cinco leguas de la ciudad de 
la Concepcion, tubieron otra fortaleza, y alli ay siete piedras a manera de piramides labradas, que fueron puestas por 
los Indios del Peru para hacer la ceremonia llamada Calpainga, que se hacia para la salud del rey Inga cada 
un afio. Era este rito a semejanza del que hacian los Cartaginenses, que como refiere el Padre Juan de Mariana, 
grave historiador, para obligar a sus dioses les sacrificaban todos los afios algunos dioses escogidos, y assi escogian 
los Ingas dos nifos de edad de seis aftos cada uno, varon y mujer, y los vestian en traje de Inga, y assi ligados 
y vivos los enterraban, diciendo que al pecado que su Rey y Sefior ubiesse echo, lo pagaban aquellos inocentes 
en aquel sacrificio.”—Historia del Chile, lib. iii. cap. 2.“ Prosecuting their conquest in Culacoya as far as the 
country of the powerful lord Quinchatipai, five leagues distant from the city of Conception, they (the Spaniards) 
found another fortress where were seven stones resembling sculptured pyramids, which had been placed there by the 
Indians of Peru for the purpose of performing the ceremony called Calpainga, which was celebrated annually to 
ensure the prosperity of the sovereign Inga. This rite resembled one in use amongst the Carthaginians, who, in 
order to gain the favour of their gods, as Father Juan de Mariana, a grave historian, relates, sacrificed every year 
some selected gods; and the Ingas accordingly selected annually two children, each of six years of age, a boy and a 
girl, and clothed them in the dress of the Inga; and in this manner, having bound them, they buried them alive, saying 
that those innocent victims would by that sacrifice ransom the sins which their king and lord had committed.” If 
our surprise is excited by the discovery that the Peruvians were not altogether ignorant of the nature of a vicarial 
sacrifice or atonement, it will be produced in no less degree when we discover that the inhabitants of New Spain 
generally believed in the coming of a future Redeemer or Saviour, whose advent as well as the last destruction of 
the world they seem to have expected at the close of certain stated periods corresponding with the artificial cycles of 
time which they employed in their calendars: that future redeemer was Quecalcoatl. The letters of Cortes to Charles 
the Fifth fully prove that about the time when the Spaniards first arrived in America, the expectation was very general 
in New Spain of the appearance of Quecalcoatl, and for many years afterwards that expectation continued: so diffi- 
cult is it to root out ancient prejudices; since we are informed that the mere report of their god having come to 

the egg of a fish, whence Venus was born.’ Sextus Empiricus also observes, (Inst. Pyrrh. lib. ili. c. 23,) that the Syrians abstain from 
eating doves; this intimates to us a period commencing in the sign of Pisces (in the winter solstice). We may further observe, that if 
Chris comes from Harisch by a chin, it will signify artificer, an epithet belonging to the sun, ‘These variations, which must have em- 
barrassed the ancients, prove it to be the real type of Jesus, as had been already remarked in the time of Tertullian. ‘ Many,’ says this

redeem them induced the Capotecas to revolt in the year 1550. Gomara, speaking of this expectation, says, “ The 
Indians viewed with attention the dress, deportment, and beards of the Spaniards; they were astonished at seeing 
the horses feed and gallop; they were terrified at the glittering of their swords, and fell to the ground at the report 
and noise caused by the artillery, thinking that heaven was bursting with thunder and lightning ; and they said of 
the ships, that it was Quecalcoatl who was coming, bringing his temples with him, (con sus templos a cuestas,) since 
he was the god of the air, who had left them, and whose return they expected.”—La Conquista de Mexico, fo. xvii. 
A most striking proof of the firmness of the faith of the Mexicans in Quecalcoatl, is afforded by the relations which 
Cortes in his third letter to Charles the Fifth, and Gomara in his Conquest of Mexico, give of the events which 
occurred during the last days of the siege of that city. Gomara, describing the state of extremity to which the 
Mexicans had been reduced, and their obstinacy in resisting the Spaniards to the last, says, “ Cortes, being desirous 
of seeing how much of the city remained yet to be gained, ascended a high tower, looked around him and perceived 
that there was an eighth part. On the following day he returned to the attack of this remaining portion: he 
commanded his troops to kill none but those who defended themselves. The Mexicans lamented their unhappy 
fate, intreating the Spaniards to conclude the work of slaughter ; and certain chiefs called to Cortes in a very pressing 
manner, who hastened to the spot, imagining that it was to treat of terms of surrender. Having placed himself by 
the side of a bridge, they addressed him, ‘Since you are the son of the sun, why do you not finish with his course : 
O sun! that canst encircle the earth in so short a space of time as a single day and one night, kill us at once, and 
relieve us from such great and protracted sufferings ; since we desire death, in order to go and rest with Quecalcoatl, 
who is expecting us.”—La Conquista de Mexico, fo. Ixxxiiii. The Mexicans and Qapotecas were not the only nations 
in New Spain who expected the coming of a future redeemer. The Totonacas, a numerous people who inhabited 
a mountainous tract of country to the east of Mexico, not far distant from Vera Cruz, believed likewise (if we may 
credit Mendieta, one of the earliest Spanish missionaries who preached the Gospel to the Indians) in this future 
Redeemer. Torquemada, citing the authority of Mendieta, says: “It was likewise found that in some provinces of 
New Spain, as in Totonaca, they expected the coming of the son of the great god, who was the sun, into the world; 
and they said that he was to come to renew all things; although they did not believe or interpret this in a spiritual, 
but in a temporal and earthly sense. They thought, for example, that on his coming, the grain would be of a purer 
and more substantial quality; that their fruit would be better flavoured, and more excellent in its kind; that the 
lives of men would be considerably prolonged, and that every thing else would become better in a corresponding 
degree. And in order to hasten the coming of the son of the great god, they sacrificed at a certain season of the year 
eighteen persons, both male and female; encouraging them, and exhorting them to consider themselves fortunate in 
being the messengers of the republic, which dispatched them to the great god to intreat and to supplicate him that he 
would vouchsafe to send them his son to free them from their many miseries and hardships, and the obligation and 
affliction laid upon them of performing human sacrifices, which, as has already been observed, they considered a 
terrible and cruel burthen; and it was an intolerable torment and grief to them, since they performed them in 
obedience to the commands of their false gods, on account of the great fear in which they held them.” It was the 
cupidity of the Spaniards that first instructed them in another essential doctrine of the Indians,—that of the resur- 
rection of the body. And here we must observe that this doctrine is peculiarly Christian : it is on hes point, and not 
on the immortality of the soul, that Christianity differs from the religions of antiquity ; and it is very singular that 
it should have been discovered in the New World. Gomara, after stating that the Peruvians deposited gold and silver 
vases in the tombs of the Ingas, says: “ When the Spaniards opened these sepulchres and scattered the bones, the 
Indians intreated them not to do so, assuring them that they would be united in the resurrection ; for they fully believe 
in the resurrection of the body, and in the immortality of the soul.”—La Istoria de las Indias, fo. Ixix. Herrera 
likewise, in several passages of his History of the Indies, asserts that the Indians maintained this belief. He says, in 
his fourth decade, page. 187, “ In the provinces of Guazacualco and Yluta they believed that the dead would come 
to life; and when the bones of such as died among them had dried up, they collected them in a basket and hung 
them to the branch of a tree, that they might be at no loss to find them when the period of the resurrection arrived.” 
He says also, “ In the province of Quimbaya they well knew that there was an immortal principle in man, although 
they thought that it was not his soul, but a (bodily) transfiguration, believing that the body would be restored to 
life. They explained further, that its future habitation would be some delightful and pleasant place, and they therefore. 
used interment like the other Indians.”"—Herrera, Historia de las Indias Occidentales, Dec. vi. lib. viii. pag. 177.

Having thus traced the resemblance which on many doctrinal points the religion of the New World presented to 
Christianity, we shall now say something of the sacraments: and it is truly surprising to discover that nearly all the 
sacraments of the primitive church were recognized by the first Spanish missionaries, as clearly shadowed out in many 
of the Indian superstitious rites and ceremonies. To begin with Baptism: Peter Martyr, in the eighth chapter of his 
fourth decade, addressing Leo the Tenth, describing the manners of the inhabitants of New Spain, says: “They report 
also another thing worth the noting, which will bee very pleasing to your Holinesse. The priestes seeme to baptise 
children, both males and females, of a yeere old, with holy ceremonyes in their temples, pouring water crosse-wise 
out of a cruet upon their heads; and although they understood not their words, yet they observed their murmurs 
and actions: neyther do they, as the Mahumetanes or Jewes, thinke their temples profaned, if any other sect be 
present at their sacrifices or ceremonyes.” 'Torquemada likewise, in his description of the Mexican baptismal cere- 
mony, says that “the midwife on bathing the infant addressed it in these words: ‘ Receive this water; for the goddess 
Chalchiuitlicue Chalchiuhtlatonac is thy mother. And may this bath wash away and remove the stain and defilement 
which thou deriyest from thy parents, and purify thy heart, and make thee of a good and holy life!’ ”—Monarquia 
Indiana, lib. 13. cap. xvi. It may here be observed that the words “manchas y suciedades que tienes de parte de tus 
padres” can only refer to original sin. This address to the infant about to be baptized, was translated from the 
Mexican language into Spanish by Bernard de Sahagun, one of the first preachers of the ‘Gospel in New Spain. Her- 
rera also asserts that in Yucatan baptismal ceremonies were performed: “ Baptism has been discovered in Yucatan 
alone of all the provinces of New Spain; and its name in their language signifies ‘regeneration’ (nacer otra vez). They 
hold it so much a matter of religion, and entertain such reverence for it, that nobody omits receiving it; they 
imagine that they receive a pure disposition in it to become good, and to escape harm from devils, and to obtain 
the glory which they hoped for ; it is administered to them from the age of three years to twelve, and no one marries 
without having received it. They fix upon a day for the celebration of it which they deem fortunate. The fathers 
fast on the three preceding days, and separate themselves from their wives: in the mean time the priests are occu- 
pied in the purification of the mother, exorcising the devil by means of certain ceremonies; which being completed, 
the children proceeded one by one, and the priest threw some ground maize and incense with his hand upon them. And 
they sent wine in a vase and censer out of the city, with orders to an Indian not to drink it or to look behind him; 
and by the performance of this ceremony they imagined that they exorcised the devil. The priest then came forth 
habited in long and grave vestments, with a branch in his hand, and placed some white cloth on the heads of the chil- 
dren, questioning the elder as to whether they had committed any sin, which on their confessing, he took them aside and 
in certain words blessed them, holding the branch in a threatening attitude towards them, and with some water which 
was kept in a bone, moistened their foreheads, cheeks, fingers, and toes: when some presents having been given, 
the baptismal ceremony was held to be complete, and the festival terminated in banquets. In addition to the three 
days before mentioned, the father and the mother remained apart nine more.”—Historia de las Indias Occidentales, 
Dec. iv. lib. x. cap. iv. 

Proceeding from baptism to the most solemn sacrament of the Church, that of the Lord’s Supper, we shall find a 
mysterious resemblance to the communion of Christians in an idolatrous rite of the Mexicans called Teoqualo, 
which literally signifies ‘to eat god.’ This ceremony consisted in eating the body and blood of Huitzilopuchtli or 
Quecalcoatl under the similitude of bread, which they named Toyoliaytlaquatl, which signifies ‘the food of our life.’ 
Torquemada, in the thirty-eighth chapter of the sixth book of his Indian Monarchy, thus describes it: “‘ Besides the 
image and statue which they had placed in the greater temple of Mexico to their false and abominable god Huitzilo- 
puchtli, which we have already mentioned, they made each year another, compounded and mixed up with different 
kinds of grain and esculent seeds, which was formed in this manner: They collected in one of the principal and 
handsomest halls of the temple, adjoining to the altar and Cu, a quantity of grain and seed of bledos and pulse, which 
they pounded with great care and devotion, and kneaded and formed into the said statue, of the size and height of 
aman. The fluid with which they moistened and worked the flour into dough was the blood of children whom they 
had sacrificed for this purpose; the intention of which was to typify, in the simplicity and innocence of the child, 
that of the god whom the statue represented. After it was made, the priests and satraps took it in their hands, and 
placed it with great reverence and veneration upon the Cu or altar which they had prepared and adorned for its 
reception ; all the ministers of their religion assisting at this act, and blowing trumpets and other instruments, which 
created a loud and tumultuous sound, whilst others went before, singing and dancing. This took place by night. 

NOTES. 7 415 

But as soon as it was morning the ministers and high priest proceeded to consecrate and to bless it, (if such an 
act can he called a consecration and benediction, although the Indians apply that very term to it in their own lan- 
guage,) at which benediction and consecration all the citizens were present, together with crowds of strangers who had 
assembled to witness the said ceremony. The consecration being over, all who could, drew near it, to touch it with, 
their hands, eyes, and mouths, as if it were to touch a relic, or the body of a saint, although that was the lurking-place 
of the Devil; and they at the same time strewed the whole of its body with jewels of gold and precious stones, of value 
proportioned to the devotion and means of each individual, which could easily be pressed into the figure of the idol, 
since the dough which composed it was fresh and soft. They made this liberal offering, thinking that they were 
rendering their god a considerable service, and that on account of it he would pardon their sins; which is what we 
are taught by the sound and Catholic doctrine of the Holy Scriptures,—that charity diminisheth sin. And if when 
done to our neighbour it possesses so much force, it will possess much greater when the offering is made unto God, 
who accordingly has chosen to declare, that it avails those who give and bestow, for their purification and the cleansing 
away of their sins; although in this place it possesses no meritorious quality, inasmuch as it was done to the Devil, 
or, to speak plainer, was done at his instigation. The day of the consecration of that infernal bread and dough being 
past, nobody was allowed to touch it, or to enter into the chapel where it was, but the high priest only. On the 
morning in which they had placed the idol on the altar, they proceeded to make a solemn offering and sacrifice to it. 
They afterwards brought forth the statue and idol of the god Paynalton, the god of war, the vicar or lieutenant of 
the said Huitzilopuchtli, which was made of wood, and was carried in the arms of a priest, who represented the god 
Quetzalcohuatl, and was dressed very richly in curious ornaments and apparel, being preceded by another, holding 
in his hands a large and thick serpent twisted in many folds, which was carried before, and was lifted up on 
high, in the manner of the cross in our processions. They made a very long procession, accompanied by all the 
citizens ; and at certain distances, and on different Cues or altars, the priests who were attached to them performed 
sacrifices as well of prisoners as of quails. The first halting-place was in the division of Teotlacho, where they killed 
two captives and many other slaves ; and approaching this part of the city where I am now writing, called Tlatelulco, 
they went forth to meet it with much solemnity, and sacrificed a great number of quails. Hence the procession 
passed on to Popotlan, where, after having offered incense to it with many ceremonies, they performed the same 
sacrifice ; whence they went to Chapultepec, which is about a league from the city, where they made a similar offering 
and sacrifice. It afterwards returned to the quarter called Tepetoca, the inhabitants of which received it with the 
same festive ceremonies and sacrifices ; and next came to another quarter, named Acachinanco, accompanied with 
the same honours and rejoicings ; from whence it proceeded to the temple from which it had set out. They then 
lifted up the statue of Paynalton, and placed it on the altar by that of Huitzilopuchtli, and there left it, together 
with the banner named Ezpaniztli, which was carried in front; the serpent alone was taken away, and deposited in a 
place allotted to it. This procession being ended, which lasted the greater part of the day, all necessary preparations 
were now ready for the sacrifice; as a commencement of which, the king or supreme lord took a censer, and throwing 
incense into it with certain ceremonies, offered incense to the image of his god, officiating himself as high priest. 
This ceremony being concluded, they took down the image of Paynalton, before which all those who were destined 
to be sacrificed were marched im files, with whatsoever else was required for the sacrifice. They then took three or 
four turns round the temple, as if in procession; and immediately afterwards made the wretched victims ascend the 
platform above, where they sacrificed them, beginning with the prisoners of war, and terminating that horrid act with 
the sacrifice of the fatted slaves who had been purchased for the occasion, tearing out their hearts, and throwing them 
at the feet of the idol. The entire of this day was dedicated to the greatest festivities and rejoicings, in which the 
priests carefully guarded the said statue, watching it during the night with much vigilance, that neither negligence 
nor omission might occur in any thing appertaining to its veneration or service. On the following day in the morning 
they took down the said statue, which being placed on its feet in a hall, the priest Quetzalcohuatl, who on the pre- 
ceding day had marched in procession with the statue of Paynalton in his arms, entered at the same time with it; and 
the king likewise, accompanied by a minister in inner attendance on the god Huitzilopuchtli, who was called Tehua, 
with four other priests of rank, and four principal young men of the number of those whose duty it was to watch 
over the other youths of the temple, who were named Telpochtlatoque, in whose presence, and in that of no others, 
Quetzalcohuatl took a spear, headed with a flint, and threw it at the breast of the idol, with which he pierced it, and 
the idol fell; which ceremony they performed, saying that it was to kill their god Huitzilopuchtli, in order to eat his 

416 NOTES. 

body. ‘The priests afterwards drew near; and one of them took out the heart and presented it to the king, and the 
others divided the body into two parts, and gave the one half to the inhabitants of this quarter of the city named Tlate- 
lulco, who distributed it in crumbs to all the people resident in these suburbs, especially to the young soldiers, without 
giving any part of the dough of the idol to the women. The remaining part, which belonged to the inhabitants of 
that part of Mexico called Tenuchtitlan, was divided amongst the inhabitants of the four quarters named Teopan, 
Atzaqualco, Quepopan, and Moyotlan. They gave it to the male portion of the community, both great and small, 
and also to children in the cradle.—This was their manner of communion, as we have said elsewhere ; and this repast 
was called Teoqualo, which signifies ‘god is eaten.’ And so the composition of this image and likeness of the Devil, 
which had been continued during so many years, ceased on one of the months dedicated to him.”
