Herrera gives a somewhat similar account: “ The Mexicans celebrated the principal festival of their god Vitzili- 
puztli in the month of May; and two days before the festival, the virgins who were shut up in the temple kneaded 
flour of hledos and roasted maize with honey, and formed a large idol of the dough, with eyes of green, blue, or 
white beads, and teeth of grains of maize. All the lords attended dressed in the same manner as the idol, who being 
seated in a blue chair was placed upon a bier in order to be carried on men’s shoulders. On the day of the festival, 
rather before the dawn of morning, the virgins came forth in new and white apparel, crowned with ears of roasted 
maize, and wearing chains of the same hanging down below their left arms, with their arms ornamented from the elbow 
to the wrist with red parrots’ feathers, and with their faces painted; and during this day they bore the name of Sisters 
of the god Vitziliputzli, and took the bier with the idol upon it and carried it to the court, where the young men 
who were educated in the temple, very splendidly dressed and crowned in the same manner, received it with great 
reverence, and carried it to the foot of the steps of the temple, when all the people humbled themselves, and taking 
dust from the ground strewed it on their heads, since this was a ceremony which was usual in their principal 
festivals. Afterwards the people went in quick procession to the mountain named Chapultepec, a league distant 
from Mexico; and there made a halt and sacrifice and then proceeded with the same haste to a place called 
Atlacuiabaia, which was the second resting-place; and passed on a league further to Cuioacan, from whence without 
stopping they returned to Mexico. This journey of four leagues was performed in four hours, and they named the 
procession Ipaina Vitzilipuztli, which signifies ‘the quick procession of Vitzilipuztli. They brought back the bier 
to the foot of the stairs, and drew it up with great reverence with ropes to the upper area of the temple, amidst the 
loud sound of drums, trumpets, horns, and pipes; for the steps were so high and narrow that they could not carry 
it up on their shoulders. The people likewise assisted with great reverence in this act. Having been drawn up 
and placed in a chamber adorned with flowers, the young men of the temple strewed many more around; and 
the virgins brought a quantity of pieces of the dough of the idol kneaded into the shape of bones, and 
placed them at its feet, calling them the flesh of Vitzilipuztli. The dignitaries of the temple then came forth 
in exact order according to seniority one after the other, attired in dresses corresponding to their offices, with 
garlands and chains of flowers. After them came the gods and goddesses, whom they worshiped under dif- 
ferent figures, habited in the same dresses. They placed themselves around the pieces or bones of dough, and 
performed over them a certain ceremony, which consisted in singing or dancing, by which they became con- 
secrated into the flesh of that god. The benediction being concluded, those who officiated in the sacrifices went 
forth, and the butchery of human victims commenced; more of whom died on that day than on any other, because 
the festival was of such a principal kind. Afterwards the young men and young women who were educated in the 
temple came forth, and placing themselves opposite to each other, danced and sang to the sound of a drum in 
praise of the festival and of the idol; and all the lords and principal persons replied to the song, dancing round 

(50) 

418 NOTES. 

them in a circle, whilst the young men and women holding each others’ hands, occupied the centre. The whole 
city flocked to this spectacle; and the festival being concluded, the priests took the idol and the pieces of dough, 
and distributed it like holy bread in the manner of a communion, and gave it to the people, great and small, men 
as well as women, who received it with great reverence, fear, and shedding of tears, declaring that they ate the flesh 
of God. They sent it likewise to the sick, and considered it a great crime to eat or drink water or any thing else 
till after noon ; and they hid water from the children, and advised all to beware of incurring the anger of God. 
This communion being over, an old man of much authority ascended some elevated place, and preached on their 
law and ceremonies.”—Herrera, Dec. iii. lib. ii. cap. xvii. Having already mentioned penance and penitence as 
doctrines introduced amongst the Indians by Quecalcoatl, it is sufficient in this place to remark, that confession 
and penance, considered as external rites and ceremonies, (and therefore recalling to our minds another sacrament of 
the Church,) were in general practice amongst the Indians. Acosta says, that throughout most of the vast provinces 
under the sceptre of the Ingas, confessors were appointed for the express purpose of hearing confession, distin- 
guished from each other by various degrees of rank, who were under a sacred obligation not to reveal any thing 
communicated to them in the discharge of their religious duties. Women also in some ‘places (as the same writer 
asserts) were accustomed to hear confession. Herrera likewise notices this custom as prevalent in Yucatan; and it 
probably existed in other provinces of New Spain —Having traced at considerable length these analogies, we shall 
now say something of the adoration of the cross, the sign of which occurs frequently in Mexican paintings, and which 
it cannot be doubted was a religious symbol among the Indians. The adoration of the cross in America, if the fact 
were well authenticated, would in itself be a strong argument of the Christian faith having been planted in the New 
World: and thetestimony of the most respectable historians may be adduced to show that crosses were discovered, 
and the adoration of them witnessed by the first Spanish settlers in America. Gomara, in concluding his description 
of a temple in the island of Acucamil, says: “ At the foot of the tower there was a wall of stone and mortar, well 
polished, and ornamented with turrets, and within this inclosure there was a cross formed of plaster about ten palms 
high, which they esteemed and adored as the god of rain; so that when no rain fell and they were in want of water, 
they went in procession to it with much devotion, and offered it sacrificed quails to appease the anger and indig- 
nation which it felt or seemed to feel against them, with the blood of that simple bird. .They likewise burned a 
certain kind of gum as incense, and sprinkled it with water, after which they felt sure that it would soon rain.”—La 
Conquista de Mexico, fo. x. 

Boturini likewise mentions the discovery of some ancient crosses in America, one of which had been found by 
himself.—Since the whole of the passage containing the account of these crosses is curious, it is here given at full 
length. Speaking of his collection of MSS. and paintings, he says, “I likewise possess some historical notices 
concerning the preaching of the Gospel in America by the glorious apostle Saint Thomas. They are contained in 
thirty-four sheets of Chinese paper, and I suppose assisted Don Carlos de Siguenza y Gongora in the composition 
of his work on the same subject, which he entitled ‘The Pheenix of the West, which I have not been able yet to 
procure, as it never was printed. Since there is some connection between the subjects,—digressing for a short time 
from my account of this class of books,—I say in reference to the above-mentioned preaching of the holy apostle, 
that I am in possession of a painting on linen of the most holy cross of the mountain Tianguiztepetl, which I have 
before spoken of in Sec. 20. No. 20, of this Catalogue, which is painted in the form of a Taw, about a cubit in size, 
and of a beautiful azure blue, intermixed with figures resembling white stars, having on its right side a shield 
likewise of a blue colour, with five white balls in the middle, undoubtedly emblematical of the five most precious 
wounds of the Redeemer, which monumients have been preserved from the time of paganism to our days, without 
the rain or the other inclemencies of the atmosphere to which they had been exposed, having been able during so 
many ages to fade the colours. I also possess a painting on linen of another most holy cross of wood, which was 
drawn by means of a machine (that was made on purpose), out of an inaccessible cave of Mizteca Baxa, and which 
is at present venerated in the conventual church of Tonala, belonging to the fathers of Saint Dominic, which had 
also been deposited in the said cave since the Pagan times, and was discovered by the music of angels being heard 
in the said cave on every vigil of the glorious apostle. The above-mentioned preaching is so clearly indicated in 
the Histories of the Indians, that it is even recorded in the paintings of the Chontales, amongst whom a most 
miraculous cross was discovered, besides the other crosses which the Spaniards found in the island of Potonchan 
and in the city of Texcalan, to which the Indians offered adoration, presenting them flowers and incense, and 

NOTES. 419 

invoking them under the name of the god Tlaloc, the god of rain. Many traces moreover of the holy feet of the 
said apostle have remained in different places of New Spain; and besides this, the above-mentioned Histories all 
declare that a white man preached among them a holy law, and the fast of forty days, which the Emperor Netza- 
hualcoyotl, in the greatest vicissitudes of his reign, frequently practised ; and they add, that at his departure from 
them he left a prophecy, that in the year of their calendar, Ce Acatl, One Cane, his sons would come from the 
East to preach again to them; which was the reason why the Indians were so disturbed at the intelligence of the 
arrival of the Spaniards exactly in the year and character Ce Acatl. And I, following the track of the Indian calendars, 
have discovered that the prophecy of the saint was verified to the letter. The Indians, availing themselves of the 
lofty metaphors of their language, have bestowed the name of Quetzalcohuatl upon the glorious apostle, which 
signifies ‘the serpent-bird, intimating by the bird, the swiftness with which he had passed from a distant country to 
theirs; and by the serpent, the wise circumspection of the law which he came to preach, the value of which was 
further denoted by the feathers of the bird, which they called Quetzalli, and infinitely esteemed; since they wore 
them not only as an ornament in war, but likewise at their public dances and solemn festivals.”—Catalogo del 
Museo Indiano, pag. 51. With reference to the tradition which Boturini mentions as prevalent in New Spain, of 
Saint Thomas having preached the Gospel in that part of America, and of the impression of his feet being visible 
in many places, it may be remarked that that tradition seems to have been general over all America. Rosales, in 
his inedited History of Chile, declares that the inhabitants of that extremely southern portion of America, situated 
at the distance of so many thousand miles from New Spain, and who did not employ paintings to record events, 
accounted for their knowledge of some of the doctrines of Christianity by saying, “ that in former times, as they 
had heard their fathers say, a wonderful man had come to that country, wearing a long beard, with shoes, and a 
mantle such as the Indians carry on their shoulders, who performed many miracles, cured the sick with water, caused 
it to rain, and their crops and grain to grow, kindled fire at a breath, and wrought other marvels, healing at once 
the sick, and giving sight to the blind; and that he spoke with as much propriety and elegance in the language of 
their. country as if he had always resided in it, addressing them in words very sweet and new to them, telling them 
that the Creator of the universe resided in the highest place of heaven, and that many men and women who were 
resplendent as the sun dwelt with him. They say that he shortly afterwards went to Peru, and that many, in 
imitation of the habit and shoes which that man used, introduced among themselves the fashion of wearing shoes, 
and the loose mantle over the shoulders, either fastened with a clasp at the breast, or knotted at the corners ; whence 
it may be inferred that this man was some apostle whose name they do not know.” ‘This is the account given by 
Rosales of that wonderful man ; and it deserves to be remarked, as quite in accordance with the gloomy and mis- 
anthropical character with which the Indians loved to invest religion, that they converted an object of reverence 
into one of horror, by assigning to him the attribute of breathing fire from his nostrils. ‘The Mexicans in the same 
way, by representing their deities surrounded with the symbols of skulls, serpents, knives and lances, and under the 
most terrific forms, endeavoured to excite fear in the minds of those who approached them, as the feeling which 
would be most grateful to stern ‘and cruel gods. Kircher * says that none of these symbols were without their 
secret meaning. The mirror in the hands of Tezcatlipoca denoted his providence, which beheld every thing as in 
a mirror: and the skull and heart, according to Torquemada, signified that he possessed equal power over life and 
death. We shall conclude these observations by adducing the testimony of Clavigero in proof of many crosses 

* Kircher notices the subject of Mexican paintings only as it were intentionally to lend the sanction of his great authority and 
learning to the popular notion, that those paintings were entirely devoid of interest, and merely a rude effort of men scarcely beyond the 
savage state at the invention of hieroglyphical writing. That celebrated Jesuit had made hieroglyphics his peculiar study, and therefore 
could not have been really ignorant of the true nature of the Mexican paintings; and that, far from being symbols meaning little or nothing, 
they contained many and great mysteries. His reserve therefore and pretended ignorance must be attributed to the same causes as 
those which so powerfully operated in effecting the almost total destruction of those paintings ; and his silence is in fact eloquent. Paint- 
ings amongst the Mexicans were a mode of religious as well as of historical instruction. It is singular that Christians should have used 
them for the former purpose in the early and middle ages; since the Nicene Council declared (proving the custom by naming it), that 
“ paintings were books for simpletons who could not read.” The Jews likewise made use of paintings; and heraldry was an art which 
sprung up in the unlettered ages of feudal grandeur. From religious paintings cut on blocks of wood, which it became the fashion before 
the art of printing was invented to form into collections and to bind up in volumes, and which in libraries assume the appellation of 
books of images, block-books, or xylographic works,—learned men have been inclined to suppose that that invaluable art took its origin. 
The Biblia Pauperum is a book of this description, the largest of its kind, which doubtless in its day was ¢ fons superstitionum.’

having been at different times discovered in America: “The crosses the most celebrated are those of Yucatan, of 
Mizteca, Queretaro, Tepique, and Tianquiztepec. Those of Yucatan are mentioned by Father Cogolludo, a 
Franciscan, in his History, book ii. cap. 12. The cross of Mizteca is taken notice of by Boturini in his work, and 
in the Chronicle of Father Burgoa, a Dominican. There is an account of the cross of Queretaro, written by a 
Franciscan of the college of Propaganda in that city ; and of that of Tepique, by the learned Jesuit Sigismund Tarabal, 
whose manuscripts are preserved in the Jesuit college of Guadalajora. That of Tianquiztepec was discovered by 
Boturini, and is mentioned in his work. The crosses of Yucatan were worshiped by the Yucatanese in obedience, 
as they said, to the instructions of their great prophet Chilam-Cambal; who desired that when a certain race of men 
with beards should arrive in that country from the east, and should be seen to adore that sign, they should embrace 
the doctrine of those strangers. We shall have an opportunity of speaking more particularly concerning these 
monuments in the Ecclesiastical History of Mexico, if Heaven vouchsafe to favour our design.”—History of Mexico, 
page 250. Besides the crosses enumerated by Clavigero, Gomara mentions brass crosses as having been discovered 
in Yucatan by the first Spaniards who visited that province, which induced some learned men of his day to suppose, 
that Christians, flying from Spain at the period of the Saracen invasion, during the reign of Roderic, and hastily 
embarking in ships to escape to other countries, might by the force of tempests have been driven on the shores of 
America, and have carried with them those peculiar symbols of their faith. It would also appear that silver vessels 
resembling sacramental chalices have been discovered in that continent; since Cabrera thus writes: “ Don Ramon 
Ordonez and the presbyter Don Gabriel Chacon y Godoy related to me, that a few years back the presbyter Don 
Patricio Chinchilla, a native Indian, gave an account to the vicar of Saint Bartholomew de los Llanos, in the 
bishopric of Chiapa, that he had discovered in a cavern many sacred vessels and utensils of silver, and repeatedly 
entreated him to go and take possession of them; but perceiving the vicar had not sufficient confidence in him to 
credit his report, he brought as a proof of his veracity a silver chalice: it was very broad at the foot, and the cup 
shaped like an inverted pyramid ; and on being compared with others of a similar make, preserved in the church, it 
is presumable it may be attributed to the times of the Apostles. The Indian died soon after this circumstance, and 
the remainder of this treasure has not since been discovered. The chalice in question, as I am informed, was 
destined by the curate for an oratory on an estate of his own, called Rosario. This discovery is of great importance, 
since it confirms the Mexican tradition before alluded to, of the Gospels having been made known in these countries 
by the apostle Saint Thomas, who was worshiped under the form of the idol Quetzalcoatl. 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN, BY M. DUPAIX. 

THE FIRST EXPEDITION IN SEARCH OF ANTIQUITIES, UNDERTAKEN IN THE YEAR 1805. 

I, Wituram Duparx, late an officer in the Mexican dragoons, left this capital (Mexico) on the 
fifth of January 1805, having been commanded by His Majesty to proceed to the investigation of 
whatever monuments of antiquity might be still in existence in this kingdom, of a date anterior to 
that of the conquest. I was accompanied by an artist, an amanuensis, and a corporal belonging 
to the auxiliary dragoons; and directing my course to the east of this city, through the towns 
of Ystapalucan, Rio-frio, Tesmelucan, and Puebla, I could not discover in my progress over 
this line of country any thing connected with the royal commission with which I was charged. 
From the latter city I continued my journey to Tepeyaca, the signification of which proper name in 
the Mexican language is The Nose of the Mountain; which was given to it from its physical 
situation, being built upon the summit of a projecting angle formed by the mountain in that 
particular place. Notwithstanding the antiquity of its foundation I could not find on the entire 
site more than four ancient monuments. 

No.1. The first number represents a stone slab, of a reddish colour and extremely hard, upon 
the surface of which is sculptured in basso-relievo a symbol one foot and a half in length, one foot 
in breadth, and the third of an inch in thickness, which possibly may allude to the ancient arms of 
this city. It is divided as it were into two quarterings: in the first or upper of which the head of 
an eagle is engraved in profile, with a hieroglyphic in front, round which there is a circle with 
mouldings; and in the second quartering, which seems to serve as a basis to the first, three pendant 
ornaments or hieroglyphics are discerned upon a striated pedestal, on which the tail of the said 
bird appears, with various rows of feathers. This stone was discovered in the foundations of an old 
building of the said city, and at present serves as an ornament to the fountain in the principal 
square.—lIt is well sculptured and in good preservation. 

No. Il. There is in the said square a sentry-box called El Rollo (The Gallows), which was built 
by the first Spanish settlers, on one side of the wall of which is imbedded another slab of the same 
quality, having a border of plain ovals, within which is a second border; three hieroglyphics or 
historical emblems occupy its centre, one of which is very singular, since it bears a partial resem- 
blance to the claw of a crab, and is accompanied with thirteen plain and solid ovals: another 
resembles a butterfly, with four ovals similar to the preceding; and the third consists of branches 
like the trunk of a palm-tree.—This piece of sculpture is also in good preservation. 

No. III. presents to our view a semi-human head of gigantic dimensions, being one foot and a half in 
length and one foot in breadth. It is formed out of a hard and very heavy piece of stone, of a dusky 
purple colour ; it is perfect, and was found in the foundation of an edifice in the higher part of this 

CoP) 

4 QQ THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

city: the forehead is ornamented with hair, the eyes and nose are in just proportion and symmetry, 
the ears cannot be seen, the mouth is destitute of proportion and monstrous, and only a single row 
of teeth is visible below the under lip.—The discovery of the other parts of this colossus, that is to 
say, of the trunk and the various limbs, would be highly interesting. 

No. IV. Ina quarter of the same city called St. Michael Tlaixtegui, (which name signifies in the 
Mexican language The Cavity of the Mountain,) at the entrance of the house of Don Sebastian 
de la Cruz Xicotencatl, we found a serpent artificially wrought out of a piece of red porphyry 
of large dimensions, in an attitude of repose, and coiled upon itself in spiral circles, so as to leave 
a hollow space or transverse axis in the middle. The head, which has a fierce expression, is 
armed with two long and sharp fangs; the tongue is double, being divided longitudinally ; whilst 
it is shaped at the extremity like an anchor. It is to be regretted that a portion of the head is muti- 
lated. The entire surface of its body is ornamented or covered with broad and long feathers, and 
the tail terminates in four rattles: its length from the head to the extremity of the tail is about 
twenty feet, and it gradually diminishes in thickness.—It was discovered a short time before our 
arrival, in a deep ravine at the foot of a mountain behind the above-mentioned house. This reptile, 
the monarch or giant of its species, was in pagan times a deity greatly esteemed under the name of 
Quetzalcoatle, or The Feathered Serpent. It is extremely well sculptured, and there are still marks of 
its having been once painted with vermilion. 

No. V. I next directed my course eastwards to the town of Tlacotepec, situated at the distance of 
a day’s journey ; and having discovered nothing remarkable there, I proceeded on the following day 
to an Indian village four leagues to the south of it, named San Christobal ‘l'eopantepec, (which name 
signifies in the Mexican language The House or Temple of God built upon the Hill) ; where, upon an 
eminence or isolated mountain close to others of greater elevation to the west of the said town, there 
is a pyramid with a quadrangular base: it consists of four bodies or stories, which gradually 
diminish in size. Of the highest, the area of which was destined for the altars of their false gods, 
nothing now remains. ‘This oratory or pyramid, the style of which is Keyptian, is built of lime and 
stone, and is a solid structure. Its exterior surface was coated with square stones when J had the 
opportunity of observing it some years ago, which at present is quite in ruins. Its four sides, which 
are rather out of the perpendicular, are turned towards the four cardinal points of the compass. ‘I'he 
staircase which faces the west deserves to be noticed on account of the peculiarity of its diagonal 
ascent from one story to another. Several pavements or floors of shining cement interspersed with 
ruins are still visible at the foot of the pyramid, which convinces me that in former times the habi- 
tations of the priests who were attached to the service of the idols were situated there. The road from 
the plain on which the village is built to the summit of the hill, is by a sort of causeway cut in the 
rocky brow of the said hill. It is to be regretted, when we consider the present state of these ancient 
monuments, that that which neither the lapse of time nor of revolving ages, nor the trunks and roots of 
large trees growing amongst them and insinuating themselves between the interstices of the stones, and 
in this manner separating them, could effect,—indiscreet religious zeal on the one hand, and on the 
other the greediness of the occupiers of the soil as well as of the inhabitants of the surrounding villages 
eager to gain possession of the materials, should have been able to accomplish, which seem to have 

conspired to dismantle and destroy works certainly worthy of lasting preservation, and calculated 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN 4.23 

to throw light on the state of the arts amongst the ancient Mexicans ;—and all for the object of plun- 
dering them of the cut stones which entered into their structure. Other ancient fabrics are greatly 
indebted to their physical situation for their preservation, since they are generally built on rugged 
and inaccessible mountains, and surrounded with precipices ; and likewise to their being far removed 
from towns and adjoining habitations,—their relentless foes,—which occasion much trouble and 
danger to those who undertake the task of investigating them. 

From this last town we proceeded to the city of Tehuacan de las Granadas, the capital of the 
district, where I was unable to discover any thing remarkable. Neither did Old Tehuacan, a place 
so named, about six miles to the east of the latter city, present to our view any remains of antiquity, 
except some spacious ruins of houses and temples built of stone and mortar, and situated upon the 
side of a mountainous declivity. 

No. VI. We found in the last-mentioned town two ancient pieces of sculpture of light green 
jasper, similar in shape and quality : they are alto-relievos, and carved carefully and with symmetry, 
each forming a separate piece. Their figure is somewhat oval; and, joining at their extremities, 
they form a sort of prolonged oval.—lIt is very difficult to ascertain the precise use of many works 
of Mexican art, or even to explain their exact shape and parts, the style of their execution being so 
very original ;—it will be necessary therefore to refer to the drawings, the view of which will be found 
more satisfactory than the most minute description. 

Quitting Orizava, we continued our journey along the rugged steeps of Zongolican or Tzongol- 
liucan, which are within the jurisdiction of that city, being itself the capital of all the hilly country. 
The city of Zongolican is situated at the distance of twelve leagues to the south of the former city, 
and the road to it lying through Teguillan, a village of native Indians, crosses over various undulating 
mountains, and winds with a difficult ascent until it reaches that city, which occupies nearly the 
centre of the hilly country, being built in a deep plain of a somewhat circular shape, and crowned 
with high rocks. Rivulets descend into the plain by cascades and waterfalls, and soon disappear in 
several subterraneous channels. It is a large city: the inhabitants employ themselves in planting 
tobacco, and it possesses an agreeable climate. I discovered a sort of sage in its vicinity, growing 
in bushy shrubs very low and broad, the taste of which is very pleasant: it is here distinguished 
by the appellation of the Sweet Herb. Here are also different sorts of earth or clay, of a very 
unctuous quality, which properly prepared might be applied to several useful purposes: some 
of them are red, others of a blue, yellow, or purple colour. This celebrated range of hilly 
country comprehends every description of climate,—cold, hot, and temperate, with all their various 
modifications : the southern portion is very fertile, and abounds in useful vegetables; the cedar and 
rosewood are very common; there are a great variety of curious plants, amongst which may be 
reckoned those which naturally twine themselves round the trunks and arms of trees, and which bear 
flowers of the most exquisite beauty and delightful scent. 

We left this city after eleven days’ stay in it, our delay having been caused by the badness of the 
weather; and reposed for the night at the residence of the proprietor of a tobacco plantation 
named Rocha, which is situated at the distance of a day’s journey from it. But before our arrival at 
the Indian village Saint Sebastian, where we intended to dine, an accident which might have proved 

of a disastrous nature befel us. In a narrow and difficult passage cut horizontally in the side of a

steep mountain on the brink of a precipice terminating in a deep abyss, the corporal and his horse, 
who were at a little distance behind me, suddenly fell and disappeared: the former, by quickly snatch- 
ing at the branches of some trees, made a successful effort to extricate himself, and escaped without 
sustaining any bodily injury; but the horse rolling downwards caused a sound like the falling of a 
heavy torrent of water, tearing up by the roots and breaking whatsoever opposed itself to the rapi- 
dity and violence of his descent, experiencing in a brief moment the powerful effects of the laws 
of gravity, until his further progress was arrested by accidentally coming into collision with some 
trees of larger growth, which served as a barrier and check to his fall. Finally, after excessive 
exertions, I was enabled, with the assistance of the Indians who accompanied me, and the united 
force of arms, bill-hooks and axes, to draw him up by means of ropes, without having received 
any other injury than a few slight cuts, which did not prevent his proceeding forwards. 

On the evening of the same day, towards nightfall, the horse of the artist, in the attempt to avoid 
some bad places in the road, approached too near its dangerous edge, which bordered on a deep 
precipice completely concealed from view by the surrounding foliage, when making a false step he 
fell: the rider had the presence of mind to throw himself from the saddle into a piece of boggy 
ground on one side; but the horse did not stop until it reached the bottom. The former was obliged 
to proceed on foot three miles to the before-mentioned plantation of Rocha, charging the magis- 
trate of a village in the vicinity where we had partaken of some refreshments, with the task of 
recovering his horse if it was still alive: the Indians accordingly brought it to him in the course 
of the night, very little hurt, our companion being happy to find himself safe and sound not- 
withstanding his fright. From this plantation we proceeded to Cordova, passing through the 
shady town of Naranjal, which is situated on the right bank of a considerable river named the 
Blanco, where we made every exertion to obtain information respecting the antiquities which might 
exist there and in the neighbouring district. We accordingly commenced our researches at the 
town of Amatlan de los Reyes, anxious to view a certain ancient edifice, which on inspecting we 
found to contain merely the ruins of an oratory; but learning that a cave formerly dedicated to 
idolatrous worship was situated at a short distance from it, we proceeded thither, accompanied by 
the curate, the vicar, and a number of Indians, notwithstanding the inconvenience to which we were 
exposed by a heavy fall of rain. The cave itself is curious, and is exceedingly picturesque: it 
may easily be perceived that Art has aided Nature ; it is situated on the declivity of a hill overgrown 
with wood, and we discovered in it various fragments of idols in stone and of baked clay. 

No. VII. From Cordova we directed our course towards Orizaba, through the Indian village of Cha- 
pulco; when passing through some beautiful forests of evergreen oak, adorned with many parasitical 
plants seemingly engrafted upon them, we arrived at another Indian village, named Alcucingo, and from 
thence came to Orizaba. We discovered there a colossal figure (No. 7.) sculptured in basso-relievo, 
on the plain and horizontal surface of an isolated piece of rock which forms part of the floor of an 
Indian cabin, which is situated on the skirts of a plain named Escamela: it lies exactly east and 
west, with its arms and legs open and apart, in the attitude as it would appear of pointing with 
them to the north and south. At its sides are two hieroglyphical figures: that on the right is a large 
fish in a vertical position, with a round unit on one side of it; the other, on the left, is a rabbit 

in a sitting posture with a hieroglyphic between its legs, with ten round units which serve as a 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 425 

border to it: the principal figure, which wears a plume of feathers and a girdle, is twenty-seven feet 
in length; the others on its sides are less. The rock itself is of a somewhat triangular shape, being 
a solid block of stone of a dark colour: its edge or base is six feet above the surface of the ground, 
and some mysterious characters are sculptured upon it. 

No. VIII. shows the profile of a head of the natural size. It has neither hair nor beard, and was 
found in the cave above mentioned, as well as the trunk described in the following number. 

No. IX. is a stone representing the trunk of a human body, of the natural size, and well proportioned 
except the feet. These two antique pieces are executed in the same kind of stone as that of which 
the cave is composed,—a sort of brown limestone. This last figure is placed upon its legs, such 
being the position in which the idols of the country were usually represented. From hence we went 
to the bridge of the river Blanco, about forty-eight miles south-east of Orizaba, in search of a large 
stone called Teololinga. 

No. X. This stone is spherical in its form, very hard (though it will not emit fire when struck by 
the steel), and of a dark blue colour. It has evidently been wrought into its present shape, and 
placed in the middle of a spacious plain, by the ancient inhabitants of the country. It is so artfully 
balanced upon its axis as to revolve at the slightest touch of the finger, but if a greater force be used 
it will stand without the least apparent motion. Its surface contains some holes capable of holding a 
small quantity of water. It appears to have anciently served as a land-mark. ‘There is another of 
these stones to the east, about six miles distant. ey 

No. XI. From the bridge of Rio Blanco we went to the native Indian village now called Santiago 
Guatusco, and formerly Huatdscle, within the jurisdiction of Cordova. This village is about thirty- 
six miles east of Cordova, and is situated on the bank of a rapid river called Xamapa, the temperature 
of which is remarkably warm. ‘The inhabitants are chiefly employed in catching the boby, a large 
and savoury fish which abounds in this river. ‘The ancient town of Guatusco was situated about two 
miles off, upon the same bank of the river, and many of its remains are yet visible on the slope of a 
high mountain called the Old Town. On its summit stands an ancient building, called by the 
neighbouring inhabitants ‘“ The Castle,” which we determined to inspect on the following day. For 
this purpose we arose very early, having engaged a number of Indians, furnished with hatchets and 
other tools, to clear our path. After a laborious and circuitous ascent of more than six miles, 
alternately walking, creeping, and leaping from stone to stone, always in danger of being bitten by 
the many venomous reptiles which abound there, we arrived at the base of that ancient monument. 
This work, intended either for a palace or a great oratory, consists of two stories. The basement 
story is very massy, and of a pyramidical form, divided into three narrow platforms intended merely 
for ornament. A broad and lofty flight of stairs leads to the porch of the second story, which forms the 
place of residence. ‘This is divided into three apartments: the first is a spacious oblong saloon, the 
roof of which is upheld by three pilasters; the other apartments are of unequal dimensions, and into 
these there do not appear to have been any other means of admitting light than through the large door 
which opened into the saloon. Several of the timbers which supported the roof are yet remaining. 
The building terminates in a kind of terrace, the walls of which are a yard in thickness. The whole 
is covered with polished cement, in which are imbedded rows of square stones placed in parallel 

lines. The frieze of each side of the building is enriched with compartments formed by round stones, 

(5a) 

426 THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

similarly imbedded, in the form of a parallelogram. ‘The sides of the saloon are rather inclining, 
those of the other rooms perpendicular. The walls are, throughout, about three yards in thickness, 
and the height of the building from the foot of the battlemented staircase to its summit is twenty- 
four yards. The basement story is about eighty yards square. The dimensions may be more 
accurately traced by the graduated scale on the annexed drawing. 

Among the causes which have assisted in the destruction of this very ancient edifice, perhaps the 
chief is the number of trees and plants which have taken root within its neglected walls, and 
compelled their massy joints to separate where they impeded the progress of vegetation. The front 
of the building is to the west; the other sides face the different points of the compass. With two or 
three exceptions, all the Mexican temples are thus placed: it is presumed, in conformity to an 
established law of their religion. We were unable to discover here more than three sculptured 
fragments. 

No. XII. This represents a goddess. Her head is richly adorned, and her neck also graced with 
a necklace of two rows.. The figure is supported by two columns. It is well executed and in 
good preservation, bearing some resemblance to the ancient statues of the Egyptians. The same 
symmetry is observable in Mexican sculpture as in Mexican architecture; and to this figure its 
due and proper proportions must have been given by instruments corresponding to our rule, level, 
and compass. 

No. XIII. The second figure is a snake curiously entwined. It is carved from a ponderous and 
fine-grained stone of a blackish colour (similar to that of the former figure): the head and body are 
fanciful. The snake was a prominent object in the ancient Mexican mythology; and we find it 
frequently carved in different shapes and sizes, coiled, extended, spiral, or entwined with great art 
and beauty ; sometimes clothed with feathers or with scales, at other times divested of any covering. 
These different representations probably denoted its different attributes. 

No. XIV. The third figure is a somewhat fanciful resemblance of a skull. It exhibits only the 
holes for the eyes, and is furnished, instead of teeth, with what appear rather like claws. It is 
executed in the same kind of stone as Figures 8 and 9 found in the cave of Amatlan. 

No. XV. In the annexed drawing under this Number is shown a sort of block, or die of baked 
clay, which we found in the same place. We may see from this that they were acquainted with the 
use of this tool; and I have in my possession two fragments of ancient blocks very finely designed, 
which were employed to stamp their calicoes and the paper which they made of the aloe-tree.. I 
have also some small figures of terracotta which prove that the ancient Mexicans were not ignorant 
of the art of modelling. 

No. XVI. Unfortunately our draftsman fell sick in this town ; and being deprived of his assistance, 
-I was unable to continue the route proposed to the Government, through the provinces of Oaxaca and 
Chiapa. Obliged to return, I determined to pass through the district of Cuernavaca. At the country- 
house called San Antonio, formerly San Andres Chachicomula, I saw an ancient edifice; and two miles 
further to the north of the country-house an oratory four stories high, in a pyramidal form, resting 
upon an oblong base. The highest story, which I conjecture was a small covered oratory, is now 
destroyed. ‘Twelve years ago when I visited this spot it was in existence. The stairs, which were 
facing the west, are also demolished, as well as the other sides, which corresponded to the cardinal points. 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 497 

The basement story was coated with volcanic stones regularly squared, and the upper stories were 
plastered and bright. ‘The exact dimensions of these ancient edifices cannot always be ascertained, 
some local circumstances occasionally rendering the operation impracticable ; but every care has been 
taken in giving the admeasurements in such cases with the nearest possible approximation to accuracy. 
The human form lives its appointed time and disappears for ever, leaving behind it its likeness: 
but the monuments of Mexican grandeur sink into decay without the chance of restoration or 
reproduction, and the time is fast approaching when their entire destruction will be effected. From 
the country-house of San Antonio we passed through the village of San Andres Chachicomula and 
Acatzingo, to Cholula. In this famous city we stopped a few days for the purpose of prosecuting our 
researches. 

No. XVII. The first thing we found was a human head of stone singularly formed into the capital 
of a column, after the manner of a caryatid. A crown adorned with plumes encircles its brow, and 
its ears are fanciful. ‘The material is a blackish volcanic stone. 

No. XVIII. On the threshold of a dwelling-house on the high road we discovered another stone 
or slab, of an ash colour, on the surface of which are various hieroglyphics. They are inclosed 
within a circle of about a foot in diameter, and deeply engraven in the stone. On the lower part of 
the circle are inscribed thirteen radii, which diverge from the same point, and terminate in ovals; on 
the upper division are two indeterminate rays, also meeting in the same centre. It is impossible to 
state with certainty the use of this symbol; but the probable conjecture is, that it was connected with 
some of the astronomical observations practised in Choldllan, or Cholula as it is now called. 

No. XIX. In this city Isaw also a mask made of dark green jasper. It rather exceeds the natural 
size, is extremely well carved and polished, and when struck is sonorous. The features, which are 
regular and well proportioned, are truly characteristic of the Mexican nation. The mouth and 
nose are pierced, and two holes are also made in the temples. This ancient relic was found, as I 
was informed, in the progress of an excavation which was made on the side of the great pyramid. 

No. XX. This stupendous work, the result of so much labour, in form resembles the celebrated 
structures of Egypt. It consists of successive stories which gradually diminish as they rise, but its 
present appearance has been somewhat changed by the all-consuming hand of Time, the four corners 
having been worn away until its outline has almost assumed a conical form. It is built of sun-dried 
bricks, and its angles, like those of similar monuments, front the cardinal points. 'The ascent was on 
the side facing the west, and the stairs evidently traversed diagonally from story to story. It is not 
easy to ascertain its original height above the city (on the level of which it stands), so extensive are 
the ravages which time has made; and it is by means of excavations in its sides that the materials 
employed in its structure have been ascertained. The Mexican oratories were usually of a pyra- 
midical form, not exceeding seven stories in height, and resting on a circular or oblong base ;—as 
I have more fully delineated and described in reference to the celebrated and truly stupendous 
pyramid of Papantla. 

No. XXI. We left Choldllan, taking the road to the town of Atlixco, where we stopped but a 
short time, and proceeded to the ancient city of Quauhquechtla. Here we found various pieces of 
sculpture. The first was inscribed on an isolated rock which stands on a plot of ground within the city: 
it is the figure of a creeping snake, executed in alto-relievo on the surface of the rock. The skin 

428 THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

appears to be smooth, and at the end of the tail are four or five rattles: the tongue is long, and 
terminates in an anchor, accompanied with a circle. The rock is formed of a hard and dark- 
coloured stone. 

No. XXII. There is another rock in the same field, somewhat similar though not so large. On 
one of its sides is carved, in basso-relievo, a shield vertically placed, and divided into four com- 
partments perpendicular to the horizon, on which are carved several small circles regularly placed. 
They are surrounded by a circular moulding which partly conceals three arrows or darts, which 
with their quiver form across. ‘The stone is similar in quality to that of which the last-mentioned — 
rock is composed. ‘These devices or trophies clearly evince the warlike character of the Mexicans ; 
and by means of such emblems of war, engraven on hard and durable stone, they probably in- 
tended to perpetuate some glorious and memorable event. 

No. XXIII. In another field I discovered, sculptured in relievo upon the four sides of a detached 
rock of a conical form, another ancient military trophy. On the front is represented a fanciful and 
monstrous head, which serves as a base to the whole. On the back there are four arrows undulated 
in imitation of lightning, crossed by a quiver; over which is a circular shield studded with figures 
somewhat resembling turbans, regularly disposed. The two lateral sides are adorned with an eagle, 
breast-plates, and other warlike symbols. This block is movable, and is composed of very hard stone 
of various colours, purple, blue, and grey. When removed, we discovered a snake and a centipede 
of great size lurking below. The height is one yard and a half, and the circumference three yards 
and three quarters. 

No. XXIV. represents a rock which is situated about a gun-shot eastward from the city. On the 
side which faces the city is carved a man’s head in relievo, rather larger than the size of nature. Its 
brow is adorned with a diadem ; its ears are monstrous, but in its other features there is design and 
proportion. 

No. XXV. From this city we travelled to the country-house called Santa Catalina, where I saw 
two pieces of sculpture. One represents a snake so entwined, that the space within the folds of its 
body forms a fent sufficiently large to contain a considerable quantity of water. The stone is volcanic, 
blackish, and somewhat porous. ‘The body of the reptile is spirally entwined, and the head probably 
served as a handle to move it. Itis decorated with circles, and the tail is that of a rattlesnake. 

No. XXVI. is the statue of a man, executed in the same kind of stone. Its attitude is expressive, 
and the mask which veils its countenance has a ludicrous expression. All the ancient statues ought not 
to be regarded as idols; some of them were the appendages of luxury, and some were designed for 
ornament or decoration. Our residence at this country-house of Santa Catalina, which is situated 
on the eastern brow of the volcano of Puebla, called by the Indians Popotepec, (or The Smoking 
Mountain,) would have afforded me an opportunity of ascending to the summit, in order to inspect 
its crater, which I had for a long while desired ; but the continuance of bad weather compelled me 
to postpone this undertaking till another visit. 

No. XXVII. We therefore directed our course to the town of Ayacapistla, and thence to the sugar- 
mill of Casasano, where we saw two ancient fragments. One is a box with a lid very well fitted, and 
made of a firm grey stone : it was found near the mill by the labourers on opening a ditch, and con- 

tained some trinkets made of flint. 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 4.29 

No. XXVIII. The other is a circular design carved upon the upper surface ofa stone. 'The division 
made in the plane of the circle is very curious, being accurately traced according to the rules of 
geometry. ‘This sufficiently proves the existence of mathematical knowledge among the ancient 
inhabitants of the country, by some erroneously called barbarians. I conjecture this cylinder to 
have been the base of an idol, or a sacrificial altar: and in treating of works of'such remote 
antiquity, the history or uses of which no written documents explain, conjecture must be admitted. 

No. XXIX. Having nothing more to examine here, we proceeded to Cuernavaca through the town 
of Yauhtepec. The magistrate of this place complied with the requisition of the Royal order by 
affording me all the assistance and information in his power. I began at that part of the town called 
San Antonio, where I found a rock of considerable size, on which the figure of a lizard was sculp- 
tured in alto relievo, accompanied by four convex circles placed at its left in a horizontal line. 

No. XXX. In the place called Chimale (or ‘‘ The spot of the shield,” as it signifies in the Mexican 
language), behind some houses associated by tradition with the name of Cortez, there is an isolated 
rock, on the northern side of which is represented, in relievo, a small turreted castle, with stairs, 
a gate, and an ornamental frieze; on the right of which are three circles or units ranged vertically. 
It is neatly worked, and its parallels are perfectly true. On the other side of the castle is a shield, 
the form of which resembles a cross, with some mouldings, and five mysterious circles placed in a 
perpendicular line to the right. 

No. XXXI. There is another rock about three miles south-east from this town, which apparently 
served as a landmark between this district and that of Quauhnahuac or Quahutetl, which name in 
the Mexican language signifies ‘The eagle of stone.” On the side of the rock facing the west is 
sculptured an eagle with a beak, wings, tail and open claws. The head is ornamented with several 
radiated circles concentric to the eye. This bird is represented too gross in the drawing; the relievo 
projects about an inch and a half, and is worked on a variegated stone of fine grain. 

No. XXXII. On the opposite side of the rock there is a circular shield, which is divided vertically. 
In the left partition are four concentric semicircles ; the right is divided into two quarters. In the 
upper appears the plan of a city situated on the bank of a lake (possibly that of Chalco). The lower 
quarter contains various ovals in close rows, while underneath the shield are five ornamented arrows 
horizontally placed. To the right appears an unfurled standard, which, it is extraordinary, should 
display on its surface a cross of the order of Malta; and at the top a helmet, on which is figured the 
head of an eagle, with a hieroglyphic appended. ‘The whole of the shield is carved with great 
regularity and symmetry. The inhabitants of Cuernavaca, or Quauhnahuac, which signifies in the 
Mexican language “ The resting place of the eagle,” intended to perpetuate their trophies by fixing 
them on the durable surface of their rocks. 

No. XXXII. From Cuernavaca we proceeded to the westward, in order to visit a village of Indians 
called Tetlama, in the Mexican language “The place of stones.” It is situated on a very sultry 
plain, about eighteen miles from that town. At three miles to the south of the village are the ruins 
of a celebrated work called Xochicalco: it was an oratory or palace built by the ancient Mexicans, 
and is a splendid monument of the genius of that people, developing their skill both in architecture 
and sculpture. It is placed on the summit of a natural and isolated mountain of a conical form. Its 
exterior is adorned with platforms of various heights and breadths, supported by massy stone walls 

CoRR) 

430 THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

gradually slanting inwards as they attain greater elevation. This peculiarity in its structure renders 
the conjecture probable, that it was designed as a fortified building capable of resisting any 
hostile attack. The ascent to the top where the monument is placed is by an old causeway, 
with a considerable inclination. The area is inclosed by a wall of loose stones, which serves as a 
parapet. The base or first story of the building is the only part now remaining; it is the 
beginning of an oblong pyramid with its plinth. This solid story is divided into three unequal 
parts ; the first, which has some declivity, serves as a base; the second is the frieze, plain and 
vertical ; and the third is a projecting cornice: the whole forming a pedestal. The outside is 
constructed with large square stones firmly united, and differing in their dimensions from three 
feet long, and appropriately wide and thick, to six feet. They are compact, and of a blackish 
colour. The four sides, like those of the other pyramids, face the four winds; the stairs occu- 
pying the western side. It is evident that the sculptural ornaments in relievo on the other three 
sides were executed after the masonry of the building was finished, since some of the figures extend 
into several courses of the work. The same designs are repeated on each side; they consist of a 
variety of hieroglyphical subjects, men, animals, plants, and other unknown figures. The whole 
building was painted over with vermilion, which now appears in various parts of its ‘surface. 
The second body or story (which was the base or pedestal) was likewise oblong, and served as a 
habitation or covered temple ; its four faces corresponding to the same cardinal points and perpen- 
dicular to the base. It is built of the same kind of stone ; but the fragments which are strewed at its 
foot denote figures of a different character to those of the first story. Its height cannot now be ascer- 
tained, but we may suppose it to have been in proportion to that of the base. The stairs were from 
five to six yards wide, and their height, rising by a gentle ascent, about thirteen yards. I could dis- 
cover only the trunks of two great idols carved in stone, lying on the floor of the large area. Here 
again I had to regret that the neighbouring trees had pushed their spreading roots into the joints of 
the masonry, and assisted in the demolition of this ancient edifice. 

In the adjacent parts, scattered without any apparent order, are many small artificial hills of cir- 
cular shape and of various heights, formed partly of masonry and partly of earth. These (if they were 
not the sepulchres of their dead) might have been the minor oratories or military posts of the 
Mexicans, like the works which encircle the greater part of the mountain. 

This sort of fortification was adapted to the mode of warfare which they practised, and, in the present 
instance, a deep fosse also encircled the base of this celebrated mountain. ‘The circumference of the 
mountain is about three miles, and its perpendicular elevation about one hundred yards. The Mexican 
name of this curious edifice (Xochicalco), which signifies ‘‘ The house of flowers,” was probably 
derived from the ornaments which enrich its exterior, of which one of the most conspicuous is a kind 
of garland encircling the walls on three sides. . 

The ancient Mexicans appear to have preferred the pyramidical form for the temples of their false 
deities ; and herein they discovered a degree of taste by no means despicable, but rather worthy the 
imitation of those who profess a purer faith. Among all the forms which architecture has devised, 
the pyramid deserves to hold the preeminence, on account of its antiquity, its massiveness, the strictly 

geometrical regularity of its structure, and its majestic height. In this stupendous monument all these 
are combined. 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. A31 

No. XXXIV. In an adit, called the Cave, which the ancient Mexicans opened in the northern 
side of the hard rock which forms the mountain Xochicalco, there is a narrow aperture, serving 
as the entrance to several galleries more than six feet in height. By the advice of the Governor of the 
Indians, who accompanied us, we unsheathed our swords before we entered, in order to defend our- 
selves from the attacks of the lions and wolves, which, he said, often harboured there: and, each 
taking a torch in his hand, we entered the mountain about six o’clock in the evening. 

This subterraneous recess contains various passages, opened in different directions; the ceilings and 
walls of which are smooth, and the pavements which yet partially exist are made with cement and 
covered with red ochre. The difficulty of proceeding from one passage to another was occasionally 
great and not unattended with danger, as we were sometimes obliged to creep along the broken ruins 
of decayed walls and roofs. | 

At the extremity of the gallery, which is about sixty yards from the entrance, are two saloons, 

divided by two pilasters formed of the hard stone of the mountain. In a corner of the innermost apart- 
ment, a conical cupola, two yards in width, and rather more in height, is constructed in the solid 
roof overhead, from the upper surface of which proceeds a tube about nine inches in diameter, which 
served the purpose of ventilation. ‘The whole interior is faced with square stones placed in circular 
rows with great precision and neatness. ‘The floor of these saloons, as well as that of the whole exca- 
vation, is nearly level. It was late when I left the cavern, thankful to Providence for our preserva- 
tion from danger, and filled with pleasing reflections on the wonders I had seen. 
- Now, who would suppose, after visiting this spacious subterranean monument of antiquity, exca- 
vated with great skill, and requiring, from the hardness of the rock, tools of considerable strength and 
temper, that the ancient Mexicans were unacquainted with the use of iron? This, nevertheless, is a 
problem which yet remains to be solved; for no person, as far as my information extends, has ever 
seen any sharp or cutting instruments of this kind of Mexican formation, such as hammers, wedges, 
&c. &c. But, whatever the fact may be, the skill and industry of the ancient Mexicans cannot fail to 
command the admiration of the present and of future generations. 

These subterranean saloons appear rather destined for the repose of the dead than the residence of 
the living, and hence I conjecture this excavation to have been an oratory or private temple consecrated 
to the souls of the departed. These mournful vaults, shrouded in sepulchral darkness, and every thing 
that I observed within them, tended to the same conclusion, that I had entered the mansion of death. 

Thus terminated our first expedition, which employed us rather more than four months, having 
quitted Mexico on the 5th of January 1805, and returned on the 10th of May. During our progress 
we remained in every city and town a sufficient time to enable us to collect from their respective 
governors or magistrates all possible information connected with the object of our commission. I 
would willingly have prolonged our journey, but the weather was now become very sultry and un- 
healthy, particularly in the districts which we had to traverse. We therefore returned to the capital, 
in order to arrange our papers and drawings, and to await the termination of the rainy season ; hold- 
ing ourselves in readiness to begin a second expedition, if the superior Government shall think fit: in 
which event, we should direct our course to the cities of Oaxaca and Chiapa, unless prevented by any 
adverse circumstances : as we are informed that those dioceses contain several important remains of 
-a date anterior to the conquest of this empire.

SECOND EXPEDITION IN SEARCH OF MEXICAN ANTIQUITIES, BY M. DUPAIX. 

Witiram Duparx, retired Captain of the Mexican Dragoons and Director of this expedition, 
left the ancient and imperial city of Mexico on the 24th of February 1806, in obedience to the 
command of our Lord the King; accompanied, as before, by Don Joseph Castaneda, engineer and 
draughtsman; Don Juan Castello, secretary ; and a dragoon. . 

In compliance with the instructions of my commission, we took the southern road from the 
capital to the ancient city of Chochimilco (which in the Mexican language signifies “A fertile 
plain”); and, guided by the information which we had received from the magistrate of the place, 
took up our abode in the old hotel facing the main road. 

No. I. The first object (connected with the purpose of the journey) which engaged my attention, 
was the figure of an animal somewhat resembling a lizard, but probably existing only in the imagi- 
nation of the sculptor, executed in alto relievo on a porous volcanic stone of a red colour. It is of 
large dimensions, and appears in the attitude of moving. The surface of the body and limbs is 
covered with scales regularly placed. 

This soft kind of stone, so well adapted for the purposes of sculpture and masonry, is found in 
various parts of New Spain; although the only use to which the ancient Mexicans seem to have 
applied it, was that of ornamenting and enriching both the exterior and interior of their temples, 
sepulchres, and palaces. It is possible, that by means of these symbolical representations they in- 
tended to designate the situation and use of the building*. 

It will readily be conceived that, in attempting to describe and explain these interesting monu- 
ments of antiquity, I must labour under great difficulty, on account of that originality and peculiarity 
in the style of the Mexican school, which superficial inquirers have spoken of with ill-placed 
contempt. But I shall not, on this account, be deterred from endeavouring to rescue them from 
the oblivion in which they-have been shrouded by the lapse of ages, and to exhibit them to the intel- 
ligent examination of the lovers of antiquity. 

In connection with this subject, I will here state my opinion as to the real cause of the ignorance 
and remarkable diversity of sentiment existing among the Indians, as to the etymology and the 
signification of the ancient names of their towns and various remains of antiquity, which, for the 
most part, were significatory and illustrative of their history. The cause of this confusion is most 
probably to be traced to the mixture, by marriage and otherwise, of their various tribes, as well as 
to the establishment of schools of instruction for the Castilian language. These causes are sufficient 
to account for the corruption of the original tongue, and the change of words and family names pecu-

liar to it: and as I have found myself unable to discriminate between the primitive meaning of the 
Mexican words and those which in later periods were substituted in their stead, ] cannot pretend to 
offer an opinion on the subject. I write the names as they are now spoken and written by all classes 
of the people; and for this reason :—the Mexican language, expressive in its character, and abounding 
with reverential forms of speech, is hastening to decay, and will by degrees be absorbed in the gulf of 
oblivion. The monuments of this nation (which, from its antiquity, language, and its cultivation of 
the arts, might rank among the most renowned of former times) will meet the same, perhaps a more 
speedy fate. The consuming hand of Time, removing even the bases of its pyramids, its temples, its 
sepulchres, and palaces, threatens their approaching and total extinction. The broken statues and 
sculptured stones will crumble away, and thus all the monuments of Mexican grandeur and greatness 
will be a chaotic heap of ruins,—the destined end of the works of man’s ephemeral creation. 

Another painful reflection suggests itself while contemplating this subject, occasioned by the irre- 
parable loss of the historical annals of this country, which were traced in hieroglyphical characters on 
a paper made of the aloe-tree and of cotton. At an early period after the conquest these documents 
were collected and publicly burnt in the square of 'Tescuco ; and thus the key which would have faci- 
litated the interpretation of every inscription and every record has been for ever lost, and all the 
remaining monuments of Mexico buried in impenetrable darkness. 

Many inscriptions on stone yet remain, in defiance of the attacks to which they have been subjected. 
Some of them are deeply engraved ; others are executed in relievo, accompanied with symbolical 
ficures: but I can only describe their appearance, without pretending to discover their meaning, or 
withdraw the mysterious veil which surrounds them. 

No. IJ. Pursuing my researches, I found at the house of Guevaras a stone in the form of a trape- 
zium, which is preserved there. On its surface are two concentric circles, and at the four corners of 
the square other circles, each having a similar convexity in its centre. The stone is hard, and of a 
brown colour. It is placed in its proper position, vertically. Its execution is conformable to the rules 
of art, and it is in a good state of preservation. ‘The design of the artist, in all probability, was to 
appropriate this slab to the decoration of some public building, judging from the purely geometrical 
style of its embellishment *. | 

No. If]. In the quarter of San Marcos in this city, are two similar figures of some monstrous and 
fanciful animal executed in hard red stone, each seated on a square base. They were intended as the 
termination of an aqueduct ; receiving the water at the back of their heads, and discharging it through 
the mouth, eyes, and nose. They are enriched with some ornamental carving on the lower part of 
the head; and the construction of the figures evinces such a theoretical and practical knowledge of 
the principles of hydraulics as was necessary to convey the water from the level of the aqueduct. 

No. IV. In the same place there are two pedestals, both alike, formed of striated limestone, and 
ornamented with alternate ovals and tassels, which are suspended from the upper surface.. The pro- 
jecting base is slightly enriched, but the carving is nearly effaced. These pedestals have been verti- 

cally divided, and the two separate sections when placed together form a semi-globe or altar.
