No. V. About two miles to the north of the city is a rock formed of red-coloured stone, and of a 
conical shape. It is accidentally intersected by the wall of the estate called La Noria. Upon it is 
engraven in relievo a shield surrounded by a circle, the field of which exhibits a device in the form 
of a cross resting upon four ornamented arrows; the lower part is adorned with a row of feathers like 
an opened fan, and several tassels are disposed around at regular intervals. On the opposite side of 
the rock is represented a sort of military kilt or apron, divided into five pendants with semicircular 
ends, crossed by smaller ones as exhibited in the drawing. Some remains of foliage ornament 
the base of the shield, which is now almost buried in the ground. It has been an immemorial 
custom among ancient and warlike nations to perpetuate by sculptured trophies the victories which 
they obtained, and to erect them on the spot where such successes were achieved. 

No. VI. In the house called Acocalco we found the representation of a curious fish carved on a 
close-grained grey stone. Its open mouth discovers a row of teeth, and its fins are regularly placed. 
Its belly, which has no scales, is flat ; and its fins, being of the thickness of the stone, would show the 
figure in relievo when built into a wall. Whether this inhabitant of the waters was formerly wor- 
shiped by the heathens I have not been able to ascertain. 

No. VII. This number refers to five fragments, of different size and colour ; three of which are 
cylindrical, one is in the form of a cross, the other square. They are all carved in relievo on the sur- 
face of the stone, the rough part being intended to be imbedded in a wall. The drawing of the devices 
is geometrically correct, and discovers good taste in the artists who designed and executed them. 

No. VIII. On the doorway of the saltpetre manufactory are carved two monstrous and fanciful 
heads, in red stone. As they are both exactly similar, a drawing of one, shown in profile, will suffice. 
It is worked with skill and delicacy, although the artist appears to have given only the leading out- 
lines of the figure. Its open mouth shows two rows of corresponding teeth and two lateral fangs. The 
proboscis or trunk describes a semicircle bending towards the wall. ‘These threatening and mon- 
strous heads were, probably, placed like sentries at the entrance of their temples and sacred caves, 
in order to inspire the people with fear of their gods. 

No. IX. In the interior of these saltpetre works, two pieces of red stone similarly carved are built 
into the buttress which supports a part of the building. On their square surface are represented two 
nosegays or bunches of herbs, with which the ancient Mexicans were accustomed to adorn the outer 
walls of their public buildings and their private houses. 

No. X. In the house of Don Francisco Solares we discovered, on a slab of dark red porphyry 
variegated with white spots, the figure of a large frog or toad built into the angle of the inner wall of 
the court, and level with the balcony. The reptile appears at rest, and has the singular addition of 
two ears extended along its body. In this respect the figure is imaginary, but its proportions are 
good, and itis well executed. It is well known that the ancient Mexicans worshiped various animals, 
particularly the feathered snake; and it would be interesting, if it were possible, to distinguish such 
human or animal figures as were the subjects of adoration among them, from those which were merely 
used for the purposes of ornament and decoration. But at present there are no sufficient data to 
guide the inquirer, and I shall hence consider them all merely as works of art. 

_ No. XI. On the site of a house now in ruins I discovered a broken slab of volcanic stone of an iron 
colour, upon the surface of which was carved the figure of a rabbit in the attitude of motion. It 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 4.35 

doubtless formed a portion of some wall, where it was placed in a vertical position. This animal was 
one of the signs of the Mexican calendar. 

No. XII. In the doorway of the house of Signor de Santa Cruz, there is inclosed a round stone in 
the form of a shield, the outer rim of which is studded with small circles. On its surface are displayed 
several hieroglyphical figures, with five numerical circles on each side, carved in alto relievo, as 
shown in the annexed drawing. Although the surface of this circle is small, being only about 18 inches 
in diameter, it may be presumed that the hieroglyphical writing, where every dot has a meaning, 
comprehends more ideas than words would be able to convey. 

No. XIII. These figures, the symbols and sad mementos of death, one of which is represented 
in profile, and the other in front, both of the size of a human skull, are built into a wall in the 
court of Donna Ana Paton’s house. The skull was an emblem in frequent use by the ancient 
Mexicans. They carved it in different kinds of stone, and in various ways displayed it on the inte- 
rior and the exterior of the tombs of their deceased relatives. The hinder part of the block whence 
these figures are carved being shaped into a form adapted for the purpose of insertion into masonry, 
shows that it was intended to be so employed. 

No. XIV. In the house of Don Joseph Ortiz there is another hieroglyphical figure of death, consist- 
ing of a gigantic skull carved from a hard red stone, which was most probably employed in the gloomy 
decoration of one of their mausoleums. 

No. XV. In the house of Don Joseph Ystapan, at this time governor of the Indians, we found the 
figure of a snake in porphyry, artificially coiled. Its long body was gracefully entwined, leaving the 
head and the tail free. There is something showy in the execution of this figure. Its head is ele- 
vated and curiously ornamented: its open mouth is defended by two long and pointed fangs ; its 
tongue, which is unusually long, is cloven at the extremity like an anchor ; its body is fancifully scaled, 
and its tail, covered with circles, ends with three rattles. 

The snake was a frequent emblem with the ancient Mexican artists. The flexibility of its figure 
being susceptible of an endless diversity of position regular and irregular, they availed themselves of 
this advantage, and varied their representations of it without limit, and without ever giving it an un- 
natural attitude. Its appellation was derived from its position and the mode of its decoration. Like 
the Egyptian Sphynx, the mystical snake of the Mexicans had its enigmas, and both are equally beyond 
our power to unravel. 

No. XVI. In the threshold of a doorway in the house of Signor Martinez is a block of red stone 
with a plain moulding, on the surface of which is sculptured in basso-relievo the figure of a strange 
amphibious animal. The scaly head and tail resemble those of a fish; four bands are placed across 
the body, the ends of which appear like paws. In our conjectures on the origin and design of these 
fanciful figures, we must be careful not to assign a mysterious character to that which may have been 
only the extravagant invention of the artist. ; 

No. XVII. In the Town-hall I saw another stone, of a dark brown colour, carved into the likeness 
of an Indian female, seated in a tranquil position with her legs doubled under her. She is clothed in 
a short garment, which is confined with a sash tasseled at each end; and her hair is formed into 
various tresses. ‘The sex of the figure is indicated by the breasts. The simplicity of the dress leads 
us to refer its date to those early periods when luxury was unknown; and, on this account, no 

436 THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

accurate conjecture can be formed whether it was intended to typify a deity, or merely some 
individual personage. It has neither ornament nor appendage by which its character may be guessed 
at ; and as there is no other way of classifying a bird but by its plumage, it is to be regretted that 
this uncertainty must, in some measure, pervade the entire series of these descriptions. 

No. XVIII. This statue, of red stone, which we discovered in the house of a shoemaker, is also 
seated in the same posture (the usual attitude of Mexican sculpture), its legs being folded under its 
body. It is entirely naked, and its forehead is encircled with a diadem adorned with bands studded 
with pearls. Its ears are also ornamented. The lower part of the figure is somewhat mutilated. 
Although its head, as well as the ornaments attached to it, are characteristic of manhood, the great 
prominence of the breasts evidently denotes its sex.; unless the artist by this ambiguous or equivocal 
design intended to represent an hermaphrodite. 

No. XIX. In a room at the entrance of the saltpetre works I found this monstrous head or skull. 
It is executed in red stone, of the natural size. The upper part of the forehead, though resembling 
a skull, is ornamented: the eyes are circular, and the nostrils highly relieved; the open mouth dis- 
covers two formidable rows of teeth, and on each side of the head the hair is separated into two long 
tassels. ‘The workmanship is excellent, and does credit to the artist. What shall we think of this 
singular production, in which life is so mixed up with death? It has no resemblance to those heads 
which adorned the walls of the ancient Mexican buildings, but had, doubtless, a different destination, 
although I am unable to assign it. 

No. XX. In the house of Joseph Pichardo, the Alcade of the Indians, a circular red stone is 
imbedded in the wall, the surface of which is divided into regular compartments surrounding a 
circle, in the centre of which is a human head, also perfectly circular, and resembling the usual 
representations of the full moon. It is surmounted by the figure of a cross. I was at a loss to con- 
jecture its design. At first sight it seemed to resemble a shield; but I was afterwards inclined to 
regard it as some astronomical emblem, on account of the apparent figure of the full moon, placed 
in the centre of its orbit. Or it may be a work of mere fancy, designed, from its masterly execution, 
to enrich, with others of equal excellence, some considerable building. 

No. XXI. From this city we proceeded to the ancient town of Cuitlahuac, a word which in the 
Mexican language means “ The deposit of the waters.” It is situated on a fine island in the middle 
of the lake of Chalco, almost on a level with its surface, and surrounded by many inhabited 
Chinampas*. The communication with the shore is by means of two causeways stretching to 
opposite points of the compass, the one to the north-east, the other to the south-west, and extending, 
in their whole length, about three miles. This noble work, which was constructed by the ancient 
natives with volcanic stone, sand, turf, and stakes, is from five to six yards wide, varying in its 
height according to the depth of the lake; and, after the lapse of so many centuries, it remains 
unimpaired, and continues to be used for the purpose of its first destination, evincing at once the 
solidity of its foundations and its skilful execution. 

In this town we discovered the following remains. At the entrance of the parish church-yard are 

two volcanic stones, of a porous substance and black colour, lying on the ground, and somewhat 

* Small floating islands. 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 437 

resembling millstones in their shape. The one which is in the best preservation has a pedestal or base, 
intended to support it perpendicularly on some solid foundation of earth or masonry. The surface of 
each side is deeply engraven. The figure carved on the stone has the singular appearance of being 
retained by its own gravity in its present position. The sculpture on each side is similar. Its form is 
partly human and partly animal ; or, probably, merely ideal, accompanied by some lines of which I 
was unable to develope the meaning. I cannot conjecture to what purpose these stones were applied 
by the ancient Mexicans; whether to that of amusement, of worship, or of sacrifice: yet being found 
in several different towns, they must have been of general use. 

No. XXII. In the hut of an Indian, situated in a Chinampa, is a pedestal or sacrificial altar, of a 
cylindrical shape, formed of a hard and dark-coloured stone. The upper surface is a plain circular 
tablet, the edge of which is ornamented with carving in relievo, and intersected by several parallel 
and regularly arranged fillets. It is probable that to each imaginary deity worshipped by these 
heathens was assigned his peculiar altar, being in shape either circular or polygon. 

No. XXIII. In the rector’s house we were shown a circular stone vase, the whole exterior of which 
discovers great skill in the artist. Its carved ornaments and mouldings are fancifully entwined around, 
displaying a graceful symmetry: the interior (of which the diameter is about eighteen inches) is 
covered with symbolical figures, disposed in the same order. The execution is neat, and the stone 
of which the vessel is formed is hard, fine-grained, and of an iron colour. It is sonorous and suffi- 
ciently hard to emit sparks when struck by the steel. The engraving on this curious isolated vessel 
has neither beginning nor end (a fit emblem of eternity); but as I have no clue by which to 
determine its use, or to decipher the hieroglyphics with which it is covered, I forbear to offer any 
superfluous conjectures. 

No. XXIV. We proceeded by water to the village of Misquique, lying only a short distance from 
Cuitlahuac, and which probably derived its name from the misquite tree, so abundant in this country. 
It is situated on an island of the same lake, somewhat larger than the last-mentioned one, and is 
surrounded by Chinampas. ‘The communication with the main land is on the western side, by means 
of a long causeway of ancient date. I found there a well-executed head, of frightful aspect, 
intended by the ancient Mexicans to project from the wall of some public edifice. There is no 
attempt at any imitation of nature; imagination alone has given existence to it. This head, carved 
out of a blackish volcanic stone, was once painted with vermilion, some of which yet adheres to it. 
The Mexicans were accustomed to give a gaudy appearance to their works, both of sculpture and 
architecture, by the use of various colours. They first applied a coat of lime or some whitish sub- 
stance, and then another of yellow ; but red, as the most brilliant of the prismatic colours, appears 
to have been most frequently used. 

No. XXV. In a wall facing the churchyard chance has introduced a stone, on the surface of which 
are designed several circles in alto-relievo, with some symmetrical ornaments, all having a common 
centre. 

No. XXVI. Another stone of the same kind is imbedded in the walls of the church steeple, exhibiting 

on its face a spiral ornament in relievo. If, divesting ourselves of prejudice, we were to enumerate 

"the various purely geometrical figures on those stones which have already been described and deli- 

neated, they would bear sufficient and ample testimony that the ancient Mexicans were acquainted 
(ee) 

438 THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

with the elements of geometry, whether it existed among them in theory or only in practice. It is 
time, therefore, that we dismiss those erroneous impressions which are merely the result of imperfect 
information, and learn to respect those intellectual powers, which enabled the natives of this vast 
continent to enrich it with works of art. 

No. XXVIII. In the parish church is preserved a large ancient vessel, formed out of a block of 
hard marble, and now used as a baptismal font. The lower part is flat, and the border is enriched 
with ornamental foliage. What an immense number of strokes must the chisel have given, to hollow out 
a space of which the circumference is thirteen feet and a half, leaving only the thickness of five inches 
in the rim, and exhibiting correctness of proportion with a highly polished surface. The exterior and 
interior of the vessel were formerly covered with a fine and burnished cement. It was, no doubt, 
designed to hold some particular liquor, but of what kind or for what use, it is difficult to conjecture. 
We know that the ancient Romans employed lustral waters to sprinkle the animal victims in their 
holocausts ; and perhaps in the New World a similar practice existed, where not only beasts but 
human beings were offered in sacrifice: or the vessel may have been applied to the purpose of 
holding water, with which to wash the bodies of the dead before they were committed to their last 
home. 

No. XXVIII. In the wall of an inclosure near the church, I discovered a brown and porous 
volcanic stone, somewhat resembling that delineated in No. 21. It differs in size as well as in 
design, but its use was probably similar to that which I have described above. 

No. XXIX. In the vestry of the old village church is a heathen altar, of an iron-grey colour and 
a cylindrical form. On the centre of the shaft is carved a snake in alto-relievo, partly coiled 
up, and adorned with a crown and plume of feathers. The mouth is open, and the tongue cloven 
at its end: the body is covered with scales, and the tail terminates with rattles. There are some 
other devices or enigmatical figures, all inclosed within two mouldings, and the whole appears to 
have been painted red. 

We cannot help pitying those dark and wretched times, when the altars of heathenism were stained 
with the smoking blood of victims, offered up in the vain hope of propitiating idol deities, alike 
insensible to hatred as to love. 

No. XXX. In the wall of a house called La Tecpan, is inclosed a slab of black and fine-grained 
volcanic stone, on which is sculptured in mezzo-relievo the figure of a wild dog, which, however, 
displays but little of that animal’s natural character. It appears to have been formerly covered with 
a varnish or wash of fine lime. The Mexican draughtsmen, in their delineations of flowers and 
animals, were generally very correct imitators of simple nature ; in works of imagination they were 
not equally expert. 

The proportions of the human form they sometimes grossly violated, evidently not from ignorance 
of their art, since many of their works display correctness of design; but rather in consequence of 
some political or religious laws existing in the Mexican empire, which compelled its artists to 
give to the statues of their deities a similarity of attitude and a uniformity of style and character ;— 
as in Egypt, where the priests prescribed fixed rules for statuary and the formation of images ; thus 
fettering the inventive genius of the artist, and checking the progress of sculpture. 

No. XXXI. In the house of an Indian, situated on the banks of the lake to the north of the church, 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 439 - 

we found a human head of the natural size, formed of a dark purple-coloured volcanic stone, and 
decorated on each side with similar ornaments and pendants. This is one of the figures so much used 
by the ancient Indians, for the purpose of fixing into their walls by means of the shaft before men- 
tioned. The Mexicans not only attempted to adorn, but in some measure to give animation to the 
fronts of their temples and palaces, by geometrical designs or the figures of animals. And they like- 
wise made use of the human form for the same purpose; thus uniting every species of embellishment 

-in the decoration of these buildings. I regard this kind of ornament as peculiar to the Mexican 
nation, and employed according to rules prescribed by their taste in architecture. 

Nos. XXXII & XXXII. These numbers refer to two small stone idols of fantastic shape, the 
originals being of the same size as the drawings. The first is in a sitting posture ; its head raised as 
if in the act of contemplation, and covered with a kind of skull-cap. Its body is without arms. A 
perpendicular hole passes through the figure, which was thus suspended by a rope. The stone is 
unctuous, glossy, and of a blackish ash colour. It appears to have been polished by being rubbed 
with another stone. 

The other figure is formed of a volcanic stone, of the colour of half heated iron. It is in a muti- 
lated state, having neither arms nor legs. On the head is placed an ornamented cap: the features 
are prominent and expressive ; the eyes are closed, and the mouth open as if singing, or expressing 
suffering ; the body appears to have been flayed to the lower extremity of the ribs. 

These figures may be considered either as household gods, or as mere toys formed for no definite 
purpose. Their forms are infinitely varied ; some being painted, others appearing in the colour of 
the substance of which they are composed. These pigmy and portable divinities, the tutelar gods of 
the Mexican houses, were common to most of the nations of antiquity. ‘The Scriptures mention the 
“images” or idols of Laban, which were probably formed of baked clay: the histories of the Egyp- 
tians and of the ancient Romans record the existence of their household deities ; and we know from 
the records of this kingdom that the Mexicans had likewise their Penates, who were always treated 
with veneration, and placed in the most honourable part of their houses. It is evident that these little 
idols were bored through for the purpose of being affixed to the walls. 

_ No. XXXIV. Having finished our researches in this village, we went to that of Tlalmanalco, where 
we found in the house of the priest a female bust. It is well executed ina sort of green stone which the 
natives name Chalchihuitl ; its size is rather beyond that of nature, and its proportions are well formed. 
The features of its face and the prominence of its breasts discover its sex. The ornaments of the head 
are carved in relievo and disposed in regular order ; the bosom contains a square concavity, well 
adapted for receiving a plate of gold or silver. This bust was probably so formed with a view to its 
being placed on the top of some temple or pyramid fronting the East, in order that the rays of the 
rising sun or moon falling on the burnished surface of the plate might reflect and diffuse a beautiful 
and brilliant light. 

No. XXXV. In the house of a neighbouring Indian we found a human figure perfect from the 
waist upwards, carved from a pale ash-coloured stone. There was nothing remarkable in its ap- 
pearance, except that its arms were raised, and the hands shut and reclining on its breast. 

No. XXXVI. This block of stone, of a somewhat cubical shape, served as a small pedestal. It is 
enriched with ornaments, and formed part of an old wall. 

44,0 THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

No. XXXVII. This is a woman’s head slightly decorated. The artist has taken nature for his model, 
and the bust is fashioned according to her unchanging rules. Its substance is a firm and finely-grained 
stone, of a lead colour. It is evident that it was originally covered with some white and glossy compo- 
sition. We found it in the curate’s house, and there the annexed drawing was made. As the contour 
of the human head is the greatest difficulty the sculptor has to surmount in the execution of a statue, 
it is to be regretted that in the present work of art, the limbs and the rest of the body should be want- 
ing ; since he who succeeded so well in the most elaborate part of the sculpture would not be likely to 
have failed in that which was of easier execution. 

Nos. XX XVIII. XXXIX. & XL. These numbers represent three stone statues, which were found 
in a wall of the mill called La Madonna del Socorro. The first is seated in an easy posture ; her 
arm is raised, as if she were lifting something with her hand (which has been broken off) to her 
mouth. 

No. XXXIX. represents the bust of a female, designed according to the ancient and primitive 
style of Egyptian sculpture. It was originally a work of skilful execution, but destructive Time has 
now very much impaired it. ’ : 

No. XL. is remarkable for its strange and monstrous formation. It consists of a head without a 
body, covered with a sort of conical cap. It stands on two legs, its hands resting on its knees. This 
very rare figure, which is probably symbolical, has in its style some resemblance to the preceding one. 

No. XLI. In the wall of a ruined house I found another stone of a cubical figure; on one 
side of which are represented in alto-relievo two bones crossed, and inclosed in a square moulding. 
I imagine that these last relics of a part of the human body were placed in some mausoleum, and 
were designed to infuse into the mind of the spectator that horror which such emblems of death are 
so well adapted to inspire. 

No. XLII. The block of stone represented in this drawing is of an oblong form, encircled with a 
moulding. In the centre of its surface is a figure of regular design, resembling a flower with six 
petals. This ornamented slab, like some before mentioned, served to enrich the front or doorway 
of some public or private building. 

No. XLII. In the hut of an Indian we found the figure of an unknown animal, represented (as in 
the annexed drawing) in profile. The stone which forms its substance is close-grained, of an iron- 
grey colour, and capable of receiving a fine polish. The lifeless attitude of this animal would seem 
to mark the appearance of an embryo extracted from the womb, while its execution displays the 
elaborate attention of the artist. I am entirely ignorant to what class of animals it should be referred, 
and equally at a loss to assign the reason for perpetuating its likeness in sculpture. 

No. XLIV. In the road from the village of Tlalmanalco to that of Mecamecan, about three miles 
eastward of the latter, and within the boundaries of the estate of Senor Don Joseph Tepatolco, there 
is an isolated rock of granite, artificially formed into a conical shape, out of which are hollowed six 
steps facing the East. The summit of the rock forms a platform or horizontal plane, well adapted to 
the observation of the stars on every side of the hemisphere. It is almost demonstrable that this very 
ancient monument was exclusively devoted to astronomical observations ; for, on the south side of the 
rock are engraved several hieroglyphical figures having a relation to that science. But the most 

striking feature in the group is the figure of a man in profile, standing erect, and directing his view 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 44,1 

to the rising of the planets in the heavens. He holds to his eyes a tube or optical instrument, 
Underneath his feet is a frieze divided into six compartments, with as many celestial signs carved on 
its surface : the results, most probably, of such observations as had been made and calculated. Some 
of these symbols have an affinity to those, which are to be found in that ancient Mexican sphere which 
is an object of such attention and admiration to all who visit the city of Mexico. In front of the figure 
is engraved the likeness of a rabbit sitting, as well as two parallel rows of numerical signs. In addition 
to these, there are two symbols connected with astronomical science. This interesting discovery will 
of itself be sufficient to convince the most incredulous, that astronomy was known and cultivated by 
the ancient Mexicans. 

No. XLV. At a short distance from Mecamecan, or Amatemecan, is situated the town of Ozumpa. 
On our arrival there we discovered in the pavement of the churchyard a circular piece of stone, of a 
hard and ferruginous substance. Its surface is divided by radii proceeding from the centre of the 
circle to its circumference. The regularity displayed in the perforation of this stone, had probably 
no other design than that of varying and adorning its appearance. 

No. XLVI. In the town of Chimalhuacan Tlachialco, not far distant from Ozumpa, I found the 
stone represented in the annexed drawing. It was discovered in the house of an Indian, behind the 
Town Hall. Its form is circular, and in its centre is carved a flower with six petals, beyond which 
extend four petals of another flower. This slab is probably one of those which the ancient Mexicans 
used for the purpose of giving some variety to the gloomy monotony of their walls. 

No. XLVII. This carving represents a human figure, apparently that of a female, seated in the 

accustomed manner. Her head resembles that of Cybele, as represented in the mythology of Greece, 
"being surmounted with a mural crown. ‘The features are very prominent: and her right hand 
grasps some unknown symbol. ‘The material is a coarse stone very much consumed by time. 

No. XLVII. This piece of stone was also found in the same town. Its form is circular, its surface 
convex, surrounded with a fanciful border. In the centre is displayed a flower with many petals, 
opening around a cross. ‘This stone, like those already mentioned, was merely designed as an orna- 
ment for some building. 

No. XLIX. In speaking of the town of Ozumpa, I should have said that in the house of the Lieu- 
tenant Don Francisco Muniain we made the drawing of a statue placed on a square base. It is 
full length. Its head is merely encircled with a band, while its ears are adorned with pendants, and 
the cartilage of its nose pierced with aring. A sash or short apron is tied round its waist. This 
figure, which is that of a male, has no visible symbols from which its character may be determined. It 
is one of the few statues of which the posture is erect ; they are usually sitting. 

No. L. From the town of Ozumpa we went to Cuauhitla Amilpa, and thence to the village of 
San Juan Ahuehuepan, lying about three miles to the west of Ozumpa. We here found the mutilated 
trunk of a statue sculptured in red stone. If we may judge of the execution of the whole from what 
remains, there is great reason to regret its mutilation. It is destitute of all ornaments and apparel with 
the exception of a sort of frill, and a sash tied in a bow, which serves the purpose of an apron. 
The trunk of this beautiful statue discovers great skill and accuracy of proportion, and was probably 
designed by the artist to represent some hero or superior deity. 

No. LI. The drawings attached to this number represent the head of a female carved in solid red

4 AD THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

stone: the one exhibits the front, and the other the back of the bust: it is of the natural size, and 
its ornaments are disposed with regularity. It is to be regretted that only a fragment of so well 
executed a figure should have been preserved. 

No. LII. From the last-mentioned villages we pursued our route to the town of Chonacatepec, 
where the magistrate showed us at his house a sort of mask, made of a white transparent and gritty 
stone, (known there by the name of Tecalle,) well proportioned and neatly finished. It seems as if the 
artist designed to portray in it the distinctive features of the Mexican face: the ears are pierced 
laterally, either for the purpose of being decorated with ear-rings, or of suspending it as an ornament 
from the neck of an idol. It was discovered on opening an ancient and deserted cave on the side of 
a mountain. The back is flat, unlike the generality of masks, which are usually formed concave so as 
to fit the face. ’ 

No. LIII. On our way to the town of Chila, at the distance of about three miles, we saw on the 
summit of a mountain called Tortuga, a pyramid of a solid mass resting upon an equilateral base, 
formed by four isosceles triangles. It was constructed with massy materials, but its primitive covering 
has mouldered away. The four sides front the four cardinal points of the compass. It does not ter- 
minate in an acute angle; the summit, at a third part of its perpendicular height, stretching into a 
spacious area, which was ascended for the purpose of prayer or sacrifice by a flight of stairs on the 
western side. 

No. LIV. At the foot of the northern angle of this pyramid, at the depth of three yards and three 
quarters from the surface of the ground, exist the ruins of a sepulchre in the form of across. We 
descended by six steps into an oblong vault, the four compartments of which, like the sides of the 
pyramid, front the four points of the compass. The walls of this subterraneous building are constructed 
of squared blocks of stone, cemented with mortar and polished. The ceiling is coated with lime, 
sand, and probably some other ingredients. We found the remains of only a few human bodies. 

No. LV. From Chilan I proceeded to the town of Huahuapan. About three miles eastward of which, 
at the top of a little hill called ‘Tallesto, I found lying on the ground a block of hard and fine-grained 
stone of a bluish colour. Its shape is prismatic, and on one of its sides is carved in relievo a circular 
shield. Its field displays some unknown symbol, and from the lower part of the circle extends an arm, 
the hand of which grasps some kind of offensive weapon resembling a dart or spear, to which certain 
ornaments are appended. ‘This shield, belonging to a class of defensive arms in general use amongst 
the ancient Mexicans, is engraved with great skill, and is probably the memorial of some deed of 
valour ; or it might have been the honourable military device of a warlike province. 

No. LVI. In the town of Yanquitlan I saw a solid red stone carved into the resemblance of a head. 
It is of the natural size, but of strange and uncouth physiognomy. It bears some resemblance to a 
skull masked and adorned. This fanciful piece of sculpture indicates a style differing from that which 
is strictly Mexican. 

No. LVII. This small vessel, in shape resembling a censer, and formed of well baked clay or some 
other hard red substance, is smooth and polished on its surface, and very neatly and tastefully executed. 
It is an ancient toy, formed of two pieces; the upper one, which serves as the cover, is cast in a 
mould and fluted: the lower, which is solid, is encircled by a moulding. There is a hole at the top 

and bottom, by means of which the two pieces may be fastened together with a string. 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 443 

No, LVIII. This number describes the barb of a dart or arrow, consisting of three sharp edges 
forming a triangular figure. The shape of this very ancient offensive missile weapon is no less 
adapted to inflict a wound than to prevent its extraction. It is made of a light grey flint stone, and 
is furnished with a shaft by which to attach it to a handle. | 

No. LIX. These figures represent a small idol, which exhibits a departure from the characteristic 
style of Mexican sculpture. They are made of a light green jasper, and are found in abundance in 
the ancient sepulchres of the Mistecas. Like Isis and Osiris, those constant appendages to the 
Egyptian mummies, they invariably present the same attitude and prismatic form, with the exception 
of one or two which have four sides. The shoulders, either straight or angular, are pierced with two 
right lines to a certain depth, which meet at a given point, and for man angle of greater or lesser 
degree, without the employment of any other than a straight instrument for this purpose. This is . 
a simple invention, but it proves the ingenuity of the artist. These figures, with the addition of beads 
or precious stones of a green colour, either round or fluted, formed the necklaces with which the 
bodies of the dead were wont to be adorned. 

No. LX. This small idol, of a similar class to those just mentioned, and sitting in a contracted 
attitude, differs somewhat from them in form, being cut down the back vertically. 

No. LXI. The sight of those instruments with which the Mexicans executed their admirable sculp- 
tures cannot fail to be highly interesting. —This number represents an heptagonal chisel, or perhaps a 
burnisher, the form of which may be seen in the annexed drawing. It is made of a very hard kind 
of touch-stone, fine-grained, and of a jet black colour. Its surface still retains a high degree of polish. 

No. LXH. This number represents a sharp-pointed instrument, which probably was the chisel 
of the Mexican sculptors. Its material is a hard stone of a dark green colour; its figure is hexa- 
gonal. One end was originally sharp, although now somewhat blunted ; the other exhibits the blows 
which were given to it by a hammer or some tool of the kind which they were accustomed to use. 

No. LXII. This last number of the antiquities of Misteca represents a kind of cylinder, made 
of a dark green stone, having an extremely smooth surface. 

The original figures indicated by the Nos. 61 to 63 are somewhat smaller than the drawings, 
as I thought they would be better understood if their proportions were rather enlarged by the 
draughtsman. The intrinsic value of works of art depends not upon size; they are not to be 
measured by the yard, nor estimated by their weight in the balance. Invention and finished 
execution are the true tests of excellence ; and to speak according to the rules of art, it is neither 
the bulk nor the material which can determine their merit, since a figure of clay may be of more 
value than one of gold ; and a work of diminutive proportions more worthy of admiration than a 
Colossus. 

After having finished my search after antiquities in Tanhuitlan, I proceeded to the city Oaxaca, 
where I prosecuted my inquiries concerning the ancient remains which yet existed in that province, 

beginning with those of Mount Alvan, which is about six miles distant from that city. The result 
will be found in the following pages. 

4 AA THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

THE ANTIQUITIES OF MOUNT ALVAN. 

TO the west of the town of Antequera, at the distance of about six miles, there is a mountain named 
Mount Alvan, the summit of which forms a table. Although apparently the work of nature, there can 
be little doubt that the art and patient industry of the Zapotecas (an Indian nation so called) has 
contributed in no small degree to its formation. It is a well known fact, that this race of Indians 
always availed themselves of the favourable disposition of the ground to erect monuments to their 
deities, their deceased kings, and their kindred ; as well as fortifications which they constructed in 
their own defence, in accordance with the usages of those remote times. In the beginning of the month 
of July I resolved to ford the dangerous river called the Atolliaque, which flows between the above- 
mentioned fixed points,—a thing not always practicable. It is true that in the dry season the waters 
of this river are so shallow, that its appearance is rather that of a gentle brook; but in the rainy 
season it not only receives a great, accession of water which flows from the valleys, but carries with 
it in its whole passage a quantity of fine sand, which sinking to the bottom by its specific gravity forms 
horizontal banks, destitute of firmness, and renders the fording of it treacherous in the extreme, as 
was experienced by our secretary, who together with his horse fell.midway in the channel, and 
would have perished had it not been for the great exertions of the Indians who attended us. Finally 
we reached the summit of this memorable place, which we found to be formed out of a group or 
assemblage of high hills, which separate the greater valley of Oaxaca from the less, where the 
following ancient ruins attracted my observation. 

No. LXIV. Upon the plane or the table formed by the above-mentioned mountain there is a 
little hill somewhat resembling a tomb, artificially raised, of a conical shape and covered with a great 
quantity of trees and shrubs. It is traversed through its centre from north to south by a very well 
planned gallery, having a semi-elliptical vault, and lined (on the left hand side as one enters) with 
many large and oblong slabs of granite, on the surface of which, sculptured in alto-relievo, appear 
several figures or human busts, rather exceeding in dimensions the common stature of man, with 
open mouths, and in various attitudes; some sitting, some standing, and all in profile, looking 
towards the north along the interior of the gallery, five only of which I have taken copies of, because 
they were found in a perfect state of preservation. 

No. LXV. The first figure is represented in a sitting position, rather in front, and without any cover- 
ing or ornaments except those which it wears on the head. 

No. LXVI. This figure resembles the first, except that its position is more in profile, and the 
attitude of the arms and legs different. 

No. LXVII. The figure represented under this number displays a greater degree of diversity, 
being in an upright position and in the act of walking: some difference is also observable m the 
ornament (or crown) which it wears on its head ; at the lower part of the legs a flourish of the chisel 

and two circles are discernible. 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. . 445 

No. LXVIII. This figure is also in the act of walking in the same direction as the foregoing, but 
the attitude of the right arm is somewhat different. Its crown is similar to those worn by the two 
first, but it is distinguished by the peculiarity (perhaps a hieroglyphic necessary for the explanation 
of this curious and enigmatical piece of history) of manifesting a superfluous sign of the sex to which 
it belongs. 

No. LXIX. This figure is represented in profile, seated with its arms crossed over its breast; its 
head armed with a sort of helmet or close cap, and a fanciful circle under the ear, with a lock of hair 
behind in the form of a cue. In the right angle of this square block of stone there appears a 
hieroglyphic of the king of birds, with a crowned head and an ornamented eye: it is in the act of 
devouring the body of a bird, upon which are six numerical signs, disposed with some degree of 
order, with three symbolical figures underneath. I directed that an excavation should be made in 
the interior of this hill, but found nothing remarkable except the fragment of a skull, a thigh bone, 
and some other small bones very much decayed. ‘There was sufficient, however, to convince me that 
this was the tomb of some king or illustrious family of the Zapotecas. But I must confess that what 
perplexed me, was the grotesque attitudes and apparent flexibility of limb displayed by these 
male figures, sculptured in relievo on the above-mentioned stones, as well as their being beardless, 
naked, without the distinctive marks of sex, and all directing their attention towards the centre of the 
tomb, with their mouths open as if in the act of exclaiming, while performing the part of mourners 
over the body there deposited. | 

No. LXX. Near this monument there is another similar to it, which was probably raised for 
the same purpose: it has a spacious gallery which traverses diametrically, in a straight line from 
south to north, the centre of the artificial hill, the interior of which is faced with square stones 
disposed in horizontal rows, whilst some large slabs which form a projecting angle over the solid 
masonry of the lateral walls resembling the ridge of a house, serve as a roof; the pavement is com- 
posed of a hard mortar of sand and lime. These sepulchral monuments evince the recollection 
and tender affection whick this nation bore to the dead. 

No. LXXI. Another monument presented itself to our view, externally of the same shape and mate- 
rials as the preceding ones, as may be seen by referring to its plan and elevation: it has likewise a 
gallery lined with wrought stones, having a somewhat concave roof. It deserves to be noticed 
that the gallery of this tomb does not follow a straight transverse line, but terminates on arriving at 
the centre of the cone, where, having formed an oblong saloon, it is divided into two equal portions, 
each following its meridian line. 

No. LXXII. At a short distance from the last’ monument, there yet exists an ancient building 
(either a temple or mansion for the dead, for it might have served both purposes). 1 found this 
great structure rested upon an immense base or terrace of hewn stone, the projection of which forms 
a quadrilateral figure, each side facing one of the four cardinal points of the compass. A tomb of a 
conical figure rises from its area: I was struck at beholding, in the interior of this solid body, 
a sort of well-constructed rotunda, from the centre of which proceeded four spacious passages 
dividing the whole plane into equal portions; and the interior walls of this famous work of art 
were formerly (judging by what is still visible) lined with uniform and perfectly even stones. It 
is to be lamented that time and vegetation,—the enemies of buildings, but more especially of 

(5x) 

4.46 THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

monuments of antiquity,—should confound art with nature, assigning to the former a brief and 
transitory existence. 

No. LXXIII. At the foot of the above-mentioned artificial hill there is a large block of granite, 
the visible surface of which contains several hieroglyphics engraved in relievo: on one of the 
sides are sculptured in profile six human figures in a row, ornamented and dressed in a uniform 
manner ; six other figures, with which I am unacquainted, are alternately placed between them. 'The 
ingenious art of transferring the thoughts to cloth or stone by means of symbolical figures, was in 
general use in the Mexican empire; and if the surface of this historical basso-relievo displays a 
difference in the order and formation of these figures, this may have originated in the diversity of 
national customs ; since as the language of the Zapotecas was totally different from the Mexican, so 
likewise the symbols by which they expressed their thoughts might have been equally different. 

No. LXXIV. I found near the same place a light and cylindrical stone, belonging to that class 
which mineralogists call breccia. This ancient piece is wrought in a simple style, and I judge it to 
have been an altar for sacrifices: it deserves its place amongst the antiquities of this country, on 
account of its having been an instrument, if I may so term it, famous in Mexican mythology, upon 
which was shed with profusion the blood of so many human victims. 

No. LXXYV. In Zocho, a town in the vicinity of Oaxaca, I was shown a copper instrument, in the 
house of an Indian labourer named Pasqual Bartolano, who a short time before my arrival discovered, 
when ploughing his field, twenty-three dozen of these tools, contained in two large earthen pots, in 
very good preservation: they are all of the same cast metal, and of similar form; they only differ 
from each other a little in length, but appear to be of equal thickness ; and the silversmiths are very 
anxious to obtain them on account of their fine alloy. It remains for me to attempt to explain (which 
I fear I shall find an impossible task) the use to which these instruments were applied; since those 
ages, the customs of which were so wholly different from ours, would likewise have had their peculiar 
usages, with which we cannot be acquainted. It is possible, therefore, that they might have employed 
them either in agriculture, war, or sacrifices ; or, perhaps, as cutting instruments in their arts,—none 
of which suppositions are improbable. 

No. LXXVI. This small and well wrought piece of sculpture, of a semi-spherical shape, formed 
of a kind of copper-coloured pyrites, possesses excellent proportion and a fine polish, particularly 
on the side intended for a mirror, or to serve as an ornament for some idol: on the convex side a hole 
has been bored for the purpose of fixing it in any situation at pleasure. This pretty little specimen of 
art confirms the opinion I have ever entertained of the ingenuity of the natives of this large portion of 
the new continent: they employed almost every known metal, especially those of a more shining na- 
ture ; and it is probable that iron, not possessing this superficial property, was not worked by them, 
and they consequently remained ignorant of its intrinsic qualities, of which we have so advan- 
tageously availed ourselves. 

No. LXXVII. Séveral chisels of red copper have also been found in the immediate environs of 
this city. We are ignorant of their mode of giving a temper to these sharp-edged tools, whatever 
may have been the purposes to which they were originally applied, whether to fashion and cut wood 
into a regular shape, or perhaps even stone itself.
