ANTIQUITIES OF SAINT PAUL OF MITLAN. 

DESIROUS of quitting as soon as possible the city of Oaxaca, in order to inspect the far-famed 
ruins of Mitlan, we set out on our journey on the first of August, 1806, leaving behind us on the road 
the town of Tlacolima.—The town of Saint Paul of Mitlan, or rather of Miguitlan, is situated in a deep 
valley surrounded with mountains in seventeen degrees and a half north latitude, and about twelve 
leagues to the south-east of the city of Oaxaca, in a warm climate; the soil being dry, venomous 
insects multiply there in excess, including many sorts of snakes and spiders, particularly tarantulas, 
of immense ‘size. The produce of the country is maize and the maguey, although of a species 
different from that which grows in the cold provinces ; the chief fruit is the pitaya. The population of 
this town has experienced the same decay as its ancient monuments, both having participated in a 
common fate. The language which they speak is the Zapotecan: its original and proper name was 
Liuba, which means, a burial place; but the Mexicans, after having subdued this nation, named it 
Miguitlan, which in the Mexican language signifies Hell, or a place of sorrow. It is evident that both 
names appear to be well adapted to each signification, if we only consider the sepulchral nature 
of its ancient monuments, the sterility of the surrounding mountains, the gloom of the valley, and 
the scarcity of water which prevails there. On my arrival in the town, I presented to the governor 
of the Indians, and to the officiating rector of the parish, Don Joseph Castillano, the civil and eccle- 
siastical orders which I bore, charging them to aid me in my antiquarian researches : they accordingly 
provided me with every thing necessary to carry into execution His Majesty’s commands. As I was 
very anxious to commence operations as soon as possible, I made diligent inquiries on the following day 
concerning the monuments of ancient architecture and sculpture which might exist in this neighbour- 
hood, desirous of comparing them with each other, that I might judge which of the sister arts here 
enjoyed the preeminence : but to my great disappointment I could only obtain the three following 
small specimens of sculpture. 

No. LXXVIII. This is a bust of terra cotta; the face of the figure is masked, and it is modelled 
after a fashion in the highest degree capricious, and novel. I must therefore dispense with the neces- 
sity of further description by referring to the drawing. Behind it we perceive a cylindrical tube 
capable of containing chips of pine, or any other combustible substance; or to express my meaning 
more clearly, to serve.as a candelabra at their pagan festivals. 

No. LXXIX. This image, formed out of greyish purple jasper, well polished, presents to our 
view a dwarf-like figure seated in a natural and easy position, with the arms crossed over the breast, 
and its forehead, neck and waist, girt with a sash; the ears consisting of curved lines, the eyes shut, 
the mouth half open, and showing the tip of the tongue, whilst the back of the figure forms a vertical 
plane. What shall we think of such a being, who appears to be filled with compunction and absorbed 
in some mental abstraction ! 

No. LXXX. This piece was brought by an Indian to me at the rector’s house, the place of our 

448 THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

temporary abode. It isa small head of baked clay, of solid consistency ; its aspect is martial, and it 
exhibits great correctness both in outline and proportions ; it is armed with a sort of graceful helmet, 
ingeniously displaying the crest of a crowned or royal eagle. In the cavity formed by the aperture 
of the beak (where are described two circles in the points of the lateral angles) the head of a warrior 
appears, beardless and without mustachios. 

It is very strange that on so renowned a site, which led us to form sanguine expections, (proceed- 
ing on the supposition that the ancient artists would have managed with equal dexterity the chisel 
and the square,) we should have been unable to discover a single fragment of sculpture; since it was 
reasonable to suppese that a soil so rich in monuments of architecture would likewise have possessed 
many valuable sculptured remains. Our surprise should cease, however, when we consider the 

causes to which their disappearance may be ascribed. It is alleged, that at the eventful period 
} immediately preceding and after the Spanish conquest, the Indians either buried their idols, or carried 
them elsewhere. But I think the true and more probable cause was, the violent and open pro- 
scription which these false gods suffered from the iconoclasts, who destroyed every thing appertaining 
to them, without sparing aught for the sake of history or from love of the arts : and thus their false zeal 
effected their entire annihilation. But if our researches after monuments of sculpture were attended 
with little success, the contemplation of architectural remains considerably lessened our disappoint- 
ment; and although these latter monuments have yielded to the ravages of time, nevertheless some 
portions possessing beautiful perfection still remain, by judging from the parts of which, we may 
form an opinion of the whole.—Let us proceed then to the examination of them, since they will 
assuredly repay our curiosity to the utmost. 

There are four edifices which have received the common appellation of the Palaces of Mitlan, of 
these two are contiguous to each other ; the third forms a part of the parish church, and the fourth 
stands upon a spacious foundation ; they are all situated at short distances from each other. With 
respect to their plans, elevations, and general geometrical dimensions, the drawing of each edifice 
contains its scale of admeasurement, to which it will be easy to refer. 

These great and splendid fabrics, partly in ruins, have been erected with a lavish magnificence 
worthy of ancient Rome. Situated in the most elevated part of the town, notwithstanding the 
destructive revolution of ages, they convey a high idea of the power of the prince who caused their 
construction, as well as of the inventive genius of the artist who planned and executed them. 

No. LXXXI. This drawing presents to our view the geometrical plan of the largest edifice, and of 
the three square buildings attached to it, of which one alone retains some traces of its ancient and 
beautiful front. 

No. LXXXII. This monument, which from its present state of preservation we are enabled more 
accurately to delineate, immediately creates the admiration of the beholder by its majestic appearance 
and mosaic decorations; the whole producing in the soul of the visitor a soft melancholy, and 
an emotion of pleasure that cannot be defined. 

Whenever in the course of this description I shall avail myself of technical terms employed in Greek 
and Roman architecture, to explain the architectural parts of these buildings,—such as pilaster, 
architrave, frieze, cornice, and others of a similar kind,—it is by no means my intention to display 

scientific knowledge, but merely to express myself in language which may be intelligible to artists: 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 449 

thus I say that the ichnography of this monument has for its foundation and base a socle of cut 
stones (the circumference of which embraces and measures, in a polygonal figure, a superficies 
extending over a vast area) of suitable dimensions and elevation above the level of the ground, 
the principal sides facing the cardinal points of the compass. On the southern front there are three 
staircases, of which the central one conducts to three doors, and the other two, placed at the projecting 
angles of the lateral extremities, serve equally to facilitate the ascent to the gallery formed along 
the upper plane: the steps consist of large and well cut stones, of a regular shape, and lead 
to the three great doors or vacant doorways, divided by as many pilasters, with their capitals 
or cornices having each a circular niche adapted to receive the head of some animal, or perhaps 
a skull; the discovery of which would have been very serviceable for the illustration of this 
description, by removing every doubt as to the destination of these edifices, and establishing cer- 
tainty on almost infallible grounds. Although I was informed that an Indian woman possessed one 
of these, and kept it concealed in the wall of her house, all my inquiries to ascertain the fact were 
fruitless. | 

The architrave, resting upon three pilasters, is a solid block of square evenly cut granite of enor- 
mous size; the base of the latter is composed of a row of stones perfectly square, with their edges well 
adjusted. The surface of the walls is covered and adorned with various entablatures or oblong compart- 
ments terminating in mouldings, which project from the vertical line of the walls, and in the planes 
of which are mosaic ornaments executed in alto-relievo and of most beautiful invention ; the designs 
presenting to the eye a series of very intricate flourishes, following in geometrical order with the most 
perfect union between the stones composing them, all of which are cut and of different shapes and 
dimensions. 'The exact evenness of this admirable mosaic work is further remarkable; and it is 
protected and crowned by a very deep moulding, whilst all the projecting angles are strengthened by 
beautiful buttresses of stone decorated with mouldings. 

The interior of the building corresponds to the magnificence of its exterior. ‘The three doors lead 
straight into a vast saloon, longitudinally divided from east to west by six granite columns, each of a 
single piece, one yard in diameter, and five yards and a half long, without base or capital. These 
columns were employed to support the transverse rows of beams which formed the roof of the saloon. 
The inside walls of this spacious room are merely covered with plaster, over which is a coat of 
fine stucco nicely spread with the trowel, and another of vermilion mixed with ochre, having a hard 
and excellent polish; the greater portion of this has crumbled to pieces, with the exception, however, 
of here and there some entire fragments, by which some estimate of its merits may be formed. We 
should not omit to remark, that the exterior as well as the interior of the whole palace, even the 
columns, was dyed or painted with the same colour. The pavement forming the floor of the entire 
edifice is a composition of lime and sand, covered with a coat of a finer and more solid cement, of 
a blueish grey colour, highly polished and shining. In that part of the inner wall which faces the 
principal door between the two centre columns, there is a square niche, in which probably was placed 
some mysterious statue. 

This saloon communicates with a quadrangular court, formed by four oblong edifices or apart- 
ments, with which there is a communication by a passage covered with large and very thick slabs 
placed horizontally. These inner apartments or long chambers, narrow in dimension, and with their 

(5x) 

ASO: THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

doors facing each other, are covered externally with the same fanciful flourishes as decorate the outer 
wall of the entire building. 

The horizontal roof or terrace which formerly covered the apartments of this edifice was com- 
posed of several rows of stout beams or trunks of the sabine tree, each one foot and a half in 
diameter, of which only three remain as a sample to posterity, the whole being now unroofed. 
Upon these strong beams was a floor of square flags, and over that a layer of mortar, composed of 
lime, sand, and earth, one foot and a half thick : and the whole was covered with a solid and smooth 
coat, forming the terrace, which is not perfectly horizontal, but has an almost imperceptible declivity, 
sufficient however to allow the rain to run off, which following its natural course flows into a pipe or 
gutter, and is conducted by this channel into a reservoir dug in an angle of the court. 

This great pile is connected with or attached to three other mferior edifices, which are built upon 
socles exactly on a level with it; and the equilateral figure described by the four principal fronts 
of these edifices, forms a square, that incloses within its compass a spacious area, the pavement 
of which is formed of cement of a good quality. It is to be regretted that only one of these 
three minor structures or saloons should exist, and that only in a very dilapidated state ; their magni- 
ficent ruins nevertheless proclaim their past splendour. We here behold an oblong saloon, of such 
narrow dimensions that it only occupies a third of its plane, divided from north to south by a row 
of five columns of the same length and diameter as those before mentioned, two of which are still 
standing. The entablatures of the wall are completely stripped of their original ornaments, but its 
three doorways still remain, with the four circular niches cut in the capitals of the pilasters, and an 
architrave of an immense block of stone, on the surface of which are engraven in basso-relievo the 
designs which are there visible. It is evident, from the traces which still remain, that when entire it 
was only ornamented with a single external frieze contained within two mouldings, having in its 
plane the same patterns in mosaic as those which are represented on the principal edifice. ‘The view 
which this ancient ruin presents when contemplated from afar has a grand effect. We recognize in 
it the features of venerable antiquity, and behold at the same time the havoc which time’s unsparing 
hand commits on the fragile works of man. 

No. LX XXIII. Under this number is represented a small fragment of the beautiful mosaic work 
which once ornamented these edifices, and which will soon disappear from the face of the earth, 
time and vegetation being its relentless foes. 

No. LXXXIV. The plan of this second palace, which is more simple, presents a perfect square, 
the sides of which are formed by four narrow long saloons; which arrangement comprises a 
spacious inner inclosure of a rectangular shape. ‘Three only of these saloons at present exist : 
all that remains of the fourth, which is in ruins, is its socle or platform; for these saloons, like 
those of the first palace, were all constructed on platforms. The three which still exist, although 
in a very dilapidated state, retain their principal parts, such as the walls, doors, and pilasters, with 
their niches. The excessive thickness of the walls is remarkable, as likewise the extreme narrowness 
of the interior apartments, which are unroofed. ‘The solid union of the rows of stone composing the 
former has been entirely destroyed, together with their mouldings, frieze, and mosaic ornaments, with 
the exception of some fragments which have escaped the hand of rapacious man, who, when desirous 
of converting the materials to his own use, is a more formidable enemy even than Time to ancient 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 451 

monuments.—The drawing contains all the information which we have been able to acquire respecting 
this palace. 

Nos. LXXXV. & LXXXVI. These drawings represent the four fronts of the saloons; and I 
should observe, for the more clear comprehension of this description, that as regards their symmetry, 
those saloons which are opposite to each other correspond in their ornaments ; since the two, the 
situation of which is diametrically the reverse of the other two, and which occupy the same line north 
and south of each other, differ in their external style of decoration from those lying east and west, 
as will easily be perceived from their plans. 

No. LXXXVII. Under the socle of the saloon facing the south there is a sepulchre or pagan mau- 
soleum, the plane of which is in the form of across. It is spacious, and the walls on the inside are 
embellished with various compartments in mosaic. A cylindrical column rises vertically from the 
central point of the plane of a square block of stone, formed by the intersection of the perpendicular 
and horizontal lines, which supports a large square stone that constitutes the ceiling ; the four angles 
of which embrace as many right angles, that divide and portion off four square rooms, the sad recep- 
tacles of the mortal remains of man, which are covered with large square slabs forming the roof. 
Every visible part of this dismal.abode was painted with vermilion : a door, subterraneous passage, 
and staircase, give admission to the tomb. I was unable to discover in this magnificent sepulchre any 
thing either artificially or naturally emblematical of death. 

No. LXXXVIII. The parish church and the rector’s house occupy the walls of this third palace ; 
and its plan may be seen in the ichnographical delineation. The materials employed in its construc- 
tion, its doorways, and ornaments, were similar to those of the other palaces, with the admission 
nevertheless of some variety, which evinces the fertile genius of the architect. 

No. LXXXIX. This, which we may designate the fourth palace, comprises in its plan two 
edifices, the walls of which are distinct. They do not constitute a single body except by their 
similarity and close proximity, being only three feet apart: the walls and doors are at present 
much decayed, and have even been propped up, which rendered the task of drawing their plan 
more easy. 

No. XC. At the distance of a league and a half to the east of Mitlan there is an ancient house 
built upon the summit of a high hill, the commencement or beginning of the Mijian range of moun- 
tains. The walls are constructed of square stones laid in rows and cemented together with lime, plain, 
and without the addition of any ornaments ; its plan is quadrilateral, and it has a court, platforms, 
and corresponding doors. At the back there is another contiguous edifice of smaller dimensions, 
which has likewise its four little platforms; and over one of the doors (that which faces the principal 
entrance) there is a stone of considerable length, on which are sculptured in basso-relievo some orna- 
ments resembling those of Mitlan. This monument is fast going to decay ; and the trees and shrubs 
which surround it will contribute by the slow and penetrating progress of their roots to the total down- 
fall of these valuable remains of antiquity. 

No. XCI. Under the principal entrance of this building, at a very little depth, there is a subterra- 
neous sepulchre ; it is constructed in a simple style, and its plane is in the form of a cross, constituting 
four square chambers, the walls of which are coated. with square stones polished and painted with 
ochre ; a flight of stairs conducts to it, and their descent faces the west. We found nothing in this 

452 THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

dismal vault but the remains of a deer and a kid, which some leopard or wolf, the present occupants of 
these ancient ruins, had dragged to this solitary spot. ; 

No. XCII. On our return from the building which we have just described, and before our arrival 
at Mitlan, I directed an excavation to be made, all the inhabitants of the town aiding me in the task ; 
when we found beneath an artificial hill, at the depth of six feet, a sepulchre, the form of which was 
oblong, and its walls lined with square hewn stones with mouldings and mosaic work of well finished 
execution : the roof was composed of large square flags ; and on the outer side, which faces the west, 
there was a small door. All that we found in this vault was a skull and some smaller bones, together 
with fragments of pitchers, jugs, and dishes of fine earthenware of a blue colour, destined for the use 

of him who could eat and drink no more. 

SEPULCHRAL ARCHITECTURE. 

The idea of absolute annihilation is repugnant to the physical constitution of man, even amongst 
savages themselves, who for the most part indulge in the fallacious hope of being able to prolong the 
body’s material existence beyond the verge of the tomb: but the love which this nation entertained 
for the bodies of their deceased friends equalled in some measure that which they bore to their gods ; 
the altar scarcely differed from the tomb. 

Experience has convinced me of the skill which this nation possessed in subterranean archi- 
tecture, which in art and in manual labour has a decided superiority over the more common kind, 
of which the sphere of operation is the open air. Let their adits, conduits, idolatrous caves, temples, 
and sepulchres, bear testimony to the truth of this assertion. It may even be doubted with respect to 
the last, whether any people of the Old Continent, the Egyptians not excepted, evinced a more tender 
affection for their deceased friends and kindred, in the solicitude which they displayed to erect suitable 
monuments to their memory, than the Capotecas ; who, besides the subterraneous sepulchres already 
mentioned, constructed artificial hills and pyramids above-ground, strengthened on the outside with 
strong masonry; whilst the interior was the sanctuary, where, as in the centre of a citadel defended 
by external works, they deposited the body of the deceased, making choice of the best materials 
for these sepulchral edifices, and employing them with method and order to ensure their longer 
duration. 

The art of subterranean architecture requires that attention should be paid to certain rules: in 
common architecture there is only one gravitating power, the column of air above; but in the former, 
of less frequent necessity, there are two, namely, earth and air; both which elements conspire to 
accelerate the sinking in and the downfall of subterraneous buildings. 

No. XCIII. There are two pyramidal oratories in this town, erected by this nation in honour of 
their false deities ; the first of which has a quadrangular base and four stories diminishing in size, and 
is of great height, being built of stones and unbaked bricks. It forms a massive and solid edifice : 
each story has a terrace, with a pavement of cement of the colour of ochre, and well polished. It 
is evident that the entire fabric was coated with square blocks of cut stone: the side on which 
the staircase is situated faces the west, and the other three sides the corresponding points of the 
compass. It has likewise a court of an oblong shape inclosed within three elevated platforms, which 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 453 

in pagan times served as socles for the quadrangular saloons destined for the habitations of the priests 
and the other ministers of this open temple. Exactly in the centre of the court there is a square 
altar built of stone and mortar, with a flight of steps opposite the stairs of the pyramid. 

No. XCIV. The other oratory has an oblong base; it consists of three stories built of unbaked 
bricks dried in the sun, placed in simple rows, with alternate layers of bricks made of a kind of com- 
position. Its revestment no longer exists, and time and the rains have diminished the bulk of its solid 
body. It serves at present as a representation of Mount Calvary, for the pious exercises of Christians, 
who ascend to the summit by a broad and beautiful staircase, furnished with landing places recently 
formed out of the spoils of the ancient palaces. This oratory in other respects resembles the 
preceding. 

From the vast number of idols, and consequently of temples or oratories erected for their worship, 
which even still remain scattered over the extensive surface of this kingdom of New Spain, without 
counting those already ruined and destroyed, we may justly characterize the Mexicans as one of the 
most religious nations which has ever existed on the face of the earth, not excluding from the compa- 
rison those of antiquity; but at the same time they were plunged in the deepest abyss of idolatry, 
until the happy arrival of their conquerors, who by rescuing them from it became their re- 
deemers. 

Nature was their prototype in the construction of their temples, the mountains themselves serving 
them as models; and they sought in this manner to exalt their gods above mankind, by placing them 
in more elevated and retired regions. From heaps of mud and shapeless mounds the majestic pyra- 
mid, consisting of a single body, took its origin; but as the genius of man advanced, the architect 
added to it progressively nine successive stories, gradually decreasing in size. At first it was formed 
simply of earth or of unbaked bricks ; but it was afterwards coated with well-cut stones disposed in 
regular rows. ‘This grand fabric served as a basis to the altars and thrones of their gods; and 
in the same way as the art of statuary has its colossal productions, so architecture can boast of the 
pyramid. I shall only further remark, that this excessive abundance of temples and idels clearly 
indicates that this great and ancient continent possessed a most numerous population. 

ARCHITECTURE. 

The destruction of so many monuments of sculpture and architecture, which might at this time have 
aided our inquiries, and guided us through the dense darkness of remote antiquity, excites our deepest 
regret. As a matter of probability, we may be permitted to hazard the conjecture, that when the Spa- 
niards first landed on these shores, Liuba and its primitive population had ceased to exist; and that 
the present are a more recent race of Indians, who replaced the ancient population by whom the struc- 
tures which we so much admire were erected. But whence did that primitive population come? and 
at what period did they people this soil? and, finally, whither have they emigrated, carrying away with 
them their arts and the instruments which they employed in them? since their first arrival and their 
subsequent disappearance are equally problematical. In order to arrive at any conclusion upon this 
great and famous question, it would be necessary to have a number of original monuments of archi- 

(5z) 

ABA THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

tecture and sculpture, by means of which we might form some plausible conjecture respecting the 
uncertain race of this most ancient people, from comparing statue with statue, building with building, 
and hieroglyphic with hieroglyphic. 

The ancient Capotecas cultivated the fine arts, were extremely religious, and entertained great 
reverence for the dead, as their own monuments, works owing their existence to a wise form of 
government, unequivocally show. But what may have been the epoch of the construction of these 
sumptuous edifices ? Were they all built at the same time, or were they founded progressively? We 
certainly find, on consulting their plans and style of ornament, that they uniformly preserved the same 
order of architecture, differing from each other only in being more or less complex in execution, 
but modelled according to the elements of the same school, which happily combined the solidity of 
the works of Egypt with the elegance of those of Greece. 

The architectural parts which immediately invite the attention of the connoisseur are, first, the 
transverse architrave, or, as we may otherwise define it, the stone which closes the upper empty spaces 
of the doors resting upon the jambs and pilasters. ‘This solid block, of the nature of granite, of enor- 
mous magnitude, forms a prism with a square base, on none of the sides of which is there any visible 
sign of its having been worked with a sharp tool or chisel; neither is this observable on any of the 
other stones which enter into the composition of these wonderful structures, all of which have a soft 
and finished evenness of surface, such as might have been produced by the grinding, or rather the 
friction, of one stone against the other. Secondly, the nice and perfect squaring of many of the stones, 
both great and small, which face and adorn the walls of the above-mentioned palaces, giving by their 
beautiful union and exact correspondence an admirable finish to the work. But what is most remark- 
able, interesting, and striking in these monuments, and which would alone be sufficient to give them 
the first rank amongst all known orders of architecture, is the execution of their mosaic relievos, very 
different from the plain mosaic, and consequently requiring more ingenious combination, and greater 
art and labour; they are inlaid on the surface of the wall, and their duration is owing to the manner 
of fixing the loose stones into it, and to their frm union. 

When the line of ornament could not be pursued along the wall, they continued it over the door- 
ways, engraving there a series of picturesque ideas. No cement or glutinous substance whatsoever can 
be discovered in the perfect union of these little stones with each other: an exactly cut square or 
level surface composes the mechanism of these mosaic works. ‘The intaglio of the stones resembles 
the figure of a wedge or of a pyramid with a quadrangular base, the vertex of which is encrusted in 
the wall, which is composed of a blackish earth well tempered. Some of these stones are laid on 
the plane, others on the edge, others vertically, and lastly some are placed diagonally, as the 
design may require. 

The interior body of the wall is a solid composition of earth and sand with a mixture of lime, into 
which the loose stones have been pressed to a certain depth. It appears to me vain to inquire when 
or from whom was borrowed the beautiful conception which still remains in the thirteen compart- 
ments which embellish the principal fronts of these monuments, or to seek to determine which of 
them was prior in foundation to the others. It is natural in works of human art that less perfect 
efforts should precede the more perfect; but these admirable structures, combining grace with majesty, 

display a style of architecture which it is impossible could be more original, since in truth we here 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 455 

behold a gigantic piece of mosaic work such as antiquity never produced. Four things are princi- 
pally deserving of notice in these palaces, of which the first is, that only two of them have socles ; 
the others are built immediately upon the surface of the ground. Secondly, the first palace occupies 
amore elevated site than the second. Thirdly, they appear to owe their situation to mere acci- 
dent, since neither symmetry nor order is observable in their disposition with respect to each other. 
Fourthly, they are built of the same materials and in the worst situation, although the highest in the 
neighbourhood ; for which, two reasons may be assigned ; one is, that a rocky soil is more fit to support 
the weight of such massive buildings ; the other, that they might not be exposed to the inundations to 
which the plains are liable in the rainy season. Lastly, considering the solid structure of these works, 
the narrowness of their chambers, and their physical situation, I am of opinion that they never were 
intended for the habitations of their kings. History informs us, and I have verified the fact, that the 
palaces of those monarchs occupied the most agreeable and delightful sites ; the proof of which may 
be found in the remains of those of Chapultepec, Ystapalapan, T'escuco, Huastepec, and others, which 
are the very reverse of Mitlan, which seems more adapted by its situation to be a receptacle and 
abode for the dead, who desire such places for their eternal rest. 

No. XCV. About three quarters of a league to the west of Mitlan, an ancient fortress towers 
over the rugged summit of a steep and isolated rock, which is only accessible on its eastern side, and 
which is crowned and circumvallated with a solid wall of stone, one and twenty feet thick and eighteen 
feet high ; forming in its wide range, which is about a league in extent, several salient and retiring 
angles, with curtains interposed: and on its assailable side, at which is the principal entrance, it is 
defended by double walls which mutually flank each other. The first, or that more advanced, 
forms an enceinte or elliptic rampart, upon which, at short distances from each other, there are heaps 
of small round stones for slinging, and in the centre of its crescent there is an oblique gate to avoid 
the enfilade or right line of arrows, darts, and stones. The second wall, which is joined at its 
extremities to that of the fortress, is of greater elevation, and forms a sort of tenaille. This wall 
differs from the other in having its sides or flanks more open ; and the second gate of the fortress is 
formed on its right side; it has likewise its rampart and heaps of stones. ‘There is besides a parapet in 
the obtuse inner angle of this work, which leaves in the recess formed by the wall a small vacant space, 
sufficiently large to admit a certain number of troops to be drawn up on a sudden attack or in defence 
of the entrance to the fortress: and for greater security in case of an attack, batteries were disposed 
according to their system of tactics, in front of the fortification, which consisted of loose round 
stones about three feet in diameter, placed on high and balanced on the upper edge of the talud, for 
the purpose of being directed to their aim by the power of the lever or united manual strength, 
and forming by their rapid rotation on their axis bounds and rebounds, so as accidentally to imitate 
the batteries named rebound. In the interior of the fortress, or the space contained within and defended 
by the above-mentioned circular wall, there exist, on the convex and plain surface of the rock, vari- 
ous ruins of square buildings and edifices of capacious size, which were the barracks of this ancient 
garrison. In the part diametrically opposite to the entrance there is a postern or sally-port, for fur- 
nishing the fortress with supplies of men and provisions, or to facilitate a forced retreat. Itis evident 
from the reasons above stated, as well as from the epoch in which this work of military architecture 

was constructed, that it was not susceptible of any other system of defence, due regard being paid to 

4.56 THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

the nature of the offensive weapons and the tactics or art of attacking then in use, as the topogra- 
phical plan and its scale will show. 

Proceeding about a league in an eastern direction from Mitlan, I discovered the ancient and 
famous quarry of stone of the nature of granite, which was the bed from whence were procured the 
voluminous masses employed in the erection of these various monuments. It extends longitudinally 
from east to west on the top of a mountain. Its naked surface forms furrows or parallel ridges, or rather 
perpendicular strata, contrary to the general order and disposition of nature. In the spaces between 
the furrows holes are visible, which were made by the ancients to serve as a point of support for the 
lever, when, dividing with the stone wedge (of so much use in their arts) the parallel strata, they after- 
wards had occasion to raise from the quarry those enormous blocks of which they formed archi- 
traves and columns; some of which, in an unfinished state, are even still scattered on the surface 
of the ground ; which proves that it was the intention of that people to execute the plans which they 
had in idea formed of other works, but that the course of circumstances prevented them. Nearly 
the same is reported by travellers in Egypt, who have found at the present day in the ancient 
quarries of granite, which supplied the materials of the colossal figures and obelisks, some in an 
unfinished state and still in the rock, and others half trimmed and detached from it. But what, we 
may inquire, was the power employed in raising these stones from their primitive bed? Experience 
has taught us that the power of the lever is unlimited; and it is probable that they employed it for 
that purpose, otherwise we must suppose that they were acquainted with some other mechanical con- 
trivance wholly unknown to us, which perhaps may be reserved for the investigations of others to 
discover : amidst so many conflicting doubts, we can only have recourse to conjectures and supposi- 
tions, which in the end leave us in the same state of uncertainty as we were in at first. If, again, 
we seriously consider the difficulty of transporting these stones, either in blocks, half worked, or 
finished, to the place of their destination, we must in each case suppose that powerful machinery 
was required to effect the object. It would be difficult to persuade me that the ancient Romans 
placed in their great and proud edifices stones comparable in magnitude to these, (and I appeal 
to their original monuments still in existence.) ‘They would have been obliged to have called to 
their aid all the powers proposed by Archimedes; whilst the Indians, barbarians as many ignorant 
writers complacently style them, who do not hesitate to apply to them that degrading epithet, with 
less parade of art attained in their works the same practical results, and who knows if not greater? 

After the conveyance of these stones, the task of lifting and fixing them in their proper places 
was further requisite; for which we must suppose the pulley was used or some other machine 
equally available. Finally, as regards the elevation of their columns, all was concerted with precision 
and skill; although, in order to give a firm foundation to them, a knowledge of their horizontal planes 
was necessary, since on the proper fixture of a column depends its being able to resist the weight 

which it is intended to support. 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 457 

INSTRUMENTS EMPLOYED IN THE ARTS. 

It may not unreasonably be expected that I should close my description of the monuments of 
Mitlan with some account of the instruments which the ancient Mexicans employed in squaring, 
cutting, and polishing the stones which entered into the composition of their monuments. Desirous 
of attaining information so highly interesting to the arts, I did not neglect making the most diligent 
inquiries respecting them, and charged the local authorities and the inhabitants of the town, to 
collect whatever stones could be found, either there or in the neighbourhood, which bore any re- 
semblance to a wedge, chisel, punch, axe, hammer, &c. My expectations were not disappointed, 
since I was so fortunate as to obtain, in the course of a few days, several stone chisels shaped like 
wedges, which I considered a propitious omen of further discoveries. The Indians displayed during 
the entire of my stay amongst them the greatest solicitude to oblige me. Availing myself of this 
favourable opportunity, I made a large collection of stone implements, with the intention of se. 
lecting out of the number the most perfect specimens: I was most desirous of obtaining metal 
instruments ; and it was not long before I procured several of copper, of various sizes and shapes. 
But what I chiefly wished to discover, were iron tools; my inquiries after this metal were, however, 
fruitless. 

Long experience proves that gold, silver, and copper, when wrought, whether exposed to the open 
air or buried underneath the surface of the earth, will remain for many ages in an uncorroded state ; 
but this is not the case with iron, which from its nature is exposed to the attacks of rust and moisture 
that in time effect its entire decomposition. 

What theory shall we advocate, or what new hypothesis propose, on this difficult question? Modern 
art certainly has never had recourse to so simple a process as that of reducing stones to proper shape 
and dimension by means of mutual friction; neither is it probable that any ancient nations of the 
Old Continent resorted to this expedient, which on the supposition that it might be found available, 
where all that was requisite was to fashion stone in a plain manner, would be totally inapplicable 
to the formation of relievos. If the Indians had ever used copper instruments, copper being ex- 
tremely ductile and not susceptible of a sharp and hard edge, they could scarcely have employed 
them for other purposes than carving wood: I should also observe, that stones which had been 
fashioned by the simple friction of one against another, would acquire a plane surface from having 
been ground, and would likewise have a certain polish, which is in fact perceptible on the surface 
of the slabs, as well as of the lesser stones, which enter into the composition of the mosaic ornaments, 
the most interesting feature in these monuments. Impressed with a full conviction of the difficult 
nature of this inquiry, I shall conclude by candidly confessing my ignorance on a subject which 
does not admit of superficial reasoning, and shall leave to others, who may be perhaps more fortunate 
in this respect than myself, the task of solving this interesting problem. In fine, having thoroughly 
investigated and taken the plans of the most ancient ruins of the venerable town of Saint Paul 
of Mitlan or Miguitlan, we resolved on our departure, and directed our course towards Zachila, 
the court and residence of the ancient sovereigns of the Zapotecan empire. 

(64) 

4.58 THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

ANTIQUITIES IN THE TOWNS OF ZACHILA AND QUILAPA. 

IN the beginning of September, 1806, we quitted Mitlan, directing our course to the towns of Saint 
Pablo Guilaa, Ocotlan, Zachila, and Quilapa. The first of these places, situated on the brow of a 
steep mountain, is remarkable for a singular willow of large dimensions and lofty height, which 
grows in that neighbourhood. ‘This venerable production of the earth forms, by the spreading of 
its roots, an oblong reservoir, the sides of which resemble basket-work, or interwoven snakes. So 
close and firm is this fibrous union, that with the exception of some apertures which are filled up 
with stones and mortar, it is capable of holding a sufficient supply of water for the town, either for 
washing linen, for bathing, or other purposes, and is ever replenished with the clear water of a peren- 
nial spring. The bottom of this curious bath or reservoir is formed by roots of the same tree, from 
which protrude several excrescences, some of which are round, some conical, and others of most 
grotesque shapes. It was impossible not to contemplate with pleasure this probably unique pro- 
duction of nature, at once so rare and so serviceable to the inhabitants of this town. From hence 
we went to the village of Ocotlan, where we remained some days, without observing any thing 
remarkable. Having arrived at the town of Zachila, we entered upon a wider field of research ; for 
here, as we had anticipated, we discovered several interesting monuments of antiquity ; this place 
having been in former times the court or residence of the ancient Zapotecan kings. Its original 
name in the Zapotecan language was Zaachillattoo, as I ascertained from the inspection of some 
old documents: but when in process of time victory followed in the train of Mexican invasion, it 
seems to have changed its appellation into that of Teozapotlan, which latter name fell likewise into 
disuse, and it was finally called Zachila, a diminutive or corruption of the primitive term, as is the 
case with almost all the proper names of places in this ancient empire. This town, being extremely 
populous, extends through a vast and smiling plain situated in the middle of the great valley of 
Oaxaca; the principal produce of which is cochineal. Here we beheld several pyramids of earth 
and stones : we commenced our researches by causing excavations to be made in some of the groups 
which tower majestically in the centre of the plain: these were probably oratories, sepulchres, or 
watch-towers. ‘The Indians, whose exertions were heightened by the presence and exhortations of 
their rector and magistrates, applied themselves with alacrity to the task. In the progress of our 
excavations we often met with human bones, as well as statues or idols made of terra ‘cotta, and. 
small earthenware vessels, such as plates, jugs, and censers. Now and then we came to the moulder- 
ing remains of massy sepulchral walls, formed of very large burnt bricks. This confirms what iI 
have elsewhere remarked, that the ancient Mexicans not only used sun-dried bricks, but such also 
as had been hardened in the furnace. 

On the southern brow of one of these hills we saw the print or impression of a human foot, cut deep 
in the rock, and pointing to the meridian. I have occasionally found similar impressions in different 

parts of this kingdom. They most probably were intended to guide travellers on the road: I have

observed on some ancient maps, traced by the Mexicans on paper made of the maguey, a series of 
impressions of the same kind directed to some of the principal points of the compass. 

I am fully persuaded that excavations conducted on a grand scale, would bring to light another 
subterraneous world buried beneath the soil of this ancient continent, the latent record of remote 
ages. I gave orders to dig holes to a considerable depth in several artificial hills, but without suc- 
cess. ‘This, however, ought not to discourage any further attempt, for it is probable that sooner or 
later some important discoveries will be made. 

No. XCVI. I found at the rector’s house a statue formed of a stone of a yellowish grey colour, 
representing an idol or human figure seated: its arms are crossed over the breast as if in the act of 
praying ; an attitude expressive of the reverence which this people felt for their gods and princes. 
The forehead is encircled with a diadem garnished with precious stonés (an ornament designedly in- 
troduced by the sculptor) ; the hair hangs loose and dishevelled ; a sash is girded round the lower part 
of the body ; the nose and chin are a little mutilated. This statue, together with a human skeleton, 
was found in a sepulchre beneath an artificial hill. The style of the carving induces me to suppose 
that it was executed by the Zapotecas, which nation is of greater antiquity than the Mexicans. 

No. XCVII. In one of the lesser pyramids, which forms part of the group already mentioned, 
and perhaps not far from the site of the greater oratory of this town, there is a large oblong slab 
of granite, encircled with a plain moulding, and containing profile representations of four human 
figures in a sitting posture. In the centre of the group (which consists of a series of basso-relievos) 
appears a kind of altar, to which the attention of each figure is directed. The first on the right 
wears a sort of cap or crown, surmounted by an eagle. It is beardless; nor could I discover any 
traces of apparel upon it: on the right arm, which is raised, are engraved two numerals, one near 
the shoulder, the other at the elbow. The head of the second figure is curiously adorned with a 
plumed turban ; ear-rings are added to the other ornaments ; the right arm, although mutilated, ap- 
pears to be pointing to the same object of veneration. This figure, like the preceding, is destitute 
of apparel ; but it is distinguished by the peculiarity of having a long and thick beard. Time has 
deprived the first figure on the left of its ornamental head-dress: the ear-rings are similar to those 
of the opposite figure. In its right hand is a branch of palm; its left is raised, and points to the 
centre. 'The last figure has suffered most from time. The upper portion of the head is mutilated, 
but the ear-rings and part of the beard are yet remaining.. Both its arms are extended as if in the 
act of adoration, and the sash which encircles its waist is distinctly visible. It would be a hopeless 
task to attempt to decypher the meaning of this mysterious and hieroglyphical stone. We must 
content ourselves therefore with admiring the excellence of its sculpture and the expressive character 
of the figures. 

No. XCVIII. This granite statue represents a human figure seated in an attitude of repose. Its 
head is ornamented with a sort of mitre, covered with relievos and fanciful decorations. The face is 
masked, and its neck is encircled with a necklace of pearls or precious stones. A peculiar dress, 
terminating in an apron, appears in front ; and its hands rest or are supported upon its knees. This 
statue must evidently be referred to a new school, since the style of its execution differs materially 
from that of the Mexicans, who, when they subjugated the Zapotecas, gave a new character to the 
arts as well as to the language of their empire. 

4.60 THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

Although the Mexicans, never attained great celebrity as artists, being a nation more addicted to 
arms than to arts, they nevertheless availed themselves of the inventive genius of the Tultecas, 
whose ancient state deserves the appellation of the Athens of the New World. At the back of this 
statue two locks of hair, a portion of the necklace, and the girdle, are visible. 

No. XCIX. This statue of white marble, well carved and in excellent preservation, was found 

in making an excavation in the parish churchyard. It appears to be a male figure, and the attitude 

in which it is represented is very strange. The head is adorned with a profusion of feathers, with . 

other ornaments intermixed. The ears are carved in a fanciful manner, and might almost be con- 
sidered a part of these ornaments. ‘The face is masked; a string of pearls is suspended round its 
neck, and a plaited mantle is thrown over the shoulders. The band which encircles its waist is 
not visible in front, and the arms are entirely concealed, displaying only the extremity of the right 

hand, in which is a vase of a globular shape, accompanied with some symbols which I cannot ex- 

plain. This statue was originally painted with vermilion or red ochre, a brilliant colour that ac-— 

corded with the national taste, as their palaces and sepulchres sufficiently declare. 

No. C. This is a block of polished grey marble, forming part of a buttress in the hermitage called 
‘* La Soledad.” he figure carved upon it is spherical, and that part which is visible exhibits a 
face resembling the image of the full moon, which is frequently symbolized by a human countenance. 
It is probable that the ancient Mexicans worshipped this planet, and that it occupied a distinguished 
place among their numerous deities. . 

No. CI. At the foot of the steps leading to the parish churchyard stands a block of marble, on 
which is carved the prominent bust of an eagle. It is represented in profile, in an erect position, 
with expanded wings; its talons grasp the tail of a snake, while it attacks with its beak the reptile’s 
head. ‘This part of the figure is much mutilated. It is probable that this ancient and well-executed 
piece of sculpture was destined to adorn some regal edifice ; since the eagle, the king of birds, has 
always been considered the type of strength and dominion, on account of which it was embroidered 
on the Roman standards, and enjoys among birds the place which is allotted to the lion amongst 
beasts. The breast exhibits a small cavity, which was doubtless filled by a plate of gold or silver: 
whence I imagine that its intended situation was the summit of some stately palace facing the east, 
in order that the rays of the rising sun might be reflected from it. 

No. CII. Of these massy blocks of stone (similarly numbered) the first was discovered in the steps 
leading to the churchyard ; the second in the south entrance of the church; the third formed part of 
the wall of the rector’s house.. They vary in size and in quality, as well as in the figure and arrange- 
ment of their relievos, which exhibit a regular and symmetrical design. It is impossible not to 
behold with regret these fragments hastening to decay; since there is every reason to suppose that 
they were originally destined for the decoration of some magnificent structure. Their surface is now 
defaced, and part of the carving has mouldered beneath the hand of time, which destroys alike the 
porphyry column and the brazen bust. 

The remains which I am now about to describe are specimens of an art which probably preceded 
that of sculpture ;—the art of forming figures in clay, either with the hand or the mould, solid or hollow, 

which were afterwards baked in the sun or hardened by fire. My reason for supposing that this art 

Ps 
Pi 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 461 

preceded that of sculpture, is, that it is so much easier to mould plastic clay, than to give shape and 
symmetry to stone, metal, or wood. 

No. CIII. The first specimen of terra cotta is a very extraordinary figure or fanciful bust. It 
serves as the cover to a square hollow pedestal resembling a box, resting upon four cylindrical and 
hollow feet. This idol, which is formed of fine and well-baked clay, is perforated by a perpen- 
dicular tube which is a sort of support to it. I should in vain attempt to explain the various de- 
signs in relievo with which this figure is embellished, since they are too complicated and too fanciful 
for my comprehension; but they exhibit (as reference to the drawing will show) the most exact 
symmetry throughout. It was found some time ago, together with four others of a similar size, 
shape, and substance, in ploughing a piece of ground near the rector’s house. For what purpose 
could it have been designed? This is a difficulty no less perplexing than the development of the 
meaning of its various hieroglyphics. The figure comprises three distinct pieces or parts; the 
pedestal or box, the lid or masked bust, and the tube. Perhaps the box was used to hold jewels 
or incense ; the bust was the cover; and the tube served to diffuse odours, or to hold some torch 
or lighted piece of wood in honour of their deities, or of the sovereigns of Zaachillattoo. 

No. CIV. The description we have just given of the preceding figure is applicable to that which is 
represented in this drawing. 

No. CV. This number represents a female figure of diminutive proportions; it is fashioned in 
lead-coloured clay. The disposition of its limbs (which are visible only at their extremities) is re- 
markable. Its garments are thrice folded round it, and enriched with a fringed border; its head is 
richly adorned with ribbons, tresses, and rings, and its neck encircled with a necklace of precious 
stones. ‘The erect and fixed attitude of this figure, resembling a mummy, its folded arms, its singular 
vestment, and the circular tube which perforates its body, seem to indicate, that like the figures last 
mentioned it was intended to hold some sort of torch. 

No. CVI. 'This small, hollow, and rather fanciful head bears some resemblance to that of a tiger or 
leopard, or perhaps it is the likeness of an unknown wild beast. It is formed of red clay ; its surface 
is smooth, its expression ferocious, and its execution finished. The dilated jaws show it to be in the 
act of seizing upon its prey, and they likewise display formidable fangs and a cloven tongue. A 
collar confines its neck, which is tied with a knot. . 

No. CVII. This strange figure, which represents a kind of mastiff, is of very finished workmanship. 
It is destitute of limbs. The ears and the belly are large; the eyes distended, and it holds in its 
mouth a human head, which it appears in the act of devouring. This figure, like those which pre- 
cede it, is attached to a tube, and was apparently destined for the same use. It is rather muti- 
lated: works formed of clay being very liable to suffer injuries from time. 

No. CVIII. This is a small hollow head very similar to that of the domestic quadruped which the 
Mexicans name the “Cacomistle”. The mouth is just opened sufficiently wide to display the teeth 
regularly arranged. The Mexican artists were better delineators of the forms and proportions of 
animals and vegetables than of the human figure ; the probable reason of which I have before at- 
tempted to explain. This figure is formed of baked clay of a reddish brown colour. . 

No. CIX. Is the head of an armadilla, forming a hollow figure of baked clay. I regret that the

body of this animal is wanting, since its execution may be presumed to have been of equal excellence 
with the head. 

No. CX. This is the head of some animal unknown to naturalists. It is moulded in solid clay of 
an ash colour, hardened in the fire. . This antique fragment is very valuable on account of its origi- 

nality, finished execution, and its animated expression. © 

Pottery, as another branch of the plastic art, next merits consideration. 

The ancient Zapotecan potters manufactured their jugs and other vessels, either by the help of 
moulds, or simply with their hands ; preparing the clay, of different qualities and colours, with appro- 
priate tools. Their workmanship was good; that of their thin plates and dishes especially, which 
might rival the celebrated wares of Sagunto in the brilliancy of their colours and the clearness: of 
their varnish. . Fragments of this description I have occasionally found under the ruins of their mag- 
nificent buildings. 

No. CXI. This common-sized jug deserves attention from its perfect symmetry, its fine material, its 
transparent varnish, and the skilful display of dark yellow and lead colour which adorns both its 
interior and exterior. It stands upon three hollow feet, shaped like the rattles of a snake, and its 
neck is encircled at top and bottom with a ring or moulding: it has no handle. The materials of 
this vessel are so well, tempered, and the baking so perfect, that when struck it emits a clear and 
brilliant sound. The ancient Zapotecas evinced the fertility of their genius, by giving a thousand 
different shapes and colours to their manufactures, and enriching them with ornamental designs of 
flowers and animals, either painted or moulded. 

No. CXII. In the cluster of artificial hills near the town of Zaachillattoo before mentioned we dis- 
covered a sepulchral vault of hewn stone; on entering which we observed a row of human skulls, 
each placed in a dish standing upon a separate pedestal: every dish also contained a small artificial 
skull with the hair longitudinally extended. I imagine these skulls to be the relics of the victims 
which were sacrificed to inhuman deities, whose nature it was to be ever thirsting after human blood. 

No. CXIII. & CXIV. These numbers describe two vessels which were employed either in the 
service of the temple or the sepulchre. The first is a portable censer, to which a long hollow handle 
is affixed. Its circular patera or bowl is perforated with several holes to admit the action of the air. 
The other, which may more properly be named a chafing-dish, rests upon three feet. ‘These ancient 
vessels were in all probability intended to fumigate the temples and the images of their deities. If 
the religious rites of this ancient people had merely consisted of these simple offerings, they would 
have been less deserving of censure ; but to propitiate their ferocious divinities with the reeking 
limbs of their fellow-creatures was an act no less barbarous than superstitious. 

No. CXV. Proceeding with our excavations, we met with a great variety of small pots of different 
shapes. Of these I shall mention only the two of which representations are given in the annexed 
drawings. The form of the first is simple and well proportioned. The bottom is flat, and the middle 
as well as the neck are neatly finished. 

No. CXVI. The form of the other vessel is more singular. The mouth resembles that of a funnel or 

trumpet. From the foot project three prongs or roots, and two similar ones extend from the body. It 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 463 

was customary with this nation to deposit in the tombs of their deceased friends various jugs, basins, 
and dishes, which vessels I have described in order to show their taste and skill in the manufacture of 
them. Nothing is insignificant which points out the origin or the merit of the arts in which they 
chiefly excelled: viewed in connection with so interesting an enquiry, every relic however minute 
forms a link in the chain of knowledge, and thus acquires value and importance. 

From this ancient imperial court of Zaachillattoo, I proceeded to that of Quilapa, the residence 
in past times of the sovereigns of the two Mistecas, whose territory, in respect to its geographical 
position, lay in an opposite direction to the Zapotecan empire: the former extending from south to 
north, the latter from north to south, as far as the city of Tehuantepec. 

Having made the necessary arrangements for commencing the task of excavation, I procured, 
through the obliging exertions of the rector of the parish, the help of some Indians, when we pene- 
trated to the centre of several artificial mounds, which the ancient inhabitants had erected in honour 
of their deities, and which were the only monuments of antiquity that continued to exist in that 
neighbourhood. Here we found the following relics. 

No. CXVII. This figure represents a musical wind-instrument, or rather a whistle, such as was in- 
use among this people, both sides of which are copied in the drawing. The first resembles the ra- 
diated and bearded face of a man, and rests upon a triangular base which composes the other extremity. 
The mouth-piece is at the lower end of the opposite side. Besides this, I have discovered several 
other different kinds of wind-instruments, upon all of which tunes might be played. Among these 
there is one which is now in my possession, resembling a German flute, of which the material is a 
very fine clay of a dark purple colour, well polished, and finished. Another is a sort of trumpet, 
formed of the same kind of earth. I might add to the list of these musical instruments, but those 
already named will be sufficient to satisfy even the careless enquirer, that the people of this country 
were not entire strangers to the charms of music. 

No. CXVIII. This is a female bust formed of terra cotta, and, as the drawing shows, gracefully 
ornamented. 

No. CXIX. In the progress of our excavations we found this small head of clay, which exhibits 
a pleasing and manly combination of features. The ears, as well as the forehead, are furnished with 
ornamental rings: a beard is visible on its chin, which contradicts the opinion of those naturalists 
who deny to the aborigines of this vast continent that characteristic sign of manhood. 

Thus empires cease, nations disappear, and last of all those monuments of art decay, which, while 
they silently proclaim their founders’ skill and genius, testify how transitory is the existence of man’s 
proudest works. 

From the province of Oaxaca we went to the town of Tehuacan de las Granadas, and thence to the 
city of ‘Tepeyacac. This journey was retarded in consequence of our party being attacked by a 
malignant fever, brought on by the dampness of a very rainy season, and by frequently inhaling the 
noxious vapours contained in the excavations and sepulchral vaults which we had explored at 
Zachila and Quilapa. This severe attack of illness, by which our draughtsman was brought to the 
point of death, delayed our progress for more than two months.
