ANTIQUITIES OF THE CITY OF TLASCALA. 

No. CXX. HAVING arrived at the town of San Pablo del Monte, near the city of La Puebla, 
T made diligent enquiries after two statues, which I had been informed existed in that neighbourhood, 
and which I found to be the figures of two Mexican vestals. They were placed upon a wall, in the 
court of a chapel named Santiago. Both are represented kneeling upon square pedestals. The 
first is almost entirely without apparel; her hands conceal her breasts : her hair is confined under a 
cap, which is formed into a bag at the back of her head. 

No. CXXI. The second statue represents a female figure of the same class. A plain collar is 
fastened round her neck, and her head and shoulders are covered with a long cloak which reaches 
to the extremities of her feet. She likewise modestly veils her person with her hands and .arms. 
These statues are sufficient to show that the ancient inhabitants of this country were not so rude 
and barbarous as some writers have falsely represented them. The same feelings of delicacy which 
suggested to the Grecian artist the attitude in which he has represented the Venus de Medici, guided 
the chisel of the Mexican sculptor. These feelings are common to human nature; and the artist 
who carved the coarse Mexican block was as much under their restraint, as he who gave form and 
beauty to the Parian marble. 

No. CXXII. In the ancient capital of this province, called Tizatlan, the Spaniards have built 
a hermitage, dedicated to the proto-martyr St. Stephen, upon the ruins of the palace which 
once belonged to Chicotencatl. An Indian showed me here a small female bust, sculptured in 
iron-grey stone, in a sitting posture, and dressed according to the ancient costume of the country. 
Destitute as this statue is of merit as a work of art, the description of it cannot be deemed useless, 
since it will be serviceable to those who may desire to acquire a more perfect knowledge of the 
history of the kingdom of New Spain, and of the manners of its inhabitants. 

No. CXXIII. Another statue, formed of a similar hard and dark-grey stone, was brought to me 
from that quarter of the city called St. Sebastian. It is of very small size, and stands on a square 
pedestal, having its body covered with a garment fastened with a girdle. Notwithstanding the 
hideous expression of its features, which in part resemble those of a man and in part those of a 
beast, its brow is encircled with an ornamented crown, which likewise covers the back of the head. 
Its hands are folded over its breasts, and discover an excrescence upon the back of each. The 
Mexican or Tlascaltecan nation, however enlightened in other respects, were not singular in as- 
sociating these monstrous images with their religion: we recognize also the same practice among the 
ancient and wise Egyptians,—I need scarcely mention their worship of Osiris, Anubis, Canopis, &c. 

No. CXXIV. In an Indian hut in the same quarter of the city I found a piece of ancient 
sculpture, the most perfect in material, execution, and proportions, that my researches in this con- 
tinent have yet discovered. It is a mask carved in green agate and finely polished ; probably the 
resemblance of one of the four chiefs who once swayed the destinies of this celebrated republic. The 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 465 

ears as well as the forehead are pierced, for the purpose of suspending some kind of rings or jewels 
from them. ‘The chin is destitute of beard. It seems to have been the intention of the artist to fill 
up the cavity left in each eye with pupils of a different substance from that of which the mask is 
composed, a custom not uncommon amongst the Greeks and Romans. The drawing represents both 
sides of this image. 

No. CXXV. In that part of the city called St. Stephen I found the flint barb of a lance, 
such as the Tlascaltecas used in their wars. This is the only weapon of its kind that I was able 
to discover in the country of that warlike and celebrated people; and this fact inclines me to be- 
lieve that they were accustomed to bury their arms in the earth. The annexed drawing will convey 
an accurate idea of its form. 

No. CXXVI. I directed an excavation to be made in the quarter of St. Sebastian above men- 
tioned, but with little success; some human bones and fragments of idols, together with a vase 
named a Popocaxtli, which signifies a fumigating vessel, were all that we discovered. This relic is 
however interesting, from its having been employed in the funeral rites of this nation. It is a 
small and well-formed vessel of fine clay, standing upon three feet. One of the borders which 
encircles its exterior is painted with a fanciful pattern; the other is perforated with regularity, in 
order to give admission to the air, and by so doing to facilitate the burning of the incense or odo- 
riferous gums which it was intended to contain. 

No. CXXVII. During our stay in this city, the Indians of the village of Tepoyango brought me 
a military musical instrument, or Teponastle, made of a dense, heavy, and dark-coloured wood. 
It is cylindrical and hollow. No ornaments are painted upon its surface; but festoons and other 
devices are carved at each extremity. In the centre, which is the part where the instrument was 
struck, are two bars longitudinally placed, which project from the surface, each of which possesses 
its distinct tone: these, when struck, return a deep and loud sound. The instrument is formed out 
of a single block of wood, and, like a drum, was intended to be beaten with two sticks. 

No. CXXVIII. This figure represents another kind of Teponastle, probably that which was most 
anciently in use among the Tlascaltecas. The material and the execution serve equally to give 
beauty and value to this instrament; the former being a hard and heavy wood of a rich purple 
colour, and susceptible of the finest polish; the latter exhibiting a specimen of that peculiar style 
of carving in wood, which the ancient Indians alone were capable of executing. It is supported 
by a human figure lying on its breast; and by striking the back of the instrument, two tones are 
produced similar to those already mentioned. The head is remarkable for the singular beauty of its 
proportions ; both the eyes and the lips are formed of mother-of-pearl, while two pendants are at- 
tached to the nostrils. The shape of this instrument is not unlike that of a canoe: it weighs about 
twenty-five pounds, and after the lapse of so many ages it is still in the most perfect state of preser- 
vation. ‘The sounds of this martial instrument were employed to animate the Indians to battle. 

These ancient drums were the first specimens of the art of carving in wood which I had met with. 
They are valuable on account of the abundant testimony which they bear to the skill and ingenuity 
of this nation. I should in vain endeavour to explain the mysterious imagery which decorates the 
latter Teponastle ; but the three drawings which are annexed will give the reader a correct estimate 

(6c ) 

466 THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

of its proportions. The first represents the head viewed in front, and the other two the different 
sides of the instrument. . : 

No. CXXIX. In the province of Tlascala there yet remain two bridges constructed by the 
ancient Indians, though now in a state of great dilapidation. One of these, situated at the distance 
of a league from the town of Los Reyes, crosses a deep ravine at the foot of a steep and lofty hill on 
the road to San Francisco Temetzontla, and is built of large stones of various sizes, of even shapes, 
and well cemented with mortar. This bridge has a sort of arch, which forms an obtuse angle springing 
from its two side walls or buttresses; the height of whichis about seven feet, its breadth the same, and 
its width forty-two feet. It had originally a parapet on both sides, of which some traces yet remain. 
The work was ornamented with four stately obelisks, built of stones and mortar within, and faced 
on the outside with large bricks disposed in circular rows, with the addition of mouldings, which 
divided the obelisks into four parts, in the highest of which there was a niche destined perhaps to 
receive the statue of some rural deity. At each angle of the bridge stood an obelisk forty-two feet 
high, and collectively they must have presented to the eye of the passenger an object of striking 
grandeur. 

No. CXXX. The other bridge is constructed over a difficult pass on the same road, about a 
mile distant. In the brick parapets of this bridge the architect has made gutters for the discharge 
of water. Its length is about one hundred and two feet, its breadth thirty-six feet, and its per- 
pendicular elevation sixty feet. The aqueduct is four feet and a half in breadth, and five feet high, 
and is covered with large slabs of stone horizontally disposed. This bridge is likewise adorned 
with four obelisks placed at its four angles. Their dimensions are larger than those before men- 
tioned, and they have no niches in the upper compartment. Their execution is equally skilful. 

What opinion shall we form of these stupendous works, which, all circumstances considered, are 
unique in their kind? Constructed amidst rugged precipices in the deep glens of mountains, they 

afford a striking proof of the population and the power of this once mighty republic. 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 467 

ANTIQUITIES OF TEHUANTEPEC. 

PROCEEDING from the city of Mexico through Puebla and Mosaque, we pursued our journey 
first to Molcaxaque, and thence to New Tepexe. Here I obtained from the magistrate of the town 
the requisite assistance to enable me to explore some ruins which still exist about three leagues 
westward of the site of Old Tepexe. 

No. I. My curiosity was gratified by the sight of several ruins which I discovered in that neigh- 
bourhood. ‘The first that attracted my attention was a massy pile of building, apparently designed 
for the defence of some interior structure. This work exhibits a system of fortification which I 
cannot persuade myself was ever known to the inhabitants of the Old Continent. The walls are 
constructed of square stones, cemented with a durable mortar composed of lime and sand, and 
present an elevation which gradually recedes from the base to the summit, forming a series of over- 
hanging platforms; thus giving each platform (of which there are eight) the command of that be- 
neath it, as may be seen in the drawing annexed. 

The space which this building covers is immense, but its situation precluded the possibility of any 
accurate admeasurement. It stands on the projecting angle of a rock, surrounded by vast precipices ; 
while innumerable serpents, fostered by a climate so intensely hot as that of Lower Misteca, lurk 
in its recesses and guard its mouldering walls from intrusion. The buildings which form the in- 
terior of this vast structure are disposed with such order and regularity, as to lead me to imagine 
that they were once the residence of some potent Indian prince; for notwithstanding its present 
state of dilapidation and decay, the traces of arrangement and design in the disposition of its several 
parts are clearly visible, while the whole building must have been executed with rule, compass, and 
level, or some instruments of a corresponding description. 

No. II. In the middle of a spacious area we found a fragment of red granite, the carved surface 
of which resembles the calendar affixed to the steeple of the cathedral at Mexico. It exhibits several 
concentric circles, two of which inclose a row of square compartments. The few hieroglyphics or 
astronomical symbols which this fragment contains (sufficient to enable us to form an opinion of 
the appearance which the perfect whole presented), show that astronomy was a favourite science 
among the ancient Mexicans. In addition to these, our attention was drawn to the transverse orifice 
in the centre, the probable receptacle of a hand or gnomon; which, supposing this dial to have 
been horizontally placed, was intended by its shadow to mark the hours through every month of the 
revolving year. 1 computed the diameter of this instrument to have been six feet, and its thickness 
nine inches; and I contemplated it with a feeling of regret, that any part of so valuable a testi- 
monial of Mexican science should have been irreparably destroyed. 

No. III. This spherical stone, about a yard and a half in diameter, which we found at the en- 
trance of the ruins above mentioned, was probably employed by the ancient inhabitants to sharpen 
the points or edges of their domestic tools and weapons of war; since we observed on its surface 

several marks which confirmed us in the opinion that it had formerly been converted to such a use. 

468 — THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

From this ancient site we proceeded to Oaxaca, being obliged to pursue a circuitous course in 
order to arrive there. 

No. IV. Some Indians of the village of Quilapan brought me a small axe of red copper, which 
had evidently been cast in a mould, of the size and shape represented in the drawing. At first sight 
it resembled a labourer’s tool, but it might also have been applied to the purposes of war or sacri- 
fice; or perhaps, when mounted on a shaft, have enjoyed the more honourable distinction of being 
borne in the hands of the civil magistrate. 

Leaving behind us the city of Antequera, and journeying by the main road to Tehuantepec, we 
arrived there without meeting with any ancient building during the whole of our journey. 

No. V. Soon after our arrival at Tehuantepec we were informed by Don Vicente Lelo, the Deputy 
Governor of the district, an enlightened man and a loyal subject of our sovereign, that within a 
few leagues of that town we should find various architectural remains. Whilst I was preparing to 
proceed thither, a military weapon was brought to me which had been found in those ruins. It is 
the barb of a sort of dart such as I had never seen, made of very hard flint, and of the size repre. 
sented in the drawing. Like our bayonets it has three edges, and the end is formed into a shaft with 
the design of its being fixed in the socket of some pole or handle. 

In furtherance of the object of the commission which had been intrusted to me, I made the 
necessary arrangements for exploring a plain three leagues to the westward of the town. Accom- 
panied by the Deputy Governor, we arrived at the base of a lofty mountain called Guingola (which 
name signifies in the Zapotecan language The High Rock), on the summit of which we observed 
some ruins. We ascended the mountain by steep, winding, and rugged paths, and our progress was 
rendered more toilsome by the intense heat of a vertical sun. Having reached the summit, not- 
withstanding the difficulty of the ascent, we discovered amidst heaps of earth and fragments of 
ruined edifices, some buildings yet remaining of a pyramidical shape, and in a state of good pre- 
servation. | 

No. VI. The first of these is a pyramid consisting of four stories, built of stone. The walls are 
coated with flags which are overspread with a cement of lime, sand, and ochre. ‘The principal ascent 
is on the western side, while two smaller flights of stairs face the north and south, all conducting to 
the horizontal surface, on which worship was paid, and barbarous sacrifices performed to false and 
imaginary gods. The second story is ornamented with stones inserted longitudinally, and at equal 
distances in the wall, the extremities of each projecting from its surface: on these the natives 
were probably accustomed to fix lighted torches, or to range the heads of their sacrificed victims. 
The dimensions of this structure may be seen by the scale. The basement story is perpendicular, 
and its form oblong: the three other stories are oblique, each receding about a yard from its base. 
The principal ascent consists of about forty steps; the height and breadth of each step is about nine 
inches. ‘he breadth of the staircases on the north and south sides is two yards. 

No. VII. The dimensions and the form of the second pyramid, though apparently built at the 
same period, differ from those of the first: the former, as I have stated, being of four stories, the 
latter of only two. The principal staircase has likewise a contrary direction, facing the east; the 
smaller ones, like the others, front the north and south; and it is remarkable that the angles of the 
basement story are curvilinear. The materials of which this monument is composed are similar to 

those of the one last mentioned; but grandeur is united with simplicity in the architectural deco- 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 469 

rations of the upper story, which consist of two parallel friezes with square mouldings, inlaid with 
large blocks of white marble, covered with hieroglyphics, now in a state of decay. There is some- 
thing painful in the reflection, that the proudest works of man must sooner or later yield to time. 

No. VIII. This monument is of a conical form, divided by stories, resembling a flight of steps. 
The base or platform upon which it stands is sixty-six feet in length, and its height twelve feet. 
Its construction is perfectly regular; the material is stone covered with a coat of lime and sand, 
painted with ochre. It is probable that the flat surface by which it is terminated, served as the 
pedestal of some heathen statue placed in this open and conspicuous situation, or it possibly might 
have been a sepulchre destined to contain the remains of some distinguished warrior. I must here 
remark, that of the many pyramidical edifices which I have had the opportunity of observing in 
my different excursions through the provinces of New Spain, none terminate in a point, but in- 
variably in a horizontal plane of greater or lesser extent. It is evident that the founders of these 
structures spared neither labour, time, nor cost, in the erection of fabrics which they consecrated to 
religion, or hallowed to the memory of their deceased kings and ancestors. 

No. IX. Before I quit this memorable spot, I shall notice another curious monument, which 
from its circular form I imagine was dedicated to the celebration of gladiatorial sacrifices. It is 
composed of stones and mortar formed into a solid mass, and its whole surface is coated with a 
hard, smooth, and white cement. It occupies the centre of a square area in front of the principal 
ascent to the second pyramid, at the distance of about one hundred paces. This position confirms 
my Conjecture that it was associated with some religious rite. It might, however, have been con- 
structed for the very different purpose of serving asa stage for the exhibition of burlesque repre- 
sentations. 

No. X. I quitted the town of Tehuantepec, having been much gratified with what I had seen in 
it, and proceeded to an Indian village named Chilhuitlan, situated at the distance of a day’s journey, 
where I found an ancient stone bridge in a state of good preservation, still serving as a passage 
over the river which flows in the neighbourhood. It is about twelve feet long, six feet wide, and its 
elevation is nine feet above the level of the stream. Its sides are provided with low parapets, which 
are intersected with gutters for the discharge of water. That which first attracts the spectator’s at- 
tention, and forms indeed the most interesting feature in this ancient piece of masonry, is its pointed 
arch, which is composed of two blocks of stone of curvilinear shape and large dimensions, com- 
prising within their span a space of nine feet. 

From this village we continued our journey to the town of St. Dominic Petapa, lying in the 
direct road to Ciudad Real, where, thank God, we arrived in safety. 

No. XI. A few days after my arrival at this city, I inquired, as was my general practice, for some 
intelligent persons from whom I might procure information on the subject of the commission with 
which I was entrusted, and I had the pleasure of finding in Don Ramon de Ordones, the Vicar- 
general of the diocese, a gentleman whose love of antiquarian research well qualified him for the 
task. He showed me two curious relics in his possession. The first is a head formed of green 
porphyry, measuring seven inches in breadth and two in thickness. It is a whimsical attempt to 
represent a man’s face in double profile, as will be better understood by reference to the annexed 
drawing. ‘The countenance is beardless, the ears fanciful, and the cap which covers the head quite 

(6p) 

470 THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

original. ‘There is a protuberance on the forehead, and to imitate nature seems never to have been 
contemplated by the artist. A semicircular fracture is visible at the top of the head, which was 
perhaps originally a circular hole, by which it was suspended like a medallion round the neck of 
some gigantic statue. The surface of this curious piece of sculpture displays an exquisite polish. 

No. XII. This number presents to our view in miniature one of the most valuable specimens in 
existence of Mexican or Guatemaltecan antiquity. We here behold an engraved copper medallion, 
about two inches in diameter and a quarter of an inch in thickness, the weight of which rather ex- 
ceeds that of a Mexican dollar, as the Vicar-general ascertained at Guatemala. He conjectures, 
and I think with reason, that its date is as ancient as the first colonization of this continent. It was 
found on that celebrated spot which in later ages received the appellation of Palenque. It is 
evidently not struck from any die, but shaped and engraved by the hand, the point made by the 
compass or some similar instrument when forming the concentric lines on its surface being still visible 
in the centre. The upper side of the medal contains an historical device, composed of a mysterious 
hieroglyphical group, of which the principal figure is that of a man kneeling in the attitude of a 
suppliant, and entirely destitute of apparel, with the exception of a turban and buskins. The beard 
denotes the sex of the figure, although the lip is without mustachios. Placed between the ferocious 
and menacing heads of two monsters, nearly resembling the alligator or the Egyptian crocodile, he 
seems, not without imminent peril, to have gained admission to this romantic, luxuriant, and fruitful 
portion of the globe, so favourable to the multiplication of the human species. 

The reverse, as I term it, of this medallion, which nevertheless may be its principal face, is 
equally enigmatical and difficult of explanation. How in attempting to escape Scylla shall we avoid 
falling into Charybdis? Its field displays the same mountainous yet luxuriant scenery ; but the effigy 
of a lofty tree in the centre, covered with fruit and spreading foliage, is that which chiefly attracts 
attention ; the size of its trunk undoubtedly indicates the fertility of the soil in which it grows. 

We perceive at the root of the tree a scaly serpent entwining itself round the trunk, which may 
possibly allude to the primitive occupation by some ancient colony of this chosen and retired spot. 
The bird of Jove, perched upon the summit of an adjoining mountain, was perhaps intended as the 
symbol of rising power. ‘These and similar conjectures must, however, be received with caution, 
since the subject to which they relate is as dark and mysterious as was the riddle proposed by the 
Theban Sphynx. If I may venture to offer an opinion, it would be, that the principal side of this 
medal records the migration of a colony, which, after encountering many difficulties, at last arrives 
at the land of its destination ; whilst the reverse signifies the flourishing and prosperous state which 
the same colony afterwards attained*. 

Having terminated our researches in this place, notwithstanding the obstacles interposed by the 
inhabitants, who designated us as traitors, we continued our journey to Ocotzingo. 

No. XIII. We observed in the town-hall of the latter place two large blocks of stone, the first of 
which is of a hard substance and of a dark grey colour. It exhibits a male figure executed in alto- 
relievo. The style of the sculpture is good, but the attitude is constrained and painful, the head 
being very much inclined to the right, while the arms and hands appear to be bound. It was im-

possible to ascertain the position of the legs, the lower part of the stone having suffered con-

shall we attempt to describe the curious crown which adorns without protecting the head? It is

No. XIV. The other basso-relievo, sculptured in a yellow stone, is probably historical. Besides 
the two principal figures that constitute the group, hieroglyphics are distributed in different parts 
of it, of which the drawing will convey a more perfect idea than any description that I could offer. 
I shall therefore confine my remarks to the former. One of these beardless figures is standing, 
and the other sitting; while the artist evidently designed to represent both personages as engaged 
in animated conversation. Each is presenting to the other some gift. The figure which is sitting 
holds in its left hand a globe surmounted by a crown: the other holds something likewise in its 
hand, but the sculpture is too much defaced to enable me to judge what it resembles. The dress, 
fashioned after nature’s simplest pattern, is disposed, as is usual in their representations of the human 
form, with a strict regard to decency. Their helmets are of very complicated workmanship. That 
of the upright figure is composed of the head and tail of some bird, probably the eagle, on the top of 
which is a circle decorated with plumes, whilst the expanded feathers of the tail hang down grace- 
fully behind : to these are added other ornaments. The helmet of the seated figure is not so elaborately 
adorned, but Iam unable to give a minute description of its parts. I have already observed that 
these figures appear to be engaged in amicable conference, in confirmation of which it may be re- 
marked that neither of them is furnished with any offensive weapon. This piece of sculpture, as 
well as that before mentioned, formed a part of the decorations of some ancient buildings situated 
two leagues eastward of the town, in a place called in the Zendal language Tonila, which signifies 
The Stone houses. 

No. XV. In our way thither, and in its immediate vicinity, we found several human figures carved 
in stone, all of them headless trunks, and scattered like rubbish over the surface of the plain. I shall 
describe the two which were in the best state of preservation. ‘The mutilated form of the first is one 
yard and half an inch in height, and of proportionate breadth. This statue is affixed to a pedestal 
of a prismatic shape, measuring two yards in length. The material is a hard ash-coloured stone ; 
and from the excellence of the workmanship, I cannot help regretting its present imperfect state, 
which also renders any conjecture as to its original design almost fruitless. The arms are folded over 
the breast, the feet are in contact with each other, and the long robe which covers the whole figure, 
with the exception of the hands, resembles a scapulary. The fixed attitude of devotion, and the 
dress, render it more probable that this was the statue of a heathen priest, than an image to which 
vows were accustomed to be addressed. It bears some resemblance, either by chance or imitation, 
to the ancient statues of the Egyptians. ; 

No. XVI. This statue, the material of which is similar to that last mentioned, is equally well 
executed. It is the mutilated figure of a female (the mere trunk being all that remains) dressed in a 
robe, covered by a sort of vest, which divides in front like a curtain drawn aside. An apron, tastefully 
ornamented, is fastened to the waist, and descends to the feet of the figure. The remains of this statue 

are sufficient to indicate the regular symmetry of its original form, although it is impossible to say 

A472 THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

what might have been its destination when new from the hands of the sculptor. It is probable that 
the Indians had their female as well as their male divinities, and that both were equally invoked by 
them in seasons of calamity. ; 

No. XVII. Having spent some time in contemplating these mutilated statues, I proceeded to 
examine the remains of their temples, which were situated in a sultry and woody spot, at the distance 
of a cannon-shot, on the slope of a gently rising eminence terminating in a flight of steps, which 
(though now in a state of dilapidation) formed the entrance to the building. Five of these temples 
are still in existence; three of which are roofed, and two open to the air. The perspective view of 
these ruins presents three points of elevation: on the first stand two small oratories, then the large 
temple, occupying the centre of the second elevation, while the two artificial hills are ranged upon 
the third. 

The three covered oratories have many points of resemblance in their structure. They are built 
in the same style, with the same materials, and the same ornaments: their porches are paved with 
large square’slabs of free-stone ; the walls and roofs are coated with a cement of lime and sand; and 
the doors and vaulted ceilings terminate in an acute angle. The four sides are decorated with a 
frieze, and the interior is divided into several different apartments. The principal building stands in 
the centre, and was formerly occupied by the idol and its altar. 

The artificial hills, which are about twenty yards in height, and which bound the perspective just 
mentioned, are built of stone and mortar, the whole occupying a space of about two hundred yards. 

These two pyramidical structures differ in one respect from all the buildings of a similar kind that 
Ihave met with. Their roofs, which are entire, terminate in an acute angle, and are destitute of 
the round or square area, usually appropriated to the celebration of their religious rites. The prin- 
cipal entrance to the largest temple fronts the west; the sides of the smaller ones face the cardinal 
points.

above. 

Having fully investigated these ancient edifices I returned to the town of Ocotzingo, intending 

to proceed thence to Palenque. 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. ang: 

ANTIQUITIES OF PALENQUE. 

AFTER a journey of eight days we reached the city of Palenque. The space which we had to 
traverse is scarcely passable for any other animal than a bird; the road winding through mountains 
and over precipices, which we crossed sometimes on the backs of mules and sometimes on foot. 
Our only vehicle was a litter or a hammock, and we were compelled to pass the streams which 
intersected our route by bridges rudely formed of trees. The country through which we travelled, 
though fertile, is uncultivated and unpeopled, except by the inhabitants of a few scattered huts: 
hence we had no other bed than the earth, nor covering than the heavens. Our baggage was trans- 
ported by the help of some Indians of extraordinary strength and agility. Loaded with a weight of 
two hundred and fifty pounds, enough for the back of a mule, they proceeded on with unslackened 
pace, and climbed like deer the passes of the mountains. 

After having encountered every kind of difficulty during this toilsome journey, we arrived, thanks 
to God! in safety at New Palenque, the principal object of this our third expedition. This city 
belongs to the diocese of Chiapa, and the principal magistrate is also Deputy Governor of Ciudad 
Real, a city distant about eighty leagues to the westward. The population is large; composed of 
natives, Europeans, and their joint offspring. It stands on an uneven site of ground, in a climate 
which, though hot, appears to be healthy and favourable to vegetation, situated in the latitude of 
sixteen degrees north. Plantations of achote, rice, cacao, and other productions peculiar to this 
climate are found here, and the pine-apple grows wild. 

The surrounding country is mountainous, interspersed with fruitful plains, which are watered by 
rivers and brooks, and produce in great abundance a lofty tree with a trunk of proportionate 
magnitude, the bark of which, naturally dry, is powdered and used as a perfume in the churches. 
It is odoriferous in the extreme, and its name in the Zendal language is Ticconti. 

As soon as the weather permitted I hastened to explore the neighbouring ruins. The name of 
the celebrated city, of which they are the remains, has not survived the oblivion in which that of 
its founders is equally involved, and the Spaniards have improperly called it Old Palenque. 
Nothing remains of this powerful nation but the mighty skeleton of those works of art which time 
has not been able to destroy. 

It was built on the brow of a chain of rugged mountains, and situated to the south-west of the 
new city occupied a space of ground seven miles and a half in extent. A situation so elevated 
rendered it easily defensible against any hostile attack, while the woods which diversified the face of 
the wide and beautiful landscape lying around it, contributed to make it an equally desirable resi- 
dence in time of peace. 

The copious streams which still pour their rich treasures through the neighbouring valleys, fall 
upon the ear with soft and gentle murmurs; and while they give beauty and variety to the lovely 
face of the surrounding scenery, adorn it yet further by nourishing a thousand gay flowers, which 

(6£) 

474 THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

fill the air with the most delightful fragrance. A spot so favoured by nature abounds with birds and 
beasts of various tribes, which here propagate their species unmolested and secure. 

Having contemplated and admired the beauties which nature has so lavishly bestowed upon this 
solitary place, I proceeded to examine those monuments of man’s skill and industry which attach 
still greater interest to it. The dimensions of these various buildings may be ascertained by the 
scales annexed to their several drawings, and the reader will be assisted by consulting the ichno- 
graphical surveys, in which it is to be observed that the arrow always indicates the north. 

I shall confine myself to the description of the ground-plans, elevations, and materials of each 
structure, reserving for the future any remarks connected with their architectural merit, and the 
figures and hieroglyphics sculptured on their walls, in order that the thread of my narrative may be 
unbroken. 

In front of the ancient palace was a spacious open square, commanding a noble view of the greater 
temple. Here we encamped, building our huts with stakes, and covering them with the leaves of 
a tree (somewhat resembling those of the tobacco plant) of more than three feet in length, and pro- 
portionably wide, but destitute of smell. 

No. XIX. The stupendous pile which supports the intricate fabric I am going to describe is of a 
pyramidical shape: its oblong base is about three hundred and sixty yards in circumference, gra- 
dually decreasing towards the summit. On the front, which faces the East, is an ample staircase 
of hewn stone, forming the principal entrance to the building. The basement story is built of square 
blocks of stone, and enriched with a very bold cornice. 

No. XX. This number represents the ground plan of this vast edifice, whence its dimensions may 
be accurately ascertained, as well as the distribution of its various apartments. The summit of the 
artificial pyramid forms a spacious platform, which served for its foundation; and the excellence of 
the materials which were employed in its structure, is apparent in the durability and strength of its 
walls. The oblong area, on which the building is situated, projects six feet on every side beyond it, 
its circumference being about three hundred and twenty-four yards. ‘The elevation is about ninety 
feet from the surface of the ground; the principal walls are four feet in thickness, the inner walls 
less. The galleries are constructed so as to admit light into the several apartments, by the vacant 
spaces which are left alternately in the walls. The door-ways vary from twelve feet to one foot and 
a half in breadth, and from fifteen feet to four feet and a half in height. They are for the most part 
without lintels. The windows also differ considerably both in size and form, as may be seen in the 
drawing; and the apartments are of very limited dimensions. 

The floors are composed of loose stones, firmly united with sand and cement, and covered with a 
thick coat of hard and polished stucco. The ceilings are curiously constructed, all of them termi- 
nating in angular vaults, closed above with slabs of stone, each a yard in length. 

The roofs are of a corresponding shape with the ceilings, on which were placed, instead of tiles, 
large slabs of stone regularly disposed, and forming a covering of great durability. The whole of 
this vast structure was plastered both within and without with shining stucco, and enriched with a 
plain deep cornice inclosed within two double mouldings. 

No. XXI. This plate represents the interior or vertical section of the corridors, saloons, and 
chambers, as well as the buildings which stand in the large quadrangle. ‘Two flights of steps, facing 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 475 

each other, descend into the grand area. They are formed of blocks of hewn stone half a yard in 
height, the same in breadth, and one yard in length. 

No. XXII. On the first flight of steps appear two rows of gigantic figures (as shown in the annexed 
drawing), placed somewhat obliquely side by side. ‘They are carved in alto-relievo out of blocks of 
granite ; some are standing, some kneeling in different attitudes. The heads are all sculptured in 
profile; the mouths, half-open, show part of the upper teeth, and all appear absorbed in admiration, 
their eyes fixed on the same elevated point. ‘Their chins are beardless, and their hair falls in tresses 
from the head, which is covered by a kind of turban, of a different fashion in each figure. The ears 
are ornamented, the wrists encircled with ruffles, and they wear girdles, two of which are of con- 
siderable breadth and covered with hieroglyphics. ‘The size of each figure is portly, and the aspect 
grave: they are all mitred, and to the neck of each is suspended a collar studded with precious 
stones, to which is fastened a locket containing some device. Nakedness among these people was 
not the effect of poverty, but of habit caused by residence in a sultry climate; neither was it con- 
nected with any feeling of indecorum. They were content with merely studying decency in their 
apparel, a due regard to which is sufficiently discernible in all the representations of the human 
figure which have fallen under my notice. 

These statues, notwithstanding the solidity of the material in which they are executed, have suf- 
fered considerably from the unrelenting hand of time. It is vain to inquire who they were originally 
intended to represent, or why they were placed in their present situation. My ignorance on these 
points obliges me to view them merely in the light of ornaments, not unworthy of a sumptuous temple. 

No. XXIII. This drawing represents a building of singular beauty and proportion. It is a square 
pyramidical tower, remarkable for its symmetry and the elegance of its construction, of which there 
remain four stories, gradually decreasing in size, and separated by deep stone mouldings covered 
with a coat of bright cement. ‘The jambs and lintels of the door-way are of chaste and finished exe- 
‘ cution. To every story there are windows on each of the four sides. The circumference of the 
tower measures one hundred and twenty feet at its base, each side being thirty feet in breadth, and its 
whole exterior has an air of simple grandeur. 

No. XXIV. This plate shows the vertical section of the tower, with the staircases leading diagonally 
to each story. The upper story being in ruins, its original height cannot be ascertained. 

No. XXV. This drawing represents an isolated interior building, which, except the roof, is in very 
good preservation. It differs in its construction from those I have already mentioned, the architrave 
being of an uncommon form, and composed of solid blocks of stone obliquely placed, forming an 
obtuse angle, and thus serving as a penthouse fit to afford shelter from the heat or rain, as well as a 
support to a broad frieze with two mouldings, the lower of which is wider than the upper one. The 
upper story of this building (if another existed) is destroyed. . 

No. XXVI. The walls of the saloon which you enter on the northern side of this isolated edifice 
are not wholly divested of their ancient ornaments. A stucco moulding tastefully executed encircles 
a tablet of stone, on the surface of which are two figures carved in alto-relievo; its lower extremity 
rests upon a square block of stone, probably an altar, whichis also ornamented with figures and 
symbols. The subject of this piece of sculpture is most rare and curious. Two female figures are 
represented as seated; the one seems to be a goddess or personage of distinction, to whom the other 

476 THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

is offering a gift, which the former is in the act of gracefully declining. This personage is seated on 
a throne carved in the form of a monstrous animal, with a head at each end of its body looking in 
opposite directions, having its two necks decorated with collars of pearls, to which other ornaments 
are appended. ‘This group was perhaps designed by the artist as an allegorical illustration of some 
part of the law or fabulous history of his countrymen. The principal figure, which is naked, is pro- 
bably emblematical of Nature. Her head is adorned with a very light and curious cap: a string of 
pearls and precious stones hangs round her neck, to which is attached an ornament surrounding a 
device resembling somewhat in form the letter T; and her arms are also decorated with bracelets. 
The other figure, represented in a sitting posture, is dressed in the usual attire of the country, a 
mantle and petticoat, which are of a pattern resembling net-work, adorned with pearls and a fes- 
tooned border. She also wears a curious cap and ear-rings. The mouth of each figure is open, as 
if they were engaged in actual conversation. The hieroglyphics which are engraved on the surface 
of the stone were doubtless intended to explain the subject of this composition. The stone itself is 
of a durable quality and dark-coloured. On the south side of this saloon is the staircase which leads 
to the subterraneous apartments. 

No. XXVII. In our descent to these apartments we remarked, over the first door-way, some plain 
yet elegant ornaments executed in stucco; the first two mouldings being in remarkably good taste. 
It is probable that they had some relation to the rites which were practised in these gloomy abodes. 

On one side we observed the body of a man joined to the head of a quadruped, resembling that 
of a wild dog, or Osiris, celebrated in ancient mythology, whose neck was surrounded by a collar 
formed of leaves arranged like feathers. On the opposite side is a corresponding figure of a naked 
man, whose head is covered with a cap of leaves; he holds in his mouth a kind of pipe. These 
hieroglyphical figures face each other, and support with their hands a table or altar resting upon two 
feet, over which is placed an ornament also formed of leaves. Under these figures are two dis- 
membered arms, two skulls, and several smaller hieroglyphical figures. 

The design of this enigmatical device was probably to awaken a feeling of awe and fear in the 
minds of all who entered these sacred precincts. It is not surprising that on approaching these 
gloomy vaults, the scenes of human sacrifice, we should encounter such emblems. The skulls and 
mangled limbs are fit devices for the portals of such a temple. 

No. XXVIII. The ornaments of the second door-way are less complicated, but of a more graceful 
character than those of the first. They consist of some curious Arabesque foliage diverging from a 
central point, whence also a human figure appears to descend. Half only of the body is revealed 
to view; the neck is encircled with a necklace, and the wrists with bracelets. We may suppose this 
figure to represent one of the aerial messengers so frequently described in the Arabian Nights as 
descending from a superior region on some important mission to the world below. The head is 
covered with a sort of cap, analogous to that with which the heathen mythology has attired the god 
Mercury. Curiosity in vain attempts to discover the meaning of these mysterious symbols. 

No. XXIX. This plate contains a ground plan of three subterraneous vaults. They are built 
with solidity, and their structure is perfectly regular. Their roofs are angular, and they are furnished 
with staircases, doors of communication, and tables or altars resting upon the floor, or built into the 

wall. The first impression, which further examination tended to confirm, led me to suppose that 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. M7 

these were chambers dedicated to the service of the dead, and that the altars were intended for the 
reception of offerings or the immolation of victims. ‘They differ in size, being from two yards 
to two yards and a half in length, and one yard and a half in breadth. Some are of smaller di- 
mensions, but all are formed of a single stone, sculptured in a simple style without any ornamental 
relievos. They are of proportionate thickness, and rest upon four square stone legs. 

It was impossible to explore the remainder of these gloomy vaults, the north end having fallen in 
and being choked up with rubbish; and we feared that an attempt to make any excavation might 
bury us in the ruins. We therefore ascended by a different staircase, affording an egress near an 
angle of the building, on the landing-place of which I discovered a stone, which I have preserved 
as a curious relic. 

No. XXX. This stone being strongly imbedded in the wall was removed with great difficulty. It 
is of calcareous substance, and is in very good preservation. ‘The surface is covered with various 
hieroglyphics, which, like the relievos placed over the door-ways before mentioned, might have been 
intended to convey a tacit admonition to persons who descended into these vaults. My only motive 
for removing this stone from its place, was the desire of possessing. some memorial of my journey, 
as well as a testimonial of the correctness of my draughtsman, whose uniform accuracy and fidelity 
I am bound to commend. 

No. XXXI. This plate exhibits some ornamental mouldings in stucco, which are executed in alto- 
relievo, with such a regard to symmetrical arrangement, that a line drawn vertically through the 
centre divides the whole into two equal and similar parts. They consist of various Arabesque 
ornaments and designs, to which are added the fanciful and symbolical figures of two birds exactly 
similar to each other, standing upon a base formed of regular geometrical figures that appear to 
have been drawn with a compass. This ornament in stucco was found in a room of inconsiderable 
size, on the wall facing the entrance; in the centre of which is a window or opening in the form of 
a cross, or rather of the letter 'T, communicating with an adjoining room, which forms part of the 
same great edifice. 

No. XXXII. This number comprises a drawing of one of the tables which were found in the 
subterranean apartments above mentioned, formed of a single slab of the same kind of stone as 
that employed in the erection of the building; and likewise specimens of the different shapes of the 
_ various windows and small recesses which this vast labyrinth contained. 

No. XX XIII. On the left side of the staircase which leads from the great court to the saloon 
above the vaults, there is a statue resembling the colossal ones which I have described above, and 
probably placed there with the same intention. The kneeling posture is similar, and the coun- 
tenance gazes upwards with an air of admiration. The head is covered with a cap of strange and 
curious fashion, and the chin is beardless. Its neck is adorned with a necklace, which is partly 
concealed by the arms folded over the breast. The ear-rings consist of long tassels, and the dress 
is merely a curiously wrought sash which reaches to the knees. This statue is carved only in 
front, its back being a tablet inserted in the wall. In material and colour it resembles the colossal 
statues before referred to. As it is a small and solitary figure, a place has been allotted to it in the 
plate which contains representations of the windows.

Thus far I have described what presented itself to my observation; but vain would be the attempt 
to explain the meaning of these mysterious relievos: the national deities or kings may perhaps be 
represented by the statues which crowd the avenues of this vast temple, or the laws of some ancient 
legislator may be recorded on the tables of granite ranged along its mouldering walls. - 

The air of authority distinguishable in most of the figures, the crown or diadem encircling their 
brows, the sceptre, the collar and the badge suspended to their necks, render it not improbable 
that they were intended to represent kings, with vassals prostrate at their feet in sunihant attitudes, 
either paying homage or imploring protection. . 

Their costume though simple is varied. Their caps, helmets, and girdles differ: and this variety 
in the dress of the kneeling and recumbent pares may be characteristic of different vanquished 
cities and states. . 

T am aware how short and unsatisfactory this explanation must appear, and that it can afford 
but little real information to the inquirer; it nevertheless must supply the place of more certain 
information. | ; 

OF THE ART OF MOULDING IN STUCCO. 

The subject at which we now arrive is so mysterious, that its elucidation would require the art of 
the diviner. Surrounded as I am with what amazes and perplexes me, I shall begin by describing 
the large historical alto-relievos which still exist in perfect preservation, although the greater part 
of those that once ornamented or illustrated these temples have mouldered beneath the hand of time. 
With the exception of a few which were carved in stone, they were all uniform in size, colour, and 
material, and were disposed at regular intervals in compartments, which occupy the inside and out- 
side walls of their respective temples. . 

No. XXXIV. Like the structures which contain them, these relievos are fast hastening to decay. 
Already their remains, mixed with dilapidated fragments of the walls to which they were attached, 
strew the surface of the ground; and if they were of an historical nature, the chain of events which 
they record is now for ever broken. All that I could do was to cause those which were still perfect 
to be copied with the utmost fidelity, the greater part having left merely an impression on the wall. 
There are many circumstances connected with these relievos worthy of attention. ‘The situations 
which they occupied, more especially in the greater temple, were happily selected; ranged in regular 
order, and filling the vacant panels between the portals on the outside of the corridor of that vast 
edifice, they invested it with an air of imposing and regal splendour. Each compartment contained 
some mysterious group of figures and hieroglyphics surrounded by a border. . 

They executed their figures in stucco in two different ways: one of which, it appears, was by 
first drawing the outline on the wall, and afterwards spreading the cement over it. ‘Traces of these 
black outlines yet remain. By the other mode a rude imitation of the human figure in stone was 
substituted for the outline, to which shape and proportion were added by moulding the limbs into 
proper form with moist stucco. This operation is called in our academies, making the skeleton of 
the statue, a practice which likewise obtained among the Indians. They afterwards painted these 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 479 

statues with vermilion, minute particles of which, as well as occasional patches, are still visible in the 
narrow folds of the drapery. The stucco employed in the composition of them was admirable in 
quality. I term it natural stucco, for it does not appear to contain either sand, powdered marble, or 
any sort of adulteration : it is hard in the extreme, besides being beautifully white. With this substance 
all the relievos which enriched the walls of these buildings and splendid monuments were executed. 

Most of the figures are erect and well proportioned: all of them are in profile, portly, and 
almost colossal, their height exceeding six feet; while their attitudes display great freedom of limb, 
with a certain expression of dignity. Their dress, though sumptuous, never wholly covers the body : 
their heads are decorated with helmets, crests, and spreading plumes; and they wear necklaces, from 
which are suspended medallions. Many of the figures hold a kind of rod or staff in one hand; at 
the feet of others smaller figures are placed in reverential postures, and some are surrounded with 
rows of hieroglyphics. 

I feel persuaded that these alto-relievos were historical representations. ‘Each compartment con- 
tains from one to three figures, tastefully grouped, and standing upon pedestals ornamented with 
hieroglyphics and other curious devices. 

The plates included under the present number are copies of the figures which are ranged along 
the principal front of the greater temple. Notwithstanding the general correctness of design which 
they discover, it is impossible to regard without surprize a striking peculiarity exhibited in the 
physiognomy of these statues, the nose and the forehead forming by their junction a perfect curve ; 
and as if to render this peculiarity more apparent, the nose is made unusually large. It is generally 
allowed that the profile of the human countenance is of more easy representation than the full face ; 
but refraining at present from indulging in conjecture, I shall content myself with remarking that 
the intelligent will view with deep interest the features of a race of men which appear to have been 
unknown either to ancient or modern historians. 

No. XXXV. Ata short distance to the south of the greater temple is another, which has received 
the vulgar appellation of “ Las Lajas,” (The Slabs) a name probably given to it from the massy slabs 
of stone of which it is built. It stands on the summit of an artificial hill, and its front faces the 
north : its elevation is well proportioned, and (like all other buildings of a similar kind) the en- 
tablatures of its walls are adorned with allegorical figures, enclosed within parallel mouldings, and 
surmounted by a broad frieze. The roof is in ruins, but the stone floor still remains. 

No. XXXVI. The four colossal figures referred to by this number are placed in the panels 
between each door-way on the principal side of the last-mentioned temple; they are apparently 
absorbed in devotion, and the faces of all are turned towards the centre of the sanctuary. ‘Two are 
placed on each side, holding in one hand a gift, and with the other supporting a child, offering it as 
it were to the Law; for it does not appear that these children were offered to any deity, since no 
statue or image of any kind is placed in this temple, its only contents being massive blocks of stone, 
full of hieroglyphics, which doubtless were tables on which were engraved their laws and ritual ob- 
servances. I regretted extremely to find that it was utterly impossible to copy these hieroglyphics : 
the rain having so injured and decayed the surface of the stones, that a fragment which we en- 
deavoured to clean for the purpose crumbled in the attempt. Each of the figures is in the act of 
presenting a branch, as well as a child, at the temple, which might either have been fo entreat 

A480 THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 

fruitfulness, or some symbol explanatory of the nature of the offering. Considerable variety is 
displayed in their dress. The chin of one of them is not wholly destitute of beard: another is a 
female figure attired in a short petticoat, elegantly adorned with net-work, pearls, and fringes, and 
wearing a rich girdle. The other two represent men, plainly and uniformly habited, in a dress which 
I am inclined to think must have been their national costume. They are all standing upon pedestals, 
decorated as usual with fanciful embellishments These emblematical relievos, formed like the 
others of stucco, are in a state of similar decay; being exposed to the open air, they have suffered 
much from the changes of the atmosphere. ‘The head of the woman, as well as those of the children, 
has completely mouldered away. ‘ 

No. XXXVII. I shall now proceed to describe a human figure executed in stucco in bold relief, 
which owing to its situation is in excellent preservation. It was discovered in an interior covered 
temple, the architecture of which scarcely differs from that of the temples in its immediate vicinity. 
It faces the east, and its subterraneous vaults are also on that side. It stands at a short distance 
to the south of the Presentation Temple, or the Temple of the Children, upon the verdant summit 
of a natural hill, to which the hand of man would seem to have given a certain regularity of form. 

This image is placed on a throne or altar; its attitude is graceful, expressive, and commanding, 
and it appears to be in the act of delivering oracles either true or false to the people. It is seated 
on a richly adorned cushion, with one leg crossed under its body: the cushion is elevated upon a 
pedestal or table of curious shape, the feet of which resemble the claws of an eagle, and serve as 
pilasters to a massy square slab, well wrought and finished. At the extremities of the table are carved 
the heads of two monstrous animals, surmounted by fanciful ornaments: their open mouths display 
the eagerness with which they are prepared to defend or to enforce due respect to the image and its 
temple. A knotted collar encircles their necks. The head of the image is not decorated in exactly 
the same style as those of the preceding figures, as will be immediately perceived on referring to 
the drawing. Its arms are ornamented with bracelets, and it wears a short vest, apron, and drawers ; 
sandals are fastened with ribbon tied in bows to its feet. On its right hand appears a row of hiero- 
glyphics ranged vertically. Complete oblivion veils its history, but it may still be presumed that 
this image represents some distinguished and extraordinary personage. 

No. XXXVIII. This temple differs from the one last mentioned, the edifice built upon its upper 
area consisting of two stories ornamented with their respective cornices; its principal side faces the 
north. Unlike other structures of this kind, there is no appearance of its ever having contained any 
figures or hieroglyphical inscriptions, either in its interior, or ranged along the outer compartments 
of its walls. It stands on the summit of a pyramid, one hundred and eighty feet high, and resting 
upon a square base. This pyramid was ascended by a staircase, of which scarcely any vestiges 
remain; it was constructed of excellent materials, and displays skilful masonry. The ground-plan of 
the temple is annexed to the plate. 

No. XXXIX. This temple, which has received the appellation of La Cruz, from the Cross which 
occupies the centre of its shrine, is likewise famed for the beauty of its architecture. It nearly re- 
sembles the former structure, though consisting only of a single story. Situated on the upper area 
of a steep and lofty pyramid, the ascent to it is difficult, and its principal side faces the north. It is 
built on the plan of the last-mentioned temple. I have remarked that no trace was there discoverable 

THE MONUMENTS OF NEW SPAIN. 481 

of any figures, either carved in stone or executed in stucco; here on the contrary we found many. 
This temple is aptly named The Sanctuary of the Cross, since it contains a representation of that 
symbol, carved in stone, and resting upon a pedestal. Beside it stand four grave personages, who 
contemplate it with an air of deep veneration. The two figures nearest to the Cross are habited in 
dresses which differ from any that I had hitherto beheld, and seem more deserving of minute atten- 
tion. The tallest of them (probably a priest) is offering to it with upraised hands a child of singular 
shape, apparently a new-born infant.: admiration is depicted in the countenance of the other. Of 
the two figures placed in the back ground, one appears to be that of a man bending under the weight 
of years, apparently in the act of blowing a musical instrument, which he holds with both hands to his 
mouth. It is a sort of trumpet, composed of different pieces longitudinally united by rings placed 
at regular intervals: from the tube of the instrument proceed three leaves or feathers; probably 
feathers, as they were a favourite ornament of the Indians. The last personage in this group is a 
grave and majestic figure, apparently an admiring spectator of the scene. 

It is impossible adequately to describe the interior decorations of this sumptuous temple; the 
sculptor and the painter seem here to have embodied the most exalted conceptions of their art. The 
hieroglyphics which adorn this mysterious shrine are innumerable; not only do they surround the 
Cross in its centre, but present themselves on all sides. They are carved on the surface of marble 
slabs, of a fine grain and of a deep buff colour, ranged in horizontal rows; they occupy the centre 
of the building, as in the sanctuary of the Presentation Temple above described. 

Our surprise was great on suddenly beholding this cross; but closer examination of it convinced 
me that it was not the holy Latin Cross which we adore, but a Greek Cross disfigured with various 
fantastical ornaments ; since the former consists of a perpendicular line intersecting a horizontal one 
rather shorter, thus forming four right angles. Neither do these whimsical embellishments corre- 
spond with the venerable simplicity and the sublime mysteries of the true Cross; we must therefore 
refer this allegorical symbol to the religion of the country, and being totally ignorant of its ritual, 
it is vain to reason about its destination. I wish that it were in my power to explain the signification 
of the historical figures which so conspicuously adorn the walls of these temples, a task less difficult 
than to decypher the meaning of the hieroglyphics. It would appear that this nation had two 
methods of expressing its ideas, the one by letters or alphabetical signs, the other by obscure and 
mysterious symbols. These symbols, infinitely diversified in form, were disposed in parallel rows, 
both vertically and horizontally on the same stone, so as frequently to form right but never acute 
angles: this peculiarity in their arrangement .is not unworthy of attention. In each kind of line 
the same symbols often occur; and the human heads, which are always in profile, are uniformly 
turned to the left; a circumstance which leads me to suppose, that like Hebrew writings, these 
inscriptions were read from right to left. It is much to be regretted that their complicated form 
would in itself render the attempt to analyze them almost wholly useless; since characters of various 
colours and substances are here glued over each other, which firmly coalescing have become as it 

were incorporated with the stone*.

The path on which I have entered is so difficult and obscure, that I would willingly quit it for the 
wider field of conjecture, were I not convinced that the result would be fruitless, the scientific key 
to these hieroglyphics having been for ever lost. It would be wrong indiscriminately to attach im- 
portance to all the relievos discovered in these: temples:. on the contrary, many of them may have 
been mere ornaments, in no wise connected with religious mysteries. Private edifices of. any con- 
siderable size or beauty I imagine could never have been numerous in Palenque; but it requires 
much ‘practical knowledge on the part of the observer to enable him to classify ancient monuments, 
and to assign to each its proper place. 

Having treated of the sister arts, Sculpture and Architecture, I must not omit to make mention 
of Painting. The skill which this nation displayed in sculpture affords the most satisfactory proof 
that they must have been proficients in the art of painting. It is therefore only necessary for me 
to remark, that the colours which they employed were mineral. Notwithstanding the lapse of ages 
and the corrosive moisture of the atmosphere, I discovered some paintings in the greater temple, 
representing animals, birds, fruits, and flowers, which cr both taste and correctness in their 
design. 

No. XL. Under this number are included two stucco tablets. They are copies taken indiscrimi- 
nately from that numerous class of relievos, which in a sort of language of their own appear to 
address the stranger... The antiquarian will view with deep interest the unknown characters which 
cover their surface: their disposition into horizontal and vertical lines is remarkable, and their form 
is quite original, since they bear not the least resemblance either to Egyptian hieroglyphics, or to 
the symbols in use amongst the ancient Mexicans. 

No. XLI. This circular stone was taken from the foundation story of the greater temple. «It, is 
perfectly plain, and without any kind of ornament or device. We found several stones similar to it 
in the vicinity of that temple, but were unable to ascertain their onigial destination. ‘They might 
have been used either as tables or altars for sacrifice. ite 

No. XLII. We discovered amongst these ruins chafing-dishes site censers, of a cylindrical shane 
and fluted, with oval covers, containing an aperture apparently for the purpose of allowing a passage 
to the smoke, when incense was burning before the idols or on their altars.: 

No. XLIIT. At a short distance to the north of the greater temple there is a bridge, built of stones 
so evenly united, that no cement is visible in their interstices: no traces of any parapet can be 
discerned. The arch, if it may be so called, is of a very peculiar construction ; being curvilinear 
below and flat above, as represented in the drawing. Although the river over which it affords a

in an eastward course, and its cold and limpid stream nourishes a shell-fish somewhat resembling a 
snail, and exceedingly palatable. | tf mid 

No. XLIV. Westward of the greater temple, at the distance of a league, we found the remains st

Now Sve A league to the westward of this spot runs a rapid stream, in which we found some 
petrified shells, and others in their natural state. It flows in a southerly direction through an aque-

We were at a loss to conjecture the use of this aqueduct, which might either have answered the

straggling suburbs of this city at the period of its greatest population. These immense ruins, scat- 
tered over a vast tract of country, and the greater portion of them buried beneath the soil, awaken 
in the mind of the spectator the liveliest feelings of curiosity and interest.

DESCRIPTION OF THE TRIUMPHAL STONE PRESERVED IN THE 
UNIVERSITY OF MEXICO. 

THIS monument, which is still preserved in the University of Mexico, is remarkable for the rich- 
ness of its hieroglyphical sculpture. It is a cylindrical block, vulgarly but erroneously called “ The 
Sacrificial Stone,” or ‘The Stone of the Dance,” since doubtless it records victories obtained by 
the Mexicans over fifteen different provinces or states, and therefore should be regarded in the light 
of a valuable historical monument. In order to transmit the fame of these victories to distant ages, 
the Mexicans caused the representation of them to be engraved on a cylindrical stone of the hardest 
grain. The upper surface of this stone is likewise carved with devices, either merely fanciful, or 
which may have some connexion with astronomical science, since they are not unlike those sculp- 
tured upon the Mexican calendar* ; but it would be impossible for me to determine this point. It 
is evident that this stone was intended to be placed in a horizontal position, with its flat surface 
resting on the ground; and it probably occupied the centre of some open court, as the most ad- 
vantageous situation for a monument consecrated to national glory. 

The ancient Romans were accustomed to erect columns and triumphal arches in honour of their 
Emperors, and the Mexicans sought in a similar manner to eternalize the fame of their martial 
monarchs. It would be a difficult task to assign any dates to the victories emblazoned on this 
triumphal stone: nor is it possible to ascertain where the series commences, since a cylindrical 
surface has no defined beginning or end. Although thirty figures are sculptured upon it, they may 
be reduced to fifteen pairs, as there are only sixteen different warriors; one of whom, who in all 
probability is the King of Mexico, is represented fifteen several times, while the remaining figures, 
symbolical of the various conquered nations, differ from each other in their dresses, arms, and 
devices. Some of the latter are represented with beards, but the attitude of each is expressive of 
the deepest reverence and submission. There is a general resemblance in their apparel, but their 
head-dresses and sandals exhibit some variety. There is some difference also in their warlike 
weapons, though in most cases they are similar; but each subjugated state is distinguished by its 
peculiar symbol or device. It is probable that the artist, having reduced the block of stone to 
proper shape and dimensions, and given it the requisite polish, sketched upon its surface the out- 
lines of his work, which he afterwards executed in basso-relievo with a metallic or stone chisel. 
The figures are all represented in profile, and exhibit a uniformly flat, and not a convex basso- 
relievo, their outlines principally consisting of straight lines. It is impossible not to admire the 
symmetrical distribution of the thirty figures into fifteen distinct groups, and the relative equality of

of sculptured granite, to which the name of The Mexican Calendar has been given from the astrological symbols carved upon its surface, 

and an engraving of it will be found in his Monumens De L’Amérique.

their proportions. Two parallel borders with different designs inclose and adorn this valuable 
ancient monument. 

The position of the principal figure, which I have already observed is fifteen times repeated, is 
such that the Mexican monarch, as I shall designate him, is only represented in profile; neither 
have we a full view of his person: the style of the sculpture is nevertheless bold and energetic. He 
is attired as a warrior, and wears a crown adorned with beautiful and spreading plumes: his vest is 
confined with a rich and broad girdle. On his feet are sandals, and that on his left foot is 
remarkable for the singularity of its shape, and unlike the other rises in the air with a high and 
graceful curve. His air and demeanour are those of a conqueror: with his left hand he grasps the 
crest of his vanquished foe, and compels him to an act of submission, while his right holds a circular 
shield, from beneath which projects a quiver of arrows in a vertical position. 

_ The second figure, which is also in profile, is shorter in stature than the first, and is habited in a 

plainer military costume, consisting of a helmet or crown of feathers, sandals, a girdle, &c. He 
seems to be in the act of presenting with his right hand some flowers as a mark of homage to the 
conqueror. It would certainly be difficult to explain the reason why mankind prefer the right 
hand to the left; but this appears to be the case amongst nations the furthest removed from each 
other. The left hand of this figure grasps some warlike weapons which differ from those of the 
other figures. 

Two things are particularly deserving of notice in the figures which represent the conquered 
nations; the one, that their eyes are either covered with a bandage or concealed by a shade*, 
probably to mark the respect due to their conqueror ; the other, that two of them have long beards 
and mustachios, a fact which would seem to indicate a diversity of national character. 

The hieroglyphical devices, or, as they may be more properly styled, the arms of the several 
states, provinces, or cities vanquished by the Mexicans, remain to be noticed. 'To each of the 
latter was assigned its distinguishing symbol; the emblem of its jurisdiction, situation, and natural 
productions. I know not whether it was intended to register on the surface of this cylindrical stone 
(as represented in the preceding plate) the dates of these memorable triumphs, but its first appearance 
certainly resembles that of the Mexican calendar. The area of the circle is divided into thirty-two 
equal parts, exhibiting a number of concentric circles exactly parallel, and eight very acute angles, 
the points of which intersect the outer circle and divide it into eight equal parts; while in like 
manner eight parallelograms and some oval figures occupy the intervening spaces between the 
angles. Immediately below these ornaments is a border divided into squares, in each of which are 
five small circles, one at each angle and one in the centre. ‘This stone in shape also resembles the 
calendar ; but its position must always have been horizontal, with its flat surface resting on the 
ground: in other respects the difference between these two Mexican monuments is sufficiently 
apparent. 

A human countenance symbolically representing the Sun is carved on the former. What a striking 
contrast does this representation of the effulgent Author of light present, when compared with the

sculptured divinities of Grecian mythology. Let us turn from their young and graceful Apollo, with

renders it difficult to conceive how it could have been executed without a compass. It is probable 
that the carving was not merely ornamental, but intended to mark, according to the calculations of 
the Mexican calendar, the precise period of the erection of this monument*.
