M. DE HUMBOLDT has described in his American Monuments the Temalacatl, or stone for the gladiatorial 
sacrifices which the Mexicans celebrated in the month Panquetzaliztli. This stone was dug up in the Plaza Mayor 
of Mexico, not many years before the baron’s visit to that city; and since a representation of it will be found in the 
fourth volume of the present work, it is only necessary to remark here, that the Mexican paintings serve to 
illustrate the ornamental figures sculptured in relievo around it. It has generally been supposed that these figures 
commemorate the triumphs of some Mexican king, who is there represented as a warrior leading to execution or 
into captivity his vanquished foe, and that the symbols placed behind the head of each prisoner denote a different 
conquered city or state. The latter part of the supposition alone appears to be correct; since in the person of the 
presumed king may be recognized, by the symbol of the smoking mirror worn as an ornament at the back of his head, 
the priest of Tezcatlipoca or Huitzilopuchtli, the supreme deity of the Mexicans, to whom prisoners taken in war 
were sacrificed as devoted victims. It was customary with the Mexican priests to dress themselves in the same 
costume as that worn by the deity whose festival they celebrated; and hence it may be inferred that this stone for 
gladiatorial sacrifices was dedicated to Tezcatlipoca:. which supposition will also serve to explain the nature of the 
ornament or symbol worn on the advanced foot of the principal figure; since the Mexicans, in allusion to their belief 
that that god had appeared to them in fire and smoke on Mount Tezca (the Mountain of the Mrror),—whence the 
proper name which they bestowed upon him of Tezcatlipoca, compounded of Tezca, the name of the mountain, 
tlil dark, and poca smoke, in reference to the manner of bis manifestation,—always represented him with the symbol 
of a smoking mirror, which was placed either on his head or his foot, and sometimes on both, as in the eighteenth 
and twenty-second pages of the Borgian MS. This god was also named by the Mexicans Yao; and the smoking 
mirror on his foot reminds us of Habakkuk’s description of the presence of Jehovah in the fifth verse of the third 
chapter of his Prophecies: “ Before him went the pestilence, and burning coals went forth at his feet :” whilst the 
proper name Tezcatlipoca recalls to our recollection the eighteenth verse of the nineteenth chapter of Exodus, 
descriptive of the descent of God upon Mount Sinai: “And Mount Sinai was altogether on a smoke, because the 
Lord descended upon it in fire: and the smoke thereof ascended as the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mount 
quaked greatly.” So important an event in Hebrew history as the promulgation of the Mosaic code of laws might, it 
may readily be conceived, have disposed the Jews, who were fond of bestowing many names upon God, either to 
use at first, or to invent i later ages, an epithet in his honour commemorative of the time when he conversed with 
Moses in the mount. They likewise emphatically styled the laws that were then given to them, the mirror of God, 
declaring that they beheld in them, as in a mirror, his will clearly revealed: and hence they argue that the old law 
has never been repealed, because the will of God must needs be wmmutable. This being the opinion of the Jews, 
it would be interesting to learn from them whether they believe that a remnant of the Canaanites, who were 
sentenced to utter destruction by Moses, exists in any corner of the earth; and whether, if they had the power, 
they would feel it to be a duty imposed upon them by Moses, to force idolaters under pain of death to become 
proselytes, and to wage war against idolatrous nations to bring them over to their faith? These questions may 
appear to be invidious; but they are intimately connected with the present subject of inquiry, the object of which is 
to discover the real origin of human sacrifices in the New World, and who were the authors of them. It is the 
spirit of Judaism, however, rather than the Jews, that we would interrogate upon these two points; since it was the 
former persuading the latter that they were the chosen people of God, whilst the rest of mankind of a different creed 
were his enemies, that constituted them the haters of nearly all their species, and too frequently made them the 

488 NOTES, ( 

cruel avengers of the pretended honour of Jehovah. Can it for a moment be doubted, whether, if any tribe or race 
of men could be impressed with the belief that some other tribe were the enemies of their god, they would not deem 
it to be a meritorious thing to make war on and to exterminate them, and consider the field of battle on which they 
fought them as a sort of table or altar of sacrifice destined to receive the blood of victims most acceptable to the 
deity? which would naturally lead to the custom of reserving prisoners taken in an engagement for a still more 
holy sacrifice at the hallowed shrine of his temple,—a custom which was common amongst the Mexicans, and which 
cannot fail to bring to mind what is recorded in the Old Testament, of Samuel hewing Agag in pieces before the 
Lord in Gilgal; which words unequivocally declare that the high priest of the Lord acted on that occasion the 
part of the Mexican Topiltzin, and stained, if he did mot profane, the shrine of Jehovah with the blood of a human 
victim. This is the only example, it is true, which-is recorded in the Old Testament of the solemn immolation of 
a prisoner of war by the hand of a Jewish high priest: but who can venture to affirm that later high priests might 
not have imitated the zeal of Samuel, although Hebrew history is silent respecting them? The ordinance in the 
last chapter of Leviticus, which expressly commands that all of man devoted by men to the Lord should surely be 
put to death, not only proves that the custom of devoting men to the Lord did exist amongst the Jews, but that it 
was approved by Moses, who no where forbids the Jews in the Pentateuch to devote men to the Lord, but only after 
having devoted them to save them alive; whilst the condition annexed to the act, implied in the first instance 
permission granted to it, since what is absolutely forbidden by the law is never made conditional. The history, 
indeed, of Jephthah offering up his own daughter as a burnt sacrifice to God, as related in the eleventh chapter of 
Judges, and the reason which he assigns for carrying his fatal vow into execution, “I have opened my mouth unto 
the Lord, and I cannot go back,” fully prove what the Jews believed to be the spirit of this ordinance, which was 
no less killing than was its letter, which is as follows: “ Notwithstanding, no devoted thing that a man shall devote 
unto the Lord of ail that he hath, both of man and beast, and of the field of his possession, shall be sold or redeemed ; 
every devoted thing is most holy unto the Lord. None devoted which shall be devoted of men shall be redeemed, 
but shall surely be put to death.” To understand more clearly the force of this ordinance, it may be proper to observe, 
that there were two kinds of devoted victims of men amongst the Jews which they were bound to put to death; the 
former class comprehended those whom God himself, speaking through the mouth of Moses, had devoted to de- 
struction, who were all the original inhabitants of the land of Canaan: the latter were those who were devoted by 
men to him. The question may well be asked, Who were these? If we may venture to offer an opinion, it would 
be, that they were either Hebrew slaves descended from Canaanitish parents, or prisoners of war captured by the 
Jews from those distant nations which were not doomed to utter destruction by Moses, whom the Hebrew soldiers 
were permitted before a battle to devote, in case they should take them prisoners in the engagement, as a sacrifice (for 
by what other name can the deed be called?) to Jehovah. The probability of this conjecture having been admitted, 
it will not be unreasonable to suppose, that the Mexican custom of sacrificing prisoners taken in war to Tezcatlipoca 
originated amongst the Jews who colonized America. If the interpretation which is here put upon the above- 
mentioned ordinance of Leviticus be disagreeable to the Rabbis, they will oblige the world by explaining its true 

signification, confining themselves strictly to the letter of the sacred text, and bearing in mind that the words “of | 

all that he hath, both of man and beast,” render it clearly impossible that the Canaanites can be alluded to. This 
doubtless is one of those many passages of Scripture that the early Fathers put without the pale of discussion, desiring 
their simple flocks to hold those who would indulge in an inquisitive train of reasoning upon them in the light of 
excommunicated persons, and to make no reply to their objections; and hence it happens that a great portion of the 
Old Testament is even at the present day but ill understood, because its contents have never yet been freely discussed 
by all classes of the community. 

In reference to a remark made above, that human sacrifices to the Deity probably originated in the notion that 
certain tribes or nations of mankind were his enemies, whose blood would be a most acceptable offering to him 
(which likewise supposes the existence of some chosen or favourite people, the executors of his will; and in fact 
every early nation were in their own estimation the chosen people of God, differing only from the Jews in not 
imagining that the rest of mankind were objects of his aversion), we shall cite some passages from the Old 
Testament, in which the field of battle is very unequivocally named a place of sacrifice. Hzekiel in the following 
passage of the thirty-ninth chapter of his Prophecies thus describes the defeat of Gog, under which name is 

NOTES. ee 489 

signified some powerful enemy of the Jews. “And, thou son of man, thus saith the Lord God; Speak unto every 
feathered fowl, and to every beast of the field, assemble yourselves, and come; gather yourselves on every side to 
my sacrifice that I do sacrifice for you, even a great sacrifice upon the mountains of Israel, that ye may eat flesh, 
and drink blood. Ye shall eat the flesh of the mighty, and drink the blood of the princes of the earth, of rams, of 
lambs, and of goats, of bullocks, all of them fatlings of Bashan. And ye shall eat fat till ye be full, and drink blood 
till ye be drunken, of my sacrifice which I have sacrificed for you. Thus ye shall be filled at my table with horses 
and chariots, with mighty men, and with all men of war, saith the Lord God. And I will set my glory among the 
heathen, and all the heathen shall see my judgment that I have executed, and my hand that I have laid upon them. 
So the house of Israel shall know that I am the Lord their God from that day and forward.” Isaiah in the sixth 
verse of the thirty-fourth chapter of his Prophecies, applies the term ‘sacrifice’ to the slaughter of God’s enemies, 
which being there said to be accomplished by the sword, it is to be supposed refers to the field of battle. “The 
sword of the Lord is filled with blood, it is made fat with fatness, and with the blood of lambs and goats, with the 
fat of the kidneys of rams: for the Lord hath a@ sacrifice in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Idumea.” 
The precise meaning of the word sacrifice in the eighth verse of the first chapter of Zephaniah, is less obvious. 
“ And it shall come to pass in the day of the Lord’s sacrifice, that I will punish the princes, and the king’s children, 
and all such as are clothed with strange apparel.” The sacrifice of prisoners taken in war, it may be presumed, 
soon led to the sacrifice of slaves ; since when once it had become an established usage to celebrate solemn festivals 
with the blood of human victims, a fanatic multitude would have been likely to deem it more criminal to let the 
festival want its accustomed rites, than to put to death some unoffending slaves. The direst of all human sacrifices 
was, however, that of children by their parents, at which extreme goal the Jews in very early ages had arrived ; 
since Scripture informs us that the valley of Tophet, which was close to the gates of Jerusalem, had acquired an 
infamous celebrity by reason of such rites. The apologists of the ancient Jews are here placed in a dilemma from which 
they will find it difficult to extricate themselves; since if they will not allow that these sacrifices were performed 
in imitation of the example of Abraham, who offered up his son Isaac to God, they must admit that the Jews, be- 
ginning with animals, waded through the blood of all kinds of sacrifices, until they finally imbrued their hands in 
the innocent blood of their own children ;—and then with what sentiments will the future perusal of many books of 
the Old Testament inspire them! The representation of human sacrifices so frequently occurs in the Mexican 
paintings, that it is unnecessary in this place to enter into any particular description of them: three things, however, 
deserve to be noticed respecting them; of which the first is, that the victim was not sacrificed at but upon the altar 
of smooth stone which stood on the upper area of the temple: secondly, that the sacrifice was performed by dividing 
him 2 the middle; and thirdly, that the Mexicans declared that Huitzilopuchtli taught them that mode of sacrifice 
when he led their ancestors forth on their pilgrimage from Aztlan, the occasion of which is more fully explained in 
the 241st page of the present volume. There was a peculiarity in the Mexican mode of laying the living victim 
upon the altar and sacrificing him there; since the general practice of ancient nations was to immolate animals 
near the altar, and afterwards to place certain parts of them as an offering upon the altar. We are informed, 
however, in the ninth and tenth verses of the twenty-second chapter of Genesis, that Abraham, when about to 
sacrifice his son Isaac, laid him upon the altar. “And they came to the place which God had told him of; and 
Abraham built an altar there, and laid the wood im order; and bound Isaac his son, and laid him on the altar upon 
the wood. And Abraham stretched forth his hand, and took the knife to slay his son.” The precise manner in 
which Abraham would have killed his son cannot be known, because he did not complete his intended sacrifice ; 
but that patriarch had on a former occasion divided the victims in the middle, when by the express command of 
God he sacrificed to him on entering into the covenant with him. The obvious interpretation, however, of the fol- 
lowing passage of the fifteenth chapter of Genesis, certainly is, that Abraham divided the victims in the middle after 
he had sacrificed them; but still fanaticism might have understood it in another sense. “And he said unto him, I 
am the Lord that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees, to give thee this land to inherit it. And he said, Lord 
God, whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it? And he said unto him, take me an heifer of three years old, and 
a she goat of three years old, and a ram of three years old, and a turtle-dove, and a young pigeon. And he took 
unto him all these, and divided them én the midst, and laid each piece one against another: but the birds divided 
he not.” In conclusion to this note we shall only observe, that the instrument with which the Mexicans’ performed

their human sacrifices was a stone knife, which perhaps resembled the sharp-edged Ethiopian stone with which the

the earliest ages made of them in circumcision. 

Nore II. 

It has been already remarked, page 377, that the words of Ezekiel, “And fire is gone out of a rod of her 
branches which hath devoured her fruit,” afford grounds for supposing that the Jews were acquainted with the 
Mexican method of kindling fire from two pieces of wood. This supposition would likewise serve to explain another 
passage in the twenty-first chapter of Ezekiel, which is thus translated in the Septuagint: “ Zrnoera Bacthevg Bav- 
Awvosg émt THY apyaay ooop, én apyne TWY dvo odwy, TOU pavrevoasbat PayvTetayv, TOU avaBpacat passoy, Kat émepwrnoar év TOLG 
yAurroug”” which Selden says that he does not clearly comprehend ; observing that he cannot see how the words rov 
avaBpaca padsoy can refer to paSouavrera, or that kind of divination which Hosea, in the twelfth verse of the 
fourth chapter of his Prophecies, says that the Jews practised by means of their staves: “My people ask counsel at 
their stocks, and their stag declareth unto them: for the spirit of whoredoms hath caused them to err, and they have 
gone a whoring from under their God.” If that learned man had known the Mexican method of kindling fire by 
means of two pieces of wood, and that one of those pieces was a staff, the rapid rotation of which between the hands 
produced ignition in the other piece, he would not have hesitated to refer the divination practised by the king of 
Babylon to zvpouavrea, or divination by fire, when the propriety of the choice of the verb dvaBpaca, to express the 
mode in which the flame proceeded from the wood, becomes apparent; and the entire passage may be translated, 
“The king of Babylon will take his station at the cross road, where an old road branches off in two directions, to 
have recourse to divination, and to kindle fire with the staff, and to interrogate images.” The object of the king of 
Babylon in using divination was, that he might thereby be guided in the choice of his captains and the operations 
of the war which he was about to undertake. It is singular that the Mexican priests,—who, as it were in obedience 
to the precept contained in the second verse of the twentieth chapter of Deuteronomy, “ And it shall be when ye are 
come nigh unto the battle, that the priest shall approach and speak unto the people,” accompanied the Mexican 
armies, and encouraged the soldiers to battle by exhortations and by the blowing of trumpets, as the Levites are said to 
have done in the sixth chapter of Joshua, when the walls of Jericho fell down at the sound,—should likewise, either 
as a mode of divination, which is very probable from the superstitious reverence which the Mexicans felt for fire 
kindled by the hands of their priests, or as a propitious omen, have drawn new fire from a piece of wood on the eve 
of an engagement, that ceremony serving as a signal for the battle to begin, as Sahagun informs us in the first section 
of the seventeenth chapter of the eighth book of his History of New Spain. We may observe, in reference to a very 
barbarous and superstitious rite practised by the Mexicans on their year of jubilee, at the commencement of every 
new cycle of fifty-two years,—that of drawing fire from the body of a sacrificed prisoner by kindling it in a piece of 
wood placed in the wound in his breast, a representation of which occurs in the fifth and sixty-ninth pages of the 
Borgian MS., although in the latter painting some miraculous circumstances appear to accompany the ceremony, 
and the painter perhaps intended to represent a living sacrifice,—that if the Jews were the institutors of this rite 
in the New World, it was probably from a fanatical desire that the denunciation contained in the twentieth verse of 
the ninth chapter of Judges should appear to be fulfilled against their enemies ; “ Let fire come out from Abimelech 
and devour the men of Shechem and the house of Millo; and let fire come out from the men of Shechem, and from 
the house of Millo, and devour Abimelech.” This denunciation was pronounced by Jotham the son of Gideon, 
who delivered the Israelites from the Midianitish yoke, against his brother Abimelech, who had usurped the title of 
king over Israel; and against the men of Shechem, who had conspired with him to deprive the Israelites of their 
liberty, and who were consequently regarded by them in the light of their bitterest enemies. Sahagun and Torquemada 
both describe the ceremonies which accompanied the above-mentioned cruel Mexican rite; the former in the tenth 

NOTES. 491 

and thirteenth chapters of the seventh book of his History, and the latter in the thirty-third chapter of the tenth book 
of his Indian Monarchy. The remarkable passage in the Book of Judges referred to, which corrupted by tradition 
possibly laid the foundation of that rite amongst the Mexicans, is thus translated in the Septuagint: “’Efed@ou zvp 
ato ABipedey, Kar Katapayou Tove avdpac Sukywwy, Kar Tov dixov BnOuaarw. Kar e£eAOoe mvp aro avopwv Likwy, Kat €k Tov 
otkov Bybuaadw, kat karaayo. tov “ABimedey.” It is not a little surprising to find, from the fifth and eighteenth verses 
of the same chapter of Judges, that Abimelech slew seventy sons of Gideon, his own brothers, wpon one stone; since 
we here have an example of the Mexican mode of immolating victims upon a stone (the piedra or tajon so often 
mentioned by Sahagun) having been practised in very early ages by the Jews. But it is even more surprising that 
after such conduct the Israelites should have allowed Abimelech to reign over them for three years, as we are 
informed was the case in the twenty-second verse of the above-mentioned chapter; and that at the expiration of that 
period it should have been the men of Shechem, and not his Hebrew subjects, who dealt treacherously with him. 
The precise manner in which Abimelech put his brothers to death upon one stone, it is impossible to know; he must 
have had a reason for causing so many as seventy persons to be led to the same place of execution, which was 
probably founded either upon the intended mode itself of their death, or upon the propriety of slaying them upon 
that particular stone. But if his conduct was on that occasion influenced by mere caprice, and if in the face of day, 
the children of Israel looking patiently on, he ventured so to act in the full confidence that the nation would not avenge 
so great a wrong, it can only be said that a people who could be guilty of such base ingratitude to their deliverer, 
well deserved so worthless a king. Whether the Jews ever immolated victims in the Mexican manner, by making 
an incision in their breasts and tearing out the heart through the wound, is no where recorded in Scripture. 
On the authority however of Maimonides, their most famous Rabbi, we affirm that they were acquainted with 
such a mode of sacrifice, since the following passage occurs in the seventh chapter of his Treatise concerning

vocantur ibidem ‘pelles cordium’.” ‘“ Maimonides observes in his notes upon Misnajot, that this was a heathen 
practice, ‘a kind of idolatry’. It would appear that the Gentiles (if the Jews are to be credited, whose sources of 
information are wholly unknown to me,) made an aperture of a round shape, or rather in the form of a heart, through 
which they tore out the heart of the victim; but if the aperture from want of dexterity (on the part of the sacrificer) 
assumed the appearance of a lengthened rent, the animal was deemed useless for the purposes of sacrifice. The 
same thing is said in Aboda Zara, chap. 11. sec. 4: ‘Rabi Simeon Ben Gamliel affirms, that when the incision is 
orbicular, the skins are forbidden ; when it is oblong, that they are lawful.’ Skins, the incision in which was oval, 
are there named ‘heart skins’.” These, however, are not the only skins which have supplied Jewish and even 
Christian writers with matter for controversy ; since the ‘ tunice pelliceze’ which God gave Adam in Paradise after 
he had discovered that he was naked, have given rise to the most absurd theories; and the question that was asked 
nearly two thousand years ago, namely, Where did these skins come from? has not yet been satisfactorily answered. 
The Rabbis, who have not scrupled to declare (in order, no doubt, to add still greater sanctity to sacrifice,) that God, 
on the occasion of having created the moon less than the sun, offered a sacrifice of atonement for himself, as it were 

492 NOTES. 

in‘confession of error, will perhaps contend that these were the skins of the victims then killed. It certainly must 
cause some surprise to find that not Maimonides alone, but a whole string of Rabbis were acquainted with a mode 
of sacrifice almost the same as that practised by the Mexicans, which had escaped the notice of the most diligent 
antiquarians. The distinction likewise which they attempt to draw between wounds made of an oval shape in the 
breasts of sacrificed animals, and longitudinal incisions, is very nice, and might induce some persons. to suppose that 
the Jews themselves occasionally sacrificed in the latter manner, and therefore that such skins were lawful. It may 
be proper to observe, that by longitudinal incisions are signified transverse wounds across the breast; since if the 
incision had been made in a straight line down the abdomen, it would have been impossible to recognize any holes 
in the hide after the animal was skinned. In the nineteenth section of the eighth chapter of Maimonides’s Treatise 
concerning Idolatry, we are informed that the Jews were not forbidden to use altars consisting of a single stone, even 
though they had previously been consecrated to idols, provided their tops were mutilated: from which permission, 
as well as from the Hebrew language assigning to such altars the peculiar name of bimos, pra, it may be inferred 
that altars of single stones were very common amongst the Jews, as they were also amongst the Mexicans; since it 
requires little study of the philosophy of language to know that words which are not proper names are the record 
of things which have had specific existence in nature, or which man has fashioned in numbers after a common 

prototype. 

Nore III. 

Whether America was known to the ancients, is a question which probably will never be satisfactorily solved : 
it may, however, confidently be said, that the assumption of the negative implies the petitio principiu, that modern 
ayes, knowing exactly what was comprised within the sphere of ancient knowledge, are qualified to judge of what 
they were ignorant. It is evident that in proportion as naval enterprise was encouraged by the most ancient states, 
the chances of the inhabitants of the Old Continent becoming acquainted with the existence of those of the New 
were increased; and it would be wrong, from the silence of Classical authors, to draw conclusive arguments justly 
liable to the charge of latitude of inference, that because the Greeks and Romans were ignorant of the existence of 
the continent of America, it must necessarily have been unknown in the elder ages of the world to the Egyptians, 
the Phcenicians, or other powerful maritime states. Referring to the page of history, we find that not only did the 
Jews and the Tyrians in the reigns of Solomon and Hiram trade to Ophir and the isles, but that the Carthaginians 
and the Tyrrhenians prosecuted their discoveries at a very remote epoch beyond the Pillars of Hercules; and that 
the Egyptians, so early as in the reign of Sesostris, possessed a powerful and numerous navy, which fact is recorded 
by Diodorus Siculus; and is the more deserving of attention, since it was the Egyptian priests of Sais who com- 
municated to Solon the tradition of the existence of the island of Atlantis, as we learn from the Timzeus and Critias 
of Plato, which, although pronounced by many persons to be merely a fiction invented by Plato, it still should be 
recollected has never been judged to be so by the greatest scholars who have been most familiar with the writings of 
that philosopher, who with a few exceptions have all been disposed to believe that at least it is founded on Egyptian 
tradition. To the objection which may be urged against the authenticity of the account of that island, as given by 
Plato in his two above-mentioned dialogues,—viz. that its extreme improbability divests it of all appearance of truth, 
whilst the compliments paid to the Athenians in the part ascribed to them in the war with the inhabitants of the 
island of Atlantis, too clearly betray a Greek and not an Egyptian origin,—it may be replied that Solon was a poet 
of transcendent genius as well as a famous legislator; and that having visited Egypt and become acquainted with 
the tradition of the Egyptians respecting the island of Atlantis, he determined to raise a poetical superstructure on 
so extraordinary a rumour, and, being eminently distinguished for the love which he bore his native country, to make 
the existence of that island redound to the glory of the Athenian name. And on this supposition the entire of the 
unfinished dialogue of Plato, entitled Critias, would appear to be merely the Argument of the epic poem which Solon 
intended to compose, and of which Plato makes express mention in the following passage of his Timeeus: “ IloAAwy pev

Siculus, lib. 1. “Sesoosis, having collected his forces, made his first expedition against the southern Ethiopians, and 
having conquered them, compelled the nation to pay him tribute of ebony, gold, and ivory: he next sent a fleet of 
four hundred ships to the Red Sea, being the first of his countrymen who caused long vessels to be built, and acquired 
possession of various islands, and subjugated that portion of the continent which bordered on the sea coast as far as 
India; and marching himself with his land forces, reduced to obedience all Asia; for he not only invaded the 
territory comprised within the later conquests of the Macedonian Alexander, but even other nations whose country 
the latter had not approached ; for he passed the river Ganges, and traversed all India till he arrived at the ocean, 
and the region of the Scythians as far as the river Tanais, which divides Europe from Asia; on which occasion it’ is 
said a certain number of the Egyptians having been left behind near the lake Mceotis, became the founders of the 
Colchian state. That the Colchians are descended from the Egyptians may be inferred from the men of that nation 
being circumcised like the Egyptians, that custom having been preserved by this colony, as it has likewise amongst 
the Jews. He subjugated in the same manner all the rest of Asia, and most of the islands named the Cyclades, and 
passing over to Europe scoured the whole of Thrace, where he ran the risk of losing his army from famine and the 
natural difficulties of the soil; wherefore having made Thrace the boundaries of his expedition, he prepared to erect 
pillars in many places which he had conquered. These pillars bore an inscription in the sacred character of the 
Egyptians : ‘Sesoosis, the king of kings and lord of lords, conquered this country with his own arms.” 
Egyptian hero flourished long before the time of Abraham, being the second of the twelfth dynasty of the Diospolitan 
kings, according to Manetho; whilst Eusebius in his Chronological Canons makes that patriarch contemporary with 
the sixteenth dynasty of Egyptian sovereigns, likewise named Diospolitan. If Egypt therefore so early as in the 
reign of Sesostris became a naval power, it is but reasonable to suppose that in later ages its maritime strength 
would have received great accessions from the attention which a wise government would have thought it necessary 
to pay to means so obviously calculated to increase national greatness. History accordingly informs us that the 
Egyptians became distinguished for their naval enterprize, and at last acquired the sovereignty of the seas, as 
Eusebius informs us in his catalogue of ancient states, to which the possession of that distinction was by general 
consent allowed, making mention of them there the eighth in order immediately after the Phcenicians. The Egyptian 
naval power was probably at its height in the reign of Apries, a short period before the invasion of Egypt by 
Cambyses, to which it even might have given rise, by causing jealousies between the Persians and the Egyptians ; 
since Diodorus Siculus asserts in the following passage of his first book, that that monarch defeated the Phcenicians 
both by sea and land, and captured Sidon. “ Mera Se Vappnriyov VorEepoy TETTAPGL yeveatc “Ampine éBactAevoev én Suot

Kat wAoLoy Keopwoy, TO MEV [LNKOG TNX wv Suakocwwy Kat oySonkorra, THY o emupavetav éyov THY PEV eEabev ery pucoy, THY 3S évdo0ev 
KaTnpyupwuerny, Kat TovTO fev aveOnke zw Oem Tw padtora év OnBate TyLWpevy.” “He also made a ship of cedar two 
hundred and eighty cubits long, which he caused to be gilded on the outside, and overlaid with silver within; this 
he presented to the god who is held in the greatest reverence at Thebes.” The ship here mentioned, the value of 
which must have been very great, was probably preserved for many ages in the temple, where it was dedicated ; and 
the safe return of an Egyptian expedition from a long and successful voyage of discovery, might have induced 
Sesostris to present such an offering. It need scarcely be remarked, that the Red or Erythrean Sea, whither that 
monarch dispatched his fleet, was the name by which the Indian Ocean was properly distinguished, and that 
the Red Sea which the Israelites crossed, usually so designated, is more generally named in profane history the 
Arabian Gulf. Some confusion indeed has originated from the great difference of names which sacred and profane 
history apply to the same persons and places; and the geographical description given by Moses in the second 
chapter of Genesis of the site of the terrestrial paradise, and of the four great rivers, the sources of which were the 
stream that watered the garden of Eden, whilst it has given rise to many curious problems in geography, does not 
serve to solve any. All that can with certainty be inferred from it is, that the Euphrates continued to flow after the 
Deluge in the same channel as it had done before it, and that the garden of Eden was situated a little beyond where 
it parted from the other three rivers. Doctor Robertson, remarking, in his notes to his History of America, that the 
ancients entertained very confused notions about geography, instances the curious fact, that when Alexander the 
Great, prosecuting his conquests in Asia, arrived at the Indus, some of those who composed his expedition imagined 
that they must be near the sources of the Nile from perceiving crocodiles in that river, an animal which they believed 
was peculiar to the Nile. Moses, however, cannot be supposed under the name of the river Gihon to mean the Nile. 
The following is the passage in the second chapter of Genesis alluded to. “And a river went out of Eden to water 
the garden; and from thence it was parted, and became into four heads. The name of the first is Pison: that is it 
which compasseth the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold; and the gold of that land is good: there is 
bdellium and the onyx stone. And the name of the second river is Gihon: the same is it that compasseth the 
whole land of Ethzopia. And the name of the third river is Hiddekel: that is it which goeth toward the east of 
Assyria. And the fourth river is Euphrates.” . 

Norte IV. 

The chapter of Gomara, entitled, The Possibility of a Shorter Passage to the Maluccas, of which the subjoined is 
the translation, is interesting, from showing that scarcely twenty years after the discovery of the continent of 
America, the best informed men in Spain, of whom Gomara certainly was one, judged that the junction of the At 
lantic with the Pacific Ocean by an artificial passage across the Isthmus of Panama, would be by no means an im- 
practicable task. 

“The voyage from Spain to the Maluccas by the Straits of Magellan is so long and hazardous, that having had 
frequent occasions to discuss the subject with men well acquainted with the Indies, as well as with other persons 
conversant with history and of an inquiring turn of mind, I have heard of another good although an expensive 
passage, which, if it were made, would be no less honourable than profitable to the maker. This passage would have 
to be opened across the main land from the one sea to the other, by whichever might appear preferable of these 
four lines ; either by the river of Lagartos, which rising in Chagre at the distance of four leagues from Panama, over 
which space of territory they proceed in cars, flows to the sea coast of Nombre de Dios; or by the channel through 
which the lake of Nicaragua empties itself into the sea, up and down which large vessels sail, and the lake is only 
distant three or four leagues from the sea; by either of these two rivers the passage is already traced and half 
made. ‘There is likewise another river which flows from Vera Cruz to Tecoantepec, along which the inhabitants of 

496 NOTES. 

New Spain tow and drag barks from the one sea to the other. The distance from Nombre de Dios to Panama is 
seventeen leagues, and from the Gulf of Urava to the Gulf of San Miguel twenty-five, which are the other two more 
difficult lines. There are mountains, it is true, but there are likewise hands; let but the wish be formed to make 
the passage, and it can be made. If inclination be not wanting, there will be no want of means: the Indies 
where the passage is to be made will supply them. To a king of Spain, with the wealth of the Indies at his 
command, when the object to be obtained is the spice trade, that which is possible is in fact easy. It appeared an 
impossibility, and really was one, to unite Brindez to Belona by a causeway over twenty leagues of the sea; yet 
Pyrrhus and Marcus Varro wished and attempted it, in order to go by land from Italy to Greece. Nicanor began to 
open a canal of more than a hundred leagues extent by land, without reckoning rivers, for the sake of transporting 
spices and other merchandize from the Caspian to the Pontic or Black Sea; but having been put to death by 
Ptolemy Ceraunus, his generous and princely design was abandoned. Nitocris, Sesostris, Psammetichus, Darius, 
Ptolemy, and other kings, projected the junction of the Red Sea with the Nile by means of a canal, in order that 
spices, perfumes, and medicines might be conveyed straight from the ocean to the Mediterranean; but being 
apprehensive lest the sea should inundate Egypt either by bursting the aqueducts, or by an over supply of water, 
they were deterred from the undertaking; and likewise because the sea might have been detrimental to the river, 
without which Egypt would be nothing. If the passage of which I have been speaking was accomplished, the 
navigation to the Maluccas would be shortened by a third of the distance, since ships proceeding thither would 
always sail by the Canaries under the equator, in a warm latitude, within the dominions of Spain, and without fear of 
meeting with a foe: nor would our Indies derive less advantage from it, since merchandize would be conveyed to 
Peru and other provinces in the same ships that brought it from Spain, and much expense and trouble would thus be 
saved.”—La Istoria de las Indias, fol. lviii. 

Note V, page 250. 

M. Chiarini, speaking of the Talmud, says, “Son génie malfaisant porte des coups funestes et invisibles au genre 
humain du milieu des ténébres epaisses qui l’environnent: qui pourrait calculer combien il a contribué et contribue 
encore & multiplier les malheurs qui affligent la terre?” “Its malignant genius aims invisible blows at the human 
race from the midst of the dense darkness in which it is enveloped: who can calculate how much it has contributed 
and still contributes to multiply the evils which afflict the earth?” The Talmud is, however, as the Rabbis contend, 
Judaism embodied into a perfect system: it contains the decisions of the greatest Jewish doctors upon difficult and 
disputed points of their law; and although it has been proscribed by many Popes and sentenced to the flames, it 
should not be forgotten that the voice of the same nation, whose veracity is fully relied upon and whose testimony is 
admitted to prove the Old Testament to be the word of God, declares that the traditions and the oral laws consigned 
to the Talmud were likewise delivered by God to Moses from Mount Sinai, and that their claim to inspiration cannot 
be affected by the circumstance of their not having been then written down; since it might as reasonably be contended 
that the written law was a forgery, as the oral Jaw an invention of the Jews; for that the national credit must be 
compromised, if at all, in both instances. This is the style in which the Jews reply to the objections of Christians. 
It must certainly be admitted that their Talmud is the development of the principles of law laid down by Moses, and 
by the sages of the nation for which his code was expressly framed; in lopping off the branches of the tree, it will 
therefore be very necessary to be careful not to injure the trunk; and to the Hebrew proverb, that “ the tree is to be 
judged of by its fruit,” none but the Jews will in this case feel inclined to yield assent. But what, it may be in- 
quired, are the doctrines of a book which Popes have so often anathematized, kings caused to be seized and burnt in 
their respective dominions, universities condemned, and learned men denounced as dangerous to civil society? Are 
the obnoxious principles which it contains one or many, and to what source may they be traced? Those who have 
turned over the pages of the Talmud must confess that absurdity, fanaticism, and universal intolerance are its leading 
doctrines. Fortunate has it been for the world that the Jews have always been an insignificant and weak state ; the 
globe would have otherwise been desolated by religious wars. And fortunate also has it been for them that other 

NOTES. 497 

religions were more tolerant than their own; since, strange as it may appear, the perverted sense in which the Rabbis 
have chosen to understand so simple an injunction as that which forbade the Jews to worship idols, associated with 
the recollection of the command which their ancestors received to extirpate the Canaanites, has led them to attempt 
to induce their countrymen to become, in almost a literal sense, the enemies and persecutors of mankind. This 
truth may shock the ears of modern Judaism, but, nevertheless, reference to the writings of some of their most famous 
Rabbis, Maimonides for example, will bear it out; wherein it will be seen, from the passages which are cited in the 
original Hebrew, what hatred of idolatry and of idolators they have endeavoured to infuse into the minds of a people, 
who have ever been led blindfold to their own and others’ destruction, and who are taught to consider nearly all 
mankind in the light of idolators, and all religions except their own, idolatry.

the Jews, the entire population of a city that proselyted from the Hebrew faith were to be put to death, men, women,

and children ; the latter, because till they attained the age of thirteen they were reckoned amongst their parents’ 
goods: and to sum up all, animals are mentioned in the next section as also adjudged to death, the plea of not 
guilty of proselytism availing them as much as the answer of the lamb to the wolf in the fable. The fanatical 
interpretation which some of the Rabbis have put on the words of the Mosaic text, “percutient omnem animam 
hominis,” is thus noticed by Dionysius Vossius: ‘In Siphre de civitate seductd dicitur: Non morientur patres 
propter filios, neque filii propter patres: juxta quam sententiam verba Scriptures, percutiendo percuties omnes habita- 
tores illius civitatis acie gladi, de reis intelligenda sint, non item, quorum nulla hic culpa est, infantibus. Super 
eddem re disputarunt R. Hlihezer et R. Aquiba: quorum ille occidi omnes, hic parvulis parcendum contendebat. 
Autor noster (Maimonides) Elihezerum sequitur; quia peccatum deserte religionis usque adeo. grave est, ut omnem 
ejus memoriam aboleri Deus velit, qué ad reliquos terror et exemplum perveniret. Unde addunt qui hane senten- 
tiam tuentur, quod Dominus omnes facultates talium absumi jusserit: liberi autem, usque ad annum xur juxta 
Thalmudistas, znter parentum facultates numerentur. Et simile est, quod Deus etiam animalia, quibuscum peccatum 
commissum est, jusserit supplicio affici.” When we consider the bitterness which the Rabbis have always displayed 
against proselytes from Judaism, by their writings, by their example, and by their appeal to passages of holy writ, 
endeavouring to excite a spirit of exterminating vengeance in the breasts of their countrymen against them, we need 
not feel at all surprised that it is a dangerous thing even still to attempt to convert the Jews resident in the East, 
who live on a more equal footing with the rest of the population, and are more powerful as a body and more 
respected as individuals, than in this country: this perhaps Mr. Wolfe will confess, if he returns safe from. his 
charitable expedition to the Holy Land. It is a very well known fact in Constantinople, that a Jew who becomes a 
proselyte not only exposes his family to certain ruin and disgrace, but himself runs imminent danger of assassina- 
tion: nor, supposing that he were dragged before the secret tribunal of Judaism, would he have a word to reply 
against the seeming justice of a sentence, which condemned him to die for an alleged offence for which the popu- 
lation of whole cities, men, women, and children, had died before him. When we read in ancient history of 
persecutions which the Jews occasionally suffered from the Romans, and reflect at the same time that the religion of 
the latter was tolerant and indulgent in the extreme to those of other nations, how can we feel surprised that the 
emperors should have become indignant on hearing that the blood of their legions had streamed in Palestine merely 
to gratify Jewish fanaticism, or that they should have taken speedy and summary vengeance? Not to have resented 
so great an indignity might have been termed by some of the early Christian historians patience; but the Romans 
would not so have judged it, and it certainly would not have been human nature: the complaints, generally speak- 
ing, brought by the Jews against the Romans were vexatious and not unfrequently seditious; ‘To render unto Cesar 
the things that were Czsar’s’ was an injunction which they obeyed with a very ill grace, as the admonition itself 
would seem to imply, which would not have been given had it not been necessary. Maimonides having been 
eulogized by M. Beugnot as a Rabbi who was an ornament to his age and country, and whose enlightened views it 
would be well if the rest of his nation could be brought to adopt, we shall take the liberty of observing, with all due 
respect for his opinion, that the Jews have long adopted them to the very spirit and letter, and that the work to 
which they are consigned may justly be entitled the most odious birth of time, since the principles it advocates do 
really aim, from the midst of the dense darkness which envelops them, invisible blows at the human race: but we 
cannot concur in the eulogium which he pronounces on Maimonides, since the following passage occurs in the 
second chapter of his Treatise concerning Idolatry, from which a due estimate may be formed of the enlightened 
views which actuated that Rabbi, who applies the contemptuous epithet of books composed by idolators to works 
written by Christians on their religion, and attempts to distort the command given by Moses to the Jews in the 
fourth verse of the nineteenth chapter of Leviticus, “Turn ye not unto idols, nor make to yourself molten gods,” into 
a positive and distinct prohibition to them against reading a particular class of books, which Moses never foresaw 
would be written. It is almost surprising that he did not go a little further, and declare to his simple flock that to 
learn to read was itself idolatrous and forbidden to all but Rabbis, who by the Lord’s special grace knew how to 
distinguish good from evil. ‘“ Multos libros composuerunt idololatre de cultu suo, quod sit fundamentum illius,

of “sed licet odii causa obstetricari,” by citing a note subjoined to the Hebrew text by Dionysius Vossius. ‘Cur ex 
odio permittit obstetricari? Num quia occasionem sic habitura interimendi foetus, vel etiam puerperz aut partu- 
rientis? Vix persuadere mihi possum, rem adeo detestabilem 4 Maimonide precipi. Vera proinde interpretatio est, 
odii causa posse obstetricari, hoc est, ad odium effugiendum, sive ne odium gliscat, sed potius occurratur iis, qui, si 
negetur hoc officium, pejus odissent, magisque malefacerent. Neque hic gratificari me Maimonide, sed revera 
hane ejus fuisse sententiam liquet ex capitis sequentis sectione secunda; ubi claré ait, si quis metuat ab iis qui 
religionis sunt disparis, posse ad odium evitandum medicam admovere manum; non gratis tamen, sed pro mercede.” 
It cannot be denied that the modern race of Jews are a charitable people, and possess, as a nation, many excellent 
qualities ; but this is owing to the inherent goodness of human nature, and not to Judaism, which strives from the 
cradle to make the Jews haters of those who are of a different creed from their own, but which never yet, we will 
venture to say, except partially and locally, has attained its end, since it is impossible for a religion, be it ever so 
‘intolerant, totally to pervert human nature; and even if it were possible for an entire generation of men to become 
the instruments of fanaticism, they would soon be succeeded by a new and innocent race, whom it would be most 
unjust even to reproach on account of the alleged crimes of their ancestors. That the charity of the modern Jews to 
strangers and persons professing a different faith does not, however, flow from the precepts of their religion as taught

Nore VI. p. 384. 

The following passage from the first chapter of the twenty-eighth book of Montesquieu’s “Esprit des Lois”, may 
be quoted to show that the clergy introduced into the barbarous codes of the dark ages many legislative enactments 
tending materially to affect the condition of the Jews. “Les évéques eurent une autorité immense a la cour des rois 
Visigoths ; les affaires les plus importantes étoient décidées dans les Conciles. Nous devons aux codes des Visigoths 
toutes les maximes, tous les principes, et toutes les vues de Inquisition @aujour@hui; et les moines wont fait que 
copier contre les Juifs des lois faites autrefois par les évéques.” “The bishops possessed immense influence in the 
court of the Visigoth kings; the most important matters were decided in Councils. To the codes of the Visigoths 
we are indebted for all the maxims, all the principles, and all the views of the modern Inquisition; and the monks 
have only copied the laws made formerly by the bishops against the Jews.” The remark made by Montesquieu 
respecting the power of Councils even in civil matters amongst the Visigoths, is generally true of all the early 
Councils ; and that power may be accounted for by the extreme bigotry of the age in which they were convened. 
As regards the present dispersed state of the Jews, it may be contended, in opposition to those who would fain dis- 
cern the fulfilment of prophecy in an event which must have had other causes than prophecy, that habits engrafted 
by time are of long duration, that a dispersed people must at last become naturalized in those countries which they 
have chosen as an asylum, even although the law does not recognize them, by language, by prejudices, or by property, 
especially in land; which latter kind the framers of the old law of Europe, as if conscious that land attaches the 
owners of it to the soil, did not allow the Jews to acquire, by kindred, by local attachments and friendships; which 
was the reason, perhaps, why the regulations of most European states excluded the Jews from becoming members of 
corporations, and assigned to them, in the several towns and cities where they resided, separate quarters from the 
other citizens, encouraging them at the same time, by forbidding them to enter into honourable professions and 
respectable trades, to seek sordid gains from following the lowest and vilest occupations, which of itself would have 
been sufficient to draw a line of demarcation between them and the other members of the community; and, finally, 
by the sepulchres of their ancestors, which the Jews have ever been accustomed so highly to revere, it is not 
unlikely that when they colonized America they carried the bones of some of their supposed patriarchs thither, 
confiding in the protection which they expected to receive from these talismans, for such they might be called, since 
a relic to which superstition ascribes occult virtues differs scarcely or at all from a talisman, although the term itself 
is not Hebrew, but Arabic. It has been already remarked that the dispersion of the Jews is no where alluded to in 
the Old Testament as a judgment with which God threatened to visit that people on account of the crucifixion of bis 
Son: those who may choose to maintain that it is, will do well to point out the passage in Scripture in which the 
allusion is contained.. But ifa nation has a right to be heard in its own defence, which the Jews certainly have, the 
argument by which they attempt to prove that their present dispersion is not owing to the cause above referred to, 
will be found to possess considerable weight with every unprejudiced mind ; since, arguing from the justice of God, 
they contend that he would not have punished a whole nation for a crime committed only by a few; the principal 
actors in which, Herod and Pontius Pilate, were not Jews of the seed of Abraham, although the former was sprung 
from a family of Jewish proselytes ; and that, even on the supposition that the whole nation were equally guilty of it 
then, their posterity eighteen hundred years afterwards must be as innocent of it as were their forefathers eighteen 
hundred years before, possessing even an advantage over them, in not being doomed to be the progenitors of so evil 
a generation.

Note VII. page 385. 

Those who seriously consider the multitudinous sects into which religion is divided in the isle which the poet, 
dipping his pen in truth, has described in the lines beginning 

“Behold yon isle, by palmers, pilgrims trod,” 

must feel surprised at the question which is not unfrequently asked, namely, what right an old East Indian (for by 
that appellation a man who has spent some twenty years of his life in the East is not unfrequently designated,) 
has to turn liberal in religious matters, and if he gains admission to the councils of his country, to advocate in 
a sort of plain matter-of-fact style of eloquence the claims of Christians, Jews, Pagans, Turks, and Infidels, to 
equal protection from the laws of this country, which, like Rome of old, is too great, and casts the shade of 
her sceptre over too many lands, to choose for herself another motto than ‘‘ Tros Tyriusque mihi nullo discrimine 
agetur.” Nothing would benefit Great Britain, or the individuals themselves more, than to send, if it were pos- 
sible, the narrow-minded few who ask this question, and who, clinging to intolerance, would prefer to drive the 
vessel of the state itself on a rock or dangerous quicksand, to steering out of the old course ona voyage to the shores 
of Hindostan, that like Ulysses they might gain wisdom by seeing the manners of many men and many cities; nor 
can it be doubted that they would return with enlarged political views, and would feel less disposed, after behold- 
ing the state of British India, mighty in numbers, but comparatively weak in effective force, from the division of its 
native population into castes, which, “for ever separate, yet for ever near,” exhibit a moral phenomenon that far 
eclipses that of Judaism in Europe, to question the right of others to disbelieve and deny the fact, that the dispersion 
of the Jews is the accomplishment of prophecy; which the Jews themselves, in reference to the particular prophecies 
which they adduce, have always denied by an appeal to arguments which have never yet been satisfactorily refuted. 
In addition to the many causes which have already been noticed in the course of these pages as conspiring to keep 
the Jews wherever they may reside a separate people, we shall mention another, which those will duly appreciate 
who have been in India, and have observed how powerfully the Hindoo laws, which prohibit some castes of. Hindoos 
from eating or even tasting the provisions of others, contribute to preserve amongst them the distinction of castes ; 
—and that is the prejudice and inflexible aversion which the Jews, of former ages at least, entertained to parta- 
king of the same fare with Christians, or those of any other sect: and this aversion, which was instilled into them 
by the Rabbis, who well knew that their own interests were inseparable from their: nation: being a distinct people, 
was grounded on the charitable sense in which they chose to understand beasts in the following ordinance of the 
twenty-second chapter of Exodus, applying the term to all those that were without the pale of Judaism: “ And 
ye shall be holy men unto me; neither shall ye eat any flesh that is torn of beasts in the field; ye shall cast it to 
the dogs.” But since to rest this prohibition on a single verse of the Old Testament, interpreted moreover so con- 
temptuously of Christians, might in some places have been attended with consequences inconvenient: to the Jews, 
their Rabbis have judged it more prudent to seek a pretext from their oral laws and from the Talmud, for forbidding 
their countrymen to eat with Christians, which might be more intelligible to the former and less’offensive to the 
latter: and hence the stress which they laid on the Jews not eating the flesh of any animal which had not been killed 
by a butcher of their own nation, and the origin of the constitutions contained in the Schechitos Ubedikos, or Book 
of the Art of Killing, as well as the necessity, in former days at least, of a butcher receiving a licence’or diploma 
from the Rabbi before he could practise a trade which amongst the Jews was a learned profession.

Selden makes a curious remark in the second chapter of the Introduction to his Treatise, that the names of the idols 
designated by the Jews ‘the Gods of the Assyrians and the Babylonians’ are really Hebrew, from which he would infer 
the primitive nature of the Hebrew tongue, and its wide diffusion over the provinces of Asia. Other persons 
may be tempted to draw a different conclusion from the following confession of that learned man. “ Pracipui 
etiam Deorum quos collegimus, Ebreeis, non Arameis, aut Babyloniis vocabulis, aut adscititid aliquaé dialecto me- 
morantur: ut Gad, Baal, Baal Peor, Baal Berith, Baalim, Baalzebub, Ashtaroth, que mere sunt Ebrea. Imo idem. 
dicendum de Teraphim, et Succoth Benoth, quorum tamen Babylonicum est hoc numen, illud Arameum ; quod nec 
leve sane est argumentum omnia illa haud recentioris fuisse evi, quam illud est quo Ebrea apud Arameos viguit et 
Babylonios pura dialectus. Religione, ni fallor, ducti, deorum ante alia inviolata nomina retinere volebant.” The 
rule of ‘audi alteram partem’ is so strictly accordant with justice, that it is to be regretted that the Syrians and the 
Babylonians cannot be heard in their own defence in reply to the charges brought against them by the Jews. What 
recrimination of idolatry and human sacrifices would undoubtedly follow, with the denial that they were the tutors, 
and the Jews merely their pupils in these atrocities! In the absence of further evidence it must however be con- 
fessed, that the Jews are most entitled to receive judgment from posterity, since their prophets bear witness against 
them, whilst the history of the Babylonians presents a blank page.

Sahagun, in the Appendix to the second book of his History of New Spain, at page 101 of the seventh volume of 
the present work, says that the form of a Mexican oath was as follows. “ ‘ Por vida del Sol y de nuestra Sefiora la 
Tierra, que no falte en lo que tengo dicho; y para mayor seguridad como esta tierra :’ y luego tocaba con los dedos en 
la tierra y llegabalos 4 la boca y lamialos; y asi comia tierra haciendo juramento.” “‘I swear by the life of the Sun 
and by our sovereign mistress the Earth, that nothing which I affirm is false; and in confirmation of my oath I eat 
this earth :’ when immediately touching the earth with his hand, he raised it to his mouth and licked it, and in this 
manner ate earth on occasion of taking an oath.” The adjuration of Moses in the nineteenth verse of the thirtieth 
chapter of Deuteronomy, “TI call heaven and earth to record this day against you that I have set before you life and 
death, blessing and cursing; therefore choose life that both thou and thy seed may live;” considered in connection 
with what is said in the first verse of the twenty-third chapter of Exodus, of a false witness making use of his hand 
when giving evidence, renders it not improbable that the form of the Mexican oath was borrowed from the Jews. 
The passage referred to in Exodus is the following: “Thou shalt not raise a false report; put not thine hand with the 
wicked to be an unrighteous witness.”

Nore X. page 334. 

We are informed by Sahagun in the thirty-seventh chapter of the second book of his History, that the Mexicans 
on the festival of Yzcalli bored the ears of their children for the purpose of putting ear-rings into them, when certain 
persons stood godfathers and godmothers to them; whence it would appear that ear-rings amongst the Mexicans 
were connected with idolatrous rites, which may serve to illustrate the fourth verse of the thirty-fifth chapter of 

Genesis, which has perplexed commentators, who have not been able to understand why Jacob should have deprived . 

his household of their ear-rings as well as of their strange gods: “And they gave unto Jacob all the strange gods 
which were in their hands, and all their ear-rings which were in their ears, and Jacob hid them under the oak which 
was by Shechem.” Another custom which the Mexicans may have borrowed from the Jews, was their solemn 
repasts on bread at the celebration of some of their greater festivals; since we learn from the fifty-fourth verse of the 
thirty-first chapter of Genesis, that Jacob, whose descendants naturally would have been inclined to imitate the 
example of the father of the house of Israel, called his brethren to eat bread when he offered a sacrifice to God upon 
the mount. “Then Jacob offered sacrifice wpon the mount, and called his brethren to eat bread, and they did eat 
bread, and tarried all night in the mount.” It is not improbable that the Mexicans circumcised their sons on the 
above-mentioned festival of Yzcalli, and the incisions which they superstitiously cut in the American aloe, when their 
object was not to obtain from it the liquor of which they made wine, might have been originally derived from the 
following passage of the nineteenth chapter of Leviticus: “And when ye shall come into the land, and shall have 
planted all manner of trees for food, then ye shall count the fruit thereof as uncircumcised. Three years shall it be as 
uncircumcised unto you: it shall not be eaten of. But in the fourth year all the fruit thereof shall be holy to praise 
the Lord withal. And in the fifth year shall ye eat of the fruit thereof, that it may yield unto you the increase 
thereof. Iam the Lord your God.” The expression ‘ uncircumcised’, here used metaphorically in reference to 
trees, may with great probability be judged to have given rise in the long course of ages to some unmeaning rite 
amongst the Jews, who, besides their proneness to multiply rites, were equally addicted with the Mexicans to seek luck 
or good fortune from omens ; and they might have imagined that if fruit, which was counted as uncircumcised, was 
unlucky and not proper to be eaten, that which could be counted as circumcised would be wholesome and good to 
eat, and accordingly have made incisions in the bark of fruit trees. It further deserves to be remarked, that the Jews, 
dividing time like the Mexicans into larger chronological cycles of fifty years, might likewise have divided it as the 
latter did into lesser periods of four years, of which some indication seems to be afforded in the provision contained 
in the twenty-fifth verse of the chapter of Leviticus referred to, permitting the Jews to eat in the fifth year the fruit 
which they were not allowed to taste during the four preceding years, since a reason for the permission then granted 
might be found in the commencement of a new cycle. It is proper however to add, that the Old Testament declares 
that both five and seven were numbers dedicated by the Jews to the holding solemn assemblies; and perhaps at the 
period of the Babylonian captivity, the number five had grown into greater public estimation. Sahagun has observed 
that the Mexicans, like the Jews, divided their months into four equal portions or weeks ; but the month of the former 
not being lunar and consisting of no more than twenty days, their week contained only five days: the people of 
Chiapa, however, whose month was lunar, counted seven days to their week. 

On the supposition that the Jews colonized America, various reasons might be assigned for their changing the 
lunar reckoning of their year soon after their arrival in that continent into a vicesimal computation of days; but the 
principal motive was probably a wish to equalize the number of days contained in each month, and to simplify their 
calendar by not regarding the changes of the moon. All the Mexican months being religious festivals, and dedicated 
to the performance of sacrifices and rites, the priest or astrologer who distributed them into twenty days each might 
moreover have wished to typify in them the greatest and most solemn Jewish festival, that of the Passover, which 
terminated on the twenty-first day of the first Hebrew month Nisan (which probably began at evening), as was ordained 
in the eighteenth verse of the twelfth chapter of Exodus: “ In the first month on the fourteenth day of the month 
at even ye shall eat unleavened bread until the one and twentieth day of the month at evening.” The Mexicans seem 
even to have borrowed some superstitious practices from the Hebrew ordinances relating to the celebration of the 
feast of the Passover. They generally performed their sacrifices in the evening or at night, and the Jews were com- 

eee 

NOTES. 505 

manded in the sixth verse of the twelfth chapter of Exodus, to kill the paschal lamb in the evening: “ And ye shall 
keep it up until the fourteenth day of the same month, and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall 
kill it in the evening.” The Mexican merchants were fearful of stirring out of their houses on certain days of the 
year; and the Jews were specially enjoined by Moses not to go out of their doors on the night of the feast of the 
Passover until morning, lest the destroyer should smite them. The Mexicans likewise computed the period of a day 
from the noon or middle of one day to that of another, as we are informed by the interpreter of the Codex Telleriano- 
Remensis, in page 152 of the present volume; and this computation assigning to the night a sort of priority over the 
day, probably induced them to keep the vigils of festivals as a part of the festival itself. Another remarkable proof 
of the predilection which the Jews and Mexicans manifested for the employment of similar numbers in their calcula- 
tions and divisions of time, is found in the former celebrating a year of jubilee at the expiration of every period of 
fifty years, and the latter at the expiration of every fifty-two years, and in both nations reckoning time and keeping a 
chronological account of historical events by cycles, so nearly agreeing in duration with each other as the Mexican 
and Hebrew jubilees. That the Mexicans preserved the recollection of the exact time when past events happened, by 
referring them to a particular year contained within a particular cycle of fifty-two years, is evident from their historical 
paintings; and that the Jews made use of an analogous method before the captivity, must clearly be understood from 
the following passage of Eusebius’s Chronological Canons: “Apud Hebraos, usque ad nativitatem Abraham, com- 
putantur anni mille nongenti quinquaginta. Usque ad diluvium enim ab Adam habent annos mpctv1, et inde 
usque ad Abraham ccxciit. Et ideo xu jobelai 4 nativitate Abraham computantur. Unus enim jobelzus quin- 
quaginta anni sunt.”—Eusebii Chronicorum Canonum, pag. 1. It is likewise the general opinion of the learned. 

In reference to an observation in a preceding paragraph respecting the number five, and the estimation in which 
that number seems to have been held by the Jews at the period of the Babylonian captivity, it may be proper to 
quote the words of Zechariah, in the fourth and fifth verses of the seventh chapter of his prophecies: “Then came the 
word of the Lord of Hosts unto me, saying, Speak unto all the people of the land, and to the priests, saying, When 
ye fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh month, even those seventy years did ye at all fast unto me, even to 
me?” Serious attention to the grave charge which God himself brings in this passage against the Jews, might 
dispose some people to wonder less, that the lost tribes cannot be discovered at the present day, than that all the 
tribes had not been lost long ago. If however it were of any real importance, as corroborative of the truth of Scrip- 
ture history, that these lost tribes should be discovered, the fact of their not having been yet discovered must also 
appear important; except in the eyes of that class of persons, who, freely admitting that if the old law had forbidden 
sacrifices they would have drawn from that circumstance an argument in proof of the divine legation of Moses, 
find on the other hand an equally strong argument in favour of it in the old law having ordained them.

‘ Viler than sea-weed ’ appears to have been a Latin proverb ; nor is it likely that the Romans held this useless marine 
production in less esteem than other nations: it is therefore the more surprising that the Peruvians, who surpassed 
every ancient and modern people in the 7zchness of the offerings which they made to the Deity, should have offered 
sea-weed with all their offerings, as Acosta expressly declares, “alge wniversis fere sacrificiis inferuntur.” This ano- 
maly in their sacrifices might perhaps have originated in the necessity imposed upon the Jews to offer salt with all 
their sacrifices, in compliance with the injunction contained in the thirteenth verse of the second chapter of Leviticus, 
* And every oblation of thy meat-offering shalt thou season with salt; neither shalt thou suffer the salt of the cove- 
nant of thy God to be lacking from thy meat-offering ; with a// thine offerings thou shalt offer salt:” since on their 
arrival in the New World, where the revival of the sacrifices prescribed by Moses probably engrossed all their atten- 
tion, they must have been at a great loss for salt; and some Rabbi might have been advised in a dream, that sea- 
weed, the taste of which is very salt, as the derivation of the Latin name implies, would be a proper substitute for 

that indispensable article.
