The following passage of the sixteenth chapter of the Gospel of Saint Matthew affords strong grounds for suppos- 
ing, that the Jews in the days of Christ believed in the doctrine of a metempsychosis: “When Jesus came into the 
coasts of Cesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, saying, Whom do men say that I the son of man am? And they 
said, Some say that thou art John the Baptist, some Elias, and others Jeremias, or one of the prophets.” Had this no- 
tion prevailed amongst them at an earlier epoch of their history, it might have caused the rabble (for Rabbis and doctors 
we here put out of the question,) to expect the coming of a future Messiah or deliverer in the person of Moses himself, 
who would re-appear to rescue the Jews from another and more oppressive bondage than the Egyptian: and then the 
proper name Mw might with great propriety be considered as the derivation of mwo. Many nations have cherished 
the idea, that the souls of those who had earned the lasting gratitude of their country, by services performed at the 
time of her greatest need, might, if the salvation of future generations was at stake, re-animate mortal bodies for the 
sake of those who were once dear to them. Thus the Chinese expect that their famous deified warrior, who has been 
dead for many centuries, will re-appear on earth: and the return of godlike mortals, rather than of immortal gods, 
may be alluded to in the line, 

“ Jam redit et Virgo, redeunt Saturnia reena:” 

which supposes happiness once more to flourish on earth under the reign of Astrea, and when Saturn should again 
sway the sceptre over the golden plains of Italy ; which country, at the time that the poet imagined to himself the com- 
mencement of a brighter era, was torn by civil wars and dissensions. The assumption of several divines, whose names 
for their own credit we shall pass over in silence, that “Virgo” means in the verse alluded to the Virgin Mary, is 
so unreasonable that it does not deserve refutation. It may be not unworthy of notice, that a philosopher so justly 
esteemed and venerated as was Pythagoras, believed in the metempsychosis ; and laying claim to the possession of 
an extraordinary memory, asserted that he recollected having been Euphorbus, and that he was killed at the time of the 
Trojan war. The doctrine of the metempsychosis is a refinement on the creed of the ancient Egyptians respecting the 
transmigration of the soul, but it is founded on the assumption, that the soul of man can only migrate into another 
rational body. Pythagoras however strictly forbade his followers to kill or to eat animals; and he only did not for- 
bid cruelty to them, because he thought it was unnecessary for Philosophy to teach what all ought to know, and that 
it would be vain for him to attempt to instil a principle, where Nature herself had been faulty in her work, and the 
soil was evil and corrupt. As the doctrine of the metempsychosis seems to have originated in the Egyptian notion 
of the soul's transmigration after death into some other body, so in its turn it appears to have given rise to the more 
mystical idea of an incarnation, or of God becoming man, or rather being born in a human form. The many incar- 
nations of Vishnou, who dignified even other species of animals by becoming one of them, is still the theme of 
exultation among Hindoo poets and philosophers. But Thibet presents a moral and political phenomenon of a nature 
truly extraordinary. That ecclesiastical state has been governed for perhaps nearly eighteen centuries by the deity 
supposed to animate, some say to become incarnate in, the body of an infant, and to inspire the person invested 
with the dignity of Grand Lama. It was either during Lord Minto’s or the Marquis of Wellesley’s government 
in India, that an embassy was sent to the Teshoo Lama, an interesting account of which will be found in the 
Annual Register. The Lama happened at that time to be an infant in arms; and the envoy, under these peculiar 
circumstances, felt at a loss respecting the forms to be observed on the ceremony of his introduction, and was at last 
ushered into the presence of a pleasing and intelligent-looking infant, quite too young to be able to speak, before 
whom, nevertheless, many Tartar Khans were prostrating themselves and doing homage; when the father of the Lama 
observed to the representative of the Governor-General of India, that although he was too young to speak, it would 
be wrong to suppose that reason. in him had not arrived at maturity. 

It certainly would be interesting to trace the history of Nestorianism in the East, since some learned men have 
supposed that the Nestorians in early ages penetrated to Thibet, and proselyted to their faith an extensive territory. 

NO 4S: 507 

it is probable that many superstitions have, in the course of revolving ages, passed from Asia to America ; but how 
truly surprising it is to find that the Mexicans, who seem to have been quite unacquainted with the doctrines of the 
migration of the soul and the metempsychosis, should have believed in the incarnation of the only son of their supreme 
god Tonacatecutle. For Mexican mythology speaking of no other son of that god except Quecalcoatle, who was born 
of Chimalman the virgin of Tula, without connection with man, and by his breath alone, (by which may be signified 
his word or his will, announced to Chimalman by word of mouth of the celestial messenger, whom he dispatched to 
inform her that she should conceive a son,) it must be presumed that Quecalcoatle was his only son. Other argu- 
ments might be adduced to show, that the Mexicans believed that Quecalcoatle was both god and man, that he had 
previously to his incarnation existed from all eternity, that he had created both the world and man, that he descended 
from heaven to reform the world by penance, that he was born with the perfect use of reason, that he preached a new 
law, and, being king of Tula, was crucified for the sins of mankind, as is obscurely insinuated by the interpreter of the 
Vatican Codex, plainly declared in the traditions of Yucatan, and mysteriously represented in the Mexican paintings. 
It would be a useless repetition of facts already stated in the preceding pages of the present volume, to undertake 
separately to prove all these points; and we shall confine ourselves in this place to the three first very important 
articles. The reflection must have suggested itself to those who have perused the New Testament, that Christ is as fre- 
quently distinguished there by the appellation of the Son of Man, as by that of the Son of God, in reference no doubt 
to his humanity, and to the famous prophecy contained in the ninth verse of the ninth chapter of Isaiah: “ For unto 

29 

us a child is born, unto us a son is given:” which Christians, on the authority of many passages in the four Gospels, 
apply to Christ, although the Jews sometimes interpret it of the Messiah, and sometimes of king Hezekiah. The 
Mexicans bestowed the appellation of Topiltzin on Quecalcoatle, the literal signification of which is ‘our son’ or ‘our 
child,’ that proper name being compounded of fo ‘our’, and pilizin, defined by Alonso de Molina in his rare and 
copious vocabulary of the Mexican and Spanish languages to be nifto 6 nifia, ‘a boy or a girl,’ and associated by him 
with the cognate terms of piltonth and piltzintia ; and it may not be unreasonably assumed, since analogies, which are 
numerous and not isolated, as their number increases increase also in their ratio of probability, not only that the Mex- 
icans were acquainted with Isaiah’s famous prophecy, but to mark their belief of the accomplishment of that prophecy 
in the person of Quecalcoatle, that they named him Topiltzin ; no less on account ot his having been born from a virgin 
of the daughters of men, than because another equally celebrated prediction of the same prophet declared, that he 
should receive a name from that very circumstance: “Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign, Behold a 
virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.” And the proper name Topiltzin does in fact 
bear a signification corresponding, if not literally, yet entirely in substance with that of Immanuel: since ‘God with 
us, which is the interpretation of the Hebrew name, means God domiciliated amongst men; and the full force of the 
expression is preserved in the term Topiltzin, which might be interpreted the Son of Man, or God on a level with men f 
for the Mexicans believed that Quecalcoatle took human nature upon him, partaking of all the infirmities of man, and 
was not exempt from sorrow, pain, or death, and that he suffered voluntarily to atone for the sins of mankind. They 
also believed that he alone of all the gods had a human body, and was of a corporeal essence; a notion which we can 
only wonder whence it could have been derived. Las Casas and Torquemada both assert that Quecalcoatle had been 
in Yucatan; and there can be little doubt, when we reflect on the mysterious history of Bacab, that the Cross discovered 
by M. Dupaix in the ancient temple of Palenque was connected with the tradition of his crucifixion. The four female 
figures, each holding in her arms an infant, which adorn the walls of another temple in the immediate vicinity of that 
just mentioned, probably represent Chimalman and the infant Quecalcoatle; which the two units conspicuously sculp- 
tured on the body of the second infant, the constant concomitants of the cane which was his sign, seem further to indi- 
cate. Smoke may perhaps also be intended to be represented as proceeding from the left foot of the female figure in 
the same plate. The prophecies contained in the Old Testament relating to the Messiah being so frequently only 
obliquely alluded to in the New, and this class being extremely difficult to trace, we must leave to others the task of 
ascertaining whether the promise of the angel Gabriel to the Virgin Mary, as recorded in the thirty-fifth verse of the 
first chapter of Saint Luke,-—“ The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow 
thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God,’—be couched in the 
language of ancient prophecy; since, should this be the case, it is not improbable that the head of the dragon which 
forms the crest of three of the female figures, as it may also be presumed that it did of the fourth when entire, (if it be 

508 NOTES. 

not a symbol which Chimalman borrowed from her son’s zame,) was intended to denote that she had been overshadowed 
by the power of Huitzilopuchtli, whose device, as we are informed by Sahagun in the first chapter of the first book of 
his History of New Spain, was the head of a dragon. Representations of the female figures here referred to, as well 
as of the Cross, will be found in the fifth volume of the present work, Part III. of the Monuments of New Spain ; and 
we shall only further observe in reference to the Cross, that similar ornaments to those sculptured on its two arms de- 
corate the symbol borne aloft by the principal figure in the twenty-eighth plate of the same Part; before whom there 
is another figure in a kneeling attitude, which may suggest the idea of that symbol being intended to represent a 
cross, although nearly as unlike one as the devices, consisting of broken lines, with which the ancient Mexicans fre- 
quently decorated their shields, and as those painted on the earthenware vases discovered by Lieutenant Hardy 
among the ruins of Las Casas Grandes. 

It is singular that the Mexicans should have viewed Quecalcoatle in the light of a god and of a man, of a father 
and of a son, of the creator of the world and of him by whom the world was finally doomed to be destroyed, since it 
is hard to reconcile such conflicting notions with each other. That they did so, will be apparent from the following 
passages extracted from the sixth book of Sahagun’s History of New Spain, which contains the prayers addressed by 
by the ancient Mexicans to their gods, as well as from what has already been said of the probable derivation of the 
proper name Topiltzin, and from what remains to be said of the belief which the Mexicans entertained, that the world 
would be destroyed when the Sun should be im the sign of four earthquakes. Quecalcoatle is emphatically styled 
Father in the exhortation which the Mexican priest addresses to the penitent who had come to make confession to him 
of his sins, whose entire speech will be found at page 359 of the fifth volume of the Antiquities of Mexico. “Quando 
fuistes criado y enviado 4 este mundo, limpio y bueno fuistes criado y enviado, y tu padre y madre Quetzalcoatl te 
form6d como una piedra preciosa y como una joya rica de oro muy resplandeciente y muy pulida; pero por tu propia 
voluntad y albedrio te ensuciastes, y te amancillastes, y te revolcastes en el estiercol y en las suciedades de los 
pecados y maldades que cometistes, y ahora has confesado.” “When thou wert created and sent into this world, thou 
wast created and sent into it pure and good, and thy father and mother Quetzalcoatl formed thee like a precious 
stone, like a rich jewel of gold, beautiful to look upon and well pclished; but thou by thine own free will and choice 
hast defiled and polluted thyself, and hast wallowed in the mire of the sins and iniquities which thou hast committed, 
and now thou hast confessed.” From this passage it is plain that the doctrine of free will, as-cpposed to absolute 
predestination, was a fundamental article of the religion of the Mexicans, although in some degree qualified by 
their notions on judicial astrology, as we learn from the following passage of the same chapter of the sixth book of 
Sahagun; where the Mexican priest or confessor, supplicating Tezcatlipoca on the behalf of the repentant sinner, 
addresses him in the following language : “En presencia de Vuestra Magestad hablo, que sabe todas las cosas, y 
sabeis que este pobre no pecé con libertad entera del libre albedrio, porque fué ayudado é inclinado de la condicion 
natural del signo en que nacid.” “I am speaking in the presence of Your Majesty who knowest all things, and 
knowest that this miserable man did not sin with the entire liberty of his free will, since he partly acted under the 
influence of the sign in which he was born.” The notion of original sin, in the acceptation in which the term is 
understood by Christians, which was totally different both in cause and quality from the frailty of human nature, 
which the ancient philosophers were all prepared to admit, was quite familiar to the minds of the Mexicans, who 
ascribed it to Suchiquecal, and to her disobedience in plucking fruit in the garden of ‘Tamoanchan; and hence a 
difficulty may arise in understanding the construction which ought to be put on that part of the speech of the 
Mexican priest to the penitent, where he says to him “when thou wert created and sent into this world, thou 
wast created and sent into it pure and good ;” which seems merely to allude to what is said in the first chapter of 
Genesis, of man having been created in the image of God, and of the works of his hands being all good, and to 
contain no denial of the doctrine of original sin, the Mexican belief in which is unequivocally declared in the 
thirty-second and thirty-seventh chapters of the same book of Sahagun’s History of New Spain, in the speeches 
which the midwife there addresses to the infant on baptizing it and washing it with water. That the Mexicans knew 
that man had been created in the image of God, may be inferred from the following passage of Sahagun, which de- 
serves to be considered in connection with the Peruvian tradition of men having been created by Viracocha after the 
likeness of images made by himself, which is perhaps after all only a sample of the artifices to which the Spanish 
clergy had recourse in order to consign to oblivion all knowledge of the ancient religion of Peru; which could more

being requested to read the sixth book of Sahagun, and to return a categorical answer to the question, “Unde Tezca-

how often, blaming themselves for the unnecessary concession of a principle, would they not feel inclined to exclaim 
“sed revocare gradum,—hoe opus hic labor est”! The Deity is said in so many passages of the Old Testament to be 
jealous of his honour, and to work miracles for his name’s sake, that many persons may feel it hard to reconcile that 
professed jealousy with the desecration of his name so common among the Jews, the profanation of his temple, and 

512 NOTES. 

the human sacrifices which they offered to him; the corollary of all which is, that though Abraham received the 
covenant from God, and Moses promulgated his laws to the Jews, still Judaism was never under such special divine 
protection as to prevent its degenerating into most abominable rites in the Old World, nor consequently in the New; 
and therefore let it not be maintained that Jehovah could not have been worshiped under the name of Tezcatlipoca 
by the Mexicans, and human sacrifices offered to him in New Spain as in Palestine of old; but even on the assumption 
that this was the case, let not God impiously be made accountable for the crimes which men may haye committed in 
his name, for the cruelty or absurdity of the religious rites by which they may have sought to honour him, or for the 
fables which they may have ridiculously invented of him. If some of those misguided men, commonly named the 
Fathers, whose writings were revered in the ages which they were so instrumental in rendering dark, but which (such 
is the vicissitude of all earthly things,) are little read or esteemed in the present day, were living, they would find 
that Christianity itself might be overthrown by the same arguments, if admitted to be valid now, which they em- 
ployed so successfully nearly two thousand years ago against Paganism, which all resolve themselves into reasoning 
against the religions of antiquity from their abuses. Those reckless sophists scrupled not to hold up to ridicule every 
thing that preceding ages of mankind had held most sacred, they invented new crimes, but did not ameliorate their 
own age, they blasphemed the First Cause at the very time that they were pretending to teach the adoration which it 
was proper to pay to the God of the universe; for who will venture to maintain, that under the name of Jupiter the 
ancients did not worship the First Cause, who was, and is, and ever will be, as Saint Paul rightly declares, the unknown 
God ; for it is a vain boast of the Jews to say that the world knew more of God when it became acquainted with the 
history of their ancestors’ flight from Egypt, and their passage across the Red Sea, than it did before, since all that 
man can know of the Deity is, that he is excellent and incomprehensible: to write, therefore, in the style of invective 
and obscenity, which Clemens Alexandrinus has employed to destroy the reverence of the Greeks and Romans for 
Jupiter, was to blaspheme the First Cause. But if the last-mentioned Father had known that mm, Yaoua, would 
be adored by the Mexicans not under the title of Yao the God of Sabbath, but of Yao the terrible God and the God 
of battles ; and that the sacrifices of the old law, the seal of which was circumcision, which would still be retained 
amongst the Indians, would degenerate into the immolation of human victims at his shrine ; he, perhaps, would have 
triumphed less at finding that Jupiter (as the poets feigned) had sometimes forsaken the seats divine, confessing the 
power of mortal charms, and have thought it less advisable to feign thereat holy horror, when it would be so neces- 
sary to reserve the feeling for another and a better occasion which the future had in store for him. The Jews are 
accused of having corrupted the Old Testament with their traditions; and if this charge has been truly brought 
against them in the Old Continent, is it at all unreasonable to suppose that in the New they may not have profaned 
it with their paintings? and, indeed, the forty-eighth verse of the third chapter of the first book of Maccabees, which 
differs materially in the Roman edition from the passage as it is rendered in our English translation of the Bible, 
makes it very doubtful whether the Jews did not in early ages disfigure the Old Testament with frightful paintings 
of idols. The following is the verse alluded to: “‘xa é€ereracay ro (iBAtoy Tov vowov wept wy eEepevvey ra eOvy ra 
opowpata Twv eldwrwy avtwy:” “and they unfolded the book of the law (that they might know likewise) whence the 
heathen borrowed the patterns of their idols.” This is the probable signification of this very obscure passage, which 
is evidently elliptical, because ro i8dt0v cannot be the antecedent to wepc wv, and the ellipsis is here supplied in a 
manner which accords with the idiom of the Greek language. It may be proper to observe, that in the Spanish 
edition of the book of Maccabees the following material variation occurs in the reading of the passage in question : 
“ é£epevvwn ra On Tov emrypapew ér avrwy ra ouowwpara :” from which it would appear that the Gentiles took the pains 
of painting their idols on the leaves of the Pentateuch, with the intention, according to commentators, of shocking the 
pure eyes of the Jews with the contemplation of their law and idols at the same time. But where is the necessity of 
supposing that the Gentiles painted idols on the leaves of a book which contained the word of God, when the Jews 
covered the walls of the temples, in which they believed that he was continually present, with paintings of the most 
deformed idols that imagination can conceive, as Ezekiel himself informs us in the eighth chapter of his book of 
prophecies? The passage which has been already quoted from the sixth book of Sahagun’s History of New Spain,

nuestro Sefior ; haga él lo que fuere servido; pongamos en él toda nuestra esperanza.” “O Lady, who art dear to 
me as my daughter or grandaughter, I am solicitous to be informed of your health; you have endured a long and 
severe trial, you have rivalled, you have imitated your mother the goddess Cioacatlquilahtli ; many thanks have we 
now to return to our Lord, because he has vouchsafed to send us this precious gem, this rich Quetzatl which has 
come to light, the image, hair, and nail of our Lords who are dead, who have long since been no more. The stock 
and scion of our Lords, Consuls, and Kings has budded, has bloomed; the thorn of the aloe and the odoriferous 
cane, which our Lords and departed Kings, who were valiant and renowned, planted deep in the earth, has sprung up, 
has appeared ; from you, Lady, our son Quetzalcoatl has received a precious gem, from you he has obtained a rich 
feather. May our Lord be praised, since he has happily preserved you from danger, and from the battle which you 
fought with death at the time of delivery; perhaps the days of the infant to which you have just given birth will 
outnumber yours; perhaps it will be the will of our Lord that he shall live, or perhaps he will die the first; perhaps, 
tender as he is, the Lord of the universe will break into atoms this precious gem, this chain of costly jewels ; perhaps 
he who made him will come and take him from us unto himself; perhaps he will pass him momentarily before the 
eyes of his kingdom and state, and deprive us of him, turning us into mockery on account of our sins, because we are 
unworthy of enjoying him. O! let the will of our Lord be done; let him do what seemeth good unto him; in him 
let us place all our hope.” It is evident from the concluding portion of this salutation, that the Mexican religion 
enjoined resignation and submission to the divine decrees, and hope in God, which after all is not an article con- 
fined to any particular creed, but a consolation that was poured into the cup of misfortune when first presented to 
man to taste, which if religion inculcates, reason nevertheless teaches without the aid of inspiration. We cannot 
omit carefully to point out here the phrase “your mother the goddess Cioacatlquilahtli,” since it is perfectly analo- 
gous to that of our mother Eve; Cioacatlquilahtli being the Eve of the New World, who, as the Mexicans believed, 
brought sin into the world, and entazled death on her posterity, as is distinctly stated in the thirty-third chapter of the 
sixth book of Sahagun. This goddess is more frequently named simply Cioacoatl or Quilahtli, she is also named 
Suchiquecal or Xochiquecal, and in the same manner as the first name seems to allude to her temptation by the 
serpent, so the last seems to refer to her having plucked the forbidden fruit, or the roses, in Xochitlicacan or the 
garden of Eden. There is also something rather equivocal in the allusion contained in the words “the stock and 
scion of our Lords, Consuls, and Kings:” the Hebrew patriarchs, judges, and kings may by possibility be here 
referred to, whose fame the Jews would speedily have spread abroad on their arrival in America. Having elsewhere 
made the observation that the Mexicans resembled the Jews in their frequent use of the same metaphors, of which 
the entire of the sixth book of Sahagun’s History of New Spain furnishes abundant proof, we shall here remark that 
the ‘hair and nail of their forefathers’, under which simile the Mexicans represented posterity, is very like the 
Hebrew metaphor of ‘flesh of flesh’ and ‘bone of bone’, which the Jews applied to their near relations and descend- 
ants, as we learn from the fourteenth verse of the twenty-ninth chapter of Genesis, where Laban addressing Jacob 
says, “Surely thou art my bone and my flesh.”. The expression “cortados de vuestros entrahas y de vuestros lomos,” 
which is applied to children in the twenty-fifth chapter of the sixth book of Sahagun, is in the pure Hebrew idiom, and 
might almost have been borrowed from the Psalms. Scripture phraseology, likewise, employing the latter term ‘loins’ 
in the famous prophecy relating to the birth of the Messiah, who was to be of the seed of David, it is probable that 
the Jews would have quickly incorporated that metaphor into the Mexican language. In the following passage of the 
thirty-third chapter of the sixth book of Sahagun, children, who are elsewhere named the gift of Tezcatlipoca, 
appear to be ascribed to Quecalcoatle. _‘ Aqui en vuestra presencia ha nacido la criatura de nuestro Sefior, que es

guos, y ha muchos dias que murieron. Hanos la dado nuestro Seftor 4 esta criatura, pero no tenemos certidumbre de

“ Here, in your presence, the infant of our Lord is born, which is like unto a precious gem or a rich feather, on whose 
face you have already fixed your eyes. This child does indeed resemble a plant set by his sires; he is, as it were, the 
fragment of a jewel cut by the ancients, who are long since no more. Our Lord has given this infant to us, but we 
cannot tell whether he will live, or be like a vision seen in a dream. Our eyes now contemplate the infant which 
has been born; he resembles a precious stone and a rich feather, which has already displayed itself to our view. 
That which I am at liberty to declare is, that our Lord Quetzalcoatl, who is the Creator, has placed a precious stone 
and one of fis rich feathers in the dust before us, and in this poor and cane-built hut; and I may likewise add, that 
he has ornamented your neck and wrists with costly gems and rich feathers, such as are rarely to be met with and 
difficult to be obtained even for a price ; and, further, that he has placed in your hands a handful of rich feathers, 
called Quetzalli, of perfect form and perfect colour. In return for so signal an act of grace, it is right that you 
should address yourself with tears, prayers, and vows to our Lord who is everywhere; sigh and weep until you 
know whether it be his will that this precious stone and rich feather, of which we are speaking like persons in a 
dream, shall live: we know not whether he will grow and arrive at maturity, or whether his term of life will be a

away, from whom he descends: we know not whether, peradventure, he will resuscitate the fortune and raise the head 
of his forefathers.” The concluding sentence of this passage is very remarkable: proceeding from the lips of the 
Mexicans, it is enigmatical and unintelligible; since, if we reflect for a moment that the Mexican empire was, ac- 
cording to the testimony of all historians, at the height of its greatness in the reign of Montezuma, the wish here 
expressed must appear alike devoid of meaning and of application, except Mexican history was something very dif- 
ferent from what historians have represented it to be: but in the mouth of a Jew the allusion would be plain, and 
would strikingly illustrate the truth of a remark previously made in page 385 of the present volume, that the 
Jews, wherever residing, and however well off in their temporal concerns, have been accustomed to indulge in a tone 
of complaint ever since the fall of their empire. It has also a tincture of Hebrew rhetoric, since children are in many 
parts of the Old Testament named the ornaments of their parents, and Christ is called in the New the image of his 
Father’s glory. He likewise compares himself, apostrophizing Jerusalem in the thirty-fourth verse of the thirteenth 
chapter of Saint Luke, to a hen ready to protect her brood beneath her wings; which metaphor, as well as the analo- 
gous simile of shading like a tree of spreading foliage, under which type Nebuchadnezzar beheld himself in the 
dream described in the fourth chapter of the book of Daniel, was very familiar to the ancient Mexicans, and was fre- 
quently employed by them in their prayers to the gods. Quecalcoatle is emphatically styled ‘ Maker and Creator’ in 
the following passage of the twenty-fifth chapter of the sixth book of Sahagun, into which brief space many Jewish 
notions are crowded: “ Nieta mia muy amada, y preciosa como piedra preciosa, como chalchiuitl y zafiro, noble y 
generosa, es cierto ahora que nuestro Sefior se ha acordado de vos, el qual esté en toda parte y hace mercedes 4 
quien quiere: ya esta claro que estds prefiada, y que nuestro Seftor os quiere dar fruto de generacion, y os quiere

Mirad, hija mia, que no os ensoberbezcais, por la merced que os ha hecho.” “My dear daughter, precious as a gem, 
and as a chalchiuitl or saphire, who art good and noble, it is now certain that our Lord, who is everywhere, and 
shows kindness to whom he will, has remembered you: it is plain that you have conceived, and that it is our Lord’s

pleasure that you should be fruitful: to whom it seems good to adorn you with a jewel, and to bestow a rich feather 
upon you. Perhaps your sighs, your tears, and the lifting up of your hands before the Lord our God, and the prayers 
and supplications which you have offered in the presence of our Lord, whose name is Obscurity and Air, in vigils at 
midnight, have merited this favour; perhaps you have watched; perhaps you have employed yourself in sweeping 
and in offering incense in his presence; perhaps for the sake of these good works our Lord hath dealt mercifully

hell, that this kindness should be shown to you; perhaps it is true that our Lord Quetzalcoatl, who is Maker and 
Creator, has shown you this kindness ; perhaps it had been decreed by the pair who inhabit heaven, the man and the

do so, you will not be able to hide your inward thoughts from our Lord, for nothing is hidden from him, be it within 
either rocks or trees; and thus you would excite his displeasure against you, and he would ‘send some chastisement 
upon you, so that we should lose that which is within you; our Lord slaying it in the womb, or causing it'to be born 
an idiot, or to die in its tender infancy; or perhaps our Lord would visit you with some disease of which you would 
die ; for the fulfilment of our wish to have children and posterity depends upon the sole mercy of God; and if our 
thoughts are at variance with this truth, imagining that it happens through our own deserts, we defraud ourselves of 
the boon which is vouchsafed to us. Perhaps, daughter, pride will render you unworthy of letting the light behold 
that which has begun and is now coming.” A Jewish tone of sentiment, it must be confessed, pervades the entire of 
this address; whilst Christian ethics, Scriptural allusions, and Hebrew customs seem all wonderfully mixed up in it. 
It was a Hebrew custom to lift up the hands in prayer, as we learn from the second verse of the hundred and forty- 
first Psalm: “Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense, and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacri- 
fices.” And David commemorates his midnight vigils in the sixty-second verse of the hundred and nineteenth Psalm : 
“ At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee, because of thy righteous judgments.” Children are named in va- 
rious parts of the Old Testament the ornaments of their parents, and compared to jewels about their necks: they were 
likewise believed by the Jews to be the gift of God, on the authority of many passages of Holy Writ; and they are 
so expressly stated to be in the third verse of the hundred and twenty-seventh Psalm, “Lo children are an heritage 
of the Lord, and the fruit of the womb is his reward.” Jacob, likewise, in the thirty-third chapter of Genesis, answers 
in reply to Esau’s question, “ Who are those with thee?” “The children which God hath graciously given thy ser- 
vant.” And Isaiah exclaims in the eighth chapter of his Prophecies, “ Behold, I and the children whom the Lord 
hath given me, are for signs and for wonders in Israel from the Lord of hosts, which dwelleth in Mount Zion.” The 
admonition towards the conclusion of the address might have suggested itself to the mind of the speaker, from the 
recollection of the example in the Old Testament of Sarah’s having incurred the displeasure of God, by laughing and 
commenting inwardly to herself on the promise made by him to Abraham, that she should bear a son; the occasion 
of which is thus described in the eighteenth chapter of Genesis: “And he said, I will certainly return unto thee 
according to the time of life; and, lo, Sarah thy wife shall have a son. And Sarah heard it in the tent-door, which 
was behind him. Now Abraham and Sarah were old, and well stricken in age; and it had ceased to be with Sarah 
after the manner of women. Therefore Sarah laughed within herself, saying, After 1 am waxed old shall I have 
pleasure, my lord being old also? And the Lord said unto Abraham, Wherefore did Sarah laugh, saying, Shall I of 
a surety bear a child, which am old? Is any thing too hard for the Lord? At the time appointed I will return unto 
thee, according to the time of life, and Sarah shall have ason. Then Sarah denied, saying, I laughed not: for she 
was afraid. And he said, Nay; but thou didst laugh.” It must have been Sarah’s fear that induced her on that 
occasion to contradict God, since, having been so long the wife of the patriarch Abraham, she could not have been 
ignorant that he knew what passed in her heart; and, except on this assumption, her want of faith would have been a 
lesser crime than her presumption; nor would a contradiction in return from God have been a punishment adequate 
to her temerity. A famous example however of pride of heart, venting itself in boastful language, and meeting with 
severe chastisement from God, is afforded in the case of king Nebuchadnezzar, who having exclaimed to himself, 
“Ts not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom, by the might of my power, and for the 
honour of my majesty?” was driven from his throne and the habitations of men, “ had a deast’s heart given unto him,” 

NOTES. 517 

and did eat grass as oven: which expressions in the fourth chapter of Daniel have induced some of the Rabbis to 
maintain that he was changed into a real ox, asking at the same time the rational question, Whether a man could 
live on grass alone? Without pausing to reply to their query, we shall proceed to observe, that the New Testament 
affords an example in Herod of exultation of heart immediately drawing down Divine vengeance: “ And upon a set 
day Herod, arrayed in royal apparel, sat upon his throne, and made an oration unto them. And the people gave a 
shout, saying, It is the voice of a god, and not of man. And immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because 
he gave not God the glory: and he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost.” The manner of Herod’s death, as 
recorded in the twenty-third verse of the twelfth chapter of the Acts, resembles that of Antiochus, who in the ninth 
verse of the ninth chapter of the Second Book of Maccabees is said to have been eaten by worms as a punishment for 
his pride. It is probable, therefore, that the extreme fear which the Mexicans entertained that God would severely 
punish them for the slightest degree of pride or presumption, was borrowed from the Jews, with whom, “Keep me, O 
Lord, from presumptuous sins” was a prayer. Their supposition, likewise, that Tezcatlipoca would punish the infant 
for the sin of its mother, was strictly in accordance with the doctrine inculcated throughout the Pentateuch; which 
induced the Jews to reproach the blind man, whose sight had been restored to him by Christ, with having been 
born in sins, as related in the thirty-fourth verse of the ninth chapter of the Gospel of Saint John: “They answered 
and said unto him, Thou wast altogether born in sins, and dost thou teach us? And they cast him out.” This prin- 
ciple of the Jewish religion is also asserted in the second commandment, where the threat, “I am a jealous God, and 
visit the sins of the fathers upon the children,” being denounced against the sz of idolatry, and not against intem- 
perance, does in fact require a very different explanation from that which most commentators have chosen to give to 
it. The notion of God not permitting children to arrive at perfection from displeasure against their parents for their 
sins, was Hebrew, as we learn from the sixteenth verse of the third chapter of the Wisdom of Solomon: “ As for the 
children of adulterers, they shall not come to their perfection; and the seed of an unrighteous bed shall be rooted 
out.” Other exceedingly curious notions respecting children were entertained by the Mexicans: they believed that 
they were dear to God, and that they interceded with him for the world and for men; that on their deaths they went 
to heaven, and were nourished by the tree distilling milk, which grew in the garden of Tonacaquahtitlan, where they 
ever abided in the presence of Tonacatecutli: the name of the tree was Chichiualquauitl, and a representation of it 
will be found in the fifth page of the larger Vatican MS. When we recollect what is said in the New Testament 
of little children, and the mysterious words of Christ in the tenth verse of the eighteenth chapter of Saint Matthew, 
“Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones: for l say unto you, that mm heaven ther angels do always 
behold the face of my Father which is in heaven,” coupled with the preceding ones in the sixth verse, “ But whoso 
shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his 
neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea,” and compare them with other similar passages contained in 
the ninth chapter of Saint Mark and the seventeenth chapter of Saint Luke ;—considering at the same time that the 
signification of Tonacaquahtitlan is, ‘the place where grows the tree of our bodies or of life’, that word being com- 
pounded of tonacayo, defined by Molina in his Lexicon of the Mexican language to be “cuerpo humano 6 nuestra 
carne,” i. e. the human body or our flesh, and guauitl, which signifies, according to the same author, “arbol 6 palo,” a 
tree or a piece of wood (quauitl nepaniuhtoc, meaning ‘a wooden cross’), to which is added a particle of local refe- 
rence ;—can a doubt remain in our mind that the Mexicans borrowed some of their notions about children from the 
Scriptures, and had heard of the tree of life which grew in the garden of Eden, the fruit of which is said in the 
twenty-second verse of the third chapter of Genesis to confer smmortalty on the taster ; and which is again mentioned 
in the following terms in the last chapter of the Revelations by Saint John, in his description of his vision of New 
Jerusalem ; “In the midst of the street of it, and on either side of the river, was there the tree of life, which bare 
twelve manner of fruits, and yielded her fruit every month: and the /eaves of the tree were for the healing of the 
nations”? which passage might have been corrupted by course of time and tradition into the doctrine, that the tree 
of life bestowed immortality upon the souls of children who died before attaining the knowledge of good and evil, or, 
as the interpreter of the Vatican MS. expresses it, “‘ che muorono senza l’uso della ragione,” and who therefore could 
not have earned it by faith or good works. The god Tonacatecutli was believed by the Mexicans to reside in the 
garden of Tonacaquahtitlan: he was the father of Quecalcoatle, and was also named Ometecutli, which signifies, the 
Most High, that name being compounded of ome, ‘twice’, which particle when prefixed to an adjective has an intensive 

(6) 

518 NOTES. 

force like the Latin fer, and tecutli, ‘lord’ or ‘king’. This observation will serve to correct an erroneous explanation 
of the proper name Hometeuli, in the note subjoined to page 156 of the present volume. The meaning of the proper 
name Tonacatecutli, is ‘the lord of our bodies or of our flesh’; and it deserves to be remarked, that the Jews styled 
Jehovah the Lord of all flesh, or of all living things, the two expressions being synonymous, because animal life cannot 
exist without flesh, nor flesh enter on its first stage of existence without life, or remain flesh any length of time after 
death : hence it is apparent that the tree of life was named with the greatest propriety by the Mexicans, Tonacaquauitl 
or Tonacaquahuitl. And since the Jews believed that the life of the flesh was the blood, grounding that notion upon 
the fourth verse of the ninth chapter of Genesis, “ But flesh with the life thereof, which is the blood thereof, shall ye 
not eat,” it is probable that the Mexicans represented the tree, described in page 127 of the present volume, bloody and 
cracked in the middle. This tree must have been very celebrated in Mexican mythology, since it has a distinct place 
assigned to it in the Tonalamatl or Mexican calendar; Suchiquecal also is recorded to have sinned by plucking its 
fruit. Having observed above that the Mexicans believed that the intercessions of children in behalf of men were effi- 
cacious with God, we shall quote a remarkable passage from the twenty-first chapter of the sixth book of Sahagun’s 
History, in confirmation of that curious fact: “ Decian, que por estos sustentaba Dios al mundo, y que ellos eran 
nuestros intercesores para con Dios.” ‘They say, that it is for their sake that God preserves the world, and that 
they (children) are our intercessors with God.” Which passage deserves to be considered in connection with what is 
said of children in the second verse of the eighth Psalm: ‘“ Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou or- 
dained strength, because of thine enemies, that thou mightest still the enemy and the avenger.” From the fifteenth 
and sixteenth verses of the hundred-and-thirty-ninth Psalm,—“ My substance was not hid from thee when I was made 
in secret, and curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth. Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being im- 
perfect ; and in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was 
none of them ;”—as well as from other parts of Scripture, it would appear that it was a Jewish doctrine that children 
were fashioned by God’s eternal decree before they had any material existence in their mother’s womb, and that there 
they became the objects of his peculiar care and love ;—that this was precisely the belief of the Mexicans is evident 
from the passage last cited from Sahagun: in reference to a curious sentence which there occurs, “ perhaps on this 
very account it was determined, before the commencement of the world, zm heaven and im hell, that this kindness 
should be shown to you,” it may be proper to observe that the Mexicans believed, like the Jews, that God was omni- 
present both in heaven and in hell; and that, therefore, that which was decreed in the one place, must necessarily have 
been decreed in the other; the latter grounding their belief on the eighth verse of the hundred-and-thirty-ninth 
Psalm: “If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there; if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there.” The omni- 
presence of the Deity is so often insisted upon in the prayers which the Mexicans addressed to Tezcatlipoca, that it is 
difficult to imagine but that they must have borrowed that notion from the Jews ; for the ancient philosophers did 
not imagine that their idea of the Deity was heightened by adding to omnipotence and omniscience the attribute of om- 
nipresence, but, on the contrary, that it was materialized and debased by it: and hence the Jews were accused, in 
very early ages, of being Ceelicole, or worshipers of the material heavens ; to which Juvenal alludes in the verse 

“ Nil preeter nubes et Coeli numen adorant,” 

in his fourteenth Satire; and Petronius, with more irony, in the line 

“Et Coeli summas advocet auriculas ;”

The Ingas of Peru wore a tassel hanging from the forehead as the insignia of royalty, which in the Peruvian language was named ¢ suntur- 
paucar’’, and by the Spaniards ‘borla’; which, considering that they accounted themselves the representatives of Viracocha, might have 
served to remind them to keep his laws, and, like the rose worn by the Mozcas, have been in imitation of the head-dress of Bochicha: 
a comparison of the royal costume of the Ingas, as represented in the plate inserted by Herrera in his General History of the Indies, 
with that of the Zippas, or sovereigns of Bogota, in the plate prefixed by Piedrahita to his History of the Conquest of the Kingdom of 
New Granada, will render this supposition more probable from the extreme similarity of the dress of the Ingas to that of the Zippas, who 
it is to be supposed imitated even more closely than their subjects the costume of Bochicha. The cleft or episcopal mitre upon the head 
of Sugamuxi, the founder of the empire of Bogota, and those upon the heads of Pachacuti Yupangui and Topaynga Yupangui, the 
tenth and eleventh Ingas of Peru, are very deserving of notice, and remind us that the Ingas of Peru and the Zippas of Bogota consi- 
dered a priest the founder of their respective dynasties. The mitre does in fact seem to have usurped the place of the crown in the New 
World, for the copilli worn by the Mexican monarch was a half-mitre; and the coincidence is curious, that all the native Indian 
monarchs, at the period of the discovery of America by the Spaniards, should have worn mitres as the ensign of royalty; for the only 
monarchies then existing worthy of the name were those of New Spain, of Peru, and of Bogota, which, though widely apart, had many 
things in common in their religion, laws, and institutions. An interesting account of the latter state, which was advanced in civilization, 
and the subjects of which made use of golden money in their dealings with each other, will be found in the Supplemental volume of this 
work; it is taken from an unpublished manuscript of the most authentic character. To an objection which may be urged against admitting 
the plates referred to in the Histories of Herrera and of Piedrahita in proof of what was the ancient costume of the Ingas, on the ground 
of the Spaniards being themselves ignorant of it, it may be observed that these plates are found in the works of two eminent historians, 
that they mutually confirm each other, and that the accuracy of another plate in Herrera, in which Acamapichtli, the first sovereign of 
Mexico, is represented in the true costume of the Mexican kings, tends further to that confirmation. A more reasonable exception may 
be taken to the crosses placed over the heads of each of the Zippas, since no such symbols are added to the portraits of the Ingas, al- 
though crosses, as Garcilaso de la Vega asserts in the second part of his Royal Commentaries, were adored in Cuzco, and found in the 
temples and the palaces of the Ingas® by the two Spaniards dispatched to that city by Pizarro. The cross being likewise immemorially 
the companion of the crozier, the acquaintance with the latter, implied by the question put by the Peruvians to the Spaniards on first 
seeing a bishop, whether he was the Guaca of the Christians? argued acquaintance on their part with the former symbol. Gomara 
incidentally records, in the following passage of his History of the Indies, this curious question of the Peruvians: ‘“ Entre sus muchas 
Guacas, assi llaman: los idolos, avia muchas con baculos y mitras de obispos.” “ Amongst their many Guacas, by which appellation 
they name their idols, there were many with bishops’ croziers and mitres.” But he immediately afterwards adds, with perhaps well 
feigned simplicity, ‘mas la causa dello aun no se sabe,” “ but the reason of this is not yet known ;” nor does it appear that the Spaniards 
took any great trouble to clear up this mystery. If, however, any proof were wanting to show that the crozier and the mitre were 
associated with the cross in the New World as well as in the Old, it would be found in the larger Vatican MS., the fifth page of which 
represents Quecalcoatle holding a crozier, and habited with a mitre, and a mantle covered with red crosses. The objection, however, that 
Spanish authors could not insert in their works plates representing the costume of the Ingas which their countrymen had never seen, 
although very futile, would be rendered in appearance even superfluous, regard being had to the weightier objection, that the portraits con- 
tained in the two plates referred to must be merely imaginary, because the sovereigns whom they represented had been dead many years 
before the arrival of the Spaniards. This is an objection that Dr. Robertson would have admitted, proceeding on his assumption that 
the Indians were barbarians in a sense almost unlimited, and that the arts of sculpture and painting were wholly unknown in America. 
That the contrary however was the case, is evident from original monuments still in existence. Neither was Europe so enlightened at the 
beginning of the sixteenth century as to justify Dr. Robertson in the parallel which he has been pleased to draw between the civilized 
population of his part of the world and the barbarous Indians. The Spaniards, it cannot be doubted, had the opportunity of seeing many 
statues and paintings of the Ingas which represented them attired in the royal costume; and embalming was carried to such perfection 
in Peru, that when they opened the tombs of the Ingas for the sake of plundering them of the gold and silver which they contained, they 
_ found the bodies of those princes preserved with such art, that, according to the testimony of Acosta and Garcilaso de la Vega, who saw 
them, they appeared to be alive ; their features were plain and distinct, and covered with a sort of varnish. Acosta remarks, that a golden 
plate was substituted for the eyes in each, shaped so as exactly to resemble them. Grarcilaso says, that the licentiate Polo Ondegardo 
showed him five of these royal bodies in a room in his house at Cuzco, observing to him, “Since you are going to Spain, come into 
this room, and you shall see some of your ancestors whom I have brought to light, that you may have something to tell when you arrive

en el Peru, cap. x. lib. 2. fol. 366.—Calancha’s Augustine Chronicle of Peru is a large folio volume, containing 922 pages: it was

tion of Pinelo, page 643 of his ¢ Bibliotheca Occidental,’ that the celebrated Spanish scholar Don Nicolas Antonio, who published the 
¢ Bibliotheca Hispana,’ doubted whether the Peruvian History of Brulius was not a translation of it. We are enabled, from possessing 
both works, to say that they are totally distinct; the latter is a book printed in Holland in the year 1652, which is also interesting, and

son que trujo de alla Yndios prisioneros de color negro, y mucho oro y plata, y mas una silla de laton y cueros de animales como caballos: 
y de parte donde se puedan traer las tales cosas, de todo punto se ignora en este Piru, y en el mar que lo va prolongando.” It must be 
admitted that this account of the voyage performed by Topa Inga is extremely curious, and it deserves to be considered in connection 
with a very remarkable passage in Gomara’s History of the Indies; where, describing at page cxvi. the province of Quivira, and the 
Spanish expedition thither in search of the seven cities reported in the first instance, by Brother Mark de Niza, to belong to a king who 
exhibited some conformity, in his adoration of the cross and homage to the Queen of Heaven, to the religion of the Spaniards, and whose 
history on that account might have been consigned to oblivion,—he observes, speaking of the coast of the Pacific Ocean, “ Vieron por la 
costa naos que trayan arcatrages de oro y de plata en las proas, con mercaderias ; y pensaron ser del Catayo y China, porque sefialavan 
aver navegado treynta dias.” But how much more curious will the following relation of Brother Antonio Tello be judged! taken from 
an original MS., which it would be wronging history to suffer to remain unpublished, in which mention is made of the north-west 
passage having been accidentally discovered in a remote century by two ships, to what nation belonging is unknown; one of which was 

2 

wrecked, while the crew of the other is recorded by native tradition to have colonized the north-west coast of America, and taught the 
Indians to adore the Cross, to wear scapularies, and to shave the crown of their heads; on which account the Spaniards, on first entering 
their province, and beholding the strange attire of the Indians, and their mode of wearing their hair, named it Provincia de los Frayles ; 
and the Indians themselves, Indios Coronados, from the round tonsure on the crown of their heads. The Indians, in confirmation of the 
truth of this tradition, which had been handed down to them from their ancestors, showed the Spaniards a large iron anchor (una ancora 
gastadisima de errumbre). ‘Tello himself supposes that these ships must have been either Dutch, English, or Spanish vessels, which, 
sailing through the Straits of Anian, entered by that route into the Pacific Ocean : and next follows, in order to render this supposition 
plausible, an assertion of an extraordinary fact unknown to the present age, which it may be proper to insert in the original Spanish.— 
“Como lo hicieron en nuestros tiempos ciertos estrangeros los quales llevados por las costas de los Bacallados y Tierra-nueva pasaron el 
Estrecho de Anian, y dieron con su navio en el Mar del Sur: y de su viage hicieron una relacion al Rey N.S. Felipe Segundo, y despues 
de su muerte el Rey N. S. Felipe Tercero viendola, mandé 4 su Virrey Conde de Monterey que 4 costa de sus reales haveres hiciese el 
descubrimiento de esta navegacion, lo qual se puso en execucion en cinco de Mayo del afio de 1602, que se hicieron 4 la vela dos naos, 
capitana y almiranta, y una fragata, y fue por General Sebastian Viscayno; y habiendo navegado y descubierto muchas yslas llegaron al 
Cabo Mendozino que esta en quarenta y dos grados de altura, y se pusieron en quarenta y tres en un cabo 6 punta que nombraron Cabo 
Blanco, junto 4 el qual se hallaron un rio caudaloso y hondable: procuraron sondearle y las corrientes no dieron lugar : entendiese que este 
rio és el que descubrieron los Holandeses viniendo derrotados, y que es el Estrechio de Anian por donde el navio que le descubrié atravesé 
y pasé del Mar del Norte al del Sur:”—the substance of which relation is briefly as follows; «That certain strangers (who, from 
the ardour displayed in Queen Elizabeth’s reign for prosecuting naval discoveries, and especially for exploring the North Pole, we must 
suppose were Englishmen), at a period not very remote from that in which Tello lived (for in this sense the phrase “en nuestros tiempos” 
must be understood, except it be opposed to the presumed antiquity of the period when the passage was first effected through the Straits 
of Anian by the two ships previously mentioned), had coasted the shores of Bacallaos and Newfoundland, and passing through the Straits 
of Anian, penetrated with their ships into the South Sea; information of which having been transmitted to Philip the Second, which was 
perused by Philip the Third, the latter monarch commanded his viceroy, the Count de Monterey, to fit out an expedition at the public 
expense to discover this passage, which was completed on the 5th of May in the year 1602, when two ships and a frigate sailed under 
the command of Sebastian Viscayno; which, having discovered many islands, arrived at Cape Mendozino in 42° north latitude, and 
prosecuted the voyage as far as a cape or point, to which they gave the name of Cabo Blanco, situated in latitude 43°, near which they 
found a great and deep river, unfathomable from the strength of the current. Tello is persuaded this was the river discovered by the Dutch, 
and the same as the Straits of Anian, through which the ships that discovered those straits sailed, and passed from the Northern into the 
Southern Ocean.” From this account it would appear that a north-west passage, of the existence of which little doubt has ever been 
entertained, but of the practicability of navigating it the greatest, has twice served as a channel of communication between the Atlantic 
and Pacific Oceans. Two reasons might be alleged for so important a fact having been buried in secresy, till it became finally forgotten ; 
but it could be only the effect of their combined action, and the jealousy which Spain must have naturally felt of the ambition of England, 
whose powerful navy in the reign of Elizabeth threatened, by effecting disembarkations in various parts of the southern continent of 
America, to revolutionize the Indian population, in the beginning but imperfectly subdued, and long impatient of the Spanish yoke. The 
reasons are these :—first, the unwillingness of Philip to cede to his rival, Queen Elizabeth, the honour of a discovery which he might have 
judged more properly belonged to himself; and, secondly, the cautious policy of that monarch, his regard to the mercantile interests of his 
kingdom, and perhaps erroneous anticipations respecting the utility which such a passage, when once declared practicable, would be of to 
the northern European powers, to the prejudice of Spanish commerce, which might have made him little eager that it should be disco- 
vered. A prince, moreover, even more inclined to protect philosophy and science than was Philip, might have deemed that one age at least 
should rest content with the great discoveries in geography which had so recently been made, and which it would be better to acquire a 
more perfect knowledge of, than to attempt new ones.— Before terminating this note we may be permitted to observe, that the only con- 
clusion which the relation of Tello seems to warrant, appealing as he does to Indian tradition and to the’ proceedings of the Spanish 
Government, in proof of ships having sailed through the northern straits into the Pacific, and thus uniting the testimony both of Spaniards 
and Indians in favour of the supposed passage, is, that there is an appearance of probability that the north-west passage has been found 

by experience to be practicable for ships.

trabajos. O Seftor nuestro, tenga por bien vuestra magestad, pues que soys Dios, y lo podeis todo, y lo ordenais todo, 
y entendeis en disponer todas las cosas, y en ordenar y disponer a que esta vuestra republica sea rica y prospera, y 
ensalzada, y honrada, y afamada en los ejercicios y valentias de la guerra.” “ And inasmuch as your majesty is Lord 
of battles, on whose will depends victory, who forsakest whom thou wilt, and standest in no need of counsel from 
any one; since so it is, I supplicate your majesty to deprive our enemies of reason and to make them drunkards, in 
order that they may throw themselves into our hands, and, without doing us any harm, may all fall into the hands of 
our soldiers and men of war, who endure poverty and hardships. O Lord, may it please your majesty, since thou art 
God and can do all things, and ordainest all things, and art ever employed in directing the affairs of the universe, 
and in ordering and providing for the riches and prosperity and glory and honour and fame of this thy republic, in 
the deeds and achievements of war.” 

It is very remarkable that the Mexicans should have prayed to Tezcatlipoca to afflict their enemies with drunken- 
ness, since that prayer accords with what is said in the twenty-fourth and twenty-fifth verses of the twelfth chapter 
of Job: “ He taketh away the heart of the chief of the people of the earth, and causeth them to wander in a wilder- 
ness where there is no way: they grope in the dark without light, and he maketh them to stagger like a drunken 
man;” and with the threat pronounced by Jeremiah in the thirteenth verse of the thirteenth chapter of his Prophecies 
against the Jews themselves, who were very fond of denouncing against others the judgments which Moses, speaking 
in the name of God, uttered against them in case of disobedience to his laws. The passage of Jeremiah referred to is 
the following: “ Then shalt thou say unto them, Behold, I will fill all the inhabitants of this land, even the kings 
that sit upon David’s throne, and the priests, and the prophets, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, with drunkenness.” 
A sort of spiritual drunkenness is certainly here signified, which in the case of the prophets, if compatible at all with 
inspiration, must nevertheless have rendered the predictions which they uttered very innocuous, and still more calcu- 
lated to excite the mirth than the fear of the Canaanites, and their other enemies, against whom they were chiefly 
directed, who would have felt inclined to pay little regard to the prophecies of these blind leaders of the blind. The 
notion of Tezcatlipoca protecting the people beneath his wings,—which metaphor was employed by the ancient Mex- 
icans, who emphatically styled themselves his people, and their kingdom God’s kingdom, and the throne of their 
kings God’s throne and the seat of judicature,—strongly assimilates itself to the language of David in the fourth verse 
of the ninety-first Psalm: “He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth 
shall be thy shield and buckler.” They likewise considered this supreme God their shield and buckler; and the 
proper name Chimalman, which is derived from chimalli the Mexican name for a shield, being compounded of that 
term with the elision of the final syllable %, and man devoid of signification, as is most probably here the case, and 
which perhaps would have been mar but that the Mexican language wants the letter 7, may not unreasonably be sup- 
posed to have been given to the Virgin of Tula, the mother of Quecalcoatle, on that account. In reference to two 
opinions of the ancient Mexicans which have already been noticed,—one of which seems related to Hebrew usages, 

5Q4, iy © Wi S, 

and the other to be strangely allied with a prejudice to which the second verse of the eighth Psalm might have given 
rise among the Jews,—we must observe, that it was customary for Hebrew women to seek the favour of Jehovah by 
ministering in the service of his temple, an example of which is recorded by Saint Luke of the prophetess Anna in 
the second chapter of his Gospel: “ And there was one Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of 
Aser: she was of a great age, and had lived with a husband seven years from her virginity ; and she was a widow 
of about fourscore and four years, which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night 
and day.” And hence perhaps the interrogation in the passage already quoted from Sahagun, “por ventura habeis 
velado ; por ventura habeis trabajado en barrer y ofrecer incienso en su presencia; por ventura por estas buenas obras 
ha hecho con vos misericordia nuestro Sefior.” The passage in the Psalms which in the English version of the Bible is 
rendered “out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou ordained strength, because of thine enemies that thou 
mightest still the enemy and the avenger,” which is translated in the Septuagint “ é« crouaroc vytwwy Kar OnraZovtwy 
Katnptisw aivoy’ éveca twv €XOpwy cov, Tov katadvoat ex Opov Kar éxducntny,” might have induced the Mexicans, borrowing 
the notion from the Jews, to imagine that through the intercession of children with God the world was preserved ; 
since if the latter had understood the enemy and the avenger to mean Satan, which it is highly probable they 
would, because he is expressly named the adversary and the accuser in many places of the Old Testament, and more 
especially in the book of Job, here we might seek the origin of this extraordinary doctrine. The English translation of 
the Bible, which although generally formed on the Hebrew text of Scripture, sometimes, and not unfrequently when 
the translators were in doubt which was the word of God, prefers the Septuagint rendering of a passage involving 
difficulty or contradiction, has in this place ‘still the enemy and the avenger,’ to which the Greek phrase tov cara- 
Avoat €xPpov Kar éxducnrny corresponds ; and it must be confessed that the word ‘still’ would be very applicable to Satan, 
who is compared elsewhere in Scripture to a roaring lion going up and down the earth to seek whom he might devour. 
‘Enemy’ and ‘adversary’ are in English synonymous terms, and literally expressive of the signification of éy8pov, which 
was a name for Satan; but ‘accuser’ and ‘avenger’ are terms of which the meaning is materially different, although 
by both these names, taken in acceptations widely different from each other, Satan was known to the ancient Jews, 
who called him the avenger of blood, and when they killed cattle were careful to cover up the blood with dust, lest 
Satan beholding it should demand vengeance at the hands of God on account of their having put to death an in- 
nocent animal. The Mexicans likewise, who were probably well acquainted with what is said in the eleventh verse of 
the fourth chapter of Genesis, of the earth having opened her mouth to receive the blood of Abel from the hand of 
Cain, and with the Hebrew custom of covering blood with dust, entertained a superstitious notion about blood being 
the beverage of the earth, as has elsewhere been observed. It may be proper however to remark that the Greek word 
éxSuntne signifies both an ‘accuser’ and an ‘avenger’, undoubtedly because a legal accuser becomes in a manner an 
avenger; and Stephanus thus defines it in the former sense, “persequutor, cujus munus est judicio experiri contra 
eos qui aurum vel argentum vel pecuniam reipublice debent ;” from which it would appear that it signified the person 
who conducted ex-officio or state prosecutions on the part of the Crown or the public when money was concerned, 
but not blasphemy ; for that was a crime which even in the age of primitive simplicity, when Rome beheld her 
dictators’ guiding the plough, Roman lawyers disdained to meddle with, and “ qui secus faxit, Deus ipse vindex 
sit” became a maxim of their jurisprudence, which, rude as was the Latin of the Twelve Tables, could not have 
come adorned from the lips of Cicero. From the name of ‘the accuser’ which the Jews bestowed upon Satan, from 
believing that his chief function was that of an accuser of men to God,—which of itself would have suggested the idea 
of a mediator, (traces of both which doctrines may perhaps be recognized in the Mexican fable of Tonatiuh or the Sun, 
who was the same as Quecalcoatle, conducting with acclamations the souls of saints to heaven, and of Miquitlante- 
cutli the god of hell endeavouring to intercept them on the way,)—the Greek word AtaBoXog is derived. But although 
the New Testament, by bestowing the name of AvaBodoc¢ upon the devil, seems to lend the strongest sanction to the 
reasons which led the Jews to name him ‘the accuser, still when we reflect that it no where inculcates the Jewish 
doctrine upon that point, inferences from the proper name Ataodoc must be considered nugatory, or be condemned as 
opposed to the silence of the Evangelists. The Book of Job places Satan before us in the light of an accuser. But the 
same Book places God himself almost in the situation of a tempter, since he it was who, at least by sufferance, afflicted 
Job with all manner of diseases to try his patience; and hence the Mexicans might have derived the notion that 
Titlacaoa or Tezcatlipoca sometimes tempted them to sin to try their obedience to his commandments; nor can it

be denied, if Moses has been named, on the authority of the sixteenth chapter of Numbers and the thirty-second 
chapter of Exodus, the first inquisitor*, that Satan has as fair a claim, on that of the Book of Job, to be styled the 
first who was zealous to take cognizance of blasphemy. Reasons for supposing that the Mexicans were acquainted 
with the Book of Job will be found at page 382 of this volume; and their custom of shaving their hair, sitting down 
upon the ground, and sprinkling dust upon their heads as a sign of humiliation, closely resembles what is said in the 
first and second chapters of that Book, of the mourning of Job and his three friends. 

To add another remark to those which we have already made on the passage in the Psalms, which might have in- 
duced the Mexicans to suppose that Tezcatlipoca spared the world at the intercession of children, we may observe, 
that the wicked are perpetually named in Scripture God’s enemies, and that éveca twv éyfpwr, in the second verse 
of the eighth Psalm, being understood to mean them, the literal translation of the entire passage would be, “ Out of 
the mouth of infants and sucklings thou hast perfected praise, for the sake of the wicked, that thou mightest confound 
the adversary and the accuser.” The propriety of understanding the verb caraAvoa in the signification here assigned 
to it, will be evident to those who consider, that to dissolve the strength or to unnerve the limbs of an adversary, is to 
confound him; and the omission of the article before éy@pov is not of the least importance, and might be justified by 
reference to innumerable passages in Scripture: the sense even of the verse as it is here translated becomes more ob- 
vious than before, and is strictly accordant with the Jewish notion, that prayers which were acceptable to God con- 
founded Satan when he presented himself before him to accuse them of sin; which was more reasonable than the 
Rabbinical doctrine that the accusations of Satan were confounded by the noise of the trumpets which Moses com- 
manded the priests to blow on their solemn festivals; and which the Mexicans,—as it were in compliance with the 
precept contained in the eighth verse of the tenth chapter of Numbers, “ And the sons of Aaron the priests shall 
blow with the trumpets; and they shall be to you for an ordinance for ever throughout your generations,”—continually 
sounded in the courts of their temple; a custom which the interpreter of the Vatican Codex believed that they borrowed 
Srom the Jews, as he unequivocally declares at page 224 of the present volume. It has been already observed, 
that the Mexicans imagined that children were the gift of Tezcatlipoca, and that he fashioned and watched over 
them in their mothers’ womb ; and itis wonderful to find how conformable their customs, as well as their opinions, in 
every thing relating to the treatment of mothers and their children, were to those of the Jews. Sahagun, in the 24th, 
34th, and 35th chapters of the sixth book of his History of New Spain, informs us, that married women amongst the 
Mexicans received two salutations from their friends and kindred, the first on their becoming pregnant, and the 
second on their safe delivery, when the mother and the infant were both saluted, and gifts were presented to the latter. 
And that this accorded with Hebrew usage is evident from what Saint Luke says, in the first chapter of his Gospel,

The deference with which women who officiated as midwives were treated by the ancient Mexicans, the appella- 
tion which they gave them of spiritual mothers, and the belief which they entertained that they were under the 
immediate inspiration of Tezcatlipoca, are so closely allied to habits and a mode of thinking’ which, with the greatest 
show of probability, may be presumed to have been Hebrew, that it is only necessary to refer to what is said in the 
first chapter of Exodus of the meritorious conduct of the Hebrew midwives, who had been commanded by Pharaoh to 
destroy the male children of the Israelites at the moment of their birth, and to the declaration contained in the twen- 
tieth verse of the same chapter, “ Therefore God dealt well with the midwives,” to render it probable that the Mexican 
usages were founded on Hebrew traditions. The treatment of lying-in women amongst the Mexicans seems likewise 
to have been the same as amongst the ancient Jews; since a comparison of the sixteenth verse of the first chapter of 
Exodus with the following passage, taken from the speech of the mother of the young married woman to the midwife 
to whose care she had been entrusted, shows that the bath was resorted to as the chief means of promoting a safe

* This box is formed out of a solid piece of wood of the colour of mahogany. Its cover consists of a sliding lid, which is ingeniously 
fastened by turning to the left the human figure in the centre of the planetary system represented on its side; its exterior has been gilt ; 
the carvings upon its sides have been executed with great care, and the subject of them all appears to be connected with the ancient re-

of the Peruvians and the first person in their trinity, riding through the universe upon some unknown animal partaking of the nature of 
the Hebrew cherub, whilst the universe itself may be not inaptly typified by the figures of animals belonging to each of the four elements

in Peruvian and Hebrew taste, or some acquaintance on the part of the former with the language of the Psalms. All Spanish authors 
describe the temple dedicated to the sun at Cuzco, as one of the most magnificent structures that man ever consecrated to religious 
worship; but while they notice the immense size of the stones of which it was built, and the incalculable riches of which Pizarro and his 
soldiers plundered it, they say little of its outward appearance or the style of its architecture, which perhaps was owing to their never having 
seen more of it than its ruins. The representation, therefore, of this temple in its perfect state, on one of the sides of this box, is very 
curious: and its Gothic look, the pointed arches of its windows, doors, and roof, resembling that of the Pantheon at Rome, with 
an aperture at the top of the cupola for the admission of light, cannot fail to interest those who may have leisure to peruse the con- 
cluding note of this volume; from which it will appear, that it is not impossible that monks of the order of Saint Columba were the 
founders of it, whom an accidental shipwreck, when returning from a pilgrimage to the Holy Land to their monastery at Iona, had 
cast on the shores of the southern continent of America. That Greenland became in early ages the resort of Christians, and that a 
flourishing monastery existed there during several ages, which probably sent forth missionaries to many parts both of North and South 
America, (which would account for the tradition, which was general throughout the New World, that Saint Thomas had preached the 
Gospel to the Indians, since the monastery in Greenland was dedicated to Saint Thomas, and the monks would have taken care to preach 
that Saint unto them,) will be apparent from the perusal of the note subjoined to page 190 of this volume. ‘The coincidence is curious, 
that the habitations of the monks should have been vaulted above and lighted from an aperture in the roof, their church in all probability 
being lighted in the same manner, and the simple vault of their dwellings changed into a cupola,—since the temple of Cuzco was built on 
this plan. Nor is it less worthy of observation, that the Mexican temazcallis, small as was their scale, must have nearly resembled, both in 
structure and appearance, the houses built by the Greenland monks, who would have been the most likely people in the world to dis- 
cover the salutary nature of steam baths, such as were the temazcallis, which were arched buildings with an aperture above for the exit 
of smoke and the admission of air, as the representation of one of them in Plate XV. of Clavigero’s History of Mexico clearly shows. 
If those monks had been animated with a spirit of enterprise, two reasons for a portion of America having been possibly long known to 
them, and their concealing all knowledge of it from the rest of the world, might be found in the jealousy which they would naturally have 
felt of all foreign interference,—a feeling which in later centuries actuated the Jesuits of Paraguay,—and in the profitable monopoly of trade 
which they might have carried on with the Indians, which would account for the lavish payments which they were able to give for arti- 
cles of mere luxury, and for the concourse of barks which came to them from Trondon (probably Drontheim) in Norway. The discovery 
of arches in America, although not so mysterious, is quite as unexplained a fact as that of crosses ; neither can their existence be accounted 
for by recurring to the old solution of all the doubts and difficulties to which the Patriarchal institutions, Mosaic laws, and Hebrew rites 
of the Mexicans and Peruvians gave rise, which proceeded on the assumption that Satan counterfeited in the New World whatever God 
had ordained in the Old and New Testament amongst Jews and Christians ; since an arch is no where mentioned in Scripture: neither 
did Moses command his countrymen to build their public or private edifices with arches, as he did with battlements, with which latter 
injunction the Mexicans seem to have been acquainted, since battlements on houses and fringes on garments were as common in Mexico 
as they were in Jerusalem. The supposition being as reasonable that America was colonized in early ages by Christians as by Jews, from
