the Peruvians were acquainted with the arch as well as the Mexicans: and although the plate in Ramusio is coarsely 
executed, still, agreeing as it does with the accounts contained in the earliest Spanish authors of the magnificence of 

the reverence in which the Indians held the sign of the cross, both parties may consider that they have an equally fair claim to the honour of 
having introduced the arch into that continent; but “non nobis est tantas componere lites” would be the only reply which the result of our 
inquiries on this interesting subject would enable us to return to either. It has been already observed, that the temple represented upon 
the side of the Peruvian box has a Gothic appearance; and a sort of mixed style of architecture, combining Gothic with Indian taste, 
- seems to be displayed in the temple of Palenque: a church or monastery appears there to occupy the summit of a teocalli, and the roofs 
of its spacious and double cloisters invariably terminate in a pointed arch, whilst the height of the pyramid afforded security to its inmates 
from any sudden hostile attack. M. Dupaix has observed, that stones of vast size were employed in the construction of the palaces of 
Mitlan; and Acosta likewise notices the prodigious size of those which he observed in the ruins of the temple of Cuzco: but, although 
the style of architecture of the former edifices is as unlike as possible to Gothic, Greek, or Roman, and displays no vestige of the pointed 
arch, while the mosaic decorations of the walls of that which is in the best state of preservation, like the devices sculptured upon the walls of 
the fortress of Xochicalco, would seem mysteriously to refer to the worship of Quecalcoatle; still the discovery of some pillars which once 
supported the roof of those palaces shows that they had something in common with the temple of Cuzco which the temple of Palenque 
was without. The use of pillars in the architecture of the New World is certainly deserving of attention; and it is extremely probable 
that the Tultecas taught the Mexicans and the Peruvians the method of fabricating them, and of afterwards raising and fixing them on 
their pedestals. The Jews employed them at the earliest period of their history, as we are informed in the twenty-sixth and twenty- 
seventh chapters of Exodus, where mention is made of the wooden pillars which supported the sides and hangings, not only of the taber- 
nacle, but of the tent of the tabernacle, otherwise named the tent of the congregation, and of the court of the tabernacle: and Acosta, 
in the twelfth chapter of his Natural History of the Indies, after noticing the rich temple of Pacachama, situated at the short distance of 
one league from Lima, proceeds to mention the still more sumptuous one of Cuzco, a pillar of which was entire, and perhaps standing in 
his time: “ Alterum in Peru templum priore mult} augustius et sanctius habebatur. Ilud olim in civitatis Cusco eo loco positum erat, 
quo nunc ceenobium S. Dominici erectum visitur. Inter ejus rudera cetera, columnam adhuc salvam et inconfractam videre licet, ex 
qua de templi magnitudine, prestantid et eminentia certissima documenta desumi possunt liquidissima. Delubrum hoc Romanorum 
Pantheo, deorum omnium domicilio, quadam tenus simile erat.” The resemblance of the temple of the Sun at Cuzco to the Roman 
Pantheon is not pointed out by Acosta in reference to the style of any portion of its architecture, but to the images of the gods of the 
conquered nations which were placed in it, asin the Pantheon. And this remark, whatever might have been the association of ideas which 
led to it, could scarcely have been expected from Acosta, who, evidently not caring how many gods the Peruvians had, provided they had

to demonstrate that the Indians had no idea of one supreme God, and that the Peruvians did not adore him under the names of Paca-

hosts, bent on the slaughter of unbelievers in the Koran,—why the latter may not have been equally profaned in the New World in hymns 
responsive to the dying groans of victims immolated at the shrine of Tezcatlipoca. Having already referred to the authority of Acosta in

add to them by observing that a garden is evidently represented in the back-ground of that temple, and the garden of the temple of the 
Sun at Cuzco was one of the most famous things belonging to it. The most respectable Spanish historians, including Garcilaso de la 
Vega, declare that there, as well as in the garden of the Ingas in the island of Puna, the plants, trees, and shrubs were of gold, made so as 
to exactly counterfeit nature; and the excessive richness of the Peruvian mines divest the accounts of these Spanish authors of the appear- 
ance of falsehood. Over the middle gate of the temple is an animal, the erect tail and head of which assimilate it to a lion, the ancient 
armorial bearing of the tribe of Judah: on another of the sides are the planets, and it is very remarkable that Saturn should be represented 
witha ring. The ancient Jews seem to have reckoned eleven the number of the planets ; since Joseph, declaring in the thirty-seventh chapter 
of Genesis his dream to his brethren, says: ‘ Behold, I have dreamed a dream more; and, behold, the sun, and the moon, and the 
eleven stars, made obeisance to me.” ‘The aggregate number of these signs it may be remarked was thirteen, a number highly esteemed 
by the Mexicans. At the four angles of the box are figures, as it has been presumed, of the Ingas, and the dress of one of them cor- 
responds exactly with the costume of the Jewish high-priest, as described in the twenty-eighth and thirty-fifth chapters of Exodus; the 
girdle, the breast-plate, the ephod, the band round the neck, the four rows of stones in the breast-plate, even the chains fastening it at the 
shoulders to the ephod, appear to be accurately represented ; but it deserves to be remarked that the stones are set vertically and not hori- 
zontally, which was perhaps the Hebrew fashion; and the bells to make a tinkling sound are wholly wanting, although the Mexican 
paintings afford evidence that a tinkling sound was considered by the Mexicans a matter of religious moment, and accordingly their 
priests occasionally wore bells on their ancles. In the thirty-ninth page of the Mexican painting preserved in the Royal Library at 
Dresden a figure occurs, with a vestment to the fringe of which are fastened bells.

Yoalliehecatl, the signification of which proper name is ‘night and wind, was an epithet which the Mexicans 
bestowed upon their supreme deity Tezcatlipoca, denoting thereby the obscurity and subtilty of the divine essence. 
Acosta has been led into the mistake, through not considering that this compound term formed a proper name, of 
asserting that the Mexicans adored, on one of their principal festivals, the winds and darkness ; but Sahagun no where 
says that they attributed divinity to the elementary portions of nature. Fire and water were in no other manner con- 
sidered sacred by them, than as being the symbols of Xiuhtecutli and of Chalchiuitlicue.

The trophy of a hand borne upon the top of a staff was used by the ancient Mexicans, and is sometimes represented 
in their mythological paintings. It is singular that a hand elevated aloft should also have been a Hebrew trophy, as 
Parkhurst informs us in his Lexicon ; who assigns, as a fourth signification to the Hebrew word 7) ‘a hand,’ that of 
atrophy. “7 is used for a trophy or monument of victory, probably because made in the shape of a large hand, the 
emblem of power, erected on a pillar. Thus Saul, after smiting the Amalekites, in the pride of his heart, 7 1) 2x0, 
erected to or for himself, not for Jehovah, a hand, 1 Sam. xv. 12; where, LXX, yea ‘a hand.’ ‘And David smote 
Hadadezer, king of Zobah, when he was going 17) 1"), to erect his hand or trophy by the river Euphrates,’ 2 Sam. 
viii. 3; 1 Chron. xviii. 3. And this appears to be the most ancient use of these memorial hands; whence Absalom 
seems to have taken the hint of erecting one merely to keep his name in remembrance, 2 Sam. xviii. 18; where 
observe that this monument is expressly called not only 7» ‘a hand’, but 72x ‘a pillar’; which, together with the 
use of the verb 2x7 in the above texts, shows that the hand was wont to be put on a pillar. See more in Bate’s 
Crit. Heb., and compare Josephus, Ant. lib. vii. cap. 10. s. 3.”

The Mexicans, according to Sahagun, were accustomed to carry their mirrors about their persons, when they 
celebrated their solemn dances in the court-yard of their greater temple; and from the eighth verse of the thirty- 
eighth chapter of Exodus, it may be inferred that the same custom prevailed at least amongst the Jewish women.— 
“And he made the laver of brass, and the foot of it of brass, of the looking-glasses of the women assembling, which 
assembled at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation.” This vanity on the part of the Jewish women who 
assembled at the door of the tabernacle, seems to have led to the consequences described in the twenty-second verse 
of the second chapter of the First Book of Samuel : “ Now Eli was very old, and heard all that his sons did unto all 
Israel; and how they lay with the women that assembled at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation.”

Bishop Cumberland estimates the value of the gold which David prepared for the House of the Lord at 507,575,000/. 
sterling, and of the silver at 353,500,000/. sterling ; the two sums added together amounting to 861,075,000). sterling. 
It may be proper to add, that the learned prelate grounds his calculation upon the following passage of the twenty- 
second chapter of the First Book of Chronicles: “ Now, behold, in my trouble I have prepared for the House of the 
Lord an hundred thousand talents of gold, and a thousand thousand talents of silver, and of brass and iron without 
weight.” How great must have been the wealth of Jerusalem in the ensuing prosperous reign of Solomon, when 
David in his trouble was able to amass such vast riches! And where is the absurdity of understanding in a literal 
sense, what most persons are inclined to consider an hyperbole, viz. that silver was really as common in Jefusalem, as 
stones in the days of the former king; which would serve to explain how the Jews could have maintained, in their 
small territory of Palestine, so large an army as that described at page 49 of this volume. 

Nore XVIII. page 191. 

It has been remarked in a preceding note, that superstitious nations are too ready to ascribe to prophetic inspiration 
things which have been foretold, merely because they were highly probable, and which accordingly afterwards came 
to pass. A fictitious case has also been recurred to at page 368, to show that true prophecies need not be always 
either miraculous or accidental in their nature. Having already quoted a passage in the chorus of one of the tragedies 
of Seneca, which, had it occurred in the Old Testament, would have been accounted a famous prophecy, we shall here 
introduce a beautiful passage of Pope’s Windsor Forest, which contains a number of accidental prophecies, and amongst 
others one the accomplishment of which we trust will be late. The greatest of poets could little have foreseen, when 
writing that admired poem, how many of his predictions time would verify ; nor would it perhaps have pleased him 
to have known, that the period would arrive when his favourite villa, and the grotto in which “St. John sat and thought,” 
would no longer be the chosen resort of the muses, but would be comprised within the suburbs of the gay metropolis. 
But who will contend that Pope, by inspiration, knew that London would be doubled in size in the course of a century ; 
that parliament would grant millions to build new churches; that the Burmese war would take place; that an expe- 
dition would be sent to the North Pole; that the ports of South America would be open to British commerce ; that 
Englishmen with capital would embark extensively in mining speculations; and that Mr. Huskisson would advocate 
the principles of free trade: yet the perusal of the following lines will convince the most sceptical, that he saw all 
these things as through a glass darkly which we now behold in the clear light of day. 

“ Hail, sacred peace! hail, long expected days 
That Thames’s glory to the stars shall raise, 
Though Tiber’s streams immortal Rome behold, 
Though foaming Hermus swells with tides of gold, 
From heaven itself though sevenfold Nilus flows, 
And harvests on a hundred realms bestows ; 
These now no more:shall be the Muse’s themes, 
Lost in my fame, as in the sea their streams. 

Let Volgas banks with iron squadrons shine, 
And groves of lances glitter on the Rhine, 
Let barbarous Ganges arm a servile train,— 
Be mine the blessings of a peaceful reign. 

532 NOTES. 

No more my sons shall dye with British blood 
Red Iber’s sands, or Ister’s foaming flood; 

Safe on my shore each unmolested swain 

Shall tend the flocks, or reap the bearded grain ; 
The shady empire shall retain no trace 

Of war or blood, but in the sylvan chace; 

The trumpet sleep, while cheerful horns are blown, 
And arms employed on birds and beasts alone. 
Behold! the ascending villas on my side 

Project long shadows o’er the crystal tide. 
Behold! Augusta’s glittering spires increase, 
And temples rise, the beauteous works of peace. 
I see, I see, where two fair cities bend 

Their ample bow, a new Whitehall ascend ! 
There mighty nations shall inquire their doom, 
The world’s great oracle in times to come ; 
There kings shall sue, and suppliant states be seen 
Once more to bend before a British Queen. 

Thy trees, fair Windsor! now shall leave their woods, 
And half thy forests rush into the floods, 

Bear Britain’s thunder, and her cross display 

To the bright regions of the rising day ; 

Tempt icy seas where scarce the waters roll, 
Where clearer flames glow round the frozen pole ; 
Or under southern shies exalt their sails, 

Led by new stars, and borne by spicy gales! 

For me the balm shall bleed, and amber flow, 
The coral redden, and the ruby glow, 

The pearly shell its lucid globe unfold, 

And Phebus warm the ripening ore to gold. 

The time shall come, when, free as seas or wind, 
Unbounded Thames shall flow for all mankind.”

The Mexican women were accustomed to anoint their faces with a yellow ointment named tecocauitl ; and we learn 
from the third verse of the third chapter of Ruth, that Naomi desired her daughter-in-law to anoint herself and put on 
raiment before she introduced herself to Boaz, in order to request him to perform the part of her near kinsman, by taking 
her for a wife. In the fourth chapter of the Fourth Book of Kings, or Second Book of Chronicles as it is more usually 
designated, the widow’s oil which was multiplied by the prophet Elisha is said to have been that which she used for 
anointing herself: “ Ovx core Ty Sovdy cov ovdev év Tw olKw, ore GAN’ 7) 0 GAerbouat éXaov.” * Thy servant hath nothing 
in the house save the oil with which I anoint myself.” Hence it would appear that the Jewish as well as the Mexican 
women were accustomed to anoint their bodies or faces, either for the sake of health or ornament.

Nore XXIII. 

In the nineteenth chapter of the fourth book of his History of New Spain Sahagun says, that the family of a Mexi- 
can merchant who had been killed in a foreign country, immediately on receiving the intelligence of his death, made 
a wooden image of him, which they adorned with paper, and carried to the temple, where it remained a short time 
previously to being burnt. The author of the Apocryphal book of Scripture entitled the Wisdom of Solomon seems 
to allude, in the fifteenth verse of the fourteenth chapter, to an analogous custom, whether existing amongst the Jews 
or Gentiles is immaterial, since the latter invented no idolatrous custom which the former did not immediately adopt: 
“ For a father afflicted with untimely mourning, when he hath made an image of his child soon taken away, now 
honoured him as a god, which was then a dead man, and delivered to those that were under him ceremonies and 
sacrifices.” 

Notr XXIV. page 227. 

“ Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints,” is an exclamation of David in the ninety-sixth 
Psalm, which occurred to the recollection of the interpreter of the Vatican MS. when explaining the meaning of 
‘Tlatzolli Tzonpantli,’ who does not appear to have recollected equally well the ejaculation with which the Book of 
Psalms may be almost said to close, where David eloquently invokes the saints to sing the praises of God with a two- 
edged sword in their hand: “Let the saints be joyful in glory: let them sing aloud upon their beds : let the high 
praises of God be in their mouth, and a two-edged sword in their hand; to execute vengeance upon the heathen, and 
punishments upon the people; to bind their kings with chains, and their nobles with fetters of iron; to execute 
upon them the judgment written : this honour have al/ his saints. Praise ye the Lord.” The royal bard could never 
have contemplated Sicilian vespers when pronouncing this ejaculation; yet we shudder at the remembrance of the 
atrocities perpetrated in a recent age by the Anabaptists, who, applying to themselves the prophecy contained in the 
eighteenth verse of the seventh chapter of Daniel,—*“ But the saints of the Most High shall take the kingdom, and 
possess the kingdom for ever, even for ever and ever,”—thought to establish the fifth monarchy, and to begin the 
millennium, by first wading through a sea of blood. The language of truth being so often mistaken for that of 
exaggeration, we cannot but entreat modern Anabaptists, who may feel disposed to doubt the fact above mentioned, 
to consult the annals of Germany; which having done, it will not be at all surprising if they should be induced to 
abandon their creed. It cannot be denied that the ancient Jews were cruel beyond belief to their vanquished enemies : 
the innocence of childhood, the sweetness of youth, admiration for valour, or respect for age, never stayed their mur- 
dering swords; and the faults of the father were too frequently visited upon his poor and unoffending babes. In 
reading the seventh and following verses of the hundred and thirty-seventh Psalm, strongly significant though 
equivocally worded, at the same time recollecting the latitude of meaning which the Rabbis assign to the phrase “the 
children of Edom,” and the great regard which the Jews have always manifested for ancient precedent, a doubt may 
reasonably be entertained whether David's apostrophe to Babylon, “Happy shall he be that taketh and dasheth thy 
little ones against the stones,” may not have led the Ingas to view with indifference the crime of infanticide, when 
the children slaughtered were those of their enemies. It is an old observation, that the code of the Pentateuch no- 
where inculeates patriotism as a virtue, which Christ appears to have had in contemplation when he uttered the words, 

2 

“ A new commandment I give unto you, that ye love one another ;” which could only have referred to the Mosaic law, 
since the laws and maxims of antiquity, which have been preserved to the present time, afford the most convincing 
proof that they inculcated patriotism and humanity. It is however even more surprising that clemency and pity for 
a fallen enemy should have found no place amongst the Levitical enactments; which strengthens our conviction that 
the ancient Jews, believing it to be impious in other nations to go to war with God’s chosen people, considered it 
virtuous to execute vengeance upon their enemies, and to show no mercy to prisoners taken in battle. Their example 

was imitated by the Mexicans, who in massacreing their captive enemies only followed the rules of Jewish warfare.

Sahagun, describing in the first paragraph of the twenty-ninth chapter of the tenth book of his History of New 
Spain the manners of the Tultecas, says, “La manera de cortarse el cabello era segun su uso pulido que traian los 
cabellos desde la media cabeza atras.” “They cut their hair in such a manner as to wear it, agreeably to their refined 
fashion, only on the hinder half of the head.” That precisely the same custom prevailed amongst the Jews, we learn 
from the following verse of the poet Nonnus’s Paraphrase of the Gospel of St. John: 

“Xpworog orio0oxopwy pepotwy Oownropr Aaw

“ Christ, an invited guest, sat in company with the revelling crew, who were bald except at the back of their heads.” 
The Galileans are here alluded to; and the epithet dio@oxouwy applied to them would seem to signify that they used

named it Ononic, according to Plutarch, from Theseus, on account of that hero having cut off the hair which grew on

of the Mosaic law. Josephus, however, was of a different opinion, and did apply the latter to his countrymen : and as

Note XXVIII. page 402. 

The Mexican goddess Cihuacohuatl, or Suchiquecal, was also named Quilaztli, as we learn from the twenty-eighth 
chapter of the sixth book of Sahagun’s History of New Spain, who there expressly declares that she was Eve: “ Esta 
és Eva, que és la muger que primero parid.” The probability of the Mexicans having been acquainted with the 
history of Cain and Abel is pointed out in page 221 of the present volume; and it seems only necessary, in order 
fully to identify Suchiquecal with the Eve of Scripture, to show that the Mexicans believed that she brought death 
into the world, which involves the supposition that they were not ignorant of the doctrine of original sin. From the 
following passage of page 469 of the preceding volume, which contains the address of the midwife to the relatives 
of a woman who had lately been delivered of a son, it may confidently be inferred that such was their belief: “Por 
cierto este negocio és una batalla en que peligramos las mugeres, porque este negocio és como tributo de muerte que 
nos echa nuestra madre Cioacoatl y Quilahtli.” “This necessity (of giving birth to children) is, indeed, a battle in 
which we who are women are exposed to great dangers, for it is as it were the tribute of death bequeathed to us by our 
mother Cioacoatl and Quilahtli.” It is singular that the Peruvians should have believed, as well as the Mexicans, that 
twins were unlucky; they, perhaps, had also a tradition that Cain had murdered his brother Abel. Cieca de Leon 
says of the former people, “Tenian por mal aguero estos Indios que una muger pariesse dos criaturas de un vientre, 
6 quando alguna criatura nasce con algun defecto natural, como es en una mano seys dedos, 6 otra cosa semejante. 
Y si, como digo, alguna muger paria de un vientre dos criaturas, 6 con algun defecto, se entristecian ella y su marido, 
y ayunavan sin comer agi, ni bever chicha que es el vino que ellos beven, y hazian otras cosas 4 su uso y como lo 
aprendieron de sus padres.”—Parte Primera de la Chronica del Peru, cap. lxv. Amongst the Jews, persons born 
with any natural defect were forbidden to discharge the Levitical functions, and Hebrew parents would probably have 
felt compunction, as well as sorrow, when such misfortunes befell their children, from the erroneous belief, which 
even some of Christ’s disciples shared, that the sins of the father were frequently visited by God upon the child; and 
hence they might, like the Peruvians, have fasted on the occasion of the birth of deformed children. 

Nore XXIX. page 449. 

M. Dupaix, in describing the palace of Mitlan, observes, that not only the inner walls, but even the pillars which 
supported the roof of that edifice, had once been painted with vermilion. That this was a Jewish custom, is evident 
from the following passage of the twenty-second chapter of Jeremiah: “Woe unto him that buildeth his house by 
unrighteousness, and his chambers by wrong; that useth his neighbour's service without wages, and giveth him not 
for his work ; that saith, I will build me a wide house and large chambers, and cutteth him out windows ; and it 
is ceiled with cedar, and painted with vermilion.” Selden, in a passage of the Introduction to his treatise De Diis 
Syris, says, on the authority of Epiphanius, that it was an Egyptian custom to dye the trees and cattle red on the 
anniversary of the Jewish passover, in commemoration of the sprinkling of the door-posts with the blood of the 
Hebrew lamb. The ancient ecclesiastical writers were so credulous, and so prone to indulge in pious frauds in their 
narrations, that it may reasonably be doubted whether such a custom ever existed amongst the Egyptians; it is at the 
same time, however, highly probable that the Jews might have dyed the pillars and walls of their houses with ver- 
milion in commemoration of the flight of their ancestors from Egypt. The following is the passage of Selden alluded 
to: “ JAoyptiis quotannis in Judaico Paschate greges et arbores minio, velut alexeterio, illinere solenne erat: id ex 
depravato traditionis sacree de Ebreeorum superliminaribus sanguine illitis intellectu manavit, quod fusius narrat Epi- 

NOTES. 53ST. 

phanius in heresi Nazareorum. Perperam accepta Mosis de aneo serpente historia ut thymiamata ei incenderentur 
effecit.” The supposition that the miracles which Moses performed, by holding up his rod that became a serpent, 
inclined his superstitious countrymen in later ages to pay adoration to that reptile, and to regard it in the light of a 
tutelary genius, has here the sanction of high authority ; and if Selden has judged it not unreasonable to refer to this 
example in Jewish history, to show the probability of Epiphanius’s narrative, who will deny the validity of the argu- 
ment by which an attempt is here made to prove that the adoption of the serpent as a sacred symbol by the Mexicans 
was in commemoration of the brazen serpent which Moses set up in the wilderness? It may be proper to add, that 
although the Mexicans carried the figure of a serpent in their religious processions, and wore it on their persons as a 
sacerdotal ornament, not scrupling to invest the image of Tezcatlipoca with a symbol so appropriate to Tetzauhteotle, 
or the terrible god, they did not adore it except as the type of Quecalcoatle. 

Nore XXX. 

The account which Gomara gives of the Spanish expedition in search of the seven cities of Sibola, and the causes 
that led to it, is interesting, not only because it records the earliest attempt made by the Spaniards to investigate the 
provinces situated to the north of Mexico, but likewise because much mystery attaches to the relation of the friars, 
from whom the intelligence of the existence of those cities was first received, who seem either themselves to have 
discovered traces of Christianity in that part of America, or to have heard rumours to that effect which they judged 
to be worthy of credit. The probability that their relation was a mere forgery, is counterbalanced by the much 
greater improbability, that, if that had been the case, they would have ventured to have stated a deliberate falsehood, 
likely to involve such serious consequences as an expedition disastrous to the Spaniards, to Cortes, and the Viceroy 
of Mexico ; or that they would have been able to deceive two persons of such great penetration as were Cortes and 
Don Antonio de Mendoza; or, finally, that those persons would have quarrelled with each other about the right which 
each claimed, Mendoza as Viceroy of Mexico, and Cortes as Captain-general of New Spain, to undertake the conquest 
of Sibola, the former of whom fitted out a numerous army of Spaniards and Indians, with a regiment of four hundred 
cavalry, to take possession of that province, and the latter retired from motives of disgust to Spain. The unfortu- 
nate result, however, of the enterprize, which did not, as was usual in such cases, lead even to the establishment of a 
settlement in the provinces which the Spanish army had traversed, furnished Gomara with the opportunity of indul- 
ging in a jest against Brother Mark de Nica, who was the friar who in the year 1539 returned to Mexico, “ diziendo 
maravillas de siete ciudades de Sibola:” which cities he proceeds thus briefly to describe; ‘“ Las famosas siete ciu- 
dades de Fray Marcos de Nica, que estan en espacio de seys leguas, ternan obra de quatro mil ombres. Las riquezas 
de su reyno es no tener que comer, ny que vestir, durando la nieve siete meses.” ‘The famous seven cities of Bro- 
ther Mark de Nica, which occupy six leagues of country, may contain a population of about four thousand men, whose 
only wealth is to have nothing to eat, and to go naked during seven winter months.” Gomara is, however, obliged 
to own that the courage of the Indians opposed a most vigorous resistance to the Spaniards, who were much disap- 
pointed on taking a town, after a siege of forty-five days, at finding that they had burnt all their turquoise-stones and 
property of value in a blazing pile which they had kindled for the purpose. It cannot be doubted that Gomara 
represents the provinces of Quivira and Sibola such as he believed them to be; but the following description, by 
Lieutenant Hardy, of the ruins which still cover a vast extent of country in the neighbourhood of Las Casas Grandes 
may induce some persons to suppose that king Tatarrax did really “adore a cross of gold, and pray to the image of 
a woman who was queen of heaven.” “Casas Grandes is one of the few ruins existing in Mexico, the original 
owners of which are said to have come from the north, and I therefore determined to devote a couple of hours on the 
morrow to its investigation. On the thirteenth I examined a ruin about half a mile from my last night’s lodgings. 
Only a portion of the external walls is standing; the building is square, and of very considerable extent; the sides 
stand accurately north and south, which gives reason to suppose that the builder was not unversed in the science of 
astronomy, having determined so precisely the cardinal points. The roof has long lain in the area of the building, 
and there are several excavations, said to have been made by the Apache Indians, to discover earthenware jars and 

(6x) 

538 NOTES. 

shells. A specimen of the jars I was so fortunate as to procure, and it is in excellent preservation. There were also 
good specimens of earthern images in the Egyptian style, which are to me at least so perfectly uninteresting that I 
was at no pains to procure any of them, The country here for the extent of several leagues is covered with the ruins 
of buildings capable of containing a population of at least twenty thousand or thirty thousand souls. Casas Grandes is 
indeed particularly favourable for maintaining so many inhabitants. Situated by the side of a large river which periodi- 
cally inundates a great part of the low surrounding lands, the verdure is perpetual. There are ruins also of aqueducts, 
and in short every indication that its former inhabitants were men who knew how to avail themselves of the advantages 
of nature and to improve them by art; but who they were and what has become of them there is no chronicle to tell, 
and conjecture is left to build as many theories respecting them, as of other extinct nations as little known. On the 
south bank of the Rio Gila there is another specimen of these singular ruins; and it may be observed that wherever 
these traces are found, the surrounding country invariably possesses great fertility of soil, water, and wood. About half 
a league to the north-west of Casas Grandes is an old convent built by the Jesuits, who were equally careful to avail 
themselves of similar advantages. It is in ruins also, and stands on an eminence; it appears to have been a very large 
building.” —Travels in the Interior of Mexico, page 465. We have availed ourselves with greater pleasure of this 
extract from Lieut. Hardy’s Travels, because the ruins of Las Casas Grandes, situated nearly a thousand miles to the 
north of Mexico, have been known rather by rumour than in any other manner to Spanish authors who have men- 
tioned them in their writings, and their existence has often been considered problematical. In a note subjoined to 
page 183 of the present volume will be found the opinion of Cardinal Lorenzana, that these ruins were the deserted 
habitations of the Mexicans; but in the same page reasons are assigned for not attaching much weight to that learned 
prelate’s opinion, whose certainty on so obscure a matter of history, resting wholly unsupported by any evidence, cannot be 
shared by the reader of his edition of the Letters of Cortes. It is to be regretted that Lieut. Hardy should not have been 
at the pains of procuring any of the little earthen images in the Egyptian style, of which he says good specimens were 
to be found in the neighbourhood of Las Casas Grandes, since it is evident, from the terms in which he mentions them, 

that disappointment at their loss would not have caused him to exclaim with Boturini, “no las trocara por oro y plata 

por diamantes y perlas;” and the comparison of them with the Mexican Penates or images of baked clay of a similar 
description, which a well-informed traveller says are still frequently found in the vicinity of Mexico, Cholula, and 
other ancient cities of New Spain, might have enabled intelligent persons to judge whether the religion of the popula- 
tion of Las Casas Grandes, and their taste for the arts, resembled that of the Mexicans. The jar, an engraving of which 
is given in page 465 of his work, is interesting, because the symmetrical lines that ornament its surface are not 
unlike those traced in mosaic on the walls of the palace of Mitlan. In Honduras, stone vases have been found em- 
bellished in a more simple manner with broken lines, representations of which will be found in the American Monu- 
ments of Baron de Humboldt. Itis probable that the town of Chihuahua, with its extensive plains, described by Lieut. 
Hardy as entirely destitute of wood, and lying on the route to Las Casas Grandes, is that to which Gomara gave the 
appellation of Cicuic.- The numerous herds of cattle grazing upon its neighbouring plains were by no means indicative 
of the poverty of the subjects of king Tatarrax : they are thus described by that historian; “De Tiguex fueron en 
quatro jornadas a Cicuic, lugar pequefio, y a quatro leguas del toparon un nuevo genero de vacas fieras y bravas, de 
las quales mataron el primer dia ochenta que bastecieron el exercito de carne. Fueron de Cicuic a Quivira, que a 
su cuenta ay casi trezientas leguas, por grandisimos llanos y arenales tan rasos y pelados que hizieron mojones de 
bofiigas, a falta de piedras y de arboles, para no perderse a la buelta, ca se les perdieron en aquella llanura tres 
cavallos y un Espafiol que se desvio a caca. Todo aquel camino y anos estan Ilenos de vacas corcobadas como la 
Serena de ovejas, pero no ay mas gente de la que los guardan; fueron gran remedio para la hambre y falta de pan que 
llevavan. Cayo les un dia por aquel Ilano mucha piedra como naranjas ; y uvo hartas lagrimas, flaqueza, y votos : 
Hegaron en fin a Quivira, y hallaron al Tatarrax que buscavan, ombre ya cano desnudo, y con una joya de cobre al 
cuello, que era toda su riqueza.”’—La Istoria de las Indias, fol. cxvz. In the first edition of Gomara’s History of the 
Indies, printed at Saragoza in 1553, from which the above extract is taken, a wood-cut is given representing a Quivira 
ox which appears to have been a real buffalo ; another domestic animal with which the Indians of that province of 
America were acquainted, and for which they might have been indebted to the Greenland monks, was a large kind of 
dog which they employed in carrying burthens. “ Ay tambien grandes perros que lidian con un toro, y que llevan 
dos arrobas de carga sobre salmas quando van a caca o quando se mudan con el ganado y hato.”——La Istoria de las 

NOTES. 539 

Indias, fol. cxvi. A very small species of dog, less than a guinea-pig, inhabits the plains of Quivira, and burrows in 
the ground like a rabbit; and here we shall take occasion to observe, that various species of dogs being known in the 
New World, it is probable that the Indians were acquainted with the hydrophobia, and perhaps with a cure for it, 
since accident frequently reveals what the greatest sagacity has failed to discover, and the medicinal properties of 
American plants which the Mexicans so well understood, many of which they used as antidotes against the bites of 
the most poisonous serpents, are yet but very imperfectly known. The account therefore which Lieut. Hardy has 
given of the mode by which an Indian woman professed to cure the hydrophobia is not undeserving of attention, and 
her notion that the complaint began with an affection of the mouth and tongue, which if removed in time, before the 
disease had extended itself through the system, would not prove fatal, acquires some plausibility from the conside- 
ration that the nerves of the mouth as well as those situated about the eye are exquisitely sensitive, and that their 
derangement or vitiated action would be likely to produce the most violent disorders. In the relation above, Lieut. 
Hardy has compared the ruins of Las Casas Grandes to others situated on the bank of the Rio Gila, a plan and de- 
scription of which we subjoin from the MS. relation of the New Discovery of the Port of Monte Rey, composed by 
the missionary Pedro Font, who accompanied the expedition which was dispatched thither from Queretaro for the 
purpose of colonization in the year 1775. In the eighth volume of the Antiquities of Mexico will be found extracts 
from valuable ancient MSS. which will throw new light on the history of the provinces situated to the north of 
Mexico, of which so very little is as yet known.

“ Determiné el Sefior Comandante que descansara oi la gente, y con esto tubimos lugar de ir 4 registrar la casa 
grande que llaman de Moctezuma, situada 4 una legua del Rio Gila, y distante del parage de la laguna unas tres 
leguas al Estsudeste 4 donde fuimos acompanados de algunos Indios, y del gobernador de Uturituc, quien en el 
camino nos cont6 una historia y tradicion que conservan de sus pasados sobre dicha casa, que toda se reduce 4 patrafias 
mescladas confusamente con algunas verdadades Catolicas. Observé este parage de la casa grande, y es sefialada en el 
mapa con la letra A. y lo hallé en 38°. 3!. y asi digo: en la casa grande del Rio Gila, dia 31 de Octubre de 1775, 
altura meridiana del bordo inferior del Sol, 42°. 25'. Registramos con todo cuidado este edificio, y sus vestigios, 
cuya planta ichnographica es la que aqui pongo; y para su mejor inteligencia doi la descripcion, y esplicacion 
siguiente. La casa grande, 6 palacio de Moctezuma, tendr4 de fundacion unos 500 afios segun las historias, y esca- 
sas noticias que hai de ello, y dn los Indios ; porque segun parece esta fundacion la hicieron los Mejicanos quando 
en su transmigracion los Ilevaba el Demonio por varias tierras, hasta llegar 4 la tierra prometida de Mexico, y en sus 
mansiones que eran largas, formaban poblacion, y edificios. El sitio donde se halla esta casa es Ilano por todas 
partes, y apartado del Rio Gila como una legua, y las ruinas de las casas que formaban la poblazion se estienden 
mas de una legua para el Oriente, y demas vientos ; y todo es de terreno : esta sembrado de pedazos de ollas, tarros, 
platos, &*., unos ordinarios, y otros pintados de varios colores, blanco, azul, colorado, &*., indicio que fué pobla- 
cion crecida, y de distinta gente de los Pimas Gilefios, pues estos no saben hacer semejante losa. Hicimos exacta 
inspeccion del edificio y de su situacion, y lo medimos con una lanza por lo prompto; cuya medida reduje despues 
& pies geométricos, y 4 poco mas 6 menos es la siguiente. 

540 NOTES. 

“Esta la casa quadrilonga, y perfectamente @ los quatro vientos cardinales, Este, Oeste, Norte, y Sur, y al rededor 
estan unas ruinas que indican algun cerco, 6 muralla, que encerraba 4 la casa, y otros edificios particularmente en las 
esquinas en donde parece habia alguna fabrica como castillo interior, 6 atalaya, pues en el esquina que cae al Sud- 
oeste hai un pedazo de pie con sus divisiones, y un alto. La cerca exterior tiene de Norte 4 Sur 420 pies*, y de 
Este 4 Oeste 260. Lo interior de la casa se compone de cinco salas; las tres iguales en medio, y una en cada 
extremo mas largas. Las tres salas tienen de Norte 4 Sur 26 pies, y de Este 4 Oeste 10. Las dos salas de los ex- 
tremos tienen de Norte 4 Sur 12 pies, y de Este 4 Oeste 38. Las salas tienen de alto 11 pies, y todas son iguales. 
Las puertas de comunicacion tienen de alto 5 pies, y de ancho 2, y son casi iguales todas, excepto las quatro primeras 
de las quatro entradas, que parece eran otro tanto anchas. Lo grueso de las paredes interiores quatro pies, y estan 
bien ensaradas, y de las externas 6 pies. La casa tiene por lo exterior de Norte 4 Sur 70 pies, y de Este 4 Oeste 50. 
Las paredes estan escarpadas por de fuera. Delante de la puerta del Oriente separada de la casa, hai otra pieza 
que tiene de Norte 4 Sur 26 pies, y de Este 4 Oeste 18, sin el grueso de las paredes. El madera era de pino por lo 
que se vé, y la sierra mas cercana que tiene pinos dista unas 25 leguas; y tambien tiene algo de mesquite. Todo 
el edificio es de tierra, y segun las senales es tapia fabricada con cajones de varios tamaftos. Viene del Rio, y de 
bien lejos, una acequia bien grande con que se socorria de agua la poblazion y esta ya mui cegada. Por-fin se 
conoce que tenia el edificio tres altos ; y si es verdad lo que se pudo rastrear de los Indios, y por los indicios que se 
vieron tenia quatro, profundizado el piso de la casa 4 modo de pieza subterranea. Para dar luz las piezas no se vén 
mas que las puertas, y unos agujeros redondos en medio de las paredes que miran al Oriente, y Poniente ; y dijeron 
los Indios que por aquellos agujeros (que sen algo grandes) miraba el Principe, que ellos llaman el hombre amargo, 
al Sol quando salia, y se ponia para saludarlo. No se hallaron rastros de escaleras, por lo que juzgamos que eran 
de madera, y se destruyeron con la quemazon que padecio el edificio por los Apaches. 

“Dia | de Noviembre salimos de la laguna 4 Jas 93 de la manaiia, y 4 la una de la tarde Ilegamos al pueblo de San 
Juan Capistrano de Uturituc haviendo caminado 4 leguas con el rumbo al Oest Noroeste. Nos recibieron los Indios, 
que regulé como mil almas puestos en dos filas, los hombres de un lado, y las mugeres del otro, y haviendonos apeado 
vinieron todos por su torno 4 saludarnos, y darnos la mano, primero los hombres, y luego las hombres digo mugeres, 
manifestando mucho contento de vernos, y nos hospedaron en una gran ramada que hicieron para este fin ; delante la 
qual plantaron una cruz grande aunque gentiles, y luego trajeron agua al real para la gente. Son estos Pimas Gilefios 
Indios mansos, y de buen corazon.”—Plan. Geo. Hist. del Nuevo Descr. de‘el Puerto del Monte Rey.

the description serves to rectify.
